2.0     INTRODUCTION

This manual describes and provides valuable safety information for operation and maintenance of rolling
mill equipment. Its primary purpose is to help point out good safety practices and warn of potential
dangers that are inherent to equipment installed, operated and maintained in the rolling mill. Mill
personnel must read and understand all safety instructions and mandatory information before entering the
mill work area.

The following safety recommendations are general guidelines based on Morgan Construction Company’s
prior mill implementation experience. These recommendations are offered as reminders only, since we
can neither anticipate all problems that may arise in a rolling mill installation, nor can we anticipate all
situations peculiar and unique to any individual mill installation. It is intended for them to enhance or
complement safety programs and procedures presently being implemented by the mill owner.

We strongly urge you to institute a recurring training and qualification program covering proper operation
and maintenance of the installed equipment with particular attention to safety procedures and features
designed into this equipment and other equipment surrounding it. Personnel trained in this program will
be safety oriented operating and maintenance personnel who should be trained and designated as such.
The equipment should not be operated or worked on except by highly trained personnel completing this
program. Morgan strongly recommends that the following information be included in your training
program.

Certain equipment such as valves, electrical controls, hydraulic cylinders, rotary actuators and couplings
are manufactured by others and should be supplied with their manufacturer's installation, operation and
maintenance instructions. This equipment is described in this manual only to the extent necessary to
define their interfaces with other mill components. Always refer to specific manufacturer’s safety,
operation and maintenance procedures for each component.

3.0     MILL SAFETY HAZARDS

Mill personnel working within the rolling mill are subject to not only exposure to running machinery
hazards, but also to general industrial environment hazards. Personnel must be trained and aware of
safeguards in place as well as potential hazards that may occur at any time. It is important to recognize
and be alert for hazards and to take precautions to avoid injury in the mill. Be aware of the following
conditions and possible hazards.

Mill personnel working within rolling areas of the mill are exposed to machinery or equipment hazards
and must be aware of the potential for accidents. In many cases, accidents with machinery are very
serious, even fatal. It is important to recognize and be alert for machine hazards and to take precautions
to avoid injury in the mill.

All mechanical motion is potentially hazardous. Motion hazards, such as rotating devices, cutting or
shearing blades, in-running nip points, reciprocating parts, linear moving belts and pulleys, meshing
gears, and uncontrolled movement of failing parts can cause severe injury. Mill operators, maintenance

personnel and others must be aware of moving parts that can cause clothing or body parts to get caught in
the machinery. Be aware of the following conditions and possible hazards.

BEWARE OF THE MILL! Do not become lax and careless to the mill environment. Always
remember dangerous conditions can emerge unexpectedly. Remember that when noise is excessive,
auditory warnings may not be heard. Realize potential dangers that may develop, and that extreme care
must be taken at ALL Times.

4.0     SHEAR AND CUTTING POINTS

Both shear and cutting points are created on machinery designed to cut and become hazards because of
their cutting forces, and because they often move so rapidly that they may not be expected. It is easy to
forget that it is operating.

Because some cutting and shearing points cannot be guarded, it is important to be aware of their hazards
and to be especially alert when they are operating. There is also a danger of thrown objects and cobbling
while operating cutting type equipment.

5.0     PINCH POINTS
Another hazard of machinery is the pinch point. Pinch points are formed when two rotating objects move
together and at least one of them moves in a circle. For example, the point at which a belt runs onto a
pulley is a pinch point. Belt drives, chain drives and gear drives are other sources of pinch points in
power transmission devices.

Fingers, hands and feet can be caught directly in pinch points, or they may be drawn into the pinch points
by loose clothing that becomes entangled. Contact may be made by simply brushing against unshielded
parts or by falling against them. Personnel can become entangled in pinch points if they take chances and
reach or work near rotating parts. Machines move too fast for personnel to get out of a pinch point once
they become caught in it.

To avoid injury from pinch points, individuals should be aware of the areas where pinch points occur and
to avoid them. They should wear clothing that fits well and is not loose or floppy. Never reach over or
work near rotating or revolving parts.

Personnel shall turn off and Lockout machinery in order to work on it. Personnel shall always replace
shields and guards if they must remove them for maintenance.

6.0     WRAP POINTS

Rotating shafts are the most common source of wrap point accidents, although any exposed machine part
that rotates can be a wrap point. Long hair, pony tail, or a cuff, sleeve, pant leg or just a thread can catch
on a rotating part and result in serious injury. Entanglement with a wrap point can pull personnel into the
machine, or clothing may be so tightly wrapped that an individual can be crushed or suffocated. In other
cases, a person could be thrown off balance and fall into other parts of the machine.

Ends of shafts, which protrude beyond bearings, are also dangerous. Universal joints, keys and fastening
devices can also snag clothing.

7.0     CRUSH POINTS

Crush points are created when two objects move toward one another or one object moves toward a
stationary one. For example, moving cylinders and raised equipment and covers create a potential crush
point.

Failure to block up equipment safely can result in a fatal crushing injury. A car jack can slip, a hose or
overhead support may break, or the equipment may roll. Personnel shall take extra precautions when
working with machinery that is raised for any reason.

To prevent being crushed or pinned, personnel must recognize the potentiality of the dangerous situation.
Personnel shall always block all machinery securely if they must work beneath it.

8.0     FREE WHEELING AND ROTATING PARTS

Many machine parts may continue to spin after the power is shut off; for instance, fans, flywheels, rollers
etc. Personnel must never touch moving parts until the part has come to a complete rest.

Springs under compression will expand with great force when released, and springs that are stretched will
contract rapidly when released. Personnel shall observe and recognize which direction the spring will
move and how it will affect other machine parts when released, and shall stay out of its path.

9.0     HYDRAULIC SYSTEMS

Hydraulic systems contain fluid under very high pressure. Before loosening, tightening, removing or
otherwise working with any fittings or parts, personnel shall relieve this pressure.
A jet stream from even pin-hole leaks can penetrate flesh. In addition, the hydraulic fluid is often
extremely hot. Before attempting any service on hydraulic systems, personnel shall shut off the motor
that powers the hydraulic pump and relieve the pressure. Personnel should always verify that all residual
energy has been dissipated. Always follow the instructions in the machines operator’s manual.

10.0    SAFETY WARNINGS

        Warning:         Consider all mill equipment as potentially hazardous at all times. Moving
                         parts are capable of crushing any body part caught in it.

        Warning:         Electrical voltages in both power and control circuits are capable of
                         rendering severe and fatal shocks.

        Beware:          The product running through the mill is hot and it should be assumed that
                         all surfaces of equipment are high temperature surfaces. Always wear
                         protective safety equipment.

11.0   NOTICE TO EMPLOYER AND SAFETY DIRECTOR

       1. Ensure that safety requirements are implemented in accordance with appropriate regulations
          (CEN, OSHA etc.).

       2. Ensure that all personnel working in the mill are safety trained and wear the proper personal
          protection equipment (PPE). Make sure everyone is informed with regard to correct use of
          safety equipment, the foreseeable dangers that may arise during operation of the equipment
          and the necessary precautions to be taken.

       3. Ensure that all personnel working in the mill are trained properly in the use the machinery
          and are aware of the dangers that may arise if they do not follow operation and safety
          instructions. Check at regular intervals, mill personnel’s awareness and compliance with
          safety requirements.

       4. Ensure that proper lockout/tagout and power supply disconnect procedures are followed in
          accordance with appropriate regulations (CEN, OSHA etc.).

       5. Ensure that safety signs and labels are in place, clearly visible and legible. Replace any
          missing or illegible signs and labels.

       6. Ensure that all safety devices are in working order before the start of each shift.

       7. Never make modifications or alterations to mill equipment. Do not by-pass safety interlocks.


12.0   NOTICE TO OPERATORS AND MAINTENANCE PERSONNEL

       1. Always wear proper safety gear when in the mill. Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
          should include safety hat, shoes and gloves as well as eye and ear protection. Dust masks

           should be worn as necessary due to accumulation of slag, dust and dirt particles in the mill
           environment.

       2. Ensure that proper lockout/tagout and power supply disconnect procedures are followed in
          accordance with appropriate regulations (CEN, OSHA, etc.) before performing any
          maintenance.

       3. Disconnect all air, hydraulic, water and electric power supply before performing any repair,
          maintenance or cleanup. Dissipate and bleed off any stored energy in cylinders and actuators.
          Verify “Zero Energy State” before working on machinery!

       4. Never put hands or other body parts in the path of moving equipment and components. Make
          sure all rotating parts come to a complete standstill and are secured against accidental restart
          before working on equipment.

       5. Make sure mill equipment is only operated when in perfect working order. Faults and
          malfunctions, particularly those that impair safety, must be remedied immediately.

       6. Ensure that all safety devices are in working order before restarting after maintenance. Make
          sure you know where all E-stop buttons are located and how to operate them.

       7. Make sure all interlocks, locking pins and covers are in correct position when operating and
          maintaining machinery.

       13.1    Signs and Labels

       Danger:         This type of warning sign indicates a situation that if not avoided could
                       result in a fatal injury.

       Warning:        This type of warning sign indicates a situation that if not avoided could
                       result in Disabling Injury or serious damage to health.

       Caution:        This type of warning sign indicates a situation that if not avoided could
                       result in injury or Damage to health. Signs and labels should be installed
                       and placed throughout the mill in accordance with applicable safety
                       standards.

       Use an acceptable sign and label format that is recognized by all personnel. Make sure personnel
       are trained and familiar with safety format and labeling criteria. Depicted below are some
       sample formats of signs and labels.

       13.2    Safety Precautions
       Ensure operating and maintenance personnel observe the following recommended general
       safety precautions:
       1. Be thoroughly familiar with all company policies concerning safety precautions for working
          on or near heavy equipment.

       2. Before starting any maintenance task, de-energize the power supply and verify that all stored
          energy has been discharged.

       3. Maintain a clean work area. Beware of fire hazards due to fluid spills and poor house
          keeping.

       4. Before restoring any pressurized air or hydraulic system, make sure that the solenoid circuit
          for that particular control valve has not been accidentally operated to shift the valve spool.

       5. Before attempting to remove any air or hydraulic system components, de-energize the control
          valve, isolate the component from the pressure supply system and vent it to remove and
          verify any residual pressure that may be entrapped.

       6. Keep exposed rotating parts shielded at all times while the mill is running. Reinstall all
          shields removed for maintenance tasks.

       7. When disassembling/reassembling heavy parts, make sure that they are fully supported by
          slings and hoists. Do not lift parts heavier than 20 Kg (45 pounds) without the aid of another
          person or hoist. Two-man lifts should not exceed 45 Kg (100 pounds).

       8. Always replace guards that have been removed for maintenance purposes, before the unit is
          put into operation.

       9. Always tighten loose bolts, nuts and screws and always replace split pins, locking washers
          etc., after maintenance.

       10. Always maintain electrical cables, hydraulic and pneumatic piping and flexes at the first sign
           of fraying, damage or leakage.

       11. Always use tongs and wear approved gloves when handling cobbles and scrap metal do not
           assume that because metal is not glowing it is not too hot to handle or touch.

       12. BEWARE OF THE MILL! Remember that when noise is excessive, auditory warnings may
           not be heard. Be Safe and Stay Alert!

       13. Use a mechanical stop or block and shore up the equipment to prevent movement before
           entering the dangerous area. Remove the shoring before operating the unit.

       14. Do not clean equipment while it is running. Isolate equipment while the work is being
           carried out.

       13.3    Fire Fighting Equipment

       1. Install appropriate fire fighting equipment, (foam CO2,
          or water hydrant, hoses and nozzles) correctly at points
          throughout the mill where the risk of fire exists (areas
          where product is exposed externally out of the along the
          equipment.).

       2. Make sure that trained personnel familiar with such
          apparatus are immediately available.

       3. Where welding or any other operation that presents a fire
          risk, is being carried out, be sure the appropriate fire
          fighting equipment is available ready for instant use and
          a fire watchman is on location at the place where the
          work is done.

14.0   HYDRAULIC AND PNEUMATIC SYSTEMS

       Hydraulic and pneumatic systems are highly complex and must be maintained by technically
       trained personnel familiar with safety, electrical lockout/tagout maintenance procedures common
       to working with automatically controlled and pressurized systems.

       Warning:         High pressure air/oil lines are potentially dangerous and may cause severe
                        injury, especially blindness, if care is not taken in the vicinity of these
                        systems.

       An oil jet may puncture the skin and enter the blood stream. This danger exists when bleeding a
       hydraulic system of air, when taking oil samples, or when joints and flanges in piping are loose or
       damaged causing leaks. USE EXTREME CARE when carrying out maintenance of this nature.
       If oil has penetrated the skin, seek medical attention immediately.

       Treat machinery and equipment that is moved or controlled by hydraulic or pneumatic systems
       with extreme caution.

       Danger:          Before making any attempt to remove the element from the Hydraulic filter,
                        or before carrying out any maintenance involving the removal, or
                        dismantling of valves etc., shut down the system and exhaust all
                        accumulators.

       Note:            Ignoring this warning may lead to danger or injury to personnel.

       14.1    Isolation of Equipment

       Warning:         High voltage and rotating parts can cause serious or fatal injury.

       Before servicing equipment, isolate the electrical or pneumatic circuit associated with a machine
       undergoing maintenance, and any other machine which presents a hazard. Switch off the
       electrical feed and padlock it in the "OFF" position. If this is not possible, take out the fuses and
       put them in a safe place from which they cannot be removed without consent. Place a "Danger"
       notice on the switchboard, or distribution board, to warn would-be operators of the danger.

       If it is not possible to isolate the machine while maintenance is being carried out, station a
       responsible person at the control of the unit. Place a notice on the controls of the machine, to
       warn a would-be operator of potential danger. NEVER by-pass safety interlocks.

       Important:       Operators must be familiar with all Main Pulpit and Local Control Station
                        switches, indicators and controls. Operators must also know where all

                       or roll and guide changes. Read Safety Instructions and Warnings for each
                       system and component prior to working on machinery. Read and refer to

                       Make sure the Mill process stations and pass line has been completely shut

       Warning:        The Pinch Roll Assembly is potentially dangerous and capable of inflicting

       Warning:        Always wear heat resistant gloves when changing guide equipment.

       Warning:        Hot Product travelling throughout the mill can make all equipment surfaces

                       throughout the mill as hot.

       14.2    Contact Water

       To isolate the cooling water, locate and manually turned off the isolation valve located in the
       water supply line. Lockout and Tagout the valve while performing maintenance and repairs.

       14.3    Mill Air and Instrument Air

       To isolate the mill and instrument air supply, locate and manually turned off the isolation
       valves located in the air supply line. Lockout /Tagout the valve while performing
       maintenance and repairs.



       14.4    Lubrication

       To isolate the internal lubrication, locate and manually turnoff the shutoff valve located in lube
       supply line. Lockout and Tagout the valve while performing maintenance and repairs.

       14.5    Hydraulic System

       To isolate the Hydraulic System, locate and manually turn off, the shutoff valve located at the
       applicable Hydraulic Valve Stand. Refer to Circuit drawings as a guide. Lockout and Tagout
       the valve while performing maintenance and repairs. Note: The hydraulic system for the
       actuator to the Cobble Covers may need to be operable to open the cover for maintenance and roll
       changes. Once the cover is open and latch pinned in place the hydraulic system can be shutoff
       and can be Locked Out and Tagged Out.

       14.6    Lifting Means

       Warning:        When using lifting machinery, ensure that items such as eye bolts are fully
                       engaged before attempting to lift.

                       Do not use any lifting means provided on motor, etc. to lift the assembly and
                       base. Lift assemblies by a sling around the base or by other lifting means
                       provided on the base.

                       In all cases, assure that the lifting will be in the direction intended in the
                       design of the lifting means.

                       Take precautions to prevent hazardous overloads due to deceleration,
                       acceleration, or shock forces.

                       Secure the load well and balance it properly in the sling or lifting device
                       before lifting more than a few inches. Never carry loads over people. Re-
                       route the load or clear the people from the area.

                       Always ensure that shackles, slings, etc., used for lifting, are in good
                       condition and adequate for the job in hand. Also, ensure that the Safe
                       Working Load of the hoist is greater than the weight of the lift.

       14.7    Floor Plating

       Always rope off an area from which floor plating has been removed, station a guard and do not
       remove the rope barrier until the floor plating has been replaced.
       Always replace floor plating as soon as possible after maintenance has been carried out. Never
       leave an opening unguarded or unprotected even for a short period.
15.0   MAINTENANCE SAFETY REMINDERS
The objectives of scheduled and planned maintenance programs are to maintain the mill in a state of
optimum readiness and performance and to ensure continued high production rates. To gain these
objectives, the Maintenance Department should develop and prepare a periodic sequence of inspections
and preventive maintenance procedures for the mill components and its supporting systems.

       Warning:        Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or
                       disconnect all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any
                       stored energy from components. Restrain and secure any moving parts of a
                       component or system that could cause injury.

       Warning:        Inspect gears and spray nozzles only when the mill equipment is stationary.

       Warning:        Solvents used for cleaning can be harmful. Follow the solvent
                       manufacturer’s recommended safety procedures for PPE, ventilation, and
                       First Aid. Petroleum based solvents and adhesives are flammable and their
                       vapors are harmful

       Caution:        Be absolutely sure to maintain a clean environment during disassembly/re-
                       assembly of all mill equipment. Dirt, scale or other foreign matter can have
                       serious adverse affects on closely tolerance, precision equipment as well as
                       contaminating the mill lube oil system.

       15.1    Housekeeping

       To the extent possible, keep all service areas clean. Do not allow oil, grease, water or dirt to
       accumulate on floors and/or around units undergoing repair

       15.2    Rigging Parts for Removal/Replacement

       Many parts in the mill are too heavy to be manhandled. Provide adequate rigging for lifting and
       supporting heavy parts before attempting to dismantle or reassemble.

       15.3    Coupling Shields - (Supplied by others)

       For protection of mill personnel, shield all exposed rotating members of mill (i.e. drive shaft
       coupling) whenever the mill is running.

       Warning:        Do not attempt to remove any shield while the mill is running. De-energize
                       the reducing/sizing mill drive motors and wait for them to stop. Close snap
                       shears immediately before the first stand. Make sure all mill equipment is
                       completely shut down.

       3.1     Safety Procedure

       Important:      All Safety Devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to
                       assure the safety of the operators.

       Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices
       make the elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the
       process and/or product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be
       constrained to follow a prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble.
       Cobbles occur at random times and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is
       unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed
       path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment, and stock temperature are also causes of
       cobbling anywhere along the length of a bar in process in the rolling train. The following
       recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe manner.

       3.2     Visibility and Communications

       Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations of
       pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment controlled from
       that point. Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight
       confirmation.

       Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper lighting can be
       used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or cloud the reflective surface and
       that the mirror location does not make it liable to breakage.

       3.3     Audible Communications

       Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as substitutes only
       when visual contact is not possible.

       3.4     Safety Stops

       Guide adjustments may be made only when the Mill Line is shut down. Mechanical or
       electrically operated stops must be used to block any stock from inadvertently entering into the
       mill.

       Ensure mill is shut down and material can not run through the stand. Ensure that stops remain in
       place as long as personnel making adjustments are in the hazard area.

       3.5     Alarms

       The alarms as described in the control specifications will have a warning system to alert the
       operators of new oncoming front ends.

       3.6     Restart of Mill

       When a service operation is completed, the Mill must be restarted in the following sequence:
       1. All mechanical stops will be moved.
       2. All Guards will be in place.
       3. All personnel will clear the hazardous area.
       4. Permissive switches will be placed in “ALLOW RESTART” position and all interlocks
          engaged.
       5. Operators at control stations will be notified that the Mill Line may be restarted.

       Operators must not restart the mill until they are completely satisfied that restarting will not
       present hazards to personnel. An audible signal will be given by the operator to indicate that
       restart is imminent.

4.0     INTRODUCTION
Each PFM consists of a roll housing assembly, cobble cover assembly, and a drive housing assembly that
connects to the drive motor. The 250 PFM connects to the drive motor via tandem couplings and the gear
reducers are contained within the mill. The roll housing assembly in turn contains the rolls, guides and
associated electrical components, oil lubrication, cooling water, and hydraulic systems. Other
components include Snap Shears before each stand, Sideloopers before each of the 250 PFMs with
scanners located between each roll housing stand.

The PFM is designed for manual and automatic operation. Operating stations (Main Pulpit and Local)
help test, monitor and adjust conditions that may occur through the automated system. Refer to Table 1

              4.1.2   Roll Housings and Rolls

              Each roll housing contains a pair of roll shaft pinions. The roll shaft pinions are driven
              by electric motors. Each motor drives a shaft which is coupled to another shaft that
              (through a series of gears) drives the individual drive pinions of each stand.

              Each roll housing mounts a pair of overhung, shell-type rolls carried on shafts. The rolls
              are supported on shafts by tapered sleeves. Each shaft is mounted in an eccentric
              cartridge and supported by Clevite type bearings. The eccentrics can be rotated to permit
              adjusting roll parting by means of a parting adjusting screw connected to the eccentrics.
              The eccentrics are linked to each other, which produces equal, and opposite adjustment in
              both shafts, thereby maintaining a constant pass.

              manner that the front end does not deviate from the pass line. Each stand will have an

              and shape of the section. In many cases it is necessary to change the guides or the guide
              components as the section size changes.

              floor. Once the guides are set, it is then the responsibility of the mill operators to install

              4.1.6   Types of Guides

              A. Roller Entry Guides

              These are usually used to guide an oval section into a round pass. A roller entry guide is
              sometimes used to guide a round section into the first stand of the PFM, especially if a
              sidelooper is located immediately ahead of the mill. The roller entry guide can have
              either 2 or 4 guide rollers and has the provision to attach a 2 roller anti-flutter guide onto
              the back of the guide assembly.

              B. Static Entry Guides

              These are usually used to guide a round section into an oval pass. All the static entry
              guides are split into two halves and are clamped together to prevent a cobble from
              breaking out into the roll bite, which if allowed will damage the roll housing.

              C. Static Delivery Guides

              This type of guide is located at the delivery end of every stand. Two types of static
              delivery guides are used in the mill

              1. Spring Clip Type

              This delivery guide is split into two halves with the top half attached to the bottom with a
              spring clip. In case of a cobble the spring clip releases allowing the cobble to breakout
              into controlled area, preventing the cobble from accumulating and damaging the roll
              housing.

              2. Solid Type

              The type of guide is split into two halves with the top half being bolted to the bottom half
              to prevent the guide halves from parting during rolling. A solid guide is used due to the
              limited space between the two sizing mill stands.

              D. Dummy Pipes

              The dummy pipes are used for when the roll unit stands are not used for rolling. They
              replace the static entry and delivery guides. The dummy pipes are mounted in holders,
              which are fitted directly onto the existing guide brackets and are therefore correctly
              aligned to the mill and pass centerline.

              4.1.7   Mounting the Guides

              A. Roller Entry Guides

              These guides are normally clamped onto an adjustable saddle, which is attached to a
              bracket located by means of a key and keyway to the housing faceplate and held in
              position by bolts, which automatically locates the bracket and roller guide on the mill
              centerline. A portable optic is supplied with the mill to help the operator accurately align
              the roller entry guide to the pass centerline by adjusting guide bracket saddle.

              A nosepiece is attached to the front of the guide to provide additional guiding as close to
              the roll bite as possible and to aid the front end of the rod into the center of the pass,
              especially at high speed. The nosepiece helps eliminate the possibility of the front end of
              the rod striking the roll pass collar, which will cause either the front end to turndown or
              cobble.

              4.1.8   Cobble Detection System

              The PFM is confined in enclosures that have a minimum amount of free space, so in the
              event of cobble, it is necessary to divert incoming stock as soon as possible. Since visual
              detection of a cobble by operator is difficult, automatic cobble detection methods are
              used in the PFM compartments. This cobble detection system consists of a monofilament
              line with a weight strung through the compartment. A cobble in either stand will break
              the line and allow the weight to drop and actuate the PFM 17/18 Cobble Detect
              proximity switches as listed in Table 1 of this chapter.

              4.1.9   Roll Cooling Water System

              The Roll Cooling Water System is designed to prevent
              damage to the PFM rolls from the hot product traveling
              through mill. PFM must never be run above 10% speed
              without water or seals for bearings will be damaged.
              Seals are only effective at preventing water ingress into
              lubrication system with PFM running above 10% top
              speed. The PFM should be run above this speed when
              rolling through it in dummy mode.

              An air cylinder operates a water valve and is controlled
              by a Roll Cooling single solenoid valve. Energizing the
              solenoid turns water on to the mill. De-energizing the
              solenoid turns water off to the mill and diverts flow to
              the flume.

              The Roll Cooling Pressure switch indicates when the correct water pressure is present at
              the pre-finishing mill. A 1.0 second time delay is used in conjunction with the pressure
              switch so that a transient drop in pressure will not produce a false low-pressure
              indication. Low water pressure indication from the pressure switch is ignored for 5
              seconds when water is first turned on to allow for normal buildup of pressure.

              4.1.10 PFM Roll Cooling Water Automatic Operation

              •   The water turns on when the PFM motor speed is equal to or greater than 10% of
                  base rated speed.

               4.1.11 Air/Oil Lube System

       4.2     PFM Interlocks

       In order for the Pre-finishing Mill to operate, certain interlocking conditions must take place. In
       addition, other interlocking steps and procedures are required at the snap shear as well as
       downstream from the PFM. Refer to other interlocking steps and procedures for existing systems
       and components that may effect the operation of the PFM. The following interlocks steps and
       procedures are required in both manual and automatic mode for operation of the PFM.

               4.2.1   PFM Cobble Guard Doors Interlocking

               •   The Snap Shears at the entry side of the Pre-finishing Mills are described in a
                   separate chapter of the Operation and Maintenance manual.

               •   Interlocking is required which permits the cobble guard door to be opened only if the
                   Snap Shear is closed.

               •   The Snap Shear is permitted to open only if the cobble guard door is closed.

               4.2.2   PFM Cooling Water Systems Interlocking

               Snap Shear at the PFM entry cannot open when water pressure in respective mill is low.

              4.2.3   PFM Lubrication Systems Interlocking

              •   Stands and rollerized turndowns whose roll bearings are lubricated by Air/Oil System

              4.2.4   250 PFM Mill Hydraulic Systems Interlocking

              •   Control circuits for operating hydraulically powered equipment are effective only
                  when a system pump is running.

                  This is to prevent unexpected movement of hydraulic cylinders or motors merely by
                  starting a hydraulic pump.

              •   If the pumps are stopped by LOW-LOW tank level, they will not restart
                  automatically by merely refilling the tank.

       4.4      Roll Parting Correction
       Note:            For roll mounting and removal procedures refer to PFM Maintenance
                        manual.

       In practice it is necessary to make some corrections to the theoretical settings to take into account
       oil film thickness, machining tolerances and roll pinion shaft deflections due to rolling load. As a
       result the roll parting adjustments required can be either positive or negative depending on rolling
       load (i.e. reduction, steel grade and temperature), product diameter and rolling speed. Due to the
       high rolling speeds the required roll parting adjustments or deviations from the theoretical
       settings are generally positive. These positive deflections are caused by the oil film strength in
       the Clevite bearings exceeding the deformation resistance of the rod, causing the mechanical
       clearance to be removed in a negative direction, i.e. inward towards the stock. As a result the roll
       parting decreases from the set value as the mill is run up to the rolling speed, producing a smaller
       than expected finished product.

       Note:            It is advantageous to derive a standard setup for each size based on the most
                        commonly rolled steel grade and entry temperature. The operator
                        responsible for adjusting the mill should keep a log of the roll parting
                        adjustments made after each change in steel grade or entry temperature.
                        This will allow a more detailed setup chart to be derived based on groups for
                        steel grade and ranges of entry temperatures. Accurate roll parting
                        adjustments can then be made prior to changes in steel grade and/or entry
                        temperature, thereby ensuring that the tolerance of the first bar after the
                        change is within specified limits.

       Deviation from standard roll partings can be caused by:

       1. Feed section size and shape outside setup parameters.

       2. Too much tension.

       3. Axial alignment of rolls being incorrect.

       4. Guide setup being incorrect.

       3.1     Safety Procedures

       Important:      All safety devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to assure
                       the safety of the operators.

       Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices
       make the elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the
       process and/or product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be
       constrained to follow a prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble.
       Cobbles occur at random times and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is
       unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed
       path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment, and stock temperature are also causes of
       cobbling anywhere along the length of a bar in process in the rolling train. The following
       recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe manner.

       3.2     Visibility and Communications

       Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations of
       pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment controlled from
       that point.

       Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight confirmation.

       Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper lighting can be
       used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or cloud the reflective surface and
       that the mirror location does not make it liable to breakage.

       3.3     Audible Communications

       Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as substitutes only
       when visual contact is not possible.

       3.4     Safety Stops

       Guide adjustments may be made only when the Mill Line is shut down. Mechanical or
       electrically operated stops must be used to block any stock from inadvertently entering into the
       mill.

       Ensure mill is shut down and material can not run through the stand. Ensure that stops remain in
       place as long as personnel making adjustments are in the hazard area.

       3.5     Alarms

       The alarms as described in the control specifications will have a warning system to alert the
       operators of new oncoming front ends.

4.0    PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE

       4.1     Introduction

       Routine and Preventive Maintenance of the PFM assembly is required to ensure extended and
       proper operation. Table 1 is provided as a quick reference guide for frequent periodic
       maintenance requirements for the PFM assembly. Refer to the General Maintenance section of
       this manual and to the applicable manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance requirements
       and procedures of specific components of Pre-Finishing Mill Area. Refer to Morgan assembly
       drawings as a guide and for additional information.

       4.2     Maintenance Facilities

       For best results provide an area where the roll housings and other components of the PFM can be
       disassembled, cleaned, inspected, and reassembled in a clean environment. The shop should have
       the capability of handling roll housings coming in for periodic inspection and rebuild as well as
       roll housing coming in for repair, and for repair of other PFM components. Ideally the following
       equipment should be installed in the shop:

       A Disassembly Bench: To support the roll housings with their flanged front surface on wooden
                            blocks. The blocks should allow a 400 mm clearance to access the
                            bottom housing components for easy removal.

       A Cleaning Tank:          Ensure tank is sufficient size for cleaning parts and an air hose for drying
                                 parts after cleaning. From the cleaning bath, the parts would be passed
                                 to the component assembly bench for subassembly of bearings, roll
                                 shafts, etc. Final assembly would be made on the housing assembly table
                                 and another table would be used for setting pass line location. Housings,
                                 when complete, would be placed on a wooden pallet for transporting to
                                 the mill.

       4.3     Maintenance Recording

       The principal maintenance problems that occur with rod mills are the result of conditions that
       develop slowly, taking many months to reach the trouble stage. Avoid potential maintenance
       troubles by keeping records and acting on them.

       Lube oil system maintenance is extremely important since the useful life of the oil film bearings
       that support the roll shafts depends mostly on the cleanliness of the lubricating oil. These
       bearings rapidly wear out and seize with contaminated lube oil. This has been especially true of
       the front Cleveite bearings on previous mills.

       4.4     Definition

       Preventive maintenance is routine maintenance that, if performed as scheduled and helps to keep
       machinery in good operating condition. Its primary purpose is to reduce the incidence of
       operating failures, which require costly downtime for repairs. The recommended scheduled and

       4.5     Scheduled and Planned Maintenance

       The objectives of scheduled and planned maintenance programs are to maintain the mill in a state
       of optimum readiness and performance and to ensure continued high production rates. To gain
       these objectives, the maintenance department should develop and prepare a periodic sequence of
       inspections and preventive maintenance procedures for the pre-finishing mill and its supporting
       systems. The objective of corrective maintenance is to return equipment to operational status as
       quickly as possible following a malfunction. Replacing faulty parts with spare new or
       refurbished parts and restoring the mill back to full operation best does this.

       The most important single factors conducive to maximum mean-time-between-failure are
       lubrication and cooling. Consequently, the most important task of preventive maintenance is to
       ensure a clean and adequate supply of lube oil at all times while the mill is running and to
       frequently lubricate those points, which require grease lubrication, and keep the cooling system
       functioning properly.

       Based on many years of experience in the development and manufacture of rod and bar mills,
       Morgan Construction Company has developed a set of scheduled maintenance activities to
       provide guidance to the maintenance department in developing and implementing a planned
       maintenance program of their own.

              4.6.10 Roll Housing and Seals

              Roll housings are the most vulnerable part of the mill because of their proximity to the
              product. Use one of the two following methods for the prevention of roll housing
              breakdown:

              1. Make periodic inspections of roll housings in the maintenance shop.

              2. Take weekly in-the-mill lift test for every roll shaft and record the results. Use the
                 lift test to determine if the ball thrust bearings are deteriorating. The lift tests also
                 will determine if the deterioration warrants removal of the housing for rebuilding.

              3. Whenever the mill is in operation be on the alert for oil leaking from roll necks,
                 indicating a defective seal. A drip would be tolerable, possibly indicating an
                 accumulation of oil in the flinger. Frequently check the water leg sight glass in the
                 lube oil drain piping from each roll stand. Signs of water in the lube oil system
                 indicate a defective roll neck seal. Replace defective seals immediately to prevent
                 contaminating the reducing/sizing mill lube oil system.

              4. All roll shaft seals must be replaced on a regular schedule. An interval of three
                 months is not uncommon. Such practices demonstrate the importance of preventing
                 cooling water into the lube oil system.

              4.6.11 Hoses and Connections

              Inspect hoses daily for any leaks, cuts, or abrasions and replace if necessary. Check
              connections for any leaks and tighten or replace if necessary.

               Ball and roller bearings are not repairable. Either they are good and suitable for reuse or

               roll housing.

       Caution:        Because a used bearing may be defective without the defect being visually
                       evident, during any maintenance task, replace all bearings removed from
                       their respective shafts with new bearings at re-assembly.

       Note:           For ease of installation of bearings, adhere to the following guidelines and
                       procedures:

               1. Observe a "NO SUBSTITUTION" policy because of the special design requirement
                  for these bearings.

               2. New bearings are packed with rust-preventive grease (or other protective coating)
                  and wrapped in grease-resistant paper before they are shipped. Do not unwrap
                  bearings until time for installation. Then, unwrap, and thoroughly wash the new
                  bearing and air dry. Pre-lubricate immediately with oil from the mill lube system.

               3. When pressing a bearing on or off a shaft, do not apply pressure to the outer race.
                  Use a bearing installation tool whenever possible. Apply pressure only to the race
                  that is a tight fit.

               4. Installation of large bearings is simplified by heating the bearing in clean oil to a
                  temperature of 250°F (120°C) maximum. Do not exceed this temperature. Allow
                  sufficient time to ensure that the bearing is heated throughout. This will sufficiently
                  expand the bearing and allow it to slide easily over the shaft to its proper location.
                  Take care to prevent cocking of the inner race as this may cause the bearing to seize
                  before it is properly seated.

               5. Heat the bearings at a maximum temperature of 120°C (250°F) in oil for 1 hour
                  minimum, or in an electric furnace for 1-1/2 hours minimum, or by electric induction
                  for 15 minutes minimum.

              4.7.3   Shaft Couplings

              Unless the oil seals are leaking, couplings require very little maintenance other than
              lubrication. To remove and replace coupling, the following guidelines are provided.

              1. For the floating shaft coupling, rig the floating half section for lifting. Take up the
                 slack in the lifting rig, but do not strain.

              2. Slide the floating shaft section away from the driving hub. Lift the floating shaft
                 section free of the coupling hubs.

              3. Consult Morgan for assistance if coupling problems develop.

              4. Mount the coupling hubs on spline shafts and secure with the clamp plate or
                 centering probe. Securely tighten the fasteners.

              5. After reassembling the floating shaft sections to the drives, inspect the coupling lube
                 spray tubes. Be certain the tubes are directed at the coupling teeth.

              4.7.4   Coupling Shields

              For protection of mill personnel, shield all exposed rotating couplings of the pre-finishing
              mill (the drive motor to drive housing floating shaft coupling) whenever the mill is
              running.

                      the PFM drive motors and wait for them to stop. Close Snap Shears
                      immediately before the fist stand. Ensure all mill equipment is completely
                      shut down.

              4.7.5   Internal Lube Oil Piping

              Handle piping that supplies lube oil to bearings and gears with extreme care to prevent
              damage. Replace any damaged tubing with stainless steel tubing of the same wall
              thickness and length and form it to the same exacting standards as the original. An
              incorrect material could possibly be a source of blocked orifices through the release of
              scale.

5.0    CORRECTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS

       5.1     Definition

       Corrective maintenance encompasses those repair procedures required to return the Pre-Finishing
       Mill assembly to satisfactory operating condition. Such repairs do not necessarily return the
       equipment to like-new condition. Rather, the objective is to make it operational again as soon as
       possible. It is recommended to replace faulty parts/components and sub-assemblies with new or
       previously refurbished spare parts/components and sub-assemblies. Those parts removed may
       then be refurbished or reconditioned after the main equipment has been returned to service.

       Important:      Always isolate, shutoff, and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic, and
                       electrical power supply sources before performing any repairs, maintenance
                       or roll, and guide changes. Read all safety instructions and warnings for
                       each system and component prior to working on machinery. Read and refer
                       to Safety Section of this manual before performing any maintenance or
                       repairs.

       5.2     Introduction

       Corrective Maintenance of the Pre-Finishing Mill (as defined above) is intended to keep down
       time at a minimum by replacing components and then dismantling and overhauling the removed
       component in a service area away from the mill. Once refurbished, the component becomes a
       spare shelf part, ready to be utilized as a replacement when needed. Disassembly procedures are
       given herein of components being replaced. Components that require overhaul/refurbishment
       should be maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Refer to the
       manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance and torque requirements and procedures of
       specific components of the PFM.

       General guidelines and maintenance criteria are provided below when corrective maintenance of
       a component or sub-assembly is required. These are minimum guidelines and should be used in
       conjunction for the specific maintenance requirements from the component manufacturer. Upon
       re-assembly, tighten all bolts, screws, nuts and fasteners in accordance with Morgan reference
       drawings torque requirements. Torque specific components in accordance with the
       manufacturer’s requirements.

       Warning:        Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or
                       disconnect all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate, and exhaust any
                       stored energy from components. Restrain and secure any moving parts of a
                       component or system that could cause injury.

       Warning:        The PFM assembly is potentially dangerous and capable of inflicting severe
                       bodily injuries and fatal electric shock. Before starting any maintenance
                       task, comply with all company policies relating to safety.

       5.3       General Maintenance Criteria

       The following is a list of maintenance actions to perform whenever dismantling equipment for
       repairs:

       1. Electric controls and power cables: Before disconnecting any wiring that does not have plug-
          in connectors, make sure that color-coding is clearly identifiable or tag each wire carefully for
          reference at re-assembly.

       2. Rigging parts for removal/replacement: Many parts that make up this equipment are much
          too heavy to be handled by one person. Provide adequate rigging for lifting and supporting
          heavy parts before attempting to dismantle any equipment.

       3. Cleaning: Clean all parts with a suitable solvent (mineral spirits, SAVASOL no.5, or
          equivalent) to remove all scale, grease, grime, or dirt. Use a clean wiper; do not use cotton
          waste. Air dry after cleaning.

       4. Bearings and Sealing Surfaces: Closely inspect bearings and sealing surfaces for signs of
          wear, nicks, scratches, gouges, or build-up of scale or other foreign substances. Replace
          bearings that show any signs of deterioration. Scrape bushings slightly, being careful not to
          exceed the tolerance limits.

             To clean roller bearings, soak in clean solvent long enough to loosen any sludge, then gently
             slosh each bearing around near the top of the container to dislodge all pockets of grease.
             Scrub away stubborn accumulations with a small brush that has bristles that do not break off.
             Do not spin dirty bearings, but rotate races slowly while washing and scrubbing.

             Rinse the bearings in clean solvent and air dry. Hold both races when blowing with clean,
             dry compressed air. Do not allow the air jet to spin the bearing; rather, turn each race by
             hand to expose all surfaces to the drying air. If the bearing is to be stored for later reuse,
             wrap it in wax paper or other greaseproof wrapping.

       Caution:          A bearing may be defective without the defect being visually evident:
                         replace any bearing removed during any maintenance task with new or
                         cleaned bearing at reassembly.

             New bearings are packed with rust-preventative grease (or other protective coating) and
             wrapped in grease-resistant paper before they are shipped. Do not unwrap the bearing until
             time for installation. Unwrap and thoroughly wash the new bearing and air dry. Pre-
             lubricate immediately with Mobil 533 (or equivalent).

       Note:             For ease of installation of bearings, heat the bearings at a maximum
                         temperature of 121°C (250°F) in oil for one hour minimum, or in an electric
                         furnace for 1-1/2 hours minimum, or by bearing induction heater for 15
                         minutes minimum.

       5.5     Roll Removal and Mounting

       The following roll removal and mounting procedures are designed only for use with the hydraulic
       tools and pump unit supplied by Morgan. Note: The roll and sleeve should be individually
       wrapped in a protective covering to prevent dirt from adhering to the clean surfaces prior to
       mounting.

       Note:           For further roll removal, handling, and mounting procedures refer to the
                       applicable drawings as listed in Section 2.0 of this manual.

               5.5.1   Roll Shop Responsibilities

               The roll shop should be responsible for cleaning (Refer to “Cleanliness”) and assembling
               the rolls and tapered sleeves (Refer to “Using Spacers”) prior to being transported to the
               mill floor.

       Important       It is recommended that each tapered sleeve be assigned to a given stand and
                       remain with that stand throughout the life of the sleeve. In addition if
                       multiple roll widths are used on a particular stand then a dedicated sleeve
                       should also be assigned to that stand and roll width. This ensures that the
                       contact between the sleeves and shaft taper is optimized.

                       The assembled rolls and sleeves must be clearly marked with the pass to be
                       used and the stand on which the roll assembly is to be mounted.

               5.5.2   Cleanliness

               Cleanliness is the highest priority when mounting the rolls on the roll shafts. If dirt is
               present on the roll, sleeve and shaft assembly the wear process on the tapered sleeve and
               the roll pinion shaft is rapidly accelerated. As the taper on the shaft and sleeve wear the
               amount of contact between the two surfaces decreases, eventually decreasing the amount
               of torque that can be transmitted and increasing the likelihood of roll slippage or
               breakage. To achieve the best results it is necessary to clean the pinion shaft tapers every
               time a roll is changed. This should be done using Scotch-Brite or Crocus Cloth. Any oil
               residue should be removed by using non-petroleum based cleaning fluid. Clean, lint-
               free type cleaning cloths should be used.

       Important:      Always use a new cloth to help prevent the shaft tapers from damage by
                       debris and particles in cloth acting as an abrasive.

                       If a roll is removed and then remounted on the mill without going to the roll
                       shop, then the bore of the roll and the tapered sleeve should be cleaned before
                       they are reassembled. The pinion shaft taper must also be cleaned as well as both
                       faces of the roll as it is important that the roll contacts the flinger or the spacers,

               5.5.6   Roll Parting Correction

               In practice it is necessary to make some corrections to the theoretical settings to take into
               account oil film thickness, machining tolerances and roll pinion shaft deflections due to
               rolling load. As a result the roll parting adjustments required can be either positive or
               negative depending on rolling load (i.e. reduction, steel grade and temperature), product
               diameter and rolling speed. Due to the high rolling speeds the required roll parting
               adjustments or deviations from the theoretical settings are generally positive. These
               positive deflections are caused by the oil film strength in the Clevite bearings exceeding
               the deformation resistance of the rod, causing the mechanical clearance to be removed in
               a negative direction, i.e. inward towards the stock. As a result the roll parting decreases
               from the set value as the mill is run up to the rolling speed, producing a smaller than
               expected finished product.

       Note:           It is advantageous to derive a standard setup for each size based on the most
                       commonly rolled steel grade and entry temperature. The operator
                       responsible for adjusting the mill should keep a log of the roll parting
                       adjustments made after each change in steel grade or entry temperature.
                       This will allow a more detailed setup chart to be derived based on groups for
                       steel grade and ranges of entry temperatures. Accurate roll parting
                       adjustments can then be made prior to changes in steel grade and/or entry
                       temperature, thereby ensuring that the tolerance of the first bar after the
                       change is within specified limits.

               Deviation from standard roll partings can be caused by:

               1. Feed section size and shape outside setup parameters.

               2. Too much tension.

               3. Axial alignment of rolls being incorrect.

               4. Guide setup being incorrect.

               5. Roll parting settings being incorrect or incorrectly measured.

               5.5.7   Setting Roll Partings

               Accurately setting the roll partings is an essential aspect for obtaining the correct finished
               section and having a trouble free start-up after a size change. Time spent to achieve an
               accurate set-up is time well spent. The following steps and procedures should be use as a
               guide for setting the roll parting.

               1. Set the mill to jog

                   A. The jog speed should be set to 30 motor R/min or slower.

                  C. If the correct parting is not obtained the first time, it will be necessary to repeat
                     steps 1 -4 until the correct parting is obtained.

              5.6.1    Handling Rolls

              Take reasonable care to avoid damage to the rolls. Do not hammer the carbide surface.
              Nicks or chips can cause failure. Transport rolls in compartment wooden boxes. Be sure

              ensure positive gripping of the rod, a finish of 0.4 to 0.8 micrometer in the pass is
              specified. A finish in the neighborhood of 0.2 micron could result in slippage in certain

              5.6.3   Pass Wear

              Some of the factors that influence pass wear are: grade of carbide, stock temperature, mill
              speed, cooling water analysis and pressure and rolling practice. In general, the softer
              grades of carbide resist breakage well but have poorer wear rates than the harder grades.
              Grade selection is a compromise between hardness for good wear and toughness for low
              breakage.

              Higher stock temperatures lead to more rapid pass wear through heat checking. Stock
              temperature is influenced by mill speed and operating practices. Maintain water pressure
              near 80 psi (5.62kg/cm sq) to minimize heat accumulation in the roll.

              Suspended solids in the water, particularly sand, can erode the pass. A well maintained
              filtration system will minimize this wear. There is some evidence that acidic water
              attacks the matrix of the carbide and increases pass wear. Treatment of the water to
              improve its quality may reduce this type of chemical erosion. Several factors in
              operating practice influence pass wear. Carefully match roll diameters to plus or minus
              0.05 mm for each pair of rolls: and match the diameters of pairs of rolls in one line to
              within 1.5 mm to minimize pull and eliminate push between stands. Too large a section
              entering the PFM can cause flutter of the section between the stands, as well as an
              excessive roll breakage. It is therefore necessary to carefully control the shape of the
              incoming section to the PFM and hold close to the diameter called for on the Diagram of
              Rolling Schedule.

              Wear rates generally fall within the range from 36 to 82 metric tons per 0.03 mm on roll
              diameter, per groove, with the lower values in the early stands, and also in the leaders and
              finishing stand due to more frequent roll changing from the surface considerations.

              5.6.4   Roll grinding

              The number of tons rolled before redressing varies from stand to stand and from mill to
              mill. A typical range is from 907 to 2733 metric tons, although the leader and finisher
              may need to be changed every 635 to 726 metric tons.

              The pass surface and outside diameter of the rolls are diamond or electrolytically ground
              on special machines so that a pair of rolls is matched dimensionally to within plus or
              minus 0.05 mm. Both plunge grinding and profile grinding techniques are used to obtain
              pass shape. The outside diameters are generally ground separately on cylindrical
              grinders. After grinding the pass to just remove all visual signs of wear, grind off an
              additional allowance (0.25 mm to 0.75 mm on the diameter) to ensure that all oxidized
              material and thermal micro-cracks have been eliminated. Initial determination of pass
              wear and checking of final pass configurations are accomplished through the use of an
              optical comparator and/or steel templates.

              On multiple pass rolls, grind the passes together or separately, as needed. If grinding the
              passes together, cover the initially unused pass or passes with a protective coating to

              5.6.5   Tapered Sleeve

              The major cause of roll breakage is lack of support of the carbide roll ring. Its strength in
              compression during rolling is dependent on it being sufficiently supported by its
              supporting tapered sleeve. To minimize premature roll breakage and maximize sleeve
              life it is critically important good surface contact between shaft, sleeve, and roll is
              maintained. To help achieve this, cleanliness in assembly of these parts is essential.
              Clean the parts prior to assembly using dry cleaning agents such as Acetone or White
              Spirit. Avoid kerosene and petroleum based solvents as they may leave an oil residue on
              the part surfaces acting as a lubricant and causing slippage between sleeve and shaft or
              sleeve and roll. Check the edges of the tapered sleeves for burrs or damage that may
              prevent a good surface contact. Carry out a visual inspection of the parts before every
              mill build.

              5.6.6   Roll Shop Records

              Etch a shop identification number onto the outer face of each roll. Keep a corresponding
              file card with pertinent data such as: date removed from mill, tonnage rolled, amount
              removed in grinding and diameter after grinding. Wear rates can easily be calculated
              from this data and are usually expressed in metric tons per 0.03 mm removed in dressing
              (on diameter).

              Also maintain roll breakage records. This information is important in the selection of roll
              materials and manufacturers, and in assessing the performance of the mill. Analysis of
              roll breakage records will pinpoint trouble areas.

              Include the following information in roll breakage records: strand, stand, shaft (upper
              and lower) pass configuration, type of break (radial, circumferential, piece broken out,
              exploded, etc.), and any special circumstance that might have contributed to the break
              (cobble, cold front end, loss of cooling water, etc.). If a radial crack has occurred, the
              location of the crack is significant in any analysis; therefore make a sketch of each
              broken roll for reference purposes.

              5.6.7   Factors Contributing to Premature Failure

              To minimize roll breakage the surface of the roll bore, the tapered sleeve and the 1:12
              mm ratio, keep the shaft taper in good condition.

              The following are other possible causes of roll breakage. A simple cause is plugged
              water spray nozzles. Thermal failure can also occur when the rolls became hot because
              the water was not on, or the hot steel of a cobble packed around a roll. Following a
              cobble the carbide will shatter if the rolls have not cooled sufficiently when the water is
              put on.

                 Examination by roll manufacturers reveals that most roll failures to date have been radial

                 conditions are fretting corrosion and faulty roll shaft tapers.

       5.7       Roll Housings

       A large part of the total pre-finishing mill maintenance time is expended on roll housings.
       Periodically replacing the roll shaft seals, Clevite bearings and ball thrust bearings helps to
       eliminate more extensive repairs.

       Warning:          Mill equipment is capable of inflicting severe and fatal injuries. Electrical
                         voltages in both the power and the control circuits can cause fatal shocks.
                         Use extreme care and observe all safety precautions

       Because of their proximity to the product, roll housings are the most vulnerable part of the mill.
       There are two methods of maintenance used for the prevention of roll housing breakdown.

       •     Periodic inspection of roll housings in the Maintenance Shop.

       •     Taking weekly, in-the-mill lift tests, and recording the results for every roll shaft in the mill
             will determine if the ball thrust bearings are deteriorating. The lift test also determines if the
             deterioration warrants removal of the housing for rebuilding.

                 5.7.1   Shaft Seals

                 One source of lube oil contamination is roll-cooling water. A defective roll shaft seal
                 will allow roll cooling water, carrying scale and grime, into the lube oil system.

                 Regularly inspect for signs of water in the lube oil system. If other equipment is served
                 by the same oil system, it is also a possible source of the water, but usually the roll shaft
                 seals are at fault. To help in detecting faulty seals, each stand should have a water leg
                 glass in the lube oil return line. If there is any sign of water in one of these glasses,
                 replace the seals of that stand.

                 Common practice at several other mills is to have all roll shaft seals replaced after a
                 certain length of time in the mill. At one mill in particular, the time interval is every
                 three months. Such practices demonstrate the importance attached to keeping cooling
                 water out of the oil system.

              5.7.3   Examining Used Clevite Bearings to Judge Oil Condition

              When the oil is very clean, there is very little wearing of the Clevite bearings. The 0.05
              mm Babbitt overlay is just polished, making the surface in the contact area more
              reflective. There will probably be a number of fine scratches in the surface. The life of
              the Clevites with such a lubricating system is unlimited.

              In contrast (as Figure 13 demonstrates), Clevites have been removed from mills with
              contaminated oil and the bearings are worn into the copper lead layer. Another sign of a
              contaminated lube oil system is deep surface score marks all the way into the copper.
              The Clevite bearings in these mills are wearing out and should be replaced frequently. If
              the Clevite bearings show such wear, the lube oil system should be cleaned.

              An examination of the material attached to the magnetic plugs in the roll housings will
              give additional evidence of oil condition. In six months time, the build-up should be no
              more than slight sludge. If there are large abrasive particles, the lube oil system is
              contaminated.

              5.7.4   Examining Used Clevite Bearings for Evidence of Misalignment

              Some Clevite seizures occur shortly after the roll housing goes into the mill. When this
              happens, review the housing rebuilding methods. Both the work side and drive side
              bearing journals are tapered to accommodate the misalignment from the overhung load
              which tips the roll shaft through the oil film clearances and from the elastic bending of
              the rather long, heavily loaded shaft. The taper compensates for both causes of
              misalignment to create a more uniform oil film thickness.

              The roll shafts are all of the same design. The work side journal taper is selected where
              the oil film is the thinnest to align the shaft and bearings.

              The test for misalignment is made by measuring the bearing wear pattern. A new bearing
              is of uniform thickness. To check the wear pattern, measure the variation in the bearing
              thickness along axial lines. Place the bearing on a surface plate and move the probe of an
              electronic measuring instrument along the axial lines. The probe is mounted on a height
              gage which slides easily on the surface plate.

              5.7.5   Rolling Housing Periodic Inspection

              To prevent roll-housing breakdown by use of this maintenance method, remove the roll
              housings after 100 turns of operation, and disassemble for inspection in the Maintenance
              Shop. Inspect all components of the roll housings. Pay particular attention to the Clevite
              bearings. The greatest threat to roll housing breakdown is seizure of the work side
              Clevite bearings. As mentioned before, the cause of Clevite deterioration is invariably
              contaminated lube oil. If the bearings are only polished and have but a scattering of fine
              surface scratches, the oil lube system is effective.

              5.7.7   Axial Roll Shaft Lift Test

              The purpose of this test is to measure and record roll shaft end play. Excessive roll shaft
              end play may cause a shoulder on the rod, or failure of the roll shaft ball thrust bearing.
              In the past the fastest stand in any mill has been the most frequently prone to wear.

              The two major sources of end play are: wear on the rear eccentric locking bar, and
              improper mounting of the thrust bearing. The following paragraphs provide some tips on
              assembling the locking bar and roll shaft thrust bearings.

              The locking bar fits into a slot on the rear eccentric bearing cartridge and is bolted to the
              roll housing rear plate. The locking bar is made slightly undersized and surface ground
              to give 0.013 mm clearance at assembly. To minimize surface conditions that could lead
              to premature wear, surface grind the locking bars rather than filing them when they are
              fitted. Be sure the eccentric slots have a good finish. Stone the corners.

              Proper adherence to these procedures will minimize end play caused by wear on the
              locking bar.

              Heat the thrust bearing to 121°C (250°F) before mounting. Mount the heated bearing on
              the roll shaft and lock it in place with its retaining plate and cap screws immediately.

       Caution:       Ensure that the oil grooves in the outer races face one another.

              Allow the bearing to cool, then tighten the retaining plate cap screws again, forcing the
              bearing against the roll shaft shoulder for proper mounting. Torque the cap screws to the
              specified value.

              This second tightening of the cap screws corrects the ball thrust bearing's tendency to
              creep away from the roll shaft radius when cooling, causing improper mounting of the
              bearing. The ball thrust bearing, properly mounted, rarely causes excessive end play.

              A minor source of end play could be grit on the surfaces of the elastomeric thrust
              bearings. Compression of these thrust bearings is negligible and not a cause of end play.
