       5.8     Drive Housing

       On the 250 pre-finishing mill the drive housing is the link in the drive train between motor and
       rolls. The Drive Housing contains an Input Shaft, two horizontal parallel integral bevel gear
       shafts, two bevel gear shafts at 45° to the horizontal shafts and 90° to each other, two idler pinion
       shafts, and Bearing Cartridge Assemblies. The gears and bearings are pressure lubricated from
       the PFM lube oil system. The basic operation of the Drive Housing Assembly is as follows [the
       numbers correlate with the numbers in Figure 22 (below)]:

       1. The Input Shaft is connected to the motor by a horizontal, floating, double coupling. The
          Input Shaft is supported by a double, tapered roller bearing cartridge at the back (driveside),
          and a single roller bearing cartridge at the front (workside) end, and an integral gear in the
          center that meshes with two helical pinion gears in the center of each Bevel Gear shaft.

       2. The Bevel Gear Shafts are oriented so that the bevel gear for Stands 13 and 15 face the front
          of PFM #1 while the bevel gear for Stands 14 and 16 face the rear of the PFM. The shafts are
          supported by a single row of roller bearings on the front (workside) end and tapered double
          roller bearings at the back (driveside) end. These bevel gears mesh with the two Drive Pinion
          Shafts at a 45° angle. Each Bevel Gear Shaft is driven by the horizontal bevel shaft through
          a set of precision spiral bevel gears.

       3. The Drive Pinions are situated at a 45° with respect to the Bevel Gear Shafts and provide a
          continuation of the drive train from the Bevel Gear Shafts to the rolls. The ratio of the spiral
          bevels are designed to give the correct speed relationship between stands based on the rolling
          schedule. The Drive Pinions are supported by a single row of roller bearings on the bottom
          (driveside) end and tapered double roller bearings at the top (workside) end. In addition to

1.0      Safety Procedures

IMPORTANT: All Safety Devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to assure the safety of the
operators.
Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices make the
elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the process and/or
product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be constrained to follow a
prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble. Cobbles occur at random times
and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently
caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment, and
stock temperature are also causes of cobbling anywhere along the length of a bar in process in the rolling
train. The following recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe manner.


        1.1     Visibility and Communications

        Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations of
        pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment controlled from that
        point.

                A. Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight.

                B. Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper
                   lighting can be used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or cloud
                   the reflective surface and that the mirror location does not make it liable to breakage.

        1.2     Audible Communications

                Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as
                substitutes only when visual contact is not possible.

        1.3     Safety Stops

                Guide adjustments may be made only when the Mill Line is shut down. Mechanical or
                electrically operated stops must be used to block any stock from inadvertently entering into
                the mill.

                Make sure mill is shut down and material can not run through the stand. Make sure that
                stops remain in place as long as personnel making adjustments are in the hazard area. For
                example, the snap shear will be closed ahead of the NTM.

INTRODUCTION Refer to Figures 1 through 4 as a guide.

A Crop and Divide shear is located in each strand of this two strand mill.

The purpose of the Crop and Divide (C & D) Shear, located upstream from No-Twist Mill (NTM) is to
cut stock and send it to the proper location as front end crops, front end samples, tail end crops, tail end
samples or divide and divert to the chopping shear. Note: Crop and Sample cuts are similar except for
preset length and the destination of the cut piece. For scrap rod cutting, the C&D shear performs a single
divide/cut causing the new front end to be deflected to a continually running chopping shear. Refer to
C&D shear switch manual for additional information on deflector and switches.

The C&D Shear consists of one pair of knives mounted on two parallel shafts arranged on 1080 mm
centers. There is one knife blade mounted on each shaft positioned at a 90° angle in the parked position
and parallel to each other (See Figure 1). The two shafts are geared together at 1:1 ratio and rotate the
knife blades to approximately 345° angle where initial contact of the rod cut occurs. The knife blade
continues rotating to the “Fully cut - 0° position” where the cut is completed. The drive motor is directly
coupled to the bottom knife shaft and geared to upper shaft.

The C&D Shear is designed for manual and automatic operation, operating stations (Main Pulpit and
Local) help test, monitor and adjust conditions that may occur through the automated system. Refer to
Table 1 for description of electrical equipment used in the C&D Shear Assembly.

1.0     Sequence of Cutting Operation
The following steps describe the intended cut sequence of the knife blades. Refer to Figure 1 as a guide.
Important: Always operate all mill equipment with Safety Guards closed.

        1.1.    The position where the knives are vertical and fully engaged is the 0° position.

        1.2.    Between cuts, the shear is held at the parked position, which is the 90° position.

        1.3.    When the shear is signaled to cut, it accelerates to the 260° position.

        1.4.    At 350° position, the approximate bite angle, the knives contact the stock and commence
                the cut.

        1.5.    At the 0° position, the position detection system signals that the cut is complete. Note:
                There is negligible speed drop at top shear speed.

        1.6.    At 10°, the positioning system signals that the knives are clear and signals the drive to
                stop by regenerative braking.

        1.7.    The shear decelerates to the 260° position.

        1.8.    The shear comes to a stop at the 270° position.

        1.9.    The shear will then reverse direction and travel from the 270° position to the 90° parked
                position.

        1.10.   When the shear has position regulated to a stop at the 90° position the position regulator
                will continue to hold the shear in position between cut cycles

Note: An over-speed adjustment, up to 25% is required for blade impact compensation and for
geometry compensation due to differences in shear (circumference) and blade speed.

1.0     C & D Shear Assembly

        1.1     Position Regulator

        A position regulator holds the shear at its parked position between cuts. This means that the same
        commutator bars always stop under the motor brushes. Good maintenance practice requires rotation of
        the motor coupling occasionally to vary the motor parked position. A positioning system must be
        designed to maintain the relationship between the motor position and the shear knife position.

        1.2     Holding Brake

        An electric operated, spring set brake is installed at the non-drive end of the shear motor. The
        brake is used for holding only. It is not used for stopping. With normal billet gap of
        approximately 5 seconds, the drive position regulator will hold the shear in parked position
        between cut cycles, while the brake is released continuously and does not operate.

        The brake will set to hold the shear when there is a longer than usual billet gap. This is
        determined by the tracking system. Whenever stock is in the mill, the brake will be energized
        and released. When there is no stock, the brake will be de-energized and set after a time delay.
        The time delay is set initially for 15 seconds.

        1.3     Cobble Detection in Shear Area

        The cobble detection system uses a mono-filament fish-line to support the Cobble Detection
        limit switch. A cobble will burn the line subsequently activate the switch and sound an alarm.
        Operation of the shear prevented.

        1.4     Safety Cage

        The Safety Cage Closed proximity switch senses that the door of the safety cage is closed. The
        door must be closed for shear operation. Whenever the safety cage door is detected open, a visual
        alarm is provided for operator.

        Note that the design must be such that loss of power to the switch or open circuit between switch
        output and control system indicates safety cage is open.

        1.5     Hot Metal Detector

        Crop HMD located ahead of the shear initiates the tracking system for front and tail end crops.

        1.6     Shear Lubrication

        The shear is lubricated by the lubrication system. A Shear Lube Pressure switch initiates an
        alarm if the lube pressure is not correct.

        1.7     Laying Head Orientation

        When a crop cut is made and the shear knives are at zero position, a signal is sent to the laying
        head drive to initiate coarse control of the laying head orientation. Refer to the description in
        control specification for laying head.

        1.8     Crop Chute

       Two scrap buckets are located at the lower level beneath the shear. Cut pieces are directed into
       one bucket or the other by the scrap chute deflector. The chute deflector is operated by an air
       cylinder which is controlled by a manual valve.

        Automatic Front Crops and Sample Cuts

        A front end at Crop HMD initiates the tracking timer. Speed is referenced from the speed of the
        first upstream active stand with roll diameter compensation. Crop length or sample length is set
        by operator as a preset. The minimum preset length is 500 mm.

        Knives must not reach cut position until front end is under deflector. The cut accuracy is +/- 50
        mm for front and tail ends for 95% of all cuts. Shear reaction time compensation subtracts
        reaction time from tracking timer preset. The reaction time is determined by the time required
        from the cut initiate signal until knives overlap at zero position.

        Automatic Tail Crops and Sample Cuts

        Tail crops and sample cuts uses pulses from NTM drive. Refer to roll pass schedule to determine
        first NTM active stand for a given product.

        front end crop system.

        activated by the auto cobble detection system for the NTM. Refer to the applicable control

CORRECTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS

DEFINITION

Corrective maintenance encompasses those repair procedures required to return the C&D shear assembly to
satisfactory operating condition. Such repairs do not necessarily return the equipment to like-new condition.
Rather, the objective is to make it operational again as soon as possible. It is recommended to replace faulty
parts/components and sub-assemblies with new or previously refurbished spare parts/components and sub-
assemblies. Those parts removed may then be refurbished or reconditioned after the main equipment has
been returned to service.

INTRODUCTION

Corrective Maintenance of the C&D Shear Assembly as defined above, is intended to keep down time at a
minimum by replacing components and then dismantling and overhauling the removed component in a
service area away from the mill. Once refurbished, the component becomes a spare shelf part, ready to be
utilized as a replacement when needed.

No disassembly procedures are given herein of components being replaced. Components that require
overhaul/refurbishment should be maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Refer to
the manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance and torque requirements and procedures of specific
components of the Chopping Shear Assembly

General guidelines and maintenance criteria are provided below when corrective maintenance of a
component or sub-assembly is required. These are minimum guidelines and should be used in conjunction
to the specific maintenance requirements from the component manufacturer.

1.0     General Maintenance Criteria

The following is a list of maintenance actions to perform whenever dismantling equipment for repairs.

        1.1     Electric controls and power cables -- Before disconnecting any wiring that does not have
                plug-in connectors, make sure that color coding is clearly identifiable or tag each wire
                carefully for reference at re-assembly.

        1.2     Rigging parts for removal/replacement -- Many parts that make up this equipment are
                much too heavy to be handled by one person. Provide adequate rigging for lifting and
                supporting heavy parts before attempting to dismantle any equipment.

        1.3     Cleaning -- Clean all parts with a suitable solvent (mineral spirits, SAVASOL no.5, or
                equivalent) to remove all scale, grease, grime, or dirt. Use a clean wiper; do not use cotton
                waste. Air dry after cleaning

        1.4     Bearings and Sealing Surfaces -- Closely inspect bearings and sealing surfaces for signs of
                wear, nicks, scratches, gouges, or build-up of scale or other foreign substances. Replace
                bearings that show any signs of deterioration.

                To clean roller bearings, soak in clean solvent long enough to loosen any sludge, and then
                gently slosh each bearing around near the top of the container to dislodge all pockets of
                grease. Scrub away stubborn accumulations with a small brush that has bristles that do not
                break off. Do not spin dirty bearings, but rotate races slowly while washing and
                scrubbing.

                Rinse the bearings in clean solvent and air dry. Hold both races when blowing with clean,
                dry compressed air. Do not allow the air jet to spin the bearing; rather, turn each race by
                hand to expose all surfaces to the drying air. If the bearing is to be stored for later reuse,
                wrap it in wax paper or other grease-proof wrapping.

                CAUTION: A bearing may be defective without the defect being visually evident.
                Replace any bearing removed during any maintenance task with new or cleaned bearing at
                reassembly.

1.0     Safety Procedures

IMPORTANT: All Safety Devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to assure the
safety of the operators.

Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices
make the elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the
process and/or product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be constrained
to follow a prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble. Cobbles occur at
random times and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is unpredictable. Cobbles are
most frequently caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed path. Improper speed regulation,
guide adjustment, and stock temperature are also causes of cobbling anywhere along the length of a
bar in process in the rolling train. The following recommended guidelines will help to produce a
quality product in a safe manner.

        1.1     Visibility and Communications

        Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations of
        pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment controlled from
        that point.

                A. Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight.

                B. Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper lighting
                   can be used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or cloud the
                   reflective surface and that the mirror location does not make it liable to breakage.

        1.2     Audible Communications

                Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as
                substitutes only when visual contact is not possible.

        1.3     Safety Stops

                Guide adjustments may be made only when the stand concerned is shut down.
                Mechanical or electrically operated stops must be used to block any stock inadvertently
                entering into the mill.

                Make sure mill is shut down and material can not run through the stand. Make sure that
                stops remain in place as long as personnel making adjustments are in the hazard area.
                For example, the snap shear will be closed ahead of the NTM.

               When a service operation is completed, the Mill must be restarted in the following sequence:

               1.      All mechanical stops will be moved.
               2.      All Guards will be in place.
               3.      All personnel will clear the hazardous area.

               5.      Operators at control stations will be notified that the MILL may be restarted.
               6.      Operators must not restart the mill until they are completely satisfied that
                       restarting will not present hazards to personnel. An audible signal will be
                       given by the operator to indicate that restart is imminent.

INTRODUCTION Refer to Figures 1through 3.

The purpose of the pivot & crop troughs and deflectors, located before and after the Crop and Divide
(C&D) Shear is to direct the stock and send it to the proper location as front end crops, front end samples,

performs a single divide/cut causing the new front end to be deflected to the chopping shear. Refer to C&D
shear section in this manual for additional information.

The C&D Switch Trough Assembly consists of a pivot trough assembly, located before the C&D
shear, and a crop trough with deflectors and a sample box located after the C&D shear.

The C&D Switch Trough Assembly consists of the pivot trough before the C & D shear and crop trough and
switch and sample deflectors after the shear. The Switch Trough Assembly is designed for manual and
automatic operation, operating stations (Main Pulpit and Local) help test, monitor and adjust conditions that

2. 0   Pivot (Switch) and Crop Trough Assemblies

       2.1      Pivot Trough Lift (vertical motion)

       The pivot (switch) trough ahead of the C&D shear must be in its lowered position during
       front end crop and sample cuts. The trough is raised to its horizontal running position a
       short time delay after front cuts to reduce wear. It remains in its up position for scrap
       cutting, tail cutting, and normal running.

       Up-down motion is produced by an air cylinder. This is controlled by Switch Trough Lift
       double solenoid valve. Switch Trough Lift Position proximity switches indicate the two
       positions.

       2.2      Upper Crop Deflector following C&D shear

       Immediately following the C&D shear, as part of the crop trough, there is a fixed deflector
       that directs crop cut pieces to the crop box. After cutting, the new front end passes over this
       deflector toward the NTM®. Immediately following this fixed deflector there is a pivoting
       upper deflector that directs stock either to the mill or to the chopping shear. For normal
       rolling, the crop deflector remains in its up position at all times. It is lowered only for tail
       end cuts and scrap cutting.

       In the down position, stock goes to the chopping shear. In the up position, stock goes to the
       NTM®. The upper crop deflector is pivoted vertically to its two positions by a pneumatic
       cylinder that is controlled by Upper Crop Deflector double solenoid valve. The Upper
       Crop Deflector Position proximity switches indicate the two positions.

       If necessary to chop a billet during the course of rolling, the upper deflector moves down,
       the C&D shear makes a divide cut and the upper deflector directs the new front end to
       chopping shear. The Upper Crop Deflector Down Position proximity switch senses the
       down position to signal the shear to make a divide cut. A timer is also used as a backup
       (initially set at 1 second) just in case the proximity switch does not sense the down position
       after a predetermined time following the upper deflector “Down” command signal.

       2.3      Lower Crop Deflector following C&D shear

       The lower crop deflector is operated by an air cylinder that has a vertical up and down
       motion. The cylinder is controlled by the Lower Crop Deflector double solenoid valve.
       Each position is indicated by the Lower Crop Deflector Position proximity switches.

       The lower crop deflector is normally in the up position except for front end sample, tail end
       sample cut and scrap cutting.

       In the down position, the lower crop deflector directs the front end sample cut or a tail end
       sample cut to the chopping shear.

3.0       Sequence of Operation

Front End Crop Cut Refer to figure 5.

      •   The tracking system signals the pivot (switch) trough ahead of the shear to move to the
          down position.

      •   The upper crop deflector after the shear is up, the lower crop deflector after the shear is up
          and the sample deflector is retracted.

      •   The front end enters the shear and is directed below the fixed deflector in the crop trough
          after the C&D shear.

      •   The C&D shear makes a divide cut. The cropped front end goes down the scrap chute; the
          new front end is lifted upward by the deflector mounted on the shear knife and passes to the
          mill.

      •   The pivot trough ahead of the shear raises to the up position 1 second after the cut is made.


Front End Sample Cuts Refer to figure 6.

      •   The operation of front end sample cuts is the same as explained above for front end crop
          cuts, except that the lower crop deflector is placed in the down position to direct pieces
          through the chopping shear to the sample box. Additionally, the sample box deflector after
          the chopping shear will be extended.

      •   There are individual length presets for crop cuts and sample cuts as described in the control
          specification for the C&D shear.

      •   Whenever the operator wishes to obtain a front end sample piece he pushes the SAMPLE
          button after the tail end has passed the C&D shear and before the next front end reaches the
          Crop HMD.

      •   After the sample cut, the sample cut function is canceled automatically.

      •   The sample deflector is to retract a time delay after the front end passes the C&D shear for
          two reasons:

                  To limit the crop pieces in the sample box.

                  To be ready to direct crop pieces to the scrap chute in the event of a cobble.

PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS
DEFINITION

Preventative maintenance is routine maintenance that, if performed as scheduled helps to keep the
C&D switch trough assembly in good operating condition. Its primary purpose is to reduce the
incidence of operating failures, which require costly downtime for repairs. The recommended
routine maintenance schedule below represents the anticipated minimum requirements for
maintaining the pivot, crop and switch troughs.
IMPORTANT
Always isolate shutoff and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic and electrical power supply sources before
performing any repairs or maintenance. Read all safety instructions and warnings for each system and
component prior to working on machinery. Refer to safety section in this manual.
INTRODUCTION
Routine and preventive maintenance of the C&D switch trough assembly is required to ensure extended and
proper operation. Table 3 is provided as a quick reference guide for frequent periodic maintenance
requirements for the C&D Shear assembly. Refer to the safety and general maintenance section and to the
applicable manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance requirements and procedures of specific
components of the equipment. Refer to Morgan assembly drawings as a guide and for additional
information.

assembly to satisfactory operating condition. Such repairs do not necessarily return the equipment to

refurbished spare parts/components and sub-assemblies. Those parts removed may then be
refurbished or reconditioned after the main equipment has been returned to service.

              then gently slosh each bearing around near the top of the container to dislodge all pockets

              clean, dry compressed air. Do not allow the air jet to spin the bearing; rather, turn each

Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices make the
elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the process and/or
product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be constrained to follow a
prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble. Cobbles occur at random times
and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently
caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment, and
stock temperature are also causes of cobbling anywhere along the length of a rod in process in the rolling
train. The following recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe manner.

        1.1     Visibility and Communications

                Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations
                of pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment
                controlled from that point.

                    A. Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight.

                    B. Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper
                    lighting can be used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or cloud
                    the reflective surface and that the mirror location does not make it liable to breakage.

        1.2     Audible Communications

                Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as
                substitutes only when visual contact is not possible.

        1.3     Safety Stops

                Guide adjustments may be made only when the Mill Line is shut down. Mechanical or
                electrically operated stops must be used to block any stock from inadvertently entering into
                the mill.

                Make sure mill is shut down and material can not run through the stand. Make sure that
                stops remain in place as long as personnel making adjustments are in the hazard area. For
                example, the snap shear will be closed ahead of the NTM.

        1.4     Alarms

                The alarms as described in the control specifications will have a warning system to alert
                the operators of new oncoming front ends.

INTRODUCTION Refer to Figures 1 and 2 as a guide.

The purpose of the Chopping Shear, located downstream from the Crop and Dividing Shear (C & D Shear)
is to cut diverted stock into short pieces for easy disposal. Scrap rod is diverted to the chopping shear
when a cobble occurs beyond the C & D Shear location.

The Chopping Shear consists of three pairs of knives mounted on two parallel shafts arranged on 380 mm
centers. There are three knives mounted on each shaft positioned at 120° apart from each other. The two
shafts are geared together at 1:1 ratio so that the knives become engaged at each 120° of shaft rotation.
The drive motor is directly coupled to the bottom knife shaft and geared to the upper shaft.

The Chopping Shear runs continuously in the ready mode to chop when necessary. The Chopping Shear is
designed for manual and automatic operation, operating stations (Main Pulpit and Local) help test, monitor
and adjust conditions that may occur through the automated system. Refer to Table 1 for a description of
the electrical devices used in the Chopping Shear Assembly.

       1.1     Tail End Acceleration

       When cobble cutting at slow product speeds, the end of the bar sometimes can stall in the delivery
       troughs going to the chopping shear. Accelerating the shear once the product tails out of the
       upstream water box provides additional inertia to the remaining piece of bar so that it does not
       stall.

       Acceleration begins as the product tail end is detected at Crop & Divide HMD. The shear
       accelerates to an operator-adjustable speed between 100% and 200% of shear reference speed.

       The Drive limits top speed is no more than top rated speed of motor and no more than 100%
       current during acceleration. The Chopping Shear returns to the preset speed once product has
       tailed out of the shear.

CORRECTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS
DEFINITION

Corrective maintenance encompasses those repair procedures required to return the chopping shear
assembly to satisfactory operating condition. Such repairs do not necessarily return the equipment to like-
new condition. Rather, the objective is to make it operational again as soon as possible. It is
recommended to replace faulty parts/components and sub-assemblies with new or previously refurbished
spare parts/components and sub-assemblies. Those parts removed may then be refurbished or
reconditioned after the main equipment has been returned to service.
INTRODUCTION
Corrective maintenance of the chopping shear assembly as defined above is intended to keep down time at
a minimum by replacing components and then dismantling and overhauling the removed component in a
service area away from the mill. Once refurbished, the component becomes a spare shelf part, ready to be
utilized as a replacement when needed.

        1.3     Cleaning -- Clean all parts with a suitable solvent (mineral spirits, SAVASOL no.5, or
                equivalent) to remove all scale, grease, grime, or dirt. Use a clean wiper; do not use cotton
                waste. Air dry after cleaning.

        1.4     Bearings and Sealing Surfaces -- Closely inspect bearings and sealing surfaces for signs of

       3.1     Safety Procedures

       Important:       All safety devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to assure
                        the safety of the operators.

       Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices
       make the elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the
       process and/or product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be
       constrained to follow a prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble.
       Cobbles occur at random times and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is
       unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed
       path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment, and stock temperature are also causes of
       cobbling anywhere along the length of a bar in process in the rolling train. The following
       recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe manner.

       3.2     Visibility and Communications

       Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations of
       pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment controlled from
       that point.

       Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight confirmation.

       Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper lighting can be
       used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or cloud the reflective surface and
       that the mirror location does not make it liable to breakage.

       3.3     Audible Communications

       Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as substitutes only
       when visual contact is not possible.

       3.4     Safety Stops

       Guide adjustments may be made only when the Mill Line is shut down. Mechanical or
       electrically operated stops must be used to block any stock from inadvertently entering into the
       mill.

       Ensure mill is shut down and material can not run through the stand. Ensure that stops remain in
       place as long as personnel making adjustments are in the hazard area.

       3.5     Alarms

       The alarms as described in the control specifications will have a warning system to alert the
       operators of new oncoming front ends.

4.0    OPERATION

       Important:      Always read all safety instructions and warnings for each system and
                       component prior to operating and working on machinery. Refer to the
                       Safety Section for general safety steps and procedures.

       4.1     Introduction

       The purpose of the Snap Shear located at the entry to the No-Twist Mill is to close the rod travel
       path and sever the rod. The Snap Shear is used as a safety device to prevent stock from entering
       the NTM when interlock safety systems are activated (i.e. Safety Guards Open). It also protects
       the downstream mechanical mill equipment in the event of low lubrication, cooling water
       malfunction, and electrical power loss. The Snap Shear must be closed when performing any
       maintenance on the downstream mill machinery.

       The Snap Shear is also used as an emergency cutting shear when a cobble occurs in the NTM or
       beyond. This prevents excess material from entering the NTM when rod travel has slowed down
       or stopped downstream.

       The Snap Shear is designed for manual and automatic operation, operating stations (Main Pulpit
       and Local) help test, monitor, and adjust conditions that may occur through the automated

       4.2     Components (Snap Shear before the NTM)

               4.2.1. Snap Shear Assembly Operation

               The Snap Shear single solenoid valve controls the Snap Shear. The Shear Opened and
               Shear Closed proximity switches indicate the open and closed positions. The valve is
               energized to open the knives’ air actuating cylinder from the rod travel path and de-
               energized to close and cut the rod (spring loaded return in the cylinder). The air cylinder
               rotates the knife into the cut position with sufficient force to bite into the traveling rod.
               The rod then pulls the knife to the final closed position, against the stop, and the knife
               blade severs the rod.

               The following condition causes immediate closing of the Snap Shear:

                   1. Operation of a SNAP SHEAR CLOSE button.
               Conversely, once the Snap Shear is closed, the following conditions will prevent the
               opening of the Snap Shear:

                   1.   Loss of power on the No-twist Mill drives.
                   2.   FAULT in the NTM lubrication system.
                   3.   FAULT in the roller entry guide lubrication system.
                   4.   No-twist Mill cobble guard door not closed.
                   5.   Low pressure in the No-twist Mill roll cooling water.

              Time delayed closing of the Snap Shear:

              •   Snap shear must not close before the divide cut has been made; otherwise a cobble
                  will occur in the C&D shear.

              •   Time delay starts when the C&D shear knives are at the zero, cut position.

              •   Time delay can be adjusted in the program; initially set for 1 second.

                       For better accuracy, the timer function is speed compensated.

                       It can be set very short if it is desired to minimize the amount of tail end stock
                       fed into the NTM.

                       Alternately, the time delay can be set long enough so that the tail end passes the
                       snap shear before it closes.

                       As an aid to setting the timer, the reaction time of the snap shear can be measured
                       by checking the time from de-energization of the Cut solenoid valve until the
                       Shear Closed proximity switch indicates the shear has closed.

              •   A backup timer starts when the C&D shear is signaled to make a divide cut. The
                  timer is set long enough, 2 or 3 seconds, to close the snap shear in the event the C&D
                  shear fails to operate.

              •   Any of the following conditions cause the snap shear to close a time delay after the
                  C&D shear scrap cutting function has been initiated and the C&D shear has made a
                  divide cut.

                  1.   Automatic initiation of the "scrap cut" function.
                  2.   LOW-LOW Lube lube pressure in the mill lube system.
                  3.   Auto Cobble Detection limit switch in mill.
                  4.   LOW Mill Cooling Water pressure.
                  5.   Stelmor® conveyor stopped while rod is detected at the NTM exit.

                       For this situation, C&D shear scrap cutting function is initiated, but the snap
                       shear does not close.

                       Ignore temporary stoppage when TAIL END STOP feature of Stelmor® is
                       active.

                  6. Stopping of the laying head drive while rod is detected at the pre-finishing mill
                     exit.

                  7. E-STOP of the mill lube system pumps.

5.0    MONITORING

       5.1      Monitoring (Snap Shear before the NTM)

       The Snap Shear is designed for manual and automatic operation, operating stations (Main Pulpit
       and Local) help test, monitor and adjust conditions that may occur through the automated system.

       Note:            For efficient operation of the Snap Shear, operators are required to
                        constantly monitor all components and control systems.

       A. Ensure the following elevated warning devices are working properly.
             1. Shear Open Signal (Green Lamp) and Shear Closed Signal (Red Lamp) indicators.
       B. Ensure compressed air supply is at proper pressure and that the lubricator is at its full mark.

       C. Test and monitor all interlock systems for proper operation. See Section 4.2.2 above. Make
          sure mill elevated warning lights and alarm is functioning.
       D. Monitor Main Control Pulpit. Refer to the following switches and indicators for proper
          operation.

             1. Snap Shear CUT selector button and indicator: Activates (with indicator) the knives to
                cut position.
             2. Snap Shear OPEN indicator. Indicator light shows shear is in open position.
       E. Monitor Local Station. Refer to the following switches and indicators for proper operation of
          snap shear.

             1. CUT indicator: Indicator light that shows snap shear knives in closed position.
             2. OPEN selector and indicator: Opens snap shear knives and indicates position. Note:
                Opening of snap shear can only be initiated at local station.
       F. Ensure water is flowing through spray tube and cooling knife assembly.

       G. Ensure cylinder is actuating properly. Test without stock for complete knife travel/rotation.
          Adjust flow control valves if necessary, so that knife assembly opens and closes quickly and
          completely against stops.

       H. Check that knifes closes completely with a maximum gap of 1.0 mm. Adjust and shim if
          necessary.

6.0    PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS
       6.1     Definition
       Preventive maintenance is routine maintenance that if performed as scheduled helps to keep the
       Snap Shear assembly in good operating condition. Its primary purpose is to reduce the incidence
       of operating failures, which require costly downtime for repairs. The recommended routine
       maintenance schedule below represents the anticipated minimum requirements for maintaining
       the Snap Shear. As you accumulate operating experience, it may be feasible to reduce the
       frequency of checks and inspections, however, do not reduce the lubrication frequency.
       Important:      Always isolate, shutoff, and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic, and
                       electrical power supply sources before performing any repairs or
                       maintenance. Read safety instructions and warnings for each system and
                       component prior to working on machinery. Refer to Safety Section in this
                       manual.
       6.2     Introduction
       Routine and preventive maintenance of the Snap Shear assembly is required to ensure extended
       and proper operation. Table 2 is provided as a quick reference guide for frequent periodic
       maintenance requirements for the Snap Shear assembly. Refer to the General Maintenance
       Section and applicable manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance requirements and
       procedures for specific components. Refer to Morgan assembly drawings as a guide for
       additional information.

       Warning:        Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or
                       disconnect all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any
                       stored energy from components. Restrain and secure any moving parts of a
                       component or system that could cause injury.

       Warning:        Exposed moving parts can cause severe injury. Lock out and tag out power
                       before removing guards or performing maintenance. Never remove a
                       guard, shield cover, or other protective devices while the equipment is
                       running!
       Warning:        The Snap Shear assembly is potentially dangerous and capable of inflicting
                       severe bodily injuries. Before starting any maintenance task, comply with
                       all company policies relating to safety. Also, be thoroughly familiar with the
                       general safety requirements.

       Warning:        Always stop machinery before entering or adjusting the equipment. Know
                       where all e-stop buttons are located before operating or performing
                       maintenance on this equipment.

       6.3     Maintenance Schedule

       Refer to the Morgan drawings listed in Section 2.0 of this Manual Chapter for guidance.

       Important:      A maintenance program must be implemented for tracking of all bearing
                       lubrication. A general deterioration of in service grease results in build up
                       of lubricant residue and consequent destruction of bearings. Apply fresh
                       grease to bearings on a regular basis and record date of lubrication to
                       establish regular lube routine.

       Note:           Setting up a maintenance plan that designates certain zones to be lubricated
                       on a specific day of the week will minimize down time and still accomplish
                       the required lubrication and maintenance interval.

       Important:      Always isolate, shutoff, and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic, and
                       electrical power supply sources before performing any repairs or
                       maintenance. Read safety instructions and warnings for each system and
                       component prior to working on machinery. Refer to the Safety section in
                       this manual.

       6.4     Lubrication

       Per Shift

       1. Inspect air regulator/lubricator/filter system for correct pressure and fluid level. Adjust
          lubricator as required.

       Weekly

       1. Lubricate bushings to knife assemblies with Mobile AW-1 or equivalent. Grease fittings are
          located on working side of assemblies. Refer to Figure 3 for guidance.

       Note:           Snap shear cover does not need to be opened to access grease fitting.

       6.5     Air Cylinder
       Daily

       1. Test for proper operation. Repair or replace as necessary. See Corrective Maintenance
          section for removal and refurbishment steps and procedures.

       2. Inspect all air connections and hoses for leaks, cuts, abrasions, and excess wear. Tighten
          connections and replace hoses as required.

7.0    CORRECTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS

       7.1     Definition
       Corrective maintenance encompasses those repair procedures required to return the Snap Shear
       assembly to satisfactory operating condition. Such repairs do not necessarily return the
       equipment to like-new condition. Rather, the objective is to make it operational again as soon as
       possible. It is recommended to replace faulty parts/components and sub-assemblies with new or
       previously refurbished spare parts/components and sub-assemblies. Those parts removed may
       then be refurbished or reconditioned after the main equipment has been returned to service.

       Important:      Always isolate, shutoff, and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic, and
                       electrical power supply sources before performing any repairs, or
                       maintenance. Read safety instructions and warnings for each system and
                       component prior to working on machinery. Refer to Safety Section in this
                       manual.

       7.2     Introduction
       Corrective maintenance of the Snap Shear assembly as defined above is intended to keep down
       time at a minimum by replacing components and then dismantling and overhauling the removed
       component in a service area away from the mill. Once refurbished, the component becomes a
       spare shelf part, ready to be utilized as a replacement when needed.

       No disassembly procedures are given herein of components being replaced. Components that
       require overhaul/refurbishment should be maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s
       instructions. Refer to the manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance and torque
       requirements and procedures of specific components of the Snap Shear Assembly.

       General guidelines and maintenance criteria are provided below when corrective maintenance of
       a component or sub-assembly is required. These are minimum guidelines and should be used in
       conjunction with the specific maintenance requirements from the component manufacturer.

       Upon re-assembly, tighten all bolts, screws, nuts, and fasteners in accordance with Morgan
       reference drawings torque requirements. Torque specific components in accordance with the
       manufacturer’s requirements.

       Warning:        Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or
                       disconnect all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any
                       stored energy from components. Restrain and secure any moving parts of a
                       component or system that could cause injury. Ensure covers are secure with
                       locking pin before performing any maintenance.

       Warning:        The Snap Shear assembly is potentially dangerous and capable of inflicting
                       severe bodily injuries. Before starting any maintenance task, comply with
                       all company policies relating to safety. Also, be thoroughly familiar with the
                       general requirements.

       7.3     General Maintenance Criteria
       The following is a list of maintenance actions to perform whenever dismantling equipment for
       repairs.

       1. Electric controls and power cables: Before disconnecting any wiring that does not have plug-
          in connectors, make sure that color coding is clearly identifiable or tag each wire carefully for
          reference at re-assembly.

       2. Rigging parts for removal/replacement: Many parts that make up this equipment are much
          too heavy to be handled by one man. Provide adequate rigging for lifting and supporting
          heavy parts before attempting to dismantle any equipment.

       3. Cleaning: Clean all parts with a suitable solvent (mineral spirits, SAVASOL no.5, or
          equivalent) to remove all scale, grease, grime, or dirt. Use a clean wiper; do not use cotton
          waste. Air dry after cleaning.

       4. Bearings and sealing surfaces: Carefully inspect bearings and sealing surfaces for signs of
          wear, nicks, scratches, gouges, or build-up of scale or other foreign substances. Replace
          bearings that show any signs of deterioration.

       5. Air cylinder seals: Replace (mandatory replacement) all seals, O-rings, and gaskets that are
          removed or disturbed during disassembly procedure. Ensure seals and o-rings seat properly
          upon re-assembly.

       6. Pre-lubrication prior to re-assembly: Lightly lubricate all seals, bearings, bushings, and gears
          with oil before installation

       7. Aligning parts during re-assembly: Because of the weight of large parts, use guide studs
          during re-assembly to ensure proper bolt hole and /or dowel pin alignment as necessary.
       8. Clean all parts and inspect for scratches, cracks, burrs, flaking, pitting, scaling or
          discoloration of mating or load-bearing surfaces.

       9. Hand scrape any bushing that have not become out-or-round to remove burrs, small scratches
          or accumulated foreign substances. Replace any bushing showing gross deformation or
          cracking.

       10. Check shafts and pivot pins for straightness with v-blocks and dial indicator. It is possible to
           straighten bent shafts in a hydraulic press, but if spares are available, it is much better to
           replace the parts. Never straighten bent castings; replace them. Weld cracked steel castings
           only if no spares are available, but replace them whenever possible.

              7.4.3. Air Cylinder Re-installation and Set-up

                      Refer to Figure 6 and Figure 7 (below) for guidance.

       Important:     The special heavy duty designed air cylinder must be replaced with exactly
                      the same model. Any substitute model air cylinder may cause damage to the
                      Snap Shear and other mill equipment.
                      A. Rotate knife assembly to closed position with knife holder against stops.

                      B. Install clevis onto spherical cylinder rod until both pieces are aligned
                         properly. Align holes and insert parallel pin into clevis and cylinder rod and
                         tighten locking bar.
                      C. Assemble pin and locking bar with knife holder against stop. Adjust cylinder
                         position with shims if necessary to ensure cylinder does not bottom out when
                         fully retracted.
                      D. Connect hoses and apply air to cylinder to check rotation of linkage. The
                         knife should pivot freely (open and close without interference). Note: When
                         closed, the gap between the knife blade tip and side wear plate should be 1
                         mm. The knife holder should contact the stop when closed.

       Important:     To prevent damage to the air cylinder: with the Knife Holder against the
                      stop (closed position), adjust the Clevis to ensure cylinder is not at the end of

3.0    SAFETY

       Important:     Always Read Safety Instructions and Warnings for each system and
                      component prior to operating and working on machinery. Follow all safety
                      precautions to avoid personal injury or property damage during system
                      operation. Refer to this section and the Safety Sections of each component
                      manual for general safety steps and procedures. Read all instructions,
                      warnings, and cautions carefully.

       Important:     Only trained personnel should operate and maintain mill equipment and
                      tools including rigging and lifting procedures. Do not work on equipment if
                      you have never been trained on!

       Important:     All Safety Devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to
                      assure the safety of the operators.

       Important:     Always wear personal protection equipment. Always wear proper safety
                      gear when in the mill. Minimum Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
                      should include safety hat, boots and gloves as well as eye and ear protection.
                      Wear proper protective gear when operating and maintaining mill
                      equipment.

       Caution:       Equipment throughout the mill produces excessive noise. Always wear
                      hearing protection.

       Warning:       Consider all equipment as potentially hazardous at all times. It is capable of
                      crushing any body part caught in it.

       Caution:       Working with high pressure may be dangerous if equipment is misused.
                      Never use faulty equipment.

       Danger:        Electrical voltages in both power and control circuits are capable of
                      rendering severe and fatal shocks.

       Warning:       Hot product traveling throughout the mill can make all equipment surfaces
                      a high temperature condition. Consider all surfaces throughout the mill to
                      be hot!

       Warning:       Beware of pinch points. Block and restrain rotating parts before removal
                      and mounting equipment.

       Warning:       Do not exceed equipment ratings. Never attempt to press on or lift a load
                      weighing more than the capacity of the cylinder. Overloading causes
                      equipment failure and possible personal injury.

       Caution:       Working with high pressure may be dangerous if equipment is misused.
                      Never set the relief valve to a higher pressure than the maximum rated
                      pressure of the pump. Higher settings may result in equipment damage
                      and/or personal injury.

       Warning:       The system operating pressure must not exceed the pressure rating of the
                      lowest rated component in the system. Check pressure gauges in the system
                      to monitor operating pressure.

       Caution:       Avoid damaging connected hoses. Avoid sharp bends and kinks when
                      routing hoses. Using a bent or kinked hose will cause severe back-pressure.
                      Sharp bends and kinks will internally damage the hose leading to premature
                      hose failure.

                      Do not drop heavy objects on hoses. A sharp impact may cause internal
                      damage to hose wire strands. Applying pressure to a damaged hose may
                      cause it to rupture. DO NOT lift or pull equipment by hoses or couplers.
                      Rig and secure equipment for safe transport.

       Caution:       Keep hydraulic equipment away from flames and heat. Excessive heat will
                      soften packing and seals, resulting in fluid leaks. Heat also weakens hose
                      materials and packing. For optimum performance do not expose equipment
                      to temperatures of 65°C [150°F] or higher. Protect all hoses and cylinders
                      from weld spatter and extreme heat.

       Danger:        Do not handle pressurized hoses. Escaping oil under pressure can penetrate
                      the skin, causing serious injury. If oil is injected under the skin, see a doctor
                      immediately.

       Warning:       Only use hydraulic cylinders in a coupled system. Never use a cylinder with
                      unconnected couplers. If the cylinder becomes extremely overloaded,
                      components can fail catastrophically causing severe personal injury. Never
                      bleed system to exposed atmosphere.

       Warning:       Immediately replace worn or damaged parts.

       Important:     Qualified trained technicians must only service Mill equipment.

       Warning:       Do not use electric pumps in an explosive atmosphere. Adhere to all local
                      and national electrical codes. Start the pump with the valve in the neutral
                      position to prevent accidental cylinder operation. Keep hands clear of
                      moving parts and pressurized hoses.

       Caution:       To prevent damage to electric motors, check specifications. Use of incorrect
                      power source will damage the motor.

       3.1     Safety Procedures

       Important:       All Safety Devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to
                        assure the safety of the operators.

       Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices
       make the elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the
       process and/or product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be
       constrained to follow a prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble.
       Cobbles occur at random times and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is
       unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed
       path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment, and stock temperature are also causes of
       cobbling anywhere along the length of a bar in process in the rolling train. The following
       recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe manner.

       3.2     Visibility and Communications

       Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations of
       pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment controlled from
       that point. Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight
       confirmation.

       Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper lighting can be
       used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or cloud the reflective surface and
       that the mirror location does not make it liable to breakage.

       3.3     Audible Communications

       Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as substitutes only
       when visual contact is not possible.

       3.4     Safety Stops

       Guide adjustments may be made only when the Mill Line is shut down. Mechanical or
       electrically operated stops must be used to block any stock from inadvertently entering into the
       mill.

       Ensure mill is shut down and material can not run through the stand. Ensure that stops remain in
       place as long as personnel making adjustments are in the hazard area.

       3.5     Alarms

       The alarms as described in the control specifications will have a warning system to alert the
       operators of new oncoming front ends.

       A prominently located light board should be used with the warning system to indicate the strand
       in use and the progress of the stock in the mill.

       3.6     Restart of Mill

       When a service operation is completed, the Mill must be restarted in the following sequence:
       1. All mechanical stops will be moved.
       2. All Guards will be in place.
       3. All personnel will clear the hazardous area.
       4. Permissive switches will be placed in “ALLOW RESTART” position and all interlocks
          engaged.
       5. Operators at control stations will be notified that the Mill Line may be restarted.

       Operators must not restart the mill until they are completely satisfied that restarting will not
       present hazards to personnel. An audible signal will be given by the operator to indicate that
       restart is imminent.

       3.7     Safety Shutoff and Lockout/Tag out

                       switches, indicators and controls. Operators must also know where all
                       power supply shutoff and isolation locations are in the water, air, hydraulic,
                       lubrication and electrical systems.

       Important:      Always isolate, shutoff, and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic and electrical
                       power supply sources before performing any repairs, maintenance or roll
                       and guide changes. Read all safety instructions and warnings for each
                       system and component prior to working on machinery. Read and refer to
                       Safety section of this manual before performing and maintenance or repairs.

                       Lockout and Tagout isolation valves located in the supply lines before
                       performing maintenance, or repairs. Lockout and Tagout control switches at the
                       Local Control Station and Main Pulpit.

       Important:      Ensure the Mill process stations and pass line has been completely shut
                       down and interlocks are working properly. All Safety devices must be
                       properly maintained and never bypassed to assure the safety of the
                       operators. ALWAYS - Verify Zero Energy State before working on
                       equipment.

       Warning:        The Mill Equipment is potentially dangerous and capable of inflicting severe
                       bodily injuries and fatal electric shock. Before starting any maintenance
                       task, comply with all company policies relating to safety. Also, be
                       thoroughly familiar with all safety requirements.

       Warning:        Always wear heat resistant gloves when changing guide equipment.
       Warning:        Hot product travelling throughout the mill can make all equipment surfaces
                       a high temperature condition and cause injury. Consider all surfaces
                       throughout the mill as hot!

4.0    INTRODUCTION

       The No-Twist Mill (NTM) consists of eight 230 mm stands arranged in a ‘Vee” type
       configuration, a cobble cover assembly, and a breakout box at the end of the mill. The mill is
       driven by a single motor that is coupled to a drive assembly which through a series of gears
       converts the rotation 90° to a gear that turns the driven shaft which meshes with a high-speed
       output shaft and a low speed output shaft. These are the shafts that turn the roll housing pinions.
       The roll housing assembly in turn contains the rolls, guides, and associated electrical components
       (i.e. oil lubrication, cooling water, and hydraulic systems).

       The NTM is designed for manual and automatic operation, operating stations (Main Pulpit and
       Local) help test, monitor and adjust conditions that may occur through the automated system. Refer
       to Table 1 for a description of electrical equipment used in the NTM.

       4.1     Systems and Components

       Refer to Figures 1 through 3 for guidance.

       Note:            For efficient operation of the No-twist Mill Area, operators are required to
                        constantly monitor all components. Listed below are operation descriptions
                        of the NTM and preventive steps/procedures to help ensure optimal
                        operation.

               4.1.1.   Cobble Guard Cover Assembly NTM

               The cobble guard door encloses the roll housing and helps prevent cobbles that occur
               from breaking out of the mill area. The cobble guard door is opened and closed by two
               screw jacks, one at each end of the cover. A squirrel cage induction motor powers each
               screwjack and is equipped with a built-in brake. Motors are high slip type for load
               sharing. Each motor has a FVR control and a Screwjack Incremental encoder located at
               the drive coupling to check motor motion.

       Note:            Motor revolutions are compared with each other and if the variation reaches
                        12 revolutions, the motors must stop to prevent unleveled motion and
                        twisting of the door.

               Under normal running conditions a drive mismatch should not occur unless there is some
               binding or other mechanical or electrical problem. To avoid unnecessary fault detection,
               make sure the pulses do not accumulate continuously from cycle to cycle. Also, reset to
               zero error when motion starts in each direction, up or down and stop synch checking
               when either drive actuates its travel limit.

               A reset pushbutton is required on the local control station to restore operation in the case
               of a fault stop. Operation of this button will cause the lagging drive to catch up. Then,
               normal operation can be resumed.

               Screwjack Limit of travel will be set through applicable software utilizing the encoder
               signal. In the close direction, there is a 0.5 second delay to make sure the door fully
               closes and seals. The end limits will also signal safety alarms when the door is not fully
               open or closed. Operating time for full travel is approximately 12.5 seconds.

               4.1.2.   Door Position Proximity Sensors

               The door is designed with (3) Door Position proximity sensors. These sensors indicate
               when the door is fully OPEN and fully CLOSED. One sensor is located on the upstream
               arm to indicate when the doors are fully open. The two other sensors, one located on
               each arm, indicate when the door is fully closed.

              4.1.4.   Roll Housings and Rolls

              Each housing contains a pair of roll shaft pinions that do not mesh with one another, but
              are independently driven by the drive pinions in the drive housing. Each roll housing
              mounts a pair of overhung, shell-type rolls carried on shafts. Each paired set of stands
              are centered at 45° to the horizontal axis, then aligned and rotated 90 ° to each other. The
              rolls are supported on shafts by tapered sleeves. Each shaft is mounted in an eccentric
              cartridge and supported by Clevite type bearings. The eccentrics can be rotated to permit
              adjusting roll parting by means of a parting adjusting screw connected to the eccentrics.
              The eccentrics are linked to each other, which produces equal and opposite adjustment in
              both shafts, thereby maintaining a constant pass.

              4.1.5.   Drive and Bevel Gear Assemblies

              The Drive Assembly is the link between the drive motor and the bevel gear assembly that is
              a continuation of the drive that operates the rolls. The drive assembly is coupled directly to
              the motor shaft and power is transmitted through gearing and pinions to the bevel gear
              assembly.

              The bevel gear assembly continues the drive train from the drive assembly to the rolls. The
              bevel gear shaft is driven by the line shaft through a pair of bevel gears that are designed to
              give the correct speed relation between the stands and the rolling pass schedule.

              4.1.6.   Guides

              The basic function of the guide is to direct the section through the mill stand in such a
              manner that the front end does not deviate from the pass line. Each stand will have an
              entry and delivery guide. The type of guide used at each stand will differ due the size
              and shape of the section. In many cases it is necessary to change the guides or the guide
              components as the section size changes.

              It is normal in many mills that the guides are prepared in a work area away from the mill
              floor. Once the guides are set, it is then the responsibility of the mill operators to install
              them. It is essential that the correct components be used in the guides for each position
              and size being rolled. Refer to the guide tabulation drawing for a list of the guides and
              components required at each stand position for the product size to be rolled. Listed
              below is a general description of types of guides used in a typical rolling mill.

              4.1.7.   Types of Guides

              A. Roller Entry Guides

              These are usually used to guide an oval section into a round pass. A roller entry guide is
              sometimes used to guide a round section into the first stand of the NTM, especially if a
              sidelooper is located immediately ahead of the mill. The roller entry guide can have
              either 2 or 4 guide rollers and has the provision to attach a 2 roller anti-flutter guide onto
              the back of the guide assembly.

              B. Static Entry Guides

              These are usually used to guide a round section into an oval pass. All the static entry
              guides are split into two halves and are clamped together to prevent a cobble from
              breaking out into the roll bite, which if allowed will damage the roll housing.

              C. Static Delivery Guides

              This type of guide is located at the delivery end of every stand. Two types of static
              delivery guides are used in the mill

              1. Spring Clip Type

              This delivery guide is split into two halves with the top half attached to the bottom with a
              spring clip. In case of a cobble the spring clip releases allowing the cobble to breakout
              into controlled area, preventing the cobble from accumulating and damaging the roll
              housing.

              2. Solid Type

              The type of guide is split into two halves with the top half being bolted to the bottom half
              to prevent the guide halves from parting during rolling. A solid guide is used due to the
              limited space between the two sizing mill stands.

              D. Dummy Pipes

              The dummy pipes are used for when the roll unit stands are not used for rolling. They
              replace the static entry and delivery guides. The dummy pipes are mounted in holders,
              which are fitted directly onto the existing guide brackets and are therefore correctly
              aligned to the mill and pass centerline.

              4.1.8.   Mounting the Guides

              A. Roller Entry Guides

              These guides are normally clamped onto an adjustable saddle, which is attached to a
              bracket located by means of a key and keyway to the housing faceplate and held in
              position by bolts, which automatically locates the bracket and roller guide on the mill
              centerline. A portable optic is supplied with the mill to help the operator accurately align
              the roller entry guide to the pass centerline by adjusting guide bracket saddle.

              A nosepiece is attached to the front of the guide to provide additional guiding as close to
              the roll bite as possible and to aid the front end of the rod into the center of the pass,
              especially at high speed. The nosepiece helps eliminate the possibility of the front end of
              the rod striking the roll pass collar, which will cause either the front end to turndown or
              cobble.

              B. Static Entry & Delivery Guides

              The static entry and delivery guides are mounted on a bracket, which is automatically
              aligned on the mill and pass centerline by a key and keyway.

              4.1.9.   Cobble Detection System

              The NTM is confined in enclosures that have a minimum
              amount of free space, so in the event of cobble, it is
              necessary to divert incoming stock as soon as possible.
              Since visual detection of a cobble by operator is
              difficult, automatic cobble detection methods are used in
              the NTM compartment and breakout box. This cobble
              detection system consists of a monofilament line with a
              weight strung through the compartment. A cobble in
              either stand will break the line and allow the weight to
              drop and actuate the NTM Cobble Detect proximity
              switch.

              The Cobble Detection System also provides a back-up
              method through the Hot Metal Detectors as follows:

              •   The tail end is sensed at the NTM Exit HMD before
                  it is sensed at the NTM Entry HMD.

              •   After the front end is sensed at NTM Entry HMD,
                  it is not sensed by the NTM Exit HMD within a
                  preset time.

              4.1.10. Roll Cooling Water System

              The Roll Cooling Water System is designed to prevent damage to the NTM rolls from the
              hot product traveling through mill. Each water valve is operated by an air cylinder. Each
              cylinder is controlled by a Roll Cooling single solenoid valve. Energizing the solenoid
              turns water on to the mill. De-energizing the solenoid turns water off to the mill and
              diverts flow to the flume.

              The Roll Cooling Pressure switch indicates when the correct water pressure is present at
              the No-twist Mill. A 0.5 second time delay is used in conjunction with the pressure
              switch so that a transient drop in pressure will not produce a false low-pressure
              indication. Low water pressure indication from the pressure switch is ignored for 5
              seconds when water is first turned on to allow for normal buildup of pressure. The NTM
              drive will stop if water pressure fault persists for 10 seconds.

       4.5      Roll Parting Correction

       Note:             For roll mounting and removal procedures refer to NTM Maintenance
                         manual.

       In practice it is necessary to make some corrections to the theoretical settings to take into account
       oil film thickness, machining tolerances and roll pinion shaft deflections due to rolling load. As a
       result the roll parting adjustments required can be either positive or negative depending on rolling
       load (i.e. reduction, steel grade and temperature), product diameter and rolling speed. Due to the
       high rolling speeds the required roll parting adjustments or deviations from the theoretical
       settings are generally positive. These positive deflections are caused by the oil film strength in
       the Clevite bearings exceeding the deformation resistance of the rod, causing the mechanical
       clearance to be removed in a negative direction (i.e. inward towards the stock). As a result the
       roll parting decreases from the set value as the mill is run up to the rolling speed, producing a
       smaller than expected finished product.

       Note:             It is advantageous to derive a standard setup for each size based on the most
                         commonly rolled steel grade and entry temperature. The operator
                         responsible for adjusting the mill should keep a log of the roll parting
                         adjustments made after each change in steel grade or entry temperature.
                         This will allow a more detailed setup chart to be derived based on groups for
                         steel grade and ranges of entry temperatures. Accurate roll parting
                         adjustments can then be made prior to changes in steel grade and/or entry
                         temperature, thereby ensuring that the tolerance of the first bar after the
                         change is within specified limits.

       Deviation from standard roll partings can be caused by:

                1.   Feed section size and shape outside setup parameters.
                2.   Too much tension.
                3.   Axial alignment of rolls being incorrect.
                4.   Guide setup being incorrect.
                5.   Roll parting settings being incorrect or incorrectly measured.

       4.6      Manual Roll Parting Under Load

       The NTM has the ability to make adjustments to the roll parting during rolling operations. This
       roll parting mechanism features a Gear Head to multiply the torque and a self-resetting manual
       torque limiter (to prevent over torquing). Results of roll parting corrections must be taken using a
       sampling method.
