       3.1      Safety Procedures

       Important:      All safety devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to assure
                       the safety of the operators.

       Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices
       make the elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the
       process and/or product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be
       constrained to follow a prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble.
       Cobbles occur at random times and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is
       unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently caused when the front end of stock fails to follow a
       prescribed path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment, and improper stock temperature
       are also causes of cobbling anywhere along the length of a bar in process in the rolling train. The
       following recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe manner.

       3.2      Visibility and Communications

       Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations of
       pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment controlled from
       that point.

       Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight confirmation.

       Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper lighting can be
       used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or cloud the reflective surface and
       that the mirror location does not make it liable to breakage.

       3.3      Audible Communications

       Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications should be used to supplement or as substitutes
       only when visual contact is not possible.

       3.4      Safety Stops

       Guide adjustments may be made only when the mill line is shut down. Mechanical or electrically
       operated stops must be used to block any stock from inadvertently entering into the mill.

       Ensure mill is shut down and material can not run through the stand. Ensure that stops remain in
       place as long as personnel making adjustments are in the hazard area.

       3.5      Alarms

       The alarms as described in the control specifications will have a warning system to alert the
       operators of new oncoming front ends.

       A prominently located light board should be used with the warning system to indicate the strand
       in use and the progress of the stock in the mill.

4.0    PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE

       4.1      General Description

       The No-Twist Mill (NTM) consists of eight 230 mm stands in a ‘V’ type configuration. Each
       NTM consists of a roll housing assembly, cobble cover assembly, and drive assembly that
       connect to the drive motor through means of a tandem coupling. The roll housing assembly in
       turn contains the rolls, guides, and associated electrical components (i.e. oil lubrication, cooling
       water, and hydraulic systems). Refer to the NTM Operation Chapter of this manual for further
       information and details of the No-twist Mill’s systems and components.

       4.2      Introduction

       Routine and preventive maintenance of the NTM assembly is required to ensure extended and
       proper operation. Table 1 is provided as a quick reference guide for frequent periodic
       maintenance requirements for the NTM assembly. Refer to the General Maintenance section of
       this manual and to the applicable manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance requirements
       and procedures of specific components of the NTM Area. Refer to Morgan assembly drawings
       as a guide and for additional information.

       4.3      Maintenance Facilities

       For best results provide an area where the roll housings and other components of the No-twist
       Mill. Can be disassembled, cleaned, inspected, and reassembled in a clean environment. Figure
       4 illustrates one possible roll housing maintenance shop. The shop should have the capability of
       handling roll housings coming in for periodic inspection and rebuild, roll housings coming in for
       repair, and repair of other No-twist Mill components. Ideally the following equipment should be
       installed in the shop:

       A Disassembly Bench:       To support the roll housings with their flanged front surface on

       4.5      Definition

       Preventive maintenance is routine maintenance that, if performed as scheduled helps to keep
       machinery in good operating condition. Its primary purpose is to reduce the incidence of
       operating failures, which require costly downtime for repairs. The recommended scheduled and
       planned maintenance procedures below represent the anticipated minimum requirements for
       maintaining the NTM.

       Important:      Always isolate, shutoff, and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic, and
                       electrical power supply sources before performing any repairs or
                       maintenance. Read all safety instructions and warnings for each system and
                       component prior to working on machinery. Refer to the Safety Section in
                       this manual.

       4.6      Scheduled and Planned Maintenance

       The objectives of scheduled and planned maintenance programs are to maintain the mill in a state
       of optimum readiness and performance and to ensure continued high production rates. To
       achieve these objectives, the Maintenance Department should develop and prepare a periodic
       sequence of inspections and preventive maintenance procedures for the No-twist Mill and its
       supporting systems. The objective of corrective maintenance is to return equipment to
       operational status as quickly as possible following a malfunction. The best way to bring the mill
       back to full operation always replace fault parts with new, or refurbished spare parts.

       Proper maintenance of the lubrication and cooling systems is the most important factor conducive
       to achieving the maximum mean-time-between-failures. Consequently, the most important task
       of preventive maintenance is to ensure a clean and adequate supply of lube oil at all times (while
       the mill is running) and to frequently lubricate the points, requiring grease lubrication, and
       keeping the cooling system functioning properly.

       Based on many years of experience in the development and manufacture of rod and bar mills,
       Morgan Construction Company has developed a set of scheduled maintenance activities to
       provide guidance to the Maintenance Department in developing and implementing a planned
       maintenance program of their own.

5.0    CORRECTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS

       5.1      Definition

       Corrective maintenance encompasses those repair procedures required to return the No-twist Mill
       assembly to satisfactory operating condition. Such repairs do not necessarily return the
       equipment to like-new condition. Rather, the objective is to make it operational again as soon as
       possible. It is recommended to replace faulty parts/components and sub-assemblies with new or
       previously refurbished spare parts/components and sub-assemblies. Those parts removed may
       then be refurbished or reconditioned after the main equipment has been returned to service.

       Important:      Always isolate, shutoff, and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic, and
                       electrical power supply sources before performing any repairs, maintenance,
                       or roll and guide changes. Read all safety instructions and warnings for
                       each system and component prior to working on machinery. Read and refer
                       to the Safety Section of this manual before performing any maintenance or
                       repairs.

       5.2      Introduction

       Corrective Maintenance of the No-twist Mill (as defined above) is intended to keep down time at
       a minimum by replacing components and then dismantling and overhauling the removed
       component in a service area away from the mill. Once refurbished, the component becomes a
       spare shelf part, ready to be utilized as a replacement when needed. Disassembly procedures are
       given herein of components being replaced. Components that require overhaul/refurbishment
       should be maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Refer to the
       manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance and torque requirements and procedures of
       specific components of the NTM.

       General guidelines and maintenance criteria are provided below when corrective maintenance of
       a component or sub-assembly is required. These are minimum guidelines and should be used in
       conjunction to the specific maintenance requirements from the component manufacturer. Upon
       re-assembly, tighten all bolts, screws, nuts and fasteners in accordance with Morgan reference
       drawings torque requirements. Torque specific components in accordance with the
       manufacturer’s requirements.

       Warning:        Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or
                       disconnect all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate, and exhaust any
                       stored energy from components. Restrain and secure any moving parts of a
                       component or system that could cause injury.

       Warning:        The NTM assembly is potentially dangerous and capable of inflicting severe
                       bodily injuries and fatal electric shock. Before starting any maintenance
                       task, comply with all company policies relating to safety.

          heavy parts before attempting to dismantle any equipment.

          wear, nicks, scratches, gouges, or build-up of scale or other foreign substances. Replace
          bearings that show any signs of deterioration. Scrape bushings slightly, be careful not to
          exceed the tolerance limits.

             To clean roller bearings, soak in clean solvent long enough to loosen any sludge then gently
             slosh each bearing around near the top of the container to dislodge all pockets of grease.
             Scrub away stubborn accumulations with a small brush that has bristles that do not break off.
             Do not spin dirty bearings, instead rotate races slowly while washing and scrubbing.

             Rinse the bearings in clean solvent and air dry. Hold both races when blowing with clean,
             dry compressed air. Do not allow the air jet to spin the bearing; rather, turn each race by
             hand to expose all surfaces to the drying air. If the bearing is to be stored for later reuse,
             wrap it in wax paper or other greaseproof wrapping.

                5.5.1   Roll Shop Responsibilities

                The roll shop should be responsible for cleaning (refer to Section 5.5.2) and assembling
                the rolls and tapered sleeves (refer to Section 5.5.3) prior to being transported to the mill
                floor.

       Important        It is recommended that each tapered sleeve be assigned to a given stand and
                        remain with that stand throughout the life of the sleeve. In addition if
                        multiple roll widths are used on a particular stand then a dedicated sleeve
                        should also be assigned to that stand and roll width. This ensures that the
                        contact between the sleeves and shaft taper is optimized.

                        The assembled rolls and sleeves must be clearly marked with the pass to be
                        used and the stand on which the roll assembly is to be mounted.

                5.5.2   Cleanliness

                Cleanliness is the highest priority when mounting the rolls on the roll shafts. If dirt is
                present on the roll, sleeve, and shaft assembly the wear process on the tapered sleeve and
                the roll pinion shaft is rapidly accelerated. As the taper on the shaft and sleeve wear the
                amount of contact between the two surfaces decreases, eventually decreasing the amount
                of torque that can be transmitted and increasing the likelihood of roll slippage or
                breakage. To achieve the best results clean the pinion shaft tapers every time a roll is
                changed. This should be done using Scotch-Brite or Crocus Cloth. Any oil residue
                should be removed by using non- petroleum based cleaning fluid. Clean, lint- free type
                cleaning cloths should be used.

       Important:       Always use a new cloth to help prevent the shaft tapers from damage by
                        debris and particles in cloth acting as an abrasive.

                If a roll is removed and then remounted on the mill without going to the roll shop, then
                the bore of the roll and the tapered sleeve should be cleaned before they are reassembled.
                The pinion shaft taper must also be cleaned as well as both faces of the roll as it is
                important that the roll contacts the flinger or the spacers, squarely. If dirt gets between
                the flinger and roll face (or spacer) this may damage the roll neck seals as well as cause
                axial misalignment.

                5.5.3   Using Spacers

                Carbide rolls can have between 1 and 4 grooves cut in the barrel depending on the width
                of the groove and the width of the roll.

                When using the outside grooves on a multi-groove roll, a spacer must be mounted
                between the roll face and flinger to maintain a constant pass line. When placing the roll
                assembly onto the roll shaft ensure that the spacer is squarely positioned between the
                flinger and drive side roll face. When using the inside grooves on a multi-groove roll the
                spacer must be mounted on the work side of the roll face.

       5.6      Roll Inspection

                5.6.1    Handling Rolls

                Take reasonable care to avoid damage to the rolls. Do not hammer the carbide surface.
                Nicks or chips can cause failure. Transport rolls in compartmented wooden boxes.
                Ensure each roll has an individual identifying number as well as a pass number as shown
                in the detail drawing.

                5.6.2    Pass Finish

                There is often a tendency to machine carbide to produce a mirror-finish on the pass. To
                ensure positive gripping of the rod, a finish of 0.4 to 0.8 micrometer in the pass is
                specified. A finish in of less than of 0.2 micron could result in slippage in certain stands.

                5.6.3   Pass Wear

                Some of the factors that influence pass wear are: grade of carbide, stock temperature, mill
                speed, cooling water analysis, and pressure and rolling practice. In general, the softer
                grades of carbide resist breakage well but have poorer wear rates than the harder grades.
                Grade selection is a compromise between hardness for good wear and softness for low
                breakage.

                Higher stock temperatures lead to more rapid pass wear through heat checking. Stock
                temperature is influenced by mill speed and operating practices. Maintain water pressure
                near 80 psi (5.62kg/cm sq) to minimize heat accumulation in the roll.

                Suspended solids in the water, particularly sand, can erode the pass. A well maintained
                filtration system will minimize this wear. There is some evidence that acidic water
                attacks the matrix of the carbide and increases pass wear. Treatment of the water to
                improve its quality may reduce this type of chemical erosion. Several factors in
                operating practice influence pass wear. Carefully match roll diameters to plus or minus
                0.05 mm for each pair of rolls: and match the diameters of pairs of rolls in one line to
                within 1.5 mm to minimize pull and eliminate push between stands. Too large a section
                entering the No-twist Mill can cause flutter of the section between the stands, as well as
                an excessive roll breakage. To prevent these problems, carefully control the shape of the
                incoming section to the No-twist Mill and hold close to the diameter called for on the
                Diagram of Rolling Schedule.

                Wear rates generally fall within the range from 36 to 82 metric tons per 0.03 mm on roll
                diameter, per groove, with the lower values in the early stands, and also in the leaders and
                finishing stand due to more frequent roll changing from the surface considerations.

                5.6.4   Roll grinding

                The number of tons rolled before redressing varies from stand to stand and from mill to
                mill. A typical range is from 907 to 2733 metric tons, although the leader and finisher
                may need to be changed every 635 to 726 metric tons.

                The pass surface and outside diameter of the rolls are diamond or electrolytically ground
                on special machines so that a pair of rolls is matched dimensionally to within plus or
                minus 0.05 mm. Both plunge grinding and profile grinding techniques are used to obtain
                pass shape. The outside diameters are generally ground separately on cylindrical
                grinders. After grinding the pass to just remove all visual signs of wear, grind off an
                additional allowance (0.25 mm to 0.75mm on the diameter) to ensure that all oxidized
                material and thermal micro-cracks have been eliminated. Initial determination of pass
                wear and checking of final pass configurations are accomplished through the use of an
                optical comparator and/or steel templates.

                On multiple pass rolls, grind the passes together or separately, as needed. If grinding the
                passes together, cover the initially unused pass or passes with a protective coating to
                prevent corrosion while the first pass is being used. One such protective coating is Rust
                Veto A2.

                5.6.5   Tapered Sleeve

                The major cause of roll breakage is lack of support of the carbide roll ring. Its strength in
                compression during rolling is dependent on it being sufficiently supported by its
                supporting tapered sleeve. To minimize premature roll breakage and maximize sleeve
                life it is critically important good surface contact between shaft, sleeve, and roll is
                maintained. To help achieve this, cleanliness in assembly of these parts is essential.
                Clean the parts prior to assembly using dry cleaning agents such as acetone or white
                spirit. Avoid kerosene and petroleum based solvents as they may leave an oil residue on
                the part surfaces acting as a lubricant and causing slippage between sleeve and shaft or
                sleeve and roll. Check the edges of the tapered sleeves for burrs or damage that may
                prevent a good surface contact. Carry out a visual inspection of the parts before every
                mill build.

                5.6.6   Roll Shop Records

                Etch a shop identification number onto the outer face of each roll. Keep a corresponding
                file card with pertinent data such as: date removed from mill, tonnage rolled, amount
                removed in grinding and diameter after grinding. Wear rates can easily be calculated
                from this data and are usually expressed in metric tons per 0.03 mm removed in dressing
                (on diameter).

                Also maintain roll breakage records. This information is important in the selection of roll
                materials and manufacturers, and in assessing the performance of the mill. Analysis of
                roll breakage records will pinpoint trouble areas.

                Include the following information in roll breakage records: strand, stand, shaft (upper
                and lower) pass configuration, type of break (radial, circumferential, piece broken out,
                exploded, etc.), and any special circumstance that might have contributed to the break
                (cobble, cold front end, loss of cooling water, etc.). If a radial crack has occurred, the
                location of the crack is significant in any analysis; therefore make a sketch of each
                broken roll for reference purposes.

                5.6.7   Factors Contributing to Premature Failure

                To minimize roll breakage the surface of the roll bore and the shaft taper must be kept in
                good condition.

                The following are other possible causes of roll breakage: A simple cause is plugged
                water spray nozzles. Thermal failure can also occur when the rolls became hot because
                the water was not on, or the hot steel of a cobble packed around a roll. Following a
                cobble the carbide will shatter if the rolls have not cooled sufficiently when the water is
                put on.

                A cold piece of steel left in the troughs before the No-twist Mill will break the rolls,
                usually several rolls on the first stands, upon entering the No-twist Mill. The rolls will
                fracture in many places.

                 Examination by roll manufacturers reveals most roll failures on record have been radial
                 breaks. These breaks are tension fatigue failures starting at either corner of the roll bore
                 and progress across the cross section of the roll. The principal source of the tension
                 stress is the separating force. This large load bends the roll locally, creating tension

                 by the tapered sleeve and shaft. The two major items that contribute to poor joint
                 conditions are fretting corrosion and faulty roll shaft tapers.

       5.7       Roll Housings

       A large part of the total No-twist Mill maintenance time is expended on roll housings.
       Periodically replacing the roll shaft seals, Clevite bearings and ball thrust bearings helps to
       eliminate more extensive repairs.

       Warning:          Mill equipment is capable of inflicting severe and fatal injuries. Electrical
                         voltages in both the power and the control circuits can cause fatal shocks.
                         Use extreme care and observe all safety precautions.

       Because of their proximity to the product, roll housings are the most vulnerable part of the mill.
       There are two methods of maintenance used for the prevention of roll housing breakdown.

       •     Periodic inspection of roll housings in the Maintenance Shop.

       •     Taking weekly, in-the-mill lift tests, and recording the results for every roll shaft in the mill
             will determine if the ball thrust bearings are deteriorating. The lift test also determines if the
             deterioration warrants removal of the housing for rebuilding.

                 5.7.1   Shaft Seals

                 Roll cooling water is one source of lube oil contamination. A defective roll shaft seal
                 will allow roll cooling water, carrying scale and grime, into the lube oil system.

                 Regularly inspect for signs of water in the lube oil system. If other equipment is served
                 by the same oil system, it is also a possible source of the water, but usually the roll shaft
                 seals are at fault. To help in detecting faulty seals, each stand should have a water leg
                 glass in the lube oil return line. If there is any sign of water in one of these glasses,
                 replace the seals of that stand.

                 Common practice at several other mills is to have all roll shaft seals replaced after a
                 certain length of time in the mill. At one mill in particular, the time interval is every
                 three months. Such practices demonstrate the importance attached to keeping cooling
                 water out of the oil system.

                5.7.4   Examining Used Clevite Bearings for Evidence of Misalignment

                Some Clevite seizures occur shortly after the roll housing goes into the mill. When this
                happens, review the housing rebuilding methods. Both the work side and drive side
                bearing journals are tapered to accommodate the misalignment from the overhung load
                which tips the roll shaft through the oil film clearances and from the elastic bending of
                the rather long, heavily loaded shaft. The taper compensates for both causes of
                misalignment to create a more uniform oil film thickness.

                The roll shafts are all of the same design. The work side journal taper is selected where
                the oil film is the thinnest to align the shaft and bearings.

                The test for misalignment is made by measuring the bearing wear pattern. A new bearing
                is of uniform thickness. To check the wear pattern, measure the variation in the bearing
                thickness along axial lines. Place the bearing on a surface plate and move the probe of an
                electronic measuring instrument along the axial lines. The probe is mounted on a height
                gage which slides easily on the surface plate.

                5.7.5   Rolling Housing Periodic Inspection

                To prevent roll-housing breakdown by use of this maintenance method, remove the roll
                housings after 100 turns of operation, and disassemble for inspection in the Maintenance
                Shop. Inspect all components of the roll housings. Pay particular attention to the Clevite
                bearings. The greatest threat to roll housing breakdown is seizure of the work side
                Clevite bearings. As mentioned before, the cause of Clevite deterioration is invariably

                5.7.7   Axial Roll Shaft Lift Test

                The purpose of this test is to measure and record roll shaft end play. Excessive roll shaft
                end play may cause a shoulder on the rod, or failure of the roll shaft ball thrust bearing.
                In the past the fastest stand in any mill has been the most frequently prone to wear.

                Wear on the rear eccentric locking bar, and improper mounting of the thrust bearing are
                the two major sources of end play. This section provides some tips on assembling the
                locking bar and roll shaft thrust bearings.

                The locking bar fits into a slot on the rear eccentric bearing cartridge and is bolted to the
                roll housing rear plate. The locking bar is made slightly undersized and surface ground
                to give 0.013 mm clearance at assembly. To minimize surface conditions that could lead
                to premature wear, surface grind the locking bars rather than filing them when they are
                fitted. Be sure the eccentric slots have a good finish. Stone the corners.

                Proper adherence to these procedures will minimize end play caused by wear on the
                locking bar.

                5.7.12 Roll Shaft Taper

                The very stiff carbide rolls (three times as stiff as steel rolls) must have full backing.
                When wear in the joints under the roll causes gaps in this support, the separating force
                can create high tension stress in the roll bore. This is an on-off stress. Because the roll is
                stiff, small amounts of wear can result in a serious loss of support. An important source
                of steady hoop tension in the roll is the driving home of the tapered sleeve. If wear or
                taper fault gives a "poor" joint condition, this stress can also be quite high. Make a
                contact check to decide when a roll assembly needs attention.

                1. Coat the roll shaft taper and the bore of the roll with a very thin layer of an orange-
                   brown marking compound.

                2. Coat the tapered sleeve, inside tapered diameter with a very thin layer of Prussian
                   blue dye.

                3. Assemble the parts. Use the hydraulic roll mounting tool to install the sleeve and roll
                   on the roll shaft. Wrench tightening of the locking screw will not create enough axial
                   force to reveal the contact pattern.

                4. When the parts are disassembled using the hydraulic roll removal tool, the exact
                   nature of the joint contact is revealed by the transfer of the blue to the orange-brown
                   gear compound. If the layer of gear compound just touches the layer of bluing, the
                   surfaces are about 0.010 mm apart.

       Note:            It is necessary to use very thin layers of compound and bluing for the above
                        statement to be true, and to accurately show the existing contact.

                5. Make a record of the contact by putting transparent tape (Scotch or equivalent) on the
                   orange-brown surface (i.e., on the shaft taper and in the roll bore). Remove the tape
                   and stick it on white cardboard, to obtain an exact contact picture. The tape picks up
                   the bluing and gear compound from the metal surface.

                6. To check the shafts in the mill, put the gear compound on the shaft taper and coat the
                   inside of the tapered diameter of a perfect tapered sleeve with Prussian blue dye.
                   Check a new solid carbide roll and use it.

                1. Check Clevite bearing lift clearances each time a housing is removed from the No-

       with or without optical equipment. After the check is made, shimming changes can be made to
       the bevel gear housing, if necessary. Morgan provides optical kits for setting the pass alignment.

                5.8.1   Optical Pass Alignment

                1. Remove rolls and guide (not brackets) from all three stands. Remove the delivery
                   guide bracket from the stand where the telescope will be mounted.

                2. Fit the adjusting bracket on the stand that is to carry the telescope, using the delivery
                   guide bracket mounting holes. Remove the rolls and place the telescope support
                   block between the sleeves. A similar block is used on the other stands. Make sure
                   the face of the block is clean. Push the block back against the flinger and retainer
                   then close the rolls until the block is gripped. Slide the nose of the telescope through
                   the adjusting bracket and into the support block. Set both perpendicular viewing axes
                   at 45°, in line with the mill roll shafts. Close the three adjusting bracket screws until
                   they grip the telescope lightly.

                3. On the other two stands, insert target blocks 1 and 2 between the sleeves, pressing
                   them firmly against the flingers after checking cleanliness of the mating faces. Screw
                   down and grip the blocks lightly. In target support block 1, fit an aluminum target in
                   the counter-bores provided.

                4. Using the focusing adjustment, sight the telescope on target 1. Check that the
                   micrometer screws on the barrel are both set to zero. Adjust the screws on the
                   adjusting bracket until the cross hairs on the telescope coincide with the center of the
                   target. This is the datum line, which is a straight line through the pass lines of the
                   housings carrying the telescope and target 1.

                5. Remove target from block 1 and place in block 2. Refocus the telescope to pick up
                   target 2.

                6. The center of target 2 will probably not coincide with the telescope's line of sight.
                   Adjust the micrometer adjusting screws on the telescope to align the cross hairs with
                   the target. Each screw causes a shift in one plane. The value shown on the adjusting
                   screw is the amount of shift that was required to return the cross hairs back to the
                   target center.

                7. Refer to Morgan pass alignment drawing. The intersection of the X and Y axes,
                   shown as Point A, represents the datum line established between the telescope and
                   target 1 while point B on the right is the pass line of the new stand on target 2. In the
                   example shown, a movement of 0.087 mm was required in the Y-axis and 0.069 mm
                   in the X-axis. The misalignment between the two original stands and the newly
                   installed one is the straight-line distance between Point A and B.

                8. The maximum permissible misalignment for the entire mill is 0.775 mm diameter
                   tolerance circle. For only three stands the recommended tolerance is 0.525 mm. If
                   the misalignment exceeds this value, re-shim the housing accordingly.

                9. To check the pass alignment right through the mill, place a 0.18 mm shim behind all
                   target blocks and the telescope nose support block. This puts the telescope and
                   targets on the operating position of the pass line.

       5.9      Bevel Gear Drive Housing

       Each bevel gear housing carries a segment of lineshaft that is supported by rolling element
       bearings, as is the driven bevel shaft, which is driven by the lineshaft through a pair of precision
       spiral bevel gears. The ratio of the spiral bevels is designed to give the correct speed relationship
       between stands, based on the rolling schedule. In addition to the bevel gear, the driven bevel
       shaft also carries a helical pinion, which meshes with a similar pinion carried on an idler shaft.
       These two pinions form the drive for the roll shafts.

       The line-shaft segments of the odd-numbered stands are coupled in tandem and the drive end
       line-shaft is coupled to one of the output shafts of the mill drive assembly through a shaft
       coupling. Similarly, the drive end of the line-shaft segments, even-numbered stands, are coupled
       directly to the other output shaft of the mill drive assembly.

       Note:           Some illustrations in this Section show the lineshafts from housings 1-6 and
                       9-10. The lineshafts from housings 7 & 8 are similar to 1-6, with only slight
                       differences in the size of the bevel gears. Always refer to the Morgan
                       drawings for the most accurate representation of the part in question.

       5.10     Lube Oil Piping Arrangement

       The gears and bearings of each bevel gear drive are pressure lubricated from the No-Twist Mill
       lube oil system. Lube oil enters each housing by way of a piping system with a flange connection
       bolted to the housing. A short piping passage connected to a long cross passage forms a header.
       This header directs lube oil to the bevel gear spray nozzles, the line-shaft bearings and couplings,
       the idler shaft bearings and the bevel gear shaft bearings.

       5.11     Drive Housing Safety Procedures

       Warning:        Before attempting any maintenance task on No-twist Mill components, close
                       the Snap Shear immediately before the appropriate stand to prevent
                       accidental entry of rod into the No-twist Mill. De-energize all drive motors
                       and comply with all company procedures relating to safety.

       Warning:        This equipment is capable of inflicting severe and fatal injuries. Electrical

       5.21     Cleaning, Inspection, and Refurbishment

       After completely disassembling the drive housing, thoroughly clean the inside of the drive box
       and protect until reassembly. Discard any gaskets, thrust washers or seals removed during
       disassembly and replace with new spare parts at reassembly. Inspect teeth of gears and pinions
       for excessive wear or damage

       The following is a list of cleaning and inspection actions to perform whenever dismantling
       equipment for repairs:

       1. Cleaning: Clean all parts with a suitable solvent (mineral spirits, SAVASOL No. 5, or
          equivalent) to remove scale, grease, grime, or dirt. Use lint-free rags; do not use cotton
          waste. Air dry after cleaning.

       Warning:         Petroleum based solvents are flammable and their vapors are harmful.

       Warning:         Blowing out the lube oil passages with compressed air can be dangerous.
                        Use caution when using compressed air.

           To clean roller bearings, soak in clean solvent long enough to loosen any sludge, then gently
           slosh each bearing around near the top of the container to dislodge all pockets of grease.
           Scrub away stubborn accumulations with a small brush that has bristles that do not break off.
           Do not spin dirt y bearings, but rotate races slowly while washing and scrubbing.

           Rinse the bearings in clean solvent and air dry. Hold both races when blowing with clean, dry
           compressed air. Do not allow the air jet to spin the bearing; instead, turn each race by hand to
           expose all surfaces to the drying air. If the bearing is to be stored for later reuse, wrap it in wax
           paper or other grease-proof wrapping.

       Caution:         A bearing may be defective without the defect being visually evident. Good
                        maintenance practices dictate replacing any bearing removed during any
                        maintenance task with new bearing at re-assembly.

       2. Housekeeping: To the extent possible, keep all service areas clean. Do not allow oil,
          grease, water or dirt to accumulate on floors and/or around units undergoing repair, not only
          for the reasons stated above, but also for personnel safety.

       3. Bearing and Sealing Surfaces: Inspect bearing and sealing surfaces closely for signs of
          wear, nicks, scratches, gouges and build-up of scale or other foreign substances. Remove
          light scratches, gouges and scale by polish grinding the surfaces as long as design tolerances
          are not exceeded.

                5.21.1 Bearing Inspection

                Worn bearings can be checked by measuring the amount of movement of the uncoupled
                shaft while the shaft is still installed in the housing. The appearance of bright spots on
                the bearing will indicate high spots or a hard bearing area of the local surface. Lightly
                scrape and polish the bearing and then check contact area.

                Fatigue cracks and metal particles removed from the bearing are attributed to vibration

                Scoring is the result of dirt or metal particles in the oil or scratches on the shaft that affect
                the bearing contact area. Examine bearings for burrs or blemishes. Check the oil

                5.21.2 Gear Housings and Shaft Assemblies Inspection and Refurbishment

                Inspect the sealing and bearing surfaces of the shaft and spacers for signs of nicks,
                scratches, or other defects. Polish grind slight scratches to provide a suitable surface.
                Replace shafts that have deep scratches or nicks in these areas.

                Check shafts and pins for straightness with v-blocks and dial indicator. Replace shaft
                assemblies if necessary.

                Mount the shaft on the “DEAD” centers in a lathe. Using a dial indicator, zero to bearing
                diameters and check the axial and radial runout of the gear. Ensure the gear runs true to
                the total runout etched on the gear datum surface. See the gear drawings for the special
                tolerance for each stand.

       Note:            If runout is excessive, check the mounting for burrs, or foreign matter
                        between the mating surfaces. If necessary, remove the gear, clean the
                        mating surfaces, and ensure the shaft gear seat is running true.

                If gears were removed and after obtaining a satisfactory runout value, run a drill through
                one of the three holes in the head of each cap screw and into the bevel gear shaft flange.
                Install the lock pins in the cap screws. Ream the dowel holes and fit dowels, peen lock
                pins and dowel pins in place.

                Inspect Bearing Cartridge bores. Remove any burrs or light scratches using a fine grit
                crocus cloth. Wash out cartridges and clean out lube oil holes. If cartridges are
                damaged, replace them with new spares.

       Caution:         Do not use an emery wheel to remove burrs or scratches in bores.

       Note:            It is too easy to remove surface stock with an emery, or grinding wheel.
                        Check the alignment of the bearing cartridge bores using Vee blocks and
                        indicators. Cover all subassemblies with plastic or other grease resistant
                        material while awaiting reassembly.

                2. Internal Lube Oil Piping: Handle piping, fittings and hoses that supplies lube oil to
                   bearings and gears with extreme care to prevent damage. Replace any damaged
                   tubing with stainless steel tubing of the same wall thickness and length and form it to
                   the same exacting standards as the original. An incorrect material could possibly be a
                   source of blocked orifices through the release of scale.

                   passages with compressed air. Clean all internal passages to loosen scale, oxides or
                   other contaminants that could impede or block passage of oil flow. After cleaning,

                5.21.4 Gear Inspection

                1. Inspect teeth of gears and pinions for excessive wear or damage. Hand stone any
                   minor damage to gear teeth, such as burr or bruise, carefully removing just enough
                   material to correct the damage without reducing the contact area of the teeth.

                2. Inspect gear teeth for wear or damage. If gears were nicked or burred during
                   disassembly, remove by hand stoning. Do not remove material from tooth flanks
                   which would change the shape of the tooth.
                3. Check contact patterns are centered on the face of the gear. A contact pattern that is
                   off to one side may indicate improper tolerances or excessive load on the output
                   shaft. Heavy load on the output shaft also could occur due to lube deficiencies
                   (Quantity and Quality).

                Gear Inspection Conditions:

                1. Destructive pitting occurs due to overload and poor lubrication. Large pits in the
                   tooth face will reduce the contact area and eventually destroy the gear tooth.

                2. Scoring produces vertical scratches and grooves from the pitch line to the tooth tip,
                   Scoring results from insufficient lubrication and loading. Check the quality and
                   condition of the oil as well as the spray flow to the gear.

       5.22     Reassembly Procedures

                5.22.1 Summary of Recommended Assembly Sequence:

                The following is a general overview of steps and procedures that should be done for
                installing bevel gear assembly and components.

                1. Thoroughly clean all components and housing.

                2. Install components to bevel gear shaft assembly.

                3. Install bevel gear shaft assembly into housing.

                4. Install components onto line shaft assembly.

                5. Install line shaft assembly into housing.

                6. Set mounting distances.

                7. Check gear backlash.

                8. Check gear tooth contacts.

                9. Install components to Idler shaft assembly.

                10. Install Idler shaft assembly into housing.

                11. Check clearances.

                12. Install remaining components to housing assembly.

                13. Install gear drive assembly back into the mill.

                5.22.6 Checks and Measurements for Bevel Gear Meshing

       Caution:         The procedures outlined in this Section are of critical importance. Poor
                        gear contacts due to improperly positioned bevel gears can result in broken
                        teeth. Contacts that are hard on the ends of the teeth create high stresses
                        which, in turn, cause fatigue cracks.

                    Check the mounting distance of the driven shaft. Figure 34 shows Line Shaft and
                    Bevel Gear set up similar to Stands 1-6.

                1. Using an outside micrometer, determine the exact line-shaft diameter at a point
                   opposite the exposed flat face of the driven bevel gear. (Dimension "A" on Figure
                   34).

                2. Using a planer gage, determine the exact distance between the flat face of the driven
                   bevel and outside of the line-shaft. (Dimension "B" on Figure 34).

                3. Calculate the distance between the centerline of the shaft and the face of the driven
                   bevel by adding one-half of dimension “A” obtained in step 5.23.3 a to dimension
                   “B” from step 5.23.3 b.

                4. Compare the calculated value to the mounting dimension etched on the face of the
                   driven bevel. If the dimension etched on the gear is greater than the measured
                   dimension, move the driven bevel away from the line-shaft by shimming.
                   Conversely, if the dimension etched on the gear is less than the measured dimension,
                   move the driven bevel toward the Line Shaft. If necessary, increase or decrease the
                   thickness of the shim pack installed at the smaller roller bearing end of the driven
                   bevel gear shaft to accomplish this.

                    Retighten the retainer bolts to specified torque values and recheck the mounting
                    distance.

       5.23     Mill Drive Assembly

       Refer to Figure 41 and Figure 42 for guidance.

       The mill drive assembly contains three horizontally parallel gear shafts, with the two output
       (driven) gear shafts meshed with the center bevel gear set bearing on the output side. The gears
       and bearings are pressure lubricated from the Vee mill lube oil system.

       The drive is coupled directly to the main drive motor by a right angle bevel gear input shaft. The
       input is transmitted by a non-integral gear, directly to the two driven shafts thru a bevel and
       helical pinions integral with the output shafts.

       The output shaft for the odd numbered stands is coupled to one end of a floating shaft by a rigid-
       flexible, single gear coupling. The opposite end of the floating shaft couples to the line-shaft of
       the first stand by a similar coupling. The output shaft for the even numbered stands is coupled
       directly to the line-shaft of the first stand via a 2-gear flexible coupling.

       Caution:         Consider disassembly/reassembly of this equipment potentially hazardous at
                        all times. Refer to the Safety and General maintenance Sections of this
                        manual for safety recommendations.

                5.23.4    Cleaning and Inspection

                Using a suitable solvent, thoroughly clean all parts, then air dry. Remove all pipe plugs;
                pressure flush all internal oil passages; blow out with compressed air and reinstall plugs.

                wear or damage. Replace all worn or damaged parts. Inspect gaskets; replace gaskets
                that are damaged or have set in a way that impairs their sealing effectiveness.
                Thoroughly clean the mating flanges of the housing and cover, removing all traces of old
                sealing compound.

                tolerances as a temporary measure. Replace all other worn or damaged parts with
                new spares. Check runout, bearing journals, T.I.R., etc. for all shafts. Refer to shaft
                detail drawings for design tolerances. Clean all shims and be sure they are free of
                all burrs; hand stone or file, if necessary.

       Important:                Always read the safety instructions and warnings for each system and
                                 component prior to operating and maintaining this machinery. Follow all
                                 safety precautions to avoid personal injury or property damage during
                                 system operation. Refer to this section and the Safety Sections of each
                                 component manual for general safety steps and procedures. Read all
                                 instructions, warnings, and cautions carefully.

       Important:                Only trained personnel should operate and maintain mill equipment and
                                 tools including rigging and lifting procedures. Do not work on equipment
                                 on which you have not been trained!

       Important:                All safety devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to assure
                                 the safety of the operators.

       Important:                Always wear personal protection equipment. Always wear proper safety
                                 gear when in the mill. Minimum Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
                                 should include safety hat, boots and gloves as well as eye and ear protection.
                                 Wear proper protective gear when operating and maintaining mill
                                 equipment.

       Caution:                  Equipment throughout the mill produces excessive noise. Always wear
                                 hearing protection.

       Warning:                  Consider all equipment as potentially hazardous at all times. It is capable of
                                 crushing any body part caught in it.

       Caution:                  Working with high pressure components (i.e. hoses and cylinders) may be
                                 dangerous if equipment is misused. Never use faulty equipment.

       Danger:                   Electrical voltages in both power and control circuits are capable of
                                 rendering severe and fatal shocks.

       Warning:                  Hot product traveling throughout the mill can raise the temperature of all
                                 equipment surfaces. Consider all surfaces throughout the mill to be hot!

       Warning:                  Beware of pinch points. Block and restrain rotating parts before removal
                                 and mounting equipment.

       Warning:                  Do not exceed equipment ratings. Never attempt to press on or lift a load

       Caution:                  Working with high pressure may be dangerous if equipment is misused.
                                 Never set the relief valve to a higher pressure than the maximum rated
                                 pressure of the pump. Higher settings may result in equipment damage
                                 and/or personal injury.

       Warning:                  The system operating pressure must not exceed the pressure rating of the
                                 lowest rated component in the system. Check pressure gauges in the system
                                 to monitor operating pressure.

       Caution:                  Avoid damaging connected hoses. Avoid sharp bends and kinks when
                                 routing hoses. Using a bent or kinked hose will cause severe back-pressure.
                                 Sharp bends and kinks will internally damage the hose leading to premature
                                 hose failure.

                                 Do not drop heavy objects on hoses. A sharp impact may cause internal
                                 damage to hose wire strands. Applying pressure to a damaged hose may
                                 cause it to rupture. DO NOT lift or pull equipment by hoses or couplers.
                                 Rig and secure equipment for safe transport.

       Caution:                  Keep hydraulic equipment away from flames and heat. Excessive heat will
                                 soften packing and seals, resulting in fluid leaks. Heat also weakens hose
                                 materials and packing. For optimum performance do not expose equipment
                                 to temperatures of 65°C [150°F] or higher. Protect all hoses and cylinders
                                 from weld spatter and extreme heat.

       Danger:                   Do not handle pressurized hoses. Escaping oil under pressure can penetrate
                                 the skin, causing serious injury. If oil is injected under the skin, see a doctor
                                 immediately.

       Warning:                  Only use hydraulic cylinders in a coupled system. Never use a cylinder with
                                 unconnected couplers. If the cylinder becomes extremely overloaded,
                                 components can fail catastrophically causing severe personal injury. Never
                                 bleed system to exposed atmosphere.

       Warning:                  Immediately replace worn, or damaged parts.

       Important:                Only qualified and trained technicians are allowed to service mill
                                 equipment.

       Warning:                  Do not use electric pumps in an explosive atmosphere. Adhere to all local
                                 and national electrical codes. Start the pump with the valve in the neutral
                                 position to prevent accidental cylinder operation. Keep hands clear of

       3.1          Safety Procedures

       Important:                All safety devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to assure
                                 the safety of the operators.

       Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices
       make the elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the
       process and/or product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be
       constrained to follow a prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble.
       Cobbles occur at random times and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is
       unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed
       path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment, and stock temperature are also causes of
       cobbling anywhere along the length of a bar in process in the rolling train. The following
       recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe manner.

       3.2          Visibility and Communications

       Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations of
       pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment controlled from
       that point.

       Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight confirmation.

       Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper lighting can be
       used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or cloud the reflective surface and
       that the mirror location does not make it liable to breakage.

       3.3          Audible Communications

       Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as substitutes only
       when visual contact is not possible.

       3.4          Safety Stops

       Guide adjustments may be made only when the Mill Line is shut down. Mechanical or
       electrically operated stops must be used to block any stock from inadvertently entering into the
       mill.

       Ensure mill is shut down and material can not run through the stand. Ensure that stops remain in
       place as long as personnel making adjustments are in the hazard area.

       3.5          Alarms

       The alarms as described in the control specifications will have a warning system to alert the
       operators of new oncoming front ends.

       A prominently located light board should be used with the warning system to indicate the strand
       in use and the progress of the stock in the mill.

       3.6          Restart of Mill

       When a service operation is completed, the Mill must be restarted in the following sequence:
       1. All mechanical stops will be moved.
       2. All Guards will be in place.
       3. All personnel will clear the hazardous area.
       4. Permissive switches will be placed in “ALLOW RESTART” position and all interlocks
          engaged.
       5. Operators at control stations will be notified that the Mill Line may be restarted.

       Operators must not restart the mill until they are completely satisfied that restarting will not
       present hazards to personnel. An audible signal will be given by the operator to indicate that
       restart is imminent.

4.0    OPERATION

       Important:                Always read all safety instructions and warnings for each system and
                                 component prior to operating and working on machinery. Refer to Safety
                                 Section for general safety steps and procedures.

       4.1          Introduction

       The purpose of the Snap Shears, located at the entry to Reducing Sizing Mill (RSM) stands 27
       through 30 are to close the rod travel path and sever the rod. The Snap Shears are used as safety
       devices to prevent stock from entering the RSM when interlock safety systems are activated (i.e.
       Safety Guards Open). They also protect the downstream mechanical mill equipment in the event
       of low lubrication, cooling water malfunction, and electrical power loss. The Snap Shears must
       also be closed when performing any maintenance on the downstream mill machinery.

       The Snap Shears are also used as an emergency cutting shear when a cobble occurs in the RSM or
       beyond. This prevents excess material from entering the RSM when rod travel has slowed down
       or stopped downstream. The Snap Shears are designed for manual and automatic operation,
       operating stations (Main Pulpit and Local) help test, monitor and adjust conditions that may occur
       through the automated system. Refer to Table 1for a description of electrical equipment used in
       the Snap Shear Assemblies.

              Table 1 – Description of Electrical Equipment
         DESCRIPTION                                                          DESIGNATOR

         Cut Solenoid Valve                                                   -      3SS/EV1
         Shear Opened Proximity Switch                                        -      3SS/PLS1
         Shear Closed Proximity Switch                                        -      3SS/PLS2
         Shear Open Signal Lantern                                            -      3SS/VIS2
         Shear Closed Signal Lantern                                          -      3SS/VIS1
         RSM Reducing Low-Low Lube Oil Pressure Switch                        -      RSM/PS9
         RSM Sizing Low-Low Lube Oil Pressure Switch                          -      RSM/PS10
         Low Mill Cooling Water Pressure Switch                               -      RSM/PS1-2
         Local Floor Station Near Snap Shear                                  -      OS18
         Main Mill Pulpit                                                     -      CP2


       The Snap Shear can accommodate various feed size diameter stock. Knife deflectors, guide
       inserts and guide shoes are interchangeable for the applicable rod size. See Morgan reference
       drawings for appropriate guide information.

       4.2          Components

                    4.2.1. Snap Shear Assembly Operation

                    The Snap Shear single solenoid valve controls the Snap Shear. The Shear Opened and
                    Shear Closed proximity switches indicate the open and closed positions. The valve is
                    energized to open the knives (air actuating cylinder) from the rod travel path and de-
                    energized to close and cut the rod (spring loaded return in the cylinder). The air cylinder
                    rotates the knives into the vertical position with sufficient force to bite into the traveling
                    rod. The rod then pulls the knives to the final closed position, against the stops, and the
                    knife blades severs the rod.

                    •         The following conditions cause an immediate closing of the snap shear:

                              1. Operation of a SNAP SHEAR CLOSE button.

                    •         Conversely, once the snap shear is closed, the following conditions will prevent the
                              opening of the snap shear :

                              1. Loss of power on the RSM mill drive.

                              2. Fault in the mill lubrication system.

                              3. Fault in the roller entry guide lube system of the RSM.

                              4. RSM cobble guard door not closed.

                              5. Low pressure in the RSM mill roll cooling water.

                              6. Pinch Roll safety guard not closed.

                              7. Laying Head safety guard not closed.

                    Time delay closing of the Snap Shear:

                    •      Snap shear must not close before the scrap cut has been made; otherwise a cobble
                           will occur in the C&D shear if the RSM is dummied.

                    •      Time delay starts when the C&D shear knives are at the zero, cut position.

                    •      Time delay can be adjusted in the program; initially set for 1 second.

                    For better accuracy, the timer function is speed compensated.

                    It can be set very short if it is desired to minimize the amount of tail end left in the NTM.

                    Alternately, the time delay can be set long enough so that the tail end passes the NTM
                    before it closes.

                    As an aid to setting the timer, the reaction time of the snap shear can be measured by
                    checking the time from de-energization of the Snap Shear solenoid valve until the Shear
                    Position Ind Closed proximity switch indicates the shear has closed.

                    •      A backup timer starts when the C&D shear is signaled to make a scrap cut. The
                           timer is set long enough, 2 or 3 seconds, to close the snap shear in the event the C&D
                           shear fails to operate.

                    •      Any of the following conditions cause the snap shear to close a time delay after the
                           C&D shear scrap cutting function has been initiated and the C&D shear has made a
                           divide cut.

                            1.          Automatic initiation of the "scrap cut" function.

                            2.          Low-Low Lube lube pressure in the mill lube system.

                            3.          Low Mill Cooling Water pressure.

                            4.          Stelmor® conveyor stopped while rod is detected at the HMD before the C &
                                        D shear.

                                        For this situation, C&D shear scrap cutting function is initiated, but the snap
                                        shear does not close.

                                        Ignore temporary stoppage when TAIL END STOP feature of Stelmor® is
                                        active.

                           6.           Stopping of the laying head drive while rod is detected at the NTM exit.

                           7.           E-STOP of the mill lube system pumps.

                           8.           Indication that the RSM is about to be stopped due to maximum temperature
                                        fault or bearing lube flow fault in the RSM drive motor.

5.0    MONITORING

       5.1          Monitoring

       The Snap Shear is designed for manual and automatic operation, operating stations (Main Pulpit
       and Local) help test, monitor and adjust conditions that may occur through the automated system.

       Note:                     For efficient operation of the Snap Shear, operators are required to
                                 constantly monitor all components and control systems.

                    A.           Ensure the following elevated warning devices are working properly:

                                 •      Shear Open Signal and Shear Closed Signal lantern type lamps:

                                        Red = closed.
                                        Green = open.

                    B.           Monitor Main Control Pulpit. Refer to the following switch and indicators for
                                 proper operation:

                                 •      Snap shear CUT initiation and indication.

                                 •      Snap shear OPEN indication.

                    C.           Monitor Local Station. Refer to the following switch and indicators for proper
                                 operation of Snap Shear:

                                 •      CUT illuminated button.

                                 •      OPEN illuminated button.

                                        OPEN can be initiated only at this location.

                    D.           Ensure water is flowing through spray tube and cooling knife assembly.

                    E.           Make sure cylinder is actuating properly. Test without stock for complete knife
                                 travel/rotation. Adjust flow control valves if necessary, so that knife assembly
                                 opens and closes quickly and completely against stops.

                    F.           Check that knives close together with a maximum gap of 0.5 mm. Adjust and
                                 shim if necessary.

6.0    PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS

       6.1          Definition

       Preventive maintenance is routine maintenance that if performed as scheduled helps to keep the
       Snap Shear assembly in good operating condition. Its primary purpose is to reduce the incidence
       of operating failures, which require costly downtime for repairs. The recommended routine
       maintenance schedule below represents the anticipated minimum requirements for maintaining
       the Snap Shear. As you accumulate operating experience, it may be feasible to reduce the
       frequency of checks and inspections, however, do not reduce the lubrication frequency.

       Important:                Always isolate, shutoff, and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic, and
                                 electrical power supply sources before performing any repairs or
                                 maintenance. Read safety instructions and warnings for each system and
                                 component prior to working on machinery. Refer to the Safety sections in
                                 the beginning of your mill’s manual as well as in this manual chapter.

       6.2          Introduction

       Routine and Preventive Maintenance of the Snap Shear assembly is required to ensure extended
       and proper operation. Table 2 is provided as a reference guide for frequent periodic maintenance
       requirements for the Snap Shear assembly. Refer to the General Maintenance section and
       applicable manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance requirements and procedures for
       specific components. Refer to Morgan assembly drawings as a guide for additional information.

       Warning:                  Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or
                                 disconnect all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any
                                 stored energy from components. Restrain and secure any moving parts of a
                                 component or system that could cause injury.

       Warning:                  Exposed moving parts can cause severe injury. LOCK OUT and TAG OUT
                                 POWER before removing guards or performing maintenance. NEVER
                                 remove a guard, shield cover or other protective devices while the
                                 equipment is running!

       Warning:                  This equipment is potentially dangerous and capable of inflicting severe
                                 bodily injuries. Before starting any maintenance task, comply with all
                                 company policies relating to safety. Also, be thoroughly familiar with the
                                 general safety requirements.

       Warning:                  Always stop machinery before entering or adjusting the equipment. Know
                                 where all e-stop buttons are located before operating or performing
                                 maintenance on this equipment.

7.0    CORRECTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS

       7.1          Definition

       Corrective maintenance encompasses those repair procedures required to return the Snap Shear
       assembly to satisfactory operating condition. Such repairs do not necessarily return the
       equipment to like-new condition. Rather, the objective is to make it operational again as soon as
       possible. It is recommended to replace faulty parts/components and sub-assemblies with new or
       previously refurbished spare parts/components and sub-assemblies. Those parts removed may
       then be refurbished or reconditioned after the main equipment has been returned to service.

       Important:                Always isolate, shutoff, and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic, and
                                 electrical power supply sources before performing any repairs or
                                 maintenance. Read safety instructions and warnings for each system and
                                 component prior to working on machinery. Refer to Safety Section in this
                                 manual chapter.

       7.2          Introduction

       Corrective Maintenance of the Snap Shear assembly as defined above is intended to keep down
       time at a minimum by replacing components and then dismantling and overhauling the removed
       component in a service area away from the mill. Once refurbished, the component becomes a
       spare shelf part, ready to be utilized as a replacement when needed.

       No disassembly procedures are given herein of components being replaced. Components that
       require overhaul/refurbishment should be maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s
       instructions. Refer to the manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance and torque
       requirements and procedures of specific components of the Snap Shear Assembly.

       General guidelines and maintenance criteria are provided below when corrective maintenance of
       a component or sub-assembly is required. These are minimum guidelines and should be used in
       conjunction with the specific maintenance requirements from the component manufacturer.

       Upon re-assembly, tighten all bolts, screws, nuts and fasteners in accordance with Morgan
       reference drawings torque requirements. Torque specific components in accordance with the
       manufacturer’s requirements.

       Warning:                  Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or
                                 disconnect all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any
                                 stored energy from components. Restrain and secure any moving parts of a
                                 component or system that could cause injury. Make sure covers are secure
                                 with locking pin before performing any maintenance.

       Warning:                  The Snap Shear assembly is potentially dangerous and capable of inflicting
                                 severe bodily injuries. Before starting any maintenance task, comply with

       7.3          General Maintenance Criteria

       The following is a list of maintenance actions to perform whenever dismantling equipment for
       repairs.

       1. Electric controls and power cables: Before disconnecting any wiring that does not have plug-
          in connectors, make sure that color coding is clearly identifiable or tag each wire carefully for
          reference at re-assembly.

       2. Rigging parts for removal/replacement: Many parts that make up this equipment are much
          too heavy to be handled by one man. Provide adequate rigging for lifting and supporting
          heavy parts before attempting to dismantle any equipment.

       3. Cleaning: Clean all parts with a suitable solvent (mineral spirits, SAVASOL no.5, or
          equivalent) to remove all scale, grease, grime, or dirt. Use a clean wiper; do not use cotton
          waste. Air dry after cleaning.

       4. Bearings and Sealing Surfaces: Closely inspect bearings and sealing surfaces for signs of
          wear, nicks, scratches, gouges, or build-up of scale or other foreign substances. Replace
          bearings that show any signs of deterioration.

       5. Air Cylinder Seals: Replace (Mandatory Replacement) all seals, o-rings and gaskets that are
          removed or disturbed during disassembly procedure. Make sure seals and o-rings seat
          properly upon re-assembly.

       6. Pre-lubrication Prior to Re-assembly: Lightly lubricate all seals, bearings, bushings, and
          gears with oil before installation

       7. Aligning Parts During Re-assembly: Because of the weight of large parts, use guide studs
          during re-assembly to ensure proper bolt hole and /or dowel pin alignment as necessary.

       8. Clean all parts and inspect for scratches, cracks, burrs, flaking, pitting, scaling or
          discoloration of mating or load-bearing surfaces.

       9. Hand scrape any bushing that have not become out-or-round to remove burrs, small scratches
          or accumulated foreign substances. Replace any bushing showing gross deformation or
          cracking.

       10. Check shafts and pivot pins for straightness with v-blocks and dial indicator. It is possible to
           straighten bent shafts in a hydraulic press, but if spares are available, it is much better to
           replace the parts. Never straighten bent castings; replace them. Weld cracked steel castings
           only if no spares are available, but replace them whenever possible.

       7.4          Air Cylinder Assembly

                    7.4.1. Air Cylinder Removal

                    Refer to Figure 3 (below) for guidance.

                    1. De-energize the cylinder control valve solenoid circuit. Isolate and disconnect the air
                       supply. Release air pressure using the pressure relief on directional control valve.
                       Bleed both ends (flow control) of the cylinder. Disconnect the hoses at the cylinder.
                       Dissipate any stored energy left in the air cylinder.

                    2. Disconnect the rod end clevis from the pivot link arm assembly.

                    3. Remove cap screws, lock washers and locking bar plate from linking arm.

                    4. Remove pin from clevis. Use a pin driver if necessary.

                    5. Remove trunnion block and shims holding cylinder to housing. Carefully remove the
                       hydraulic cylinder to a service area for refurbishment.

                    7.4.2. Air Cylinder Refurbishment

                    1. Dismantle and repair cylinder in accordance with manufacturer’s maintenance
                       instructions.

       Caution:                  Stay clear of end caps of air cylinder when dismantling.

                    2. A compression spring inside the cylinder could cause serious injury. Place cylinder
                       in a vice and restrain caps. Remove caps with extreme care.

                    7.4.3. Air Cylinder Reinstallation

                    Refer to Figure 3 (below) for guidance.

       Important:                The special heavy duty designed air cylinder must be replaced with exact the same
                                 model. Any substitute model air cylinder may cause damage to the snap shear and
                                 other mill equipment.
                    1. Rotate knife assembly to closed position (vertical) and knife holders register against
                       stops.

                    2. Thread clevis all the way onto cylinder rod until thread bottoms out on shoulder of
                       cylinder rod. Align holes and insert parallel pin into clevis and cylinder rod.
