    The following procedures have been written to establish a standard method of operation, setup

    established it is essential that each and every operator follow these procedures. If the procedure
    is found to be incorrect then it should be revised so that the problem is resolved and all the

SAFETY CAUTIONS
IMPORTANT Always Read Safety Instructions and Warnings for each system and component prior to
operating and working on machinery. Follow all safety precautions to avoid personal injury or property
damage during system operation. Refer to this Safety Section and the Safety Section of each component
manual for general safety steps and procedures. Read all instructions, warnings, and cautions carefully.

Only trained personnel should operate and maintain mill equipment and tools, including rigging and lifting
procedures. Do not work on equipment you have never been trained on! IMPORTANT: All Safety
Devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to assure the safety of the operators.

        Warning - ALWAYS WEAR PERSONAL PROTECTION EQUIPMENT.
        Always wear proper safety gear when in the mill. Minimum Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
        should include safety hat, boots and gloves as well as eye and ear protection. Wear proper protective
        gear when operating and maintaining mill equipment.

        CAUTION: EQUIPMENT THROUGHOUT THE MILL PRODUCES EXCESSIVE NOISE.
        ALWAYS WEAR HEARING PROTECTION

        WARNING: CONSIDER ALL EQUIPMENT AS POTENTIALLY HAZARDOUS AT
        ALL TIMES. IT IS CAPABLE OF CRUSHING ANY BODY PART CAUGHT IN IT.

        CAUTION:   WORKING WITH HIGH PRESSURE MAY BE DANGEROUS IF
        EQUIPMENT IS MISUSED. NEVER USE FAULTY EQUIPMENT.

        ELECTRICAL VOLTAGES IN BOTH POWER AND CONTROL CIRCUITS ARE
        CAPABLE OF RENDERING SEVERE AND FATAL SHOCKS.

        WARNING: HOT PRODUCT TRAVELLING THROUGHOUT THE MILL CAN MAKE
        ALL EQUPIMENT SURFACES A HIGH TEMPERATURE CONDITION. CONSIDER
        ALL SURFACES THROUGHOUT THE MILL AS HOT!!

        WARNING: BEWARE OF PINCH POINTS. BLOCK AND RESTRAIN ROTATING
        PARTS BEFORE REMOVAL AND MOUNTING OF EQUIPMENT.

        WARNING: Do not exceed equipment ratings. Never attempt to press on or lift a load
        weighing more than the capacity of the cylinder. Overloading causes equipment failure
        and possible personal injury.

        Never set the relief valve to a higher pressure than the maximum rated pressure of the
        pump. Higher settings may result in equipment damage and/or personal injury.
        WARNING: The system operating pressure must not exceed the pressure rating of the
        lowest rated component in the system. CHECK pressure gauges in the system to monitor
        operating pressure.

        CAUTION: Avoid damaging connected hoses. Avoid sharp bends and kinks when routing
        hoses. Using a bent or kinked hose will cause severe back-pressure. Sharp bends and kinks
        will internally damage the hose leading to premature hose failure.

Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices make the
elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the process and/or
product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be constrained to follow a
prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble. Cobbles occur at random times
and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently
caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment,
and stock temperature are also causes of cobbling anywhere along the length of a rod in process in the
rolling train. The following recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe
manner.

INTRODUCTION

The Reducing / Sizing Mill (RSM) is located downstream of the rod finishing block or No-Twist® Mill
(NTM) and provides the mill with:

•   Increased finishing speed for small diameter product.
•   Single family rolling throughout the complete size range.
•   Precision tolerance product.
•   Thermo-mechanical rolling capability.
•   “Free size” rolling capability.

The Reducing / Sizing Mill (RSM) consists of four cantilevered mill stands in a ‘Vee” type configuration.
The four stands are split into two separate roll units, reducing and sizing. A 2-stand 230 mm reducing
unit is followed by a 150 mm 2-stand sizing unit. Normally all four stands are used in the rolling
position. However, each roll unit can be independently shifted in and out of the pass-line for setup off-
line. Split bore guide dummy troughs in the cobble cover/guard doors lower into the pass-line to take the
place of either roll unit when shifted out of position. With the aid of a transfer car, line bed assembly and
multiple off-line roll units, size change times can be reduced to as little as 5 minutes. All services such as
electrical, oil lubrication, water and hydraulic fluid are coupled automatically when the roll units are
transferred on-line.

The precision tolerance and “free sizing” capability of the Reducing / Sizing Mill (RSM) is accomplished
through the patented round-oval-round-round-round pass sequence, which utilizes the principals of
guideless rolling between successive round passes within the sizing mill roll unit. Guideless rolling simply
refers to the use of loose fitting static guides instead of roller entry guides between consecutive stands.
Conventional roller entry guides are used in the reducing mill roll unit.

The RSM is designed for manual and automatic operation, operating stations (Main Pulpit and Local) help
test, monitor and adjust conditions that may occur through the automated system. Refer to Table 1 for a
description of the electrical equipment used in the RSM.

1.0     Cobble Cover Assembly
Cobble Cover Doors

There is one cover for the 2-stand 250 mm unit and one cover for the 2-stand 150 mm unit. The covers
are operated by two ratchets which are controlled by Cobble Cover Lift gear motors. One for reducing
mill. One for sizing mill. Each squirrel cage induction motor is supplied with built-in brake. Motors
have 731:1 gear ratio. Each motor has FVR control.

Cover will move in the CLOSE or DUMMY TROUGH direction only while the Cover CLOSE or
DUMMY TROUGH pushbutton is depressed. If the pushbutton is released, the motor is de-energized
and Cover motion stops immediately. Also when a proximity switch indicates that the designated
destination has been obtained, then the motor is de-energized

Cover will move in the OPEN direction only while the Cover OPEN pushbutton is depressed. If the
pushbutton is released the cover motor shall stay energized until cover is fully open. The cover can be
stopped by the stop pushbutton which stops all motions immediately. Also when OPEN proximity
switch indicates that the designated destination has been obtained, then the motor shall be de-
energized. It is not required to move Cover from DUMMY TROUGH position to CLOSE position.

Each door has 3 positions which are indicated by Cobble Cover proximity switches:

        Open                           =   fully open
        Closed                         =   closed with roll unit in position (156° rotation from fully open)
        Dummy                          =   closed to dummy position without roll unit being used (180° rotation
                                           from fully open)

When the cover is used in the dummy trough position, it is necessary to activate locking pins to secure the
cover in place. These pins are operated by hydraulic cylinders which are controlled by Cobble Cover
Lock single solenoid valves. The solenoid is energized continuously to obtain the unlocked position and
de-energized to obtain the locked position.

Cobble Cover Lock Ind proximity switches indicate the released position. The sprocket design is to
allow opening cover without retracting the locking pins. These locking pins must be retracted whenever
the cover is being closed. These locking pins are not necessary to be retracted whenever the cover is
being opened. Sequencing of locking pins to the unlock position is automatic as part of the door
movement routine when opening or closing. When the door is signaled to open or close, the Cobble
Cover Lift solenoids should be energized 2 seconds after the cobble cover is unlocked as indicated by the
Cobble Cover Lock Ind pressure switches.

Whenever a cover is not in one of its normal operating positions, a Cover Alarm Lantern and Cover
Alarm Howler alarm is activated to alert mill personnel. The mill main drive can be run only when the

2.0     Axial Clamps for Sizing Mill Stands

The axial clamping hydraulic system is designed to remove roll shaft axial end-play in the sizing mill
stand unit. High pressure (clamped) is used during rolling, while low pressure (unclamped) is used only
during adjustment of roll parting and axial position adjustment of the roll shafts. The hydraulic system
allows control of Clamp and Unclamp pressure.

The Clamped position is used during rolling. The axial clamps must be UNCLAMP to make a parting
adjustment or axial adjustment to the rolls.

SIZING MILL AXIAL CLAMP is controlled by double solenoid valve. The "a" solenoid of SIZING
MILL AXIAL CLAMP is energized to clamp. The "b' solenoid is energized to unclamp. The solenoid
should be energized continuously.

3.0      Service Coupling

Each unit has a service coupling which automatically disconnects the; lube oil, water, hydraulic, and
electric supplies when a unit is traversed away from the on-line rolling position.

Before traversing, roll cooling water and axial clamp hydraulics (on the 150 mm unit) must be off.
The lube pumps can keep running; check valves in the coupling will seal the pressure.

The coupling also disconnects electrical connections for thermocouples, parting sensor resolvers, lube oil
pressure switches, and vibration sensors if used.

Note: The system logic must recognize that when a unit is traversed away from the rolling position, the
lube pressure switches will lose their pressure and become de-activated but this is not a fault condition.

5.0         Roll Water Cooling System
The Roll Water Cooling System is designed to prevent damage to the RSM rolls and dummy guides from
the hot product traveling through the mill and to lubricate the seals for the bearings. The RSM must never
be run above 10% speed without water or else the seals for bearings will be damaged.

Seals are only effective at preventing water ingress into the lubrication system with RSM running above
10% top speed. Cooling water should be flowing to the cobble cover when the RSM is in the off line,
dummy position.

Two water valves are used for the RSM roll cooling; one feeds the Reducing mill and the other feeds the
Sizing mill. Each valve is operated by an air cylinder controlled by Roll Cooling single solenoid valve.
Water turns on to a 2-stand unit only when it is in the on-line position.

Water turns on when the solenoid is energized. Water turns on when RSM motor speed is 10% of top
rated speed or above. When motor speed drops below 10% speed, the water will turn off following a time
delay of about 7 seconds to cool the rolls.

The Roll Cooling Pressure switch indicates when the
correct water pressure is present at the associated mill.

Low water pressure indication when the RSM is running
above 10% speed will initiate the scrap cut mode of the C&D
shear. In addition, this condition will be displayed on the mill
alarm annunciator.

A 0.5 second time delay is used in conjunction with the pressure switch so that a transient drop in
pressure will not produce a false, low pressure indication. Low water pressure indication from the
pressure switch is ignored for 5 seconds when water is first turned on to allow for normal buildup of
pressure.

The RSM drive will stop if a water pressure fault persists for 10 seconds.

Note: The RSM must never run above 10% speed without water. Lack of cooling will cause damage.

Water Sensor

A Water Sensor is mounted in the lubrication line. This detects any water in the lubrication oil feeding
the RSM. Detection of water will signal an alarm to the mill control system.

      5.1          Dummy Trough Water Cooling
      When a cobble cover door is in the dummy trough position, water cooling is applied to cool the
      dummy trough. Separate roll cooling valves are utilized for the 230 and 150 units. Water turns on
      when Dummy Trough Cooling single solenoid valve is energized. Water turns on to a 2-stand
      trough only when cover is in the dummy trough position. Water turns on if cover is in dummy trough
      position and main RSM drive is running.

6.0 Traverse To/From Rolling Line Position (Refer to E.C.S. for controls details)

Each 2-stand unit can be hydraulically traversed sideways either to the on-line rolling position or to the
off-line position. The off-line position is 2851 mm from the on-line position.

Overview of Quick Stand Change System

     • Hydraulic cylinders located below the on-line sliding bed assembly are used to traverse the stand
       assemblies to the off-line position for roll change operation.
     • Each 2-stand unit (1 x 2-stand 230 and 1 x 2-stand 150) is individually traversable (in or out)
       from the sliding bed by hydraulic cylinders.
     • The traverse cylinders are attached to the roll units with manual locking pins.

The Traverse Fast Speed single solenoid valve is energized to traverse the roll units at fast speed. The
fast speed solenoid valve is de-energized whenever the On-Line Slowdown proximity switch is
indicating.

Before traversing a 150 sizing mill unit in or out, pressure must be relieved from the shaft preload circuit.
Attempting to engage or disengage the service coupling when hydraulic pressure is present could damage
the service coupling. Sizing mill unit traverse motion is to be prevented if a pressure signal is active at
either Axial Clamping Pressure - Mill Side or Axial Clamping Pressure - Supply Side pressure
switch.

Base Locking

Each 2-stand unit is locked into the on-line rolling position with the traverse cylinders. Thus, the
traversing cylinder solenoids must be energized at all times when the roll unit is sensed in the on-line
position. Locking is indicated with pressure switches indicating high pressure (RSM/PS5-6)

Four (4) proximity switches are used with each unit to indicate positions in each direction.

When traversing in on-line direction, the unit will travel at fast speed until the On-Line Slowdown point
is reached, then travel at slow speed to the On-Line Position where it stops.

When traversing toward the off-line position, the unit will travel at fast speed until the Off-Line Position
point is reached or stop when the pushbutton is released.

The slowdown signal is only momentarily activated as the target passes the proximity switch. Between
the slowdown point and the stop point the slowdown signal will go inactive. Thus the control system
must retain the status of speed control, i.e. once a slowdown signal is received, the speed will be slow
until the travel direction is reversed.

7.0     Cobble Detection System
The RSM is confined in enclosures that have a minimum amount of free space, so in the event of cobble,
it is necessary to divert incoming stock as soon as possible. Since visual detection of a cobble by the
operator is difficult, automatic cobble detection is used.
A separate monofilament line with weight is
strung through both the reducing mill, the sizing
mill, and also through the breakout box.
A cobble in either location will break the line and
allow the weight to drop and actuate the
Reducing Mill Cobble Detect, Sizing mill
Cobble Detect proximity switch or the Breakout
box Cobble Detect proximity switch.

In addition, Cobbles are also detected as follows:

   •   Tail end sensed at the RSM Exit HMD before it is sensed at the NTM® Exit HMD.
   •   After the front end is sensed at the NTM® Exit HMD it is not sensed by RSM Exit HMD within
       a preset time.

When a cobble occurs, an alarm is actuated, the snap shear in front of the RSM is closed, the scrap cutting
mode for the shears ahead of the NTM is initiated, and the main drive is stopped.

The stand #16H is the pivot stand for speed control except breakdown mill. Cascade direction is upstream
prior to stand #16, and downstream towards the Laying head after stand #16H.

The RSM motor speed is calculated using the Finishing stock speed, the effective roll diameter of the
finishing stand and the selected ratio between the finishing stand and the RSM motor. This motor speed
is then used to calculate the stock entry speed into the RSM using the effective roll diameter of the RSM
entry stand, the entry stand reduction and the selected gear ratio between the motor and the entry stand.

On first coil after a roll change, operator initially sets the RSM delivery speed 2 m/s above the recipe
value to ensure tension between the two mills. If the NTM is dummied, the 2m/s tension should be
between the Stand that is feeding the RSM and the RSM.

When using the NTM®, the RSM speed reference is calculated as follows:

1. Initial motor speed reference for the RSM is determined by the first stand effective roll diameter and
   selected gear ratio.

2. The RSM motor speed reference is then biased based on the amount of forward slip from the NTM®
   and the amount of tension required between the NTM® and the RSM.

3. An impact speed reference is added to the RSM motor speed reference prior to arrival of the head end
   and is removed after impact at a 0.6 sec ramp rate.

4. The linear delivery speed from the RSM is calculated from the motor speed feedback to the delivery
   stand of the RSM. This delivery speed is used as the reference for the pinch roll and laying head.

Tail End Speed-Up

Speeds up larger, slower speed products to provide sufficient energy for rod tail end to clear laying head.
RSM, Pinch roll and Laying Head accelerate at same rate. The Mill control system calculates where tail
end should be when mill tracking initiates tail end speed-up. Calculation is based on required tail out
speed at laying head, run speed of RSM, reduction of stands in service and acceleration rate to be used.
This function is automatic if rolling speed is less than the speed-up preset. Tail end at laying head exit
turns off tail end speedup function.

Tail End Speed Step-down

Slows down smaller, high speed products to control the ring diameter as the product tails out of the laying
head.

Step slowdown of speed occurs when tail end clears the NTM® delivery stand as indicated by a tracking
system.

The RSM and Pinch Rolls are to decelerate at the same rate until the tail end clears the pinch roll.

8.0   Roll Parting Mechanism

Refer also to Roll Partings in Standard Operation, Section 10 as a guide.

Each stand of the Reducing Sizing Mill (RSM) is equipped with a roll parting mechanism to adjust the
roll gap.

The roll parting drive mechanism is composed of the Roll Parting Feedback device and the control
signal interface. The roll parting mechanisms are manually opened and closed. The mill control system
is to use the Roll Parting Feedback encoder (resolvers for 150 mills) for position feedback.

The operator will adjust parting using a wrench. To ensure all backlash is removed from the parting
system, the operating should always open past the desired parting position and then close.

        8.1     Roll Parting Under Load

        The RSM has the ability to make adjustments to the roll parting during rolling operations. This
        roll parting mechanism features a Gear Head to multiply the torque and a self-resetting manual
        torque limiter (to prevent over torquing). Results of roll parting corrections must be taken using a
        sampling method.

        8.2     Roll Parting Sensors (OPTIONAL EQUIPMENT)

        The mill control system uses the Roll Parting Feedback encoder (resolvers for 150 mills) for
        position feedback.

        The Roll Parting Feedback devices are used to provide a display (XX.XX mm) of the parting
        distance between roll collars. Resolvers are used for Sizing Mill stands. Encoders are used for all
        other stands.

        Parting displays for each stand are to be on the mill floor panel and main pulpit so they can be
        observed while making a parting adjustment. Each pulpit display can also be selected to indicate
        roll diameter.

        Design target accuracy is 0.0136 mm (worst case) for parting. There is a non-linear relationship
        between the adjusting screw and the roll center distance due to the eccentric geometry. The
        display must be calibrated to account for this non-linear condition.

        Refer to the referenced E.C.S for a description of the steps required to first calibrate, and then
        display, the roll parting.

9.0     External Gear Drive Arrangement Refer to the Main Drive Control ECS for additional Main
Drive Control information.

The Reducing/Sizing Mill (RSM) stands are mechanically tied through an external gear drive arrangement
and driven by a single motor. The clutch positions are obtained by servo motors and are indicated by
resolvers. By changing the clutch configurations of each stage in the external gear drive the total reduction
within the Reducing / Sizing Mill (RSM) can be varied allowing multiple finished products to be rolled.

Clutch Arrangement

•   There are several combinations of gear ratios available based on clutching arrangement selected.

•   There is one, four stage gear box with 9 clutches. Clutches 1-3 control ratio of stage A, clutches 4-5
    control stage B, clutches 6-7 control stage C and clutches 8-9 control D stage.

•   The box has an arrangement of clutches to change the gear ratios. Refer to the end of RSM Gearing
    Data for the layout diagram.

•   The following procedure is used to change any gear ratio. This procedure is controlled by the Morgan
    clutch change system with interface to the Main mill control system for Jogging and clutch position
    verification:

    1. RSM drive is at complete stop and prevented from running
    2. Shift ALL clutches to desired positions
    3. If any clutch fails to engage the Main RSM motor is jogged forward. (5rpm or less)
    4. If any clutch still fails to engage the Main RSM motor is jogged reverse. (5rpm or less)
    5. If any clutch still fails to engage that clutch is returned to neutral and the Main RSM motor is
       jogged. (5rpm or less)
    6. After jogging, the clutches are commanded to their position again and the entire sequence steps 1
       thru 5 are repeated.
    7. At end of sequence, verify ALL clutches are in desired operating position

•   The clutch positions are obtained by servo motors.

•   The clutch positions are indicated by resolvers.

•   The Morgan Gearbox control system will contain the proper clutch configuration for each product
    size.

•   Once the mill has been prepared to roll a new size, i.e. new rolls, new gaps set etc. the main mill
    operator should select the new product size ratio. Selecting this new ratio initiates the clutch change
    sequence controlled by the Morgan clutch change system.

1.0    Interlocks
The following interlock steps and procedures are required in both manual and automatic operation. Refer
to other operation sections of all mill equipment for additional interlocking steps and procedures of
specific components.

1.1    Interlocking with Mill Lubricating Oil Systems

       •   Forced oil lubrication is provided for:

               NTM® bearings and gears
               RSM bearings and gears

       • Refer to Table 3 (later page) or the Main Drive Control ECS for correct interlock performed
       for each lubrication sensor.

       •   “A1” INTERLOCK scheme causes the following to occur:

               After the associated drive motor(s) is running, a low-pressure condition initiates a 0.5
               second time delay (this time delay is used to protect against nuisance trips due to
               vibration, etc.).

               If the low-pressure condition is present after the delay time ends, the snap shear at the
               entry side of the mill is closed, cobble cutting of the upstream shears is started and a
               second time delay is started.

               After the second time delay ends, (approximately 1.0 second), the motors of the
               associated drive motor(s) are stopped.

               Associated drive motor(s) may not be started or jogged when low-pressure is detected.

       •   “A2” INTERLOCK scheme causes the following to occur:

               After the associated drive motor(s) is running, a low-pressure condition initiates a 0.5
               second time delay (this time delay is used to protect against nuisance trips due to
               vibration, etc.).

               If the low-pressure condition is present after the time delay ends, the following functions
               take place:

                     a. The “scrap cut” mode for the crop and divide shear at the entry to the NTM® is
                        initiated to divert the stock to the scrap chopping shear.

                     b. A timer (adjustable from 0-3 seconds) is started which initiates the closing of
                        the snap shears at the entry sides of the NTM® and RSM.

2.0     Roll Removal and Mounting
The following roll removal and mounting procedures are designed only for use with the hydraulic tools
and pump unit supplied by Morgan. Please refer to the reference drawings for special roll mount and
removal tools and procedures.

ROLL SHOP RESPONSIBILITIES
The roll shop should be responsible for cleaning (Refer to “Cleanliness”) and assembling the rolls and
tapered sleeves (Refer to “Using Spacers”) prior to being transported to the mill floor.

IMPORTANT It is recommended that each tapered sleeve be assigned to a given stand and remain
with that stand throughout the life of the sleeve. In addition, if multiple roll widths are used on a
particular stand, then a dedicated sleeve should also be assigned to that stand and roll width. This
ensures that the contact between the sleeves and shaft taper is optimized.

The assembled rolls and sleeves must be clearly marked with the pass to be used and the stand on which
the roll assembly is to be mounted.

The roll and sleeve should be individually wrapped in a protective covering to prevent dirt from adhering
to the clean surfaces prior to mounting.

CLEANLINESS

Cleanliness is the highest priority when mounting the rolls on the roll shafts. If dirt is present on the roll,
sleeve and shaft assembly, the wear process on the tapered sleeve and the roll pinion shaft is rapidly
accelerated. As the taper on the shaft and sleeve wear, the amount of contact between the two surfaces
decreases, decreasing the amount of torque that can be transmitted and increasing the likelihood of roll
slippage or breakage.

To achieve the best results it is necessary to clean the pinion shaft tapers every time a roll is changed.
This should be done using SCOTCH-BRITE or CROCUS CLOTH. Any oil residue should be removed
by using non- petroleum based cleaning fluid. Clean, lint free type cleaning cloths should be used.

If a roll is removed and then remounted on the mill without going to the roll shop, then the bore of the roll
and the tapered sleeve should be cleaned before they are reassembled. The pinion shaft taper must also be
cleaned as well as both faces of the roll as it is important that the roll contacts the flinger or the spacers,
squarely. If dirt gets between the flinger and roll face or spacer then this can damage the roll neck seals
on the older type NTM as well as cause axial misalignment.

USING SPACERS
Carbide rolls can have between 1 and 4 grooves cut in the barrel, depending on the width of the groove
and the width of the roll

In order to maintain a constant pass centerline a spacer must be mounted between the roll face and flinger
when using the outside grooves on a multi-groove roll. When placing the roll assembly onto the roll
shaft, ensure that the spacer is squarely positioned between the flinger and drive side roll face. When
using the inside grooves on a multi-groove roll the spacer must be mounted on the work side of the roll
face.

HYDRAULIC ROLL MOUNTING & REMOVAL EQUIPMENT Refer to Figure 8 as a guide.
Please refer to the reference drawings for special roll mount and removal tools and procedures.

The tapered sleeves are pressed onto the roll shaft using a hydraulic roll-mounting tool. A hydraulic tool
is also used to remove the rolls. There are two different sets of tools used for these procedures, they are:

        •   9" (230 mm) roll mounting and removal tools used for Reducing Mill stands.

        •   6" (150 mm) roll mounting and removal tools used for Sizing Mill stands.

    1. ROLL MOUNTING TOOLS

    The roll-mounting tool fastens onto the end of the roll shaft and applies an axial force to the roll and
    tapered sleeve, which locks the roll onto the shaft. The roll-mounting tool consists of two-pistons:
        • Piston #1 applies an axial force to the roll face to hold it against the flinger.
        •   Piston #2 applies an axial force to the tapered sleeve, pressing it between the shaft and roll
            bore thereby locking the roll in position.

    2. ROLL REMOVAL TOOLS

    The roll removal tool is locked onto the flange of the tapered sleeve and an axial force is applied to
    the end of the roll shaft, which in turn releases the tapered sleeve.

    3. ROLL HANDLING TOOL

    The Roll Handling tool is used to help lift and remove the roll from the roll housing.

    4. ELECTRO-HYDRAULIC PUMP UNIT

    The electro-hydraulic pump unit supplies the force to mount and remove the rolls.

The roll diameter deviation within the Reducing / Sizing mill is split into the following three (3)

1. DEVIATION WITHIN A STAND

      deviation is the same for all stands and roll housing types.

4.0       Roll Parting Correction
The roll partings for the RSM defined on the rolling diagrams are theoretical settings and are produced
using the following formula: Roll Parting = Hot Stock Height - [ 2 x Groove Depth] .

In practice it is necessary to make some corrections to the theoretical settings to take into account oil film
thickness, machining tolerances and roll pinion shaft deflections due to rolling load. As a result the roll
parting adjustments required can be either positive or negative depending on rolling load (i.e. reduction,
steel grade and temperature), product diameter and rolling speed.

Due to the high rolling speeds the required roll parting adjustments or deviations from the theoretical
settings are generally positive. These positive deflections are caused by the oil film strength in the clevite
bearings exceeding the deformation resistance of the rod, causing the mechanical clearance to be removed
in a negative direction, i.e. inward towards the stock. As a result the roll parting decreases from the set
value as the mill is run up to the rolling speed, producing a smaller than expected finished product.

Note: It is advantageous to derive a standard setup for each size based on the most commonly rolled steel
grade and entry temperature. The operator responsible for adjusting the mill should keep a log of the roll
parting adjustments made after each change in steel grade or entry temperature. This will allow a more
detailed setup chart to be derived based on groups for steel grade and ranges of entry temperatures.
Accurate roll parting adjustments can then be made prior to changes in steel grade and/or entry
temperature, thereby ensuring that the tolerance of the first bar after the change is within specified limits.

Deviation from standard roll partings can be caused by:

      1. Feed section size and shape outside setup parameters.

      2. Too much tension between NTM and RSM.

      3. Axial alignment of rolls being incorrect.

      4. Guide setup being incorrect.

      5. Roll parting settings being incorrect or incorrectly measured.

5.0     Setting Roll Partings

Accurately setting the roll partings is an essential aspect for obtaining the correct finished section and
having a trouble free start-up after a size change. Time spent to achieve an accurate set-up is time well
spent. The following steps and procedures should be used as a guide for setting the roll parting. Note:
Taking Dynamic roll parting samples while the mill is running, making necessary adjustments and
recording the results will further fine-tune the parting accuracy for future startups. Refer to Section 7 for
Dynamic Roll Parting Instructions.

        5.1       Set the mill to jog.

                  A. The jog speed should be set to 30 motor R/min or slower.
                  B. Wait until the mill has achieved a constant jog speed before taking the parting
                     measurements.
                  C. Do not leave the mill in jog after the roll partings have been taken, since this can reduce
                     the life expectancy of the roll neck seals.

        5.2       Collect the Jog Partings (roll parting measurement at jog speed).

                  A.      Standardize on either aluminum, copper or low carbon steel wire.
                          Note: Aluminum wire gauges are used in most applications.
                  B.      Standardize the jog parting wire diameter. Ensure that the selected wire diameter
                          provides approximately 1.0 mm of deformation on the roll parting. The ideal
                          wire diameter or thickness for the RSM should be about 3.0 mm.

              Note: Different wire diameters for different roll parting ranges can be used; however, this must
              be standardized and maintained for repeatability of setup.

                  C.      Pass the wire between one roll collar and the deformed section is the roll parting (See
                          Figure 10). If only two or more roll collars are captured, then the amount of roll
                          deflection will be giving an artificially larger roll parting measurement. Note: If this
                          occurs repeat this step.
                  D.      If multiple roll partings are taken prior to measurement, ensure that the wire used is
                          uniquely marked for each stand so that the measurements are not confused.

        5.3       Measure the roll parting.

                  A.      Measure the roll parting using a needle or standard micrometer and not a vernier
                          caliper.
                  B.      When measuring the roll partings it is important to measure the same roll collar every
                          time since there will be a slight variation in roll parting measurement between the
                          work side and drive side roll collars. Note: For bet results, measure the parting at
                          the center, vertically halfway across the parting from the entry side.

7.0     Taking Dynamic Roll Parting Measurements

Due to the high rolling speeds, the required roll parting adjustments or deviations from the theoretical
settings are generally positive. As a result, the roll parting decreases from the set value as the mill is run up
to the rolling speed, producing a smaller than expected finished product. At various speeds the RSM roll
partings deviate from the actual jog partings set into the mill prior to rolling. Depending on the speed of the
mill, the size of the product being rolled, and the reduction being taken, each stand might undergo an
increase or decrease in the actual roll parting under dynamic conditions. Due to the nature of the RSM, the
dynamic partings serve as an important tool that provides us with information that further clarifies this
condition.

Collecting Dynamic Roll Parting measurements while the mill is running under load conditions with a
bar in the mill, creates a monitoring system for more accurate product runs. Comparing parting bite data
taken from the dynamic parting tool samples, as it corresponds proportionally with actual product
measurements, allows the operators to make more precise adjustments and creates a more accurate
reference point for the next time that a particular product line is rolled. Keeping accurate historical data
and updating records with new load running measurements will help to reduce setup time for future
product lines and sizes. Additionally, the roll wear is monitored and changes can be made accordingly.
Note: It cannot be overemphasized that the dynamic partings must be taken while the bar is being
rolled in the RSM.

7.1     Dynamic Roll Parting Tools

There are three Dynamic roll parting tools used to take measurements in the RSM rolls while the mill is
rolling. An angled tool is used for roll positions 1 and 3, while separate tools are each used for positions 2
and 4 respectively. Access covers are incorporated into the cobble cover design and are located alternately
at the front and top of each cobble cover stand location.

Caution: The Cobble cover must be down and interlocks working when taking dynamic roll parting
measurements. Never by- pass interlocks and take measurements while cobble cover is open. Fatal and
severe injury could result.

7.2     Collecting Dynamic Parting

When collecting the Dynamic Partings at each stand, make sure the following guidelines are followed:

        •   Measurements for Stands 1 & 3 are taken through the 2 horizontal access covers.
        •   Measurements for stands 2 and 4 are taken from the 2 diagonal covers.
        •   Make sure to only use the 2.5 mm aluminum-parting rod in these tools. Morgan suggests that a
            2.5 mm aluminum wire rod be used for the dynamic partings. Other materials with similar
            properties can be used, but the information from one material compared with the other may
            produce different results. Aluminum wire is supplied with roll parting kit.
        •   Make sure that the aluminum rod has a hook bent into it to allow it to stretch out when the rolls
            make contact and pull on it.

8.0     Axial Roll Alignment
Accurately setting the axial roll alignment on the 150 mm roll housings is critical to produce a precision
tolerance product. If the rolls are axially misaligned it is physically impossible to produce a finished
product with ovality less than 0.15 mm. The axial alignment of the sizing mill stands must be checked
every time rolls are mounted. Use the following steps to align the sizing mill rolls:

       8.1     Mount the portable optics as shown in Figures 13 and 14.
               A. When checking the axial alignment with the portable optic, ensure that the mill is on-
                  line and the axial pre-load pressure is selected to high.
               B. Remove the entry guide and the delivery guide from the stand being checked.
               C. Blow oxygen from an acetylene torch through the roll passes to remove any dirt or
                  water droplets. This will allow a clear image of the passes to be seen through the
                  portable optics.
               D. Clean the entry and delivery guide brackets to ensure that the optic and light source
                  brackets fit flush.
               E. Focus the optic on the pass by moving it on the guide bracket such that a sharp image
                  can be seen.

       8.2     Check the correct mounting of the rolls.

               A. Unless the roll units are new or recently maintained, axial adjustments of the rolls are
                  not normally required. If axial misalignment is seen, it is usually caused by the
                  following:

                   •   Incorrect mounting of the rolls
                   •   Dirt between the roll and flinger
                   •   Worn flinger
                   •   Excessive axial clearance (check by lift test)
                   •   Incorrect pass geometry (centerline of pass to roll collar distance)

               B. Before making any axial adjustments check the above and remount the rolls

       8.3     Adjust the roll alignment

                A. Figure 15 shows examples of possible axial misalignments and the correct alignment
                   position. It is important that the roll passes are aligned with the centerline of pass
                   indicated by the vertical line on the portable optics. If both passes are misaligned, then
                   both roll axial adjustment nuts must be adjusted. Do not use the corner of the passes as
                   an indication of axial alignment since the corners of the pass are usually chamfered or
                   have a corner relief radius which is not as accurate as the bottom radius of the pass.
       Note: The images in the optic are mirrored such that the bottom roll on the optic is the top roll on
       the mill.

9.0     Guide Mounting & Alignment

The basic function of the guide is to direct the section through the mill stand in such a manner
that the front end does not deviate from the pass line. Each stand will have an entry and delivery
guide. The type of guide used at each stand will differ due to the size and shape of the section. In
many cases it is necessary to change the guides or the guide components as the section size
changes.

It is normal in many mills that the guides are prepared in a work area away from the mill floor.
Once the guides are set, it is then the responsibility of the mill operators to install them. It is the
installation into the mill that is covered in this section of the manual. Refer to the guide manual
for assembly and alignment for guides off-line.

It is essential that the correct components be used in the guides for each position and size being
rolled. Refer to the guide tabulation drawings for a list of the guides and components required at
each stand position for the product size to be rolled.

        9.1      Types of Guide used in the Reducing/Sizing Mill

                 A. ROLLER ENTRY GUIDE

                 These are usually used to guide an oval section into a round pass. A roller entry
                 guide is sometimes used to guide a round section into the first stand of the RSM
                 or NTM, especially if a sidelooper is located immediately ahead of the mill. The
                 roller entry guide can have either 2 or 4 guide rollers and has the provision to
                 attach a 2 roller anti-flutter guide onto the back of the guide assembly.

                 B. STATIC ENTRY GUIDES

                 These are usually used to guide a round section into an oval pass. All the static
                 entry guides are split into two halves and are clamped together to prevent a
                 cobble from breaking out into the roll bite, which if allowed will damage the roll
                 housing.

                 C. STATIC DELIVERY GUIDES

                 This type of guide is located at the delivery of every stand. Two types of static
                 delivery guides are used in the Reducing / Sizing Mill:

              This delivery guide is split into two halves with the top half attached to the

              E. SOLID TYPE

              This guide is split into two halves with the top half being bolted to the bottom

              F. DUMMY PIPES – OPTIONAL

              If the Reducing / Sizing Mill does not traverse on and off-line and deformed bar

              mill roll unit. Otherwise the dummy troughs in the cobble guard doors will be
              lowered into the pass-line when the respective roll units are traversed off-line.

   9.2        Mounting the Guides

              A. ROLLER ENTRY GUIDE

              These guides are normally clamped onto an adjustable saddle, which is attached
              to a bracket located by means of a key and keyway to the housing faceplate and
              held in position by bolts. This automatically locates the bracket and roller guide
              on the mill centerline. A portable optic is supplied with the mill to help the
              operator accurately align the roller entry guide to the pass centerline by adjusting
              guide bracket saddle. Refer to the Portable Optics Manual for details.

              A nosepiece is attached to the front of the guide to provide additional guiding as
              close to the roll bite as possible and to aid the front end of the rod into the center
              of the pass, especially at high speed. The nosepiece helps eliminate the
              possibility of the front end of the rod striking the roll pass collar, which will
              cause either the front end to turndown or cobble.

              B. STATIC ENTRY & DELIVERY GUIDES

              The static entry and delivery guides are mounted on a bracket, which is
              automatically aligned on the mill and pass centerline by a key and keyway.

TROUBLESHOOTING GUIDE

REDUCING / SIZING MILL ENTRY SECTION
The RSM has been designed to utilize a single roll pass family feeding multiple RSM roll pass families to
produce the complete product size range. This means that the roll pass design, roll partings and gear ratio
selections for each RSM family have been calculated based on a single entry section area and shape. Any
variations in the entry section area or shape may result in the need for additional roll parting and RSM
lead speed adjustments to the standard setup.

1. ENTRY SECTION TOLERANCE

    To maintain a repeatable and standard setup for the RSM and to ensure that the first bar through the
    RSM after a size change is within tolerance, it is essential that the feed section area to the NTM and
    RSM are within allowable limits. The allowable variation in feed section area to the RSM is ±2%
    from the nominal areas defined on the Morgan rolling diagram.

    NOTE:       1. Density of cold steel is 7.85E-6 g/cm3.
                2. All the areas shown on the Morgan rolling diagrams are hot areas.

2. INCORRECT ENTRY SECTION

    If the entry section to the RSM is too large or small, or possesses poor shape, i.e. tolerance and
    ovality, then the following problems could be encountered in achieving a precision tolerance product
    from the RSM.

    a. ENTRY SECTION SMALL

        Decreases the reduction in the RSM, increasing the interstand tension. This can result in the
        stock turning down in the roller guide and/or twisting between the sizing mill stands. Irrespective
        of RSM roll parting adjustments, no improvement in section tolerance can be achieved. See
        Adjustment # 4.

    b. ENTRY SECTION LARGE

        Increases the reduction in the RSM, decreasing the interstand tension. If the reduction is too
        high, then compression can occur between the stands causing flutter on the finished product.
        See Adjustment # 5.

    c. ENTRY SECTION SHAPE POOR

        Causes the entry section to twist onto the minor axis prior to entry into the RSM. Depending on the
        severity of the section ovality variations to the RSM standard setup may be required in order to
        maintain a precision tolerance product.

        IMPORTANT Poor entry section shape has minimal effect on the finished tolerance if the area
        of the entry section is within the limits defined in Table 4.

ADJUSTING TENSION BETWEEN NTM AND RSM

Important: Some grades of product require an increase of water pressure flow in the water box
creating a momentarily vibration of the rod as it exits the water box. This should not be confused with
lack of tension to the rod. Over adjusting the tension can cause the product to pull apart.
To date there are no proven automatic means of regulating the speed of the RSM to minimize tension
between the NTM and RSM. Therefore manual methods must be adopted to detect the presence of tension
and adjust the RSM speed reference accordingly. The following are recommended and proven on-line, real-
time methods for detecting tension.
1. MANUAL ROD DISPLACEMENT
   After the rod has entered both the NTM and RSM the operator can use a short piece of small diameter rod
   (5.5mm rod ~ 500mm long) to displace the stock towards the center of the trough between the NTM and RSM.

   a. HIGH TENSION
       If the rod is difficult to move, and once displaced quickly moves back to the mill centerline with
       little or no oscillation, then significant tension is present between the NTM and RSM. The operator
       should decrease the RSM speed slowly through the local operator station to reduce the tension.

   b. MINIMUM TENSION
       If the rod is easy to displace, and once moved floats or oscillates freely in the trough, then little
       tension is present. This is the optimum rolling condition.
   c. COMPRESSION
       If the rod starts to oscillate immediately after entering the RSM and continues to oscillate without
       manual displacement, then no tension is present. The operator should increase the RSM speed
       immediately to increase the tension and prevent the rod from cobbling in the NTM breakout box.

   d. UPSTREAM TENSION
       If the displacement of the rod becomes easier prior to the rod exiting the NTM, then
       tension exists upstream in the mill. Upstream tension problems should be eliminated
       prior to adjustment of the RSM lead speed.

2. BAR GAUGE
   If the mill is equipped with a rotating or oscillating bar gauge located after the RSM, then the output
   of the gauge can be used to detect the presence of tension between the NTM and RSM.

   IMPORTANT: The Bar Gauge should always be used in conjunction with the manual displacement of the
   rod for detecting tension.

   a. HIGH TENSION
       If the minimum dimension on the bar gauge increases rapidly on the tail end after exiting the last
       stand of the NTM, then tension is present between the NTM and RSM. The operator should
       decrease the RSM speed to reduce the tension through the local operator station.

   b. MINIMUM TENSION

       If the minimum dimension from the bar gauge does not change appreciably on the tail end, then
       little or no tension exists between the two mills.

   c. COMPRESSION

       The rod gauge cannot be used to indicate compression between the NTM and RSM. Only visual
       or manual displacement methods can be used.

       The operator should increase the RSM speed immediately to increase the tension through the
       local operator station before the rod cobbles in the NTM breakout box.

   d. UPSTREAM TENSION

       If the minimum dimension from the bar gauge gradually increases prior to the tail end exiting the
       NTM, then tension is present in the mill stands upstream of the NTM.

       The operator should then remove the tension from the upstream stands before adjusting the NTM
       speed reference.

3. NUMBER OF OVERFILLED TAIL END RINGS

   If tension exists between the NTM and RSM, then the finished section width will rapidly increase
   when the tail end exits the last stand of the NTM. If too much tension is present between the NTM
   and RSM then this could cause the RSM passes to overfill. By counting the number of tail end
   overfilled rings it is possible to identify the source of the tension.

   a. MORE RINGS

       If more overfilled rings are counted than calculated allowance, then tension is present between
       the mill stands upstream of the NTM. This tension should be removed first before adjusting the
       NTM speed reference.

   b. LESS RINGS

       If less than one or two overfilled rings are counted, then this is likely to be caused by the tension
       within the RSM stands themselves and not by tension between the NTM and RSM.

IDENTIFICATION OF FINISHED PRODUCT HEIGHT & WIDTH
Due to the oval-round-round-round pass sequence used in the RSM it becomes very difficult and, in some
cases, impossible to visually identify the height and width dimensions on the finished rod. Without the

1. BAR GAUGE
   With a rotating or oscillating bar gauge located after the RSM it is relatively easy to determine the
   height and width dimension when the measured rod has an ovality of ≥ 0.10mm.

    on the gauge display typically indicate the width or free side of the rod.

2. VISUAL INSPECTION
   If no bar gauge is available then the roller should visually compare the rod dimensions from the front
   and middle of the coil to determine the height or width of the rod. Do not use the tail end rings for
   determining the height of the coil, as this can be distorted by the pinch roll or tension induced
   between the NTM and RSM.

    The height dimension should remain fairly consistent throughout the coil with only a slight increase
    on the head end due to increased load caused by a larger tension free feed from the NTM. Note if the
    QA inspector at the coil line measures around the rod circumference the majority of similar
    dimensions measured usually indicates the height due to contact with the constant radius of the
    bottom of the pass.

       WARNING: BEWARE OF PINCH POINTS. BLOCK AND RESTRAIN ROTATING
       PARTS BEFORE REMOVAL AND MOUNTING OF EQUIPMENT.

       WARNING: Do not exceed equipment ratings. Never attempt to press on or lift a load
       weighing more than the capacity of the cylinder. Overloading causes equipment failure
       and possible personal injury.

       Never set the relief valve to a higher pressure than the maximum rated pressure of the
       pump. Higher settings may result in equipment damage and/or personal injury.
       WARNING: The system operating pressure must not exceed the pressure rating of the
       lowest rated component in the system. CHECK pressure gauges in the system to monitor
       operating pressure.

       CAUTION: Avoid damaging connected hoses. Avoid sharp bends and kinks when routing
       hoses. Using a bent or kinked hose will cause severe back-pressure. Sharp bends and kinks
       will internally damage the hose leading to premature hose failure.


       Do not drop heavy objects on hose. A sharp impact may cause internal damage to hose wire
       strands. Applying pressure to a damaged hose may cause it to rupture. DO NOT lift or pull
       equipment by hoses or couplers. Rig and secure equipment for safe transport.


       CAUTION: Keep hydraulic equipment away from flames and heat. Excessive heat will
       soften packing and seals, resulting in fluid leaks. Heat also weakens hose materials and
       packing. For optimum performance do not expose equipment to temperatures of 65°C
       [150°F] or higher. Protect all hoses and cylinders from weld spatter and extreme heat.


       DANGER: Do not handle pressurized hoses. Escaping oil under pressure can penetrate the
       skin, causing serious injury. If oil is injected under the skin, see a doctor immediately.

       WARNING: Only use hydraulic cylinders in a coupled system. Never use a cylinder with
       unconnected couplers. If the cylinder becomes extremely overloaded, components can fail
       catastrophically causing severe personal injury. Never bleed system to exposed atmosphere.

       WARNING: Immediately replace worn or damaged parts.
       IMPORTANT: Qualified trained technicians must only service Mill equipment.

       WARNING: Do not use electric pumps in an explosive atmosphere. Adhere to all local and
       national electrical codes. Start the pump with the valve in the neutral position to prevent
       accidental cylinder operation. Keep hands clear of moving parts and pressurized hoses.
       CAUTION: To prevent damage to electric motors, check specifications. Use of incorrect
       power source will damage the motor.

1.0      Safety Procedures

IMPORTANT: All Safety Devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to assure the safety of the
operators.
Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices make the
elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the process and/or
product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be constrained to follow a
prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble. Cobbles occur at random times
and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently
caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment, and
stock temperature are also causes of cobbling anywhere along the length of a bar in process in the rolling
train. The following recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe manner.


        1.1     Visibility and Communications

        Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations of
        pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment controlled from that
        point.

                A. Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight.

                B. Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper
                   lighting can be used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or cloud
                   the reflective surface and that the mirror location does not make it liable to breakage.

        1.2     Audible Communications

                Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as
                substitutes only when visual contact is not possible.

        1.3     Safety Stops

                Guide adjustments may be made only when the Mill Line is shut down. Mechanical or
                electrically operated stops must be used to block any stock from inadvertently entering into
                the mill.

OPERATION
IMPORTANT
Always read safety instructions and warnings for each system and component prior to operating and working on
machinery. Refer to Safety Section for general safety steps and procedures.

INTRODUCTION Refer to Figures 1 through 4 as a guide.

The Up and Down (pendulum) Shear is located after the billet pinch roll at the entry to stand 1H. The up
and down shear is a dividing shear consisting of a pair of knives.

The shear is used primarily to divide the billet in the event of a cobble in the mill, thus limiting the
amount of material fed into the cobble. It can also be used to manually control the length of the finished
product if required or for trial bars during mill set-up.

The Shear has one knife path for single strand operation. Upper and lower knife blades are mounted in
swinging frame assembly.

The shear is driven by a shaft which is connected through an air clutch and gearing to a continuously
running flywheel driven through a gearbox by a foundation mounted electric motor. Engagement of the
air clutch connects the shear shaft to the pinion drive. An air operated brake is used to stop the shear.

The up and down shear is designed for manual and automatic operation, operating stations (Main Pulpit
and Local) help test, monitor and adjust conditions that may occur through the automated system. Refer
to Table 1 for description of electrical devices used in the shear Assembly.

SYSTEMS AND COMPONENTS Refer to Figures 1 through 4 as a guide.

Note: For efficient operation of the shear, operators are required to constantly monitor all
components. Listed below are operation descriptions of the shear assembly and preventive
steps/procedures to help ensure optimal operation.

1.0     Up and Down Shear Assembly

A single strand up and down cut (pendulum) shear is mounted at the entry to stand 1H and is used for
emergency cutting of bar during rolling. This unit is used for cutting bars at the time of a cobble to limit
the amount of stock entering the intermediate mill.

The Shear has one knife path for single strand operation. Upper and lower knife blades are mounted in a
swinging frame assembly which allows pendulum motion when cutting a moving billet.

The shear is driven by a shaft which is connected through an air clutch and gearing to a continuously
running flywheel driven by a foundation mounted electric motor. The action of the rotating eccentric
shaft both raises the lower blade and lowers the upper blade to produce cutting action.

Engagement of the air clutch connects the shear shaft to the pinion drive. After each cut, the clutch is
disengaged and the shear stops quickly by setting an air operated brake.

Release of the air operated brake and engaging the air operated clutch accelerates the shear rapidly to
flywheel speed. After the knives have gone through the cut position, the clutch is disengaged and the
brake is set.

A spring loaded shock absorber is utilized at the base of the shear to provide a buffer when stopping the
pendulum motion of the shear following a cut.

A roller located ahead of the shear knives supports the billet entering the shear.

        1.1     Shear speed

        Shear speed reference is obtained from the previous billet roller table. Due to short throw of the
        shear knives, the bite angle is a significant factor in setting the shear speed.

        Shear speed must be set high enough above stock speed so that in the shearing process the
        pendulum motion of the lower knife frame assembly is not excessive.

        1.2     Air operated clutch and brake solenoids

        The air operated clutch and air operated brake are controlled by solenoid air valves. Energizing
        the clutch valve solenoid will apply air pressure to the clutch and cause it to engage.

        Energizing the air brake valve solenoid will exhaust air pressure to the brake and cause it to
        disengage.

       At the start of the shear cycle it is desirable to delay clutch engagement until the brake is released.
       This prevents unnecessary wear of the clutch and brake and prevents an unnecessary speed drop
       and the resultant motor loading. The time delay is initially set for 0.1 second.

       1.3     Shear Drive Gearbox Refer to figures 2 and 4.

       A gearbox which has an internal flywheel and external air operated clutch is utilized to drive the
       shear. There are two lower shafts and an upper shaft driven through a series of pinion gears.

       One of the lower shafts is the input shaft which is driven by a continuously running electric motor
       through a coupling. The input shaft also has a flywheel keyed to the shaft which provides inertia
       for the shear cutting action.

       The upper gearbox shaft is in fact two shafts which are concentric. The outer quill shaft is driven
       by a pinion gear from one of the lower shafts. Inside and concentric to the quill is the output
       shaft which has an external air operated clutch on the end opposite from the diving shaft. When
       the shear is at rest the air clutch is disengaged and an air brake on the output shaft stops the shaft
       from rotation. When a cut is initiated, the brake releases and the clutch engages to drive the
       shear.

       1.4     Scrap Chute

       A scrap bucket is located at the lower level beneath the shear. Cut pieces are directed into the
       bucket through embedded scrap chute.

       The bucket is removed and replaced with an empty bucket when full.

       1.5     Knife Gap

       The gap (in the horizontal plane) between the upper and lower knife blades is approximately 0.75
       mm when in new condition. To check the knife gap it is necessary to pry the knife holders apart.
       If this gap is found to exceed approximately 3 mm, it is necessary to determine the cause of the
       excess motion and repair or replace as required.

DEFINITION
Preventative maintenance is routine maintenance that, if performed as scheduled helps to keep the shear
assembly in good operating condition. Its primary purpose is to reduce the incidence of operating
failures, which require costly downtime for repairs. The recommended routine maintenance schedule
below represents the anticipated minimum requirements for maintaining the up and down cut shear.
IMPORTANT
Always isolate shutoff and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic and electrical power supply sources before
performing any repairs or maintenance. Read safety instructions and warnings for each system and
component prior to working on machinery. Refer to safety section in this manual.
Make sure the mill process stations have been shut down. Bleed and vent air pressure from air cylinders.
INTRODUCTION
Routine and Preventive Maintenance of the up and down shear assembly is required to ensure extended and
proper operation. Table 2 is provided as a quick reference guide for frequent periodic maintenance
requirements for the shear assembly. Refer to the General Maintenance section and to the applicable
manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance requirements and procedures of specific components. Refer
to Morgan assembly drawings as a guide.

CORRECTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS

DEFINITION

Corrective maintenance encompasses those repair procedures required to return the shear assembly to
satisfactory operating condition. Such repairs do not necessarily return the equipment to like-new condition.
Rather, the objective is to make it operational again as soon as possible. It is recommended to replace faulty
parts/components and sub-assemblies with new or previously refurbished spare parts/components and sub-
assemblies. Those parts removed may then be refurbished or reconditioned after the main equipment has
been returned to service.

INTRODUCTION

Corrective Maintenance of the up and down shear assembly as defined above, is intended to keep down time
at a minimum by replacing components and then dismantling and overhauling the removed component in a
service area away from the mill. Once refurbished, the component becomes a spare shelf part, ready to be
utilized as a replacement when needed.

No disassembly procedures are given herein of components being replaced. Components that require
overhaul/refurbishment should be maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Refer to

General guidelines and maintenance criteria are provided below when corrective maintenance of a
component or sub-assembly is required. These are minimum guidelines and should be used in conjunction
to the specific maintenance requirements from the component manufacturer.

Upon re-assembly, tighten all bolts, screws, nuts and fasteners in accordance with Morgan reference
drawings torque requirements. Torque specific components in accordance with the manufacturer’s
recommendations.

        WARNING: Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or disconnect
        all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any stored energy from

        WARNING: The up and down shear assembly is potentially dangerous and capable of
        inflicting severe bodily injuries. Before starting any maintenance task, comply with all
        company policies relating to safety. Also, be thoroughly familiar with the general

1.0     General Maintenance Criteria

The following is a list of maintenance actions to perform whenever dismantling equipment for repairs.

        1.1     Electric controls and power cables -- Before disconnecting any wiring that does not have
                plug-in connectors, make sure that color coding is clearly identifiable or tag each wire
                carefully for reference at re-assembly.

        1.2     Rigging parts for removal/replacement -- Many parts that make up this equipment are
                much too heavy to be handled by one person. Provide adequate rigging for lifting and
                supporting heavy parts before attempting to dismantle any equipment.

        1.3     Cleaning -- Clean all parts with a suitable solvent (mineral spirits, SAVASOL no.5, or
                equivalent) to remove all scale, grease, grime, or dirt. Use a clean wiper; do not use cotton
                waste. Air dry after cleaning

        1.4     Bearings and Sealing Surfaces -- Closely inspect bearings and sealing surfaces for signs of
                wear, nicks, scratches, gouges, or build-up of scale or other foreign substances. Replace
                bearings that show any signs of deterioration.

                To clean roller bearings, soak in clean solvent long enough to loosen any sludge, and then
                gently slosh each bearing around near the top of the container to dislodge all pockets of
                grease. Scrub away stubborn accumulations with a small brush that has bristles that do not
                break off. Do not spin dirty bearings, but rotate races slowly while washing and
                scrubbing.

              Rinse the bearings in clean solvent and air dry. Hold both races when blowing with clean,
              dry compressed air. Do not allow the air jet to spin the bearing; rather, turn each race by
              hand to expose all surfaces to the drying air. If the bearing is to be stored for later reuse,

              CAUTION: A bearing may be defective without the defect being visually evident.

              New bearings are packed with rust-preventative grease (or other protective coating) and

              lubricate immediately with Mobil 525 (or equivalent).

       NOTE: For ease of installation of bearings, heat the bearings at a maximum temperature of 121°C
       (250°F) in oil for one hour minimum, or in an electric furnace for 1-1/2 hours minimum, or by

       1.5    Oil Seals -- Replace all seals and gaskets that are removed or disturbed during disassembly
              procedure. Make sure seals seat properly upon re-assembly.

       1.6    Oil Passages -- Pressure flush oil passages and blow dry with compressed air. Make sure
              passages are clear of debris or blockage.

       1.7    Pre-lubrication prior to re-assembly -- Lightly lubricate all seals, bearings, bushings, and
              gears with oil before installation.

       1.8    Aligning parts during re-assembly -- Because of the weight of large parts, use guide studs
              during re-assembly to ensure proper bolt hole and /or dowel pin alignment.

       1.9    Clean all parts and inspect for scratches, cracks, burrs, flaking, pitting, scaling or
              discoloration of mating or load-bearing surfaces.

       1.10   Hand scrape any bushing that have not become out-or-round to remove burrs, small
              scratches or accumulated foreign substances. Replace any bushing showing gross
              deformation or cracking.

       1.11   Check shafts and pivot pins for straightness with v-blocks and dial indicator. It is possible
              to straighten bent shafts in a hydraulic press, but if spares are available, it is much better to
              replace the parts. Never straighten bent castings; replace them. Weld cracked steel
              castings only if no spares are available, but replace them whenever possible.

              lathe or grind them clean as long as the design tolerances are maintained. Otherwise,
              replace the parts.

        1.0      Safety Procedures

                    IMPORTANT: All Safety Devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to assure
                    the safety of the operators. Stay clear of machinery when in operation.

                    WARNING: CONSIDER ALL EQUIPMENT AS POTENTIALLY HAZARDOUS
                    AT ALL TIMES.

Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices make the
elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the process and/or
product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be constrained to follow a
prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble. Cobbles occur at random times
and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently
caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment,
and stock temperature are also causes of cobbling anywhere along the length of a rod in process in the
rolling train. The following recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe
manner.

       1.1     Visibility and Communications

       Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations of
       pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment controlled from
       that point.

               A. Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight.

               B. Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper
                  lighting can be used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or
                  cloud the reflective surface and that the mirror location does not make it liable to
                  breakage.

       1.2     Audible Communications
               Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as
               substitutes only when visual contact is not possible.

       1.3     Safety Stops
               Guide adjustments may be made only when the stand concerned is shut down.
               Mechanical or electrically operated stops must be used to block any stock inadvertently
               entered into the mill.

               Make sure mill is shut down and material can not run through the stand. Make sure that stops
               remain in place as long as personnel making adjustments are in the hazard area. For example,
               the snap shear will be closed ahead of the NTM.

               1.4     Alarms

               The alarms as described in the control specifications will have a warning system to alert the
               operators of a new oncoming front ends.

               A prominently located light board should be used with the warning system to indicate the
               strand in use and the progress of the stock in the mill.

       1.5     Restart - After a Housing Change, Roll Change, or Pass Change

               When a service operation is completed, the Mill must be restarted in the following
               sequence:

               1.      All mechanical stops will be moved.

               2.      All Guards will be in place.

               3.      All personnel will clear the hazardous area.

               4.      Permissive switches will be placed in “ALLOW RESTART” position and all
                       interlocks engaged.

               5.      Operators at control stations will be notified that the NTM may be restarted.

PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE AND INSPECTION GUIDELINES
1.0        Maintenance Guidelines
Required maintenance for specific components of the mill system may differ dramatically from each
manufacturer specifications. However, listed below are general maintenance procedures that should be
performed when any component or its subassemblies are dismantled for repairs. Refer to manufacturer’s
literature for more detailed operation and maintenance instructions for each specific component.

         1.1     GENERAL MAINTENANCE
                 A.  Cleaning: Clean all parts with a suitable solvent (mineral spirits, SAVASOL No. 5, or
                     equivalent) to remove scale, grease, grime or dirt. Use lint-free rags; do not use
                     cotton waste. Air dry after cleaning.
      WARNING: SOLVENTS USED FOR CLEANING CAN BE HARMFUL. FOLLOW THE SOLVENT
      MANUFACTURER'S RECOMMENDED SAFETY PROCEDURES FOR CLOTHING, VENTILATION,
      AND FIRST AID.
      WARNING: Petroleum based solvents are flammable and their vapors are harmful.


      CAUTION:         Be absolutely sure to maintain a clean environment during disassembly/re-
      assembly of all mill components. Dirt, scale or other foreign matter can have serious adverse
      affects on the close tolerance, precision equipment as well as causing contamination to the lube oil
      system.
                 B.    Housekeeping - To the extent possible, keep all service areas clean. Note: It cannot
                       be over-emphasized that the utmost care should be observed to keep dust and dirt out
                       of housings while they are being rebuilt to avoid the possibility of contaminating the
                       mill lube oil system.
         Caution: Do not allow oil, grease, water or dirt to accumulate on floors and/or around units
         undergoing repair, not only for the reasons stated above, but also for personnel safety.
                 C.    Bearing and Sealing Surfaces - Inspect bearing and sealing surfaces closely for signs
                       of wear, nicks, scratches, gouges and build-up of scale or other foreign substances.
                       Remove light scratches, gouges and scale by polish grinding the surfaces as long as
                       design tolerances are not exceeded. Deep gouges and nicks may require resurfacing,
                       machining and grinding to restore the units to their original condition and dimensions.
                 D.    Oil Seals and Gaskets - Discard all O-rings and gaskets removed or disturbed during
                       disassembly and replace with new ones.
                 E.    Internal Oil Passages - Pressure flush all internal oil passages and blow out the

               A. MAINTENANCE FACILITIES

               It is important that an area be provided where roll housings and other components of the
               No-Twist finishing mill can be disassembled, cleaned, inspected and reassembled in a
               clean environment. Figure 1 shows a suggested layout for finishing mill maintenance
               shop.

               The shop would have to have the capability of handling roll housings coming in for
               periodic inspection and rebuild, and those coming in for repair, as well as for the repair of
               other No-Twist mill components.

               so that the roll housings can be supported on their back plates with their thrust bearings
               projecting into the space.

               brackets, rolls and tapered sleeves, seal plates and flingers) will be readily accessible for
               removal.

               project down between the horses or into the space in the bench. The housing can then be
               further disassembled and parts taken to the component disassembly table for inspection
               and further disassembly.

               be required for drying parts after cleaning. From the tank the parts are passed to the table
               for disassembly of the eccentrics, roll shafts, etc. Final assembly would be made on the
               housing assembly table or saw horse.
