              C.    INSPECTION AND MEASUREMENT RECORDING
                    1. ROLL SHOP RECORDS
                    The principal maintenance problems that occur with mill equipment is the result of
                    conditions that develop slowly, taking many months to reach the trouble stage. Avoid
                    potential maintenance troubles by keeping records and acting on them.
                    Lube oil system maintenance is extremely important since the useful life of the oil film
                    bearings which support the roll shafts depends mostly on the cleanliness of the lubricating
                    oil. These bearings rapidly wear out and seize with contaminated lube oil. This has been
                    especially true of the front Cleveite bearings on previous mills.
                    Etch a shop identification number onto the outer face of each roll. Keep a corresponding
                    file card with pertinent data such as: date removed from mill, tonnage rolled, amount
                    removed in grinding and diameter after grinding. Wear rates can easily be calculated from
                    this data and are usually expressed in metric tons per 0.03 mm removed in dressing (on
                    diameter).
                    Also maintain roll breakage records. This information is important in the selection of roll
                    materials and manufacturers, and in assessing the performance of the mill. Analysis of roll
                    breakage records will pinpoint trouble areas.

                    Include the following information in roll breakage records: strand, stand, shaft (upper and
                    lower) pass configuration, type of break (radial, circumferential, piece broken out,
                    exploded, etc.), and any special circumstance that might have contributed to the break
                    (cobble, cold front end, loss of cooling water, etc.). If a radial crack has occurred, the
                    location of the crack is significant in any analysis; therefore make a sketch of each broken
                    roll for reference purposes.

                  2. TAKING LIFT TEST MEASUREMENTS
                  Taking in and out of-the-mill axial lift tests can be used as the determining factor for the
                  removal of roll housings to the Maintenance Shop. Measuring techniques become an
                  important part in determining the extent of wear occurring to the roll housing.
                  IMPORTANT: Many external factors are involved that affect the measurement and
                  reading of the endplay of the shaft. The ability to take measurements that are close to
                  the true value (ACCURACY) as well as the ability to consistently get the same readings
                  (PRECISION) is the key to obtaining data values that are reliable and dependable for
                  evaluation. Always take at least three measurements for each lift test to see if you can
                  repeat the test results in a consistent manner.

                  IN-THE-MILL LIFT TESTS (Radial and Axial)
                  In-the-mill lift tests must be used as the determining factor for the removal of roll
                  housings to the Maintenance Shop for roll housing rebuild. Follow a consistent test
                  procedure and carefully record the data gathered. Compare with previously recorded data,
                  as mentioned earlier, to provide the information needed to determine roll-housing
                  removal. Once the mill is operational, perform, record, and compare the lift tests on a
                  weekly basis and during housing rebuilds.

                  MAINTENANCE-SHOP LIFT TESTS (Radial and Axial)
                  Lift tests should be performed before disassembly and after completed rebuild of the
                  housing assembly (On each roll shaft of every housing removed from the mill). Keeping
                  accurate historical records of rebuilt housing assemblies is an important part of the
                  preventive maintenance program.

                  RADIAL ROLL SHAFT LIFT TESTS
                  The purpose of the radial lift test is to help prevent seizures to the clevite bearings. When
                  taking the lift test, the total lift of the roll shaft in the clevite bearing and the eccentric
                  cartridge in the roll housing is measured. Important Note: The removal of rolls and
                  tapered sleeves are required to conduct radial lift tests.
                  The use of Morgan’s special lifting tool allows for limited force to be used with the torque
                  wrench and provides for more accurate measurements. The clearance is measured in an
                  upward and downward direction. The values are recorded and compared with previous
                  existing data. Note: Excessive force when taking measurements can lead to damage to the
                  clevite bearings.
                   AXIAL ROLL SHAFT LIFT TESTS
                   The purpose of this test is to measure and record roll shaft endplay. Excessive roll shaft
                   endplay may cause a shoulder on the rod, or failure of the roll shaft ball thrust bearing.
                   Note: In the past, the fastest stand in any mill has been the most frequently prone to wear.
                   The two major sources of endplay are, excess wear on the rear eccentric locking bar and
                   improper mounting of the duplex ball thrust bearing.

                   The locking bar fits into a slot on the rear eccentric bearing cartridge and is bolted to the
                   roll housing rear plate. The locking bar is made slightly oversized and surface ground to
                   give a slight drag fit upon assembly (0,015 mm clearance). To minimize surface
                   conditions that could lead to premature wear, surface grind the locking bars rather than

       2.4     ROLL ASSEMBLY INSPECTION CRITERIA
       Each roll is mounted on a tapered steel sleeve, which, in turn, is assembled onto the tapered
       portion of the roll shaft. The assembly is designed so that while there is no radial clearance
       between the roll and sleeve or the sleeve and shaft, any radial clearance between these parts would
       cause excessive tensile stress in the roll when rolling loads are applied, leading to roll breakage
       and fretting wear of mating parts. Interference fit supplies the necessary friction for transmitting
       the rolling torque from the shaft to the roll.
       NOTE: The amount of interference fit must be limited so that safe levels of stress are not
       exceeded in the roll.

       The following are other possible causes of roll breakage. A simple cause is plugged water spray
       nozzles. Thermal failure has also occurred when the rolls became hot because the water was not
       on, or the hot steel of a cobble packed around a roll. Following a cobble the carbide will shatter if
       the rolls have not cooled sufficiently when the water is put on.
       A cold piece of steel left in the troughs before the reducing/sizing mill will break the rolls,
       usually starting at the first stands and continuing upon entering the reducing/sizing mill. The rolls
       will fracture in many places.
       Examination by roll manufacturers reveals that most roll failures to date have been radial breaks.
       These breaks are tension fatigue failures that start at either corner of the roll bore and progress across
       the cross section of the roll. The principal source of the tension stress is the separating force. This
       large load bends the roll locally, creating tension stress in the roll bore. The amount of stressing is
       dependent on the support given the roll by the tapered sleeve and shaft. The two major items that
       contribute to poor joint conditions are fretting corrosion and faulty roll shaft tapers.
                A.      ROLL COOLING
                Roll breakage and roll wear are both directly related to the effectiveness of roll cooling.
                Water is supplied from the main mill water system for cooling rolls. Since rolls would
                generally break if not water cooled, water pressure and flow must be maintained while
                steel is being rolled.
               Keep the water pressure interlock (in the water supply line to the reducing/sizing mill)
               operative at all times. If the water supply fails during rolling, keep the stands running without
               steel and allow the rolls to air cool slowly. Check for cracked or broken rolls after cooling.

               B.   HANDLING OF ROLLS

              Take reasonable care to avoid damage to the rolls. Do not hammer the carbide surface. Nicks
              or chips can cause failure. Transport rolls in compartment wooden boxes. Be sure each roll
              has an individual identifying number as well as a pass number as shown in the detail drawing.
              C. PASS FINISH
              There is often a tendency to machine carbide to produce a mirror-finish on the pass. To ensure
              positive gripping of the rod, a finish of 0,4 to 0,8 micrometer in the pass is specified. A finish
              in the neighborhood of 0,2 micrometer could result in slippage in certain stands.
              D.     PASS WEAR
              Some of the factors that influence pass wear are: grade of carbide, stock temperature, mill
              speed, cooling water analysis and pressure and rolling practice. In general, the tougher grades
              of carbide resist breakage well but have poorer wear rates than the harder grades. Grade
              selection is a compromise between hardness for good wear and toughness for low breakage.
              Higher stock temperatures lead to more rapid pass wear through heat checking. Stock
              temperature is influenced by mill speed and operating practices. Maintain water pressure near
              80 psi (5,62 kg/cm sq) to minimize heat accumulation in the roll.
              Suspended solids in the water, particularly sand, can erode the pass. A well maintained
              filtration system will minimize this wear. There is some evidence that acidic water attacks the
              matrix of the carbide and increases pass wear. Treatment of the water to improve its quality
              may reduce this type of chemical erosion.
              Several factors in operating practice influence pass wear. Carefully match roll diameters to
              plus or minus 0,05mm for each pair of rolls: and match the diameters of pairs of rolls in one
              line to within 1,5mm to minimize pull and eliminate push between stands. Too large a section
              entering the reducing/sizing mill can cause flutter of the section between the stands, as well as
              an excessive roll breakage. Therefore, carefully control the shape of the incoming section to
              the reducing/sizing mill and hold close to the diameter called for on the Diagram of Rolling
              Schedule.
              Wear rates generally fall within the range from 36 to 82 metric tons per 0,03mm on roll
              diameter, per groove, with the lower values in the early stands, and also in the leaders and
              finishing stand due to more frequent roll changing from the surface considerations.

              E.    ROLL GRINDING
              The number of tons rolled before redressing varies from stand to stand and from mill to mill.
              A typical range is from 907 to 2733 metric tons, although the leader and finisher may be
              changed every 635 to 726 metric tons.

              The pass surface and outside diameter of the rolls are diamond or electrolytically ground on
              special machines so that a pair of rolls is matched dimensionally to within plus or minus
              0,05mm. Both plunge grinding and profile grinding techniques are used to obtain pass shape.
              The outside diameters are generally ground separately on cylindrical grinders. After grinding
              the pass to just remove all visual signs of wear, grind off an additional allowance (0,25 to
              0,75mm on the diameter) to ensure that all oxidized material and thermal micro-cracks have
              been eliminated. Initial determination of pass wear and checking of final pass configurations
              are accomplished through the use of an optical comparator and/or steel templates.
              On multiple pass rolls, grind the passes together or separately, as needed. If grinding the
              passes together, cover the initially unused pass or passes with a protective coating to prevent
              corrosion while the first pass is being used
              F.    TAPERED SLEEVE
              The major cause of roll breakage is lack of support of the carbide roll ring. Its strength in
              compression during rolling is dependent on it being sufficiently supported by its supporting
              tapered sleeve. Therefore, to minimize premature roll breakage and maximize sleeve life it is
              critically important that good surface contact between shaft, sleeve, and roll be maintained.
              To help achieve this, cleanliness in assembly of these parts is essential. Clean the parts prior to
              assembly using dry cleaning agents such as Acetone or White Spirit. Avoid Kerosene’s and
              petroleum based solvents as they may leave an oil residue on the part surfaces acting as a
              lubricant and causing slippage between sleeve and shaft or sleeve and roll. Check the edges of
              the tapered sleeves for burrs or damage that may prevent a good surface contact. Carry out a
              visual inspection of the parts before every mill build. Check for the following conditions.

                  1. The clearance between the Inside Diameter of the roll and the Outside Diameter of the
                     sleeve barrel should not exceed .0015” ( 0,038 mm). Both of these dimensions can be
                     taken with ordinary micrometers so no special tooling is required. If size values are
                     OK, the surface finish of the sleeve OD must be considered. Drag marks due to local
                     seizure with resulting raised lines are cause for rejection. Minor high spots may be
                     stoned off but grinding of the OD is not recommended because an undersize or non-
                     concentric sleeve will almost certainly result.

                  2. Wear of the sleeve and shaft tapers are inevitable. As the two parts wear they tend to
                     seat together, Morgan recommends that individual sleeves be used with a particular roll
                     shaft over the life of the sleeve. If the surface finish of both tapers is not damaged wear
                     of the sleeve taper can be assessed by checking how far it goes onto the shaft taper.

       highest speeds, and approximately 1 year for 8” housings. Note: Many mills have extended the

              The principal maintenance problems that occur in the mill are the result of conditions that

              on them the bulk of the potential maintenance troubles can be avoided.

              B. ROLL SHAFT SEALS
              One source of oil contamination is the roll cooling water. It goes past a defective roll shaft
              seal and into the roll housing. The water carries scale and minerals. These seals should be
              inspected regularly. The seal inspections should be done about every two weeks. Regularly
              inspect for signs of water in the lube oil system (See Fluids Section). To help in detecting
              faulty seals each bevel gear drive has a water leg glass in the drain. If a distinct layer of
              water is seen in any of these glasses, the seals of that stand need to be changed.

              C. CLEVITE BEARINGS
              Figure 5 shows the two halves of the Clevite bearings. The principal preventive maintenance
              task is to eliminate the seizures on the heavily loaded work side bushings. These seizures
              occur when the oil film separating the roll shafts and the bushings break down. The resulting
              high rubbing friction causes a tremendous buildup of heat and melting of the white metal
              bushing surface occurs. On dismantling the roll housing, the seized bushings are usually
              fused to the roll shaft. Damage to the roll shaft and to the workside eccentric is severe. The
              roll housing front wall may also be damaged. Note: Housing bores usually collapse and
              are damaged after a bearing seizure. Housings cannot normally be reused until the bores
              have been repaired as part of a complete reconditioning and housing rebuild. Contact
              Morgan for rebuild information.

                1. EXAMINING USED CLEVITE BEARINGS TO JUDGE OIL CONDITION

                    When the oil is very clean, there is very little wear of the Clevite bearings. The Babbitt
                    overlay is just polished, making the surface in the contact area more reflective. There may
                    be a number of fine scratches in the surface. The lift of the Clevites with such a lubricating
                    oil system is unlimited.

                   In contrast, Clevites have been removed from mills with contaminated oil and the bearings
                   are worn into the copper layer. (See Figures 7 & 8) Another sign of a contaminated system
                   is deep surface score marks all the way into the copper. The Clevite bearings in these mills
                   are wearing out and should be replaced frequently. More to the point, the lube oil system
                   should be inspected and cleaned.

              2.   EXAMINING USED CLEVITE BEARINGS FOR EVIDENCE OF MISALIGNMENT

                    Some Clevite seizures occur shortly after the roll housing goes into the mill. When this
                    happens the housing rebuilding methods should be reviewed.

                    The work side bearing journals of the roll shafts are tapered. The drive side journals are
                    not. The need for the taper is caused by the overhung load which tips the roll shaft through
                    the oil film clearances. There would be misalignment at the work side bearing without the
                    taper. The elastic bending of the rather long, heavily loaded shaft would add to this
                    misalignment. The taper compensates for both misalignments. At the drive side bearing
                    the tipping slope and the bending slope are in opposite directions and the net misalignment
                    is small.

                    The early stands are much more heavily loaded than the stands at the high speed end
                    of the finishing mill.

                    The roll shafts are all of the same design and the work side journal taper was
                    selected to align the shaft and the bushing at the heavily loaded early stands where
                    the oil film is the thinnest. Figure 8 roughly shows the alignment situation at the
                    early stands and at the last stands. The Clevite bearing shown in Figure 7 has a
                    severe misalignment. It is believed that immediate seizures are the result of such
                    misalignments.

3.0    Scheduled and Planned Maintenance

INTRODUCTION

Routine and Preventive Maintenance of the roll housing assembly is required to ensure extended and proper
operation. Table 3 is provided as a quick reference guide for frequent periodic maintenance requirements
for the RSM assembly. Refer to the General Maintenance section of this manual and to the applicable
manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance requirements and procedures of specific components of
Finishing Mill Area. Refer to Morgan assembly drawings as a guide and for additional information.

DEFINITION

Preventive maintenance is routine maintenance that, if performed as scheduled, helps to keep the laying head
assembly in good operating condition. Its primary purpose is to reduce the incidence of operating failures,
which require costly downtime for repairs. The recommended scheduled and planned maintenance
procedures below represent the anticipated minimum requirements for maintaining the roll housing
assembly.

      IMPORTANT
      Always isolate shutoff and/or disconnect Water, Air, Hydraulic and Electrical power supply sources
      before performing any repairs or maintenance. Read Safety Instructions and Warnings for each system
      and component prior to working on machinery. Refer to Safety section of this manual.

OBJECTIVE

The objectives of scheduled and planned maintenance programs are to maintain the mill in a state of
optimum readiness and performance and to ensure continued high production rates. To gain these
objectives, the Maintenance Department should develop and prepare a periodic sequence of inspections
and preventive maintenance procedures for each rolling mill stand and its supporting systems. The objective
of corrective maintenance is to return equipment to operational status as quickly as possible following a
malfunction. Replacing faulty parts with spare new or refurbished parts will help keep the rod mill operating.

The most important single factors conducive to maximum mean-time-between-failure are lubrication
and temperature control. Consequently, the most important task of preventive maintenance is to ensure a clean
and adequate supply of lube oil at all times while the mill is running and to frequently lubricate those points
which require grease lubrication, and keep the oil cooling and heating systems functioning properly.

Based on many years of experience in the development and manufacture of rod and bar mills, Morgan has
developed a set of scheduled maintenance activities to provide guidance to the Maintenance Department in
developing and implementing a planned maintenance program of their own.

           3.1 ROLL HOUSING AND SEALS

               A. Make periodic inspections of roll housings in the maintenance shop.

               B. Take weekly in-the-mill lift test for every roll shaft and record the results. Use the lift
                  test to determine if the ball thrust bearings are deteriorating. The lift tests also will
                  determine if the deterioration warrants removal of the housing for rebuilding.

                   Whenever the mill is in operation be on the alert for oil leaking from roll necks,
                   indicating a defective seal. A drip would be tolerable, possibly indicating an
                   accumulation of oil in the flinger. Frequently check the water leg sight glass in the lube
                   oil drain piping from each roll stand. Signs of water in the lube oil system indicate a
                   defective roll neck seal. Replace defective seals immediately to prevent contaminating
                   the mill lube oil system.

                   All roll shaft seals must be replaced on a regular schedule. A monthly interval is
                   common. Such practices demonstrate the importance of preventing cooling
                   water into the lube oil system.

               C. Check that Cooling Water Sprays are working properly (aligned and not clogged).
                  Remove and Replace as necessary.

               D. Check Taper sleeves and roll fit every six months or as required. Inspect for excess wear
                  at every roll change.

           3.2 COUPLINGS

           The maintenance technician should inspect all mill couplings for erratic operation and
           unusual noise daily. Most couplings are of the sealed lubrication type. Fill Couplings with
           grease every 6 months. Refer to the manufacturer’s literature for applicable maintenance
           information and grease specifications to the specific coupling.

           3.3 BREATHERS AND FILTERS

           Every three months or sooner if conditions warrant, remove the breather/filter element and clean
           it in a suitable solvent. Air dry thoroughly and then reinstall. Dip element in lube oil before
           reassembling it in housing. Replace filter element if necessary. To reduce oil misting, Morgan
           recommends that the breathers be removed on the high speed stands and that the vent is piped to
           the oil drain.

4.0    INSTRUCTIONS FOR ROLL HOUSINGS
DEFINITION
Corrective maintenance encompasses those repair procedures required to return the RSM to satisfactory
operating condition. Such repairs do not necessarily return the equipment to like-new condition. Rather, the
objective is to make it operational again as soon as possible. It is recommended to replace faulty
parts/components and sub-assemblies with new or previously refurbished spare parts/components and sub-
assemblies. Those parts removed may then be refurbished or reconditioned after the main equipment has been
returned to service.
IMPORTANT
Always isolate shutoff and/or disconnect Water, Air, Hydraulic and Electrical power supply sources
before performing any repairs or maintenance. Read Safety Instructions and Warnings for each system
and component prior to working on machinery. Refer to Safety section.
INTRODUCTION
Corrective Maintenance of the Reducing and Sizing Mill as defined above, is intended to keep down time at
a minimum by replacing components and then dismantling and overhauling the removed component in a
service area away from the mill. Once refurbished, the component becomes a spare shelf part, ready to be
utilized as a replacement when needed.
Disassembly procedures are given herein of components being replaced. Components that require overhaul/
refurbishment should be maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Refer to the
manufacturers technical manual for maintenance and torque requirements and procedures of specific
components of the RSM.
General guidelines and maintenance criteria are provided in this section where corrective maintenance of a
component or sub-assembly is required. These are minimum guidelines and should be used in conjunction
with the specific maintenance requirements from the component manufacturer. Upon re-assembly, tighten all
bolts, screws, nuts and fasteners in accordance with Morgan reference drawings torque requirements. Torque
specific components in accordance with the manufacturer’s requirements.

WARNING: Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or disconnect all power
supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any stored energy from components. Restrain and
secure any moving parts of a component or system that could cause injury.

WARNING: The RSM Assembly is potentially dangerous and capable of inflicting severe bodily

         4.1    ROLL REMOVAL AND MOUNTING GUIDELINES
         The following roll removal and mounting procedures are designed only for use with the hydraulic
         tools and pump unit supplied by Morgan.

         The roll shop should be responsible for cleaning (Refer to “Cleanliness”) and assembling the rolls
         and tapered sleeves (Refer to “Using Spacers”) prior to being transported to the mill floor.

         IMPORTANT: It is recommended that each tapered sleeve be assigned to a given stand and
         remain with that stand throughout the life of the sleeve. In addition if multiple roll widths are
         used on a particular stand then a dedicated sleeve should also be assigned to that stand and roll
         width. This ensures that the contact between the sleeves and shaft taper is optimized.

         The assembled rolls and sleeves must be clearly marked with the pass to be used and the stand on
         which the roll assembly is to be mounted. The roll and sleeve should be individually wrapped in a
         protective covering to prevent dirt from adhering to the clean surfaces prior to mounting.

               A. HYDRAULIC ROLL MOUNTING & REMOVAL EQUIPMENT (Refer to Figures 9 and
               10 for guidance).

               The tapered sleeves are pressed onto the roll shaft using a hydraulic roll-mounting tool. A
               hydraulic tool is also used to remove the rolls. There are two different sets of tools
               used for these procedure, they are:

                        •     8" (230 mm) roll mounting and removal tools used for reducing stands.

                        •     6" (150 mm) roll mounting and removal tools used for Sizing stands.

                   1. ROLL MOUNTING TOOLS

                   The roll-mounting tool fastens onto the end of the roll shaft and applies an axial force to
                   the roll and tapered sleeve, which locks the roll onto the shaft.

                   The roll-mounting tool consists of two-pistons:

                    •       Piston #1 applies an axial force to the roll face to hold it against the flinger.
                    •       Piston #2 applies an axial force to the tapered sleeve, pressing it between the shaft
                            and roll bore thereby locking the roll in position.

                    2. ROLL REMOVAL TOOLS

                    The roll removal tool is locked onto the flange of the tapered sleeve and an axial force is
                    applied to the end of the roll shaft, which in turn releases the tapered sleeve.

                    3. ELECTRO-HYDRAULIC PUMP UNIT

                    The electro-hydraulic pump unit supplies the force to mount and remove the rolls.

               B. CLEANLINESS
               Cleanliness is the highest priority when mounting the rolls on the roll shafts. If dirt is present
               on the roll, sleeve and shaft assembly the wear process on the tapered sleeve and the roll
               pinion shaft is rapidly accelerated. As the taper on the shaft and sleeve wear the amount of
               contact between the two surfaces decreases, decreasing the amount of torque that can be
               transmitted and increasing the likelihood of roll slippage or breakage.

               To achieve the best results it is necessary to clean the pinion shaft tapers every time a roll is
               changed. This should be done using SCOTCH-BRITE or CROCUS CLOTH. Any oil residue
               should be removed by using non- petroleum based cleaning fluid. Clean, lint free type
               cleaning cloths should be used.

               If a roll is removed and then remounted on the mill without going to the roll shop, then the
               bore of the roll and the tapered sleeve should be cleaned before they are reassembled. The
               pinion shaft taper must also be cleaned as well as both faces of the roll as it is important that
               the roll contacts the flinger or the spacers, squarely. If dirt gets between the flinger and roll
               face or spacer then this can damage the roll neck seals as well as cause axial misalignment.

               C. USING SPACERS
               Carbide rolls can have between 1 and 4 grooves cut in the barrel depending on the width of
               the groove and the width of the roll.

               In order to maintain a constant pass centerline a spacer must be mounted between the roll face
               and flinger when using the outside grooves on a multi-groove roll. When placing the roll
               assembly onto the roll shaft ensure that the spacer is squarely positioned between the flinger
               and drive side roll face. When using the inside grooves on a multi-groove roll the spacer must
               be mounted on the work side of the roll face.

IMPORTANT: Always reference the running arrangement drawings provided with the equipment to
ensure that the correct parts are used for each roll assembly.

               C. Clean the roll shafts thoroughly using clean cloth and a non-petroleum-based solvent
                  to remove all dirt and oil film. Ensure the cleaning cloth used is clean and lint free.

               D. Ensure that the flinger is clean and seated correctly.

       For this procedure, assemble the spreader bar assembly to the ends of the roll shafts. Screw the
       special bolts into the end of each roll shaft until they bottom out in the tapped hole. It is only
       necessary to hand tighten these components. Slip the spreader bar onto the ends of the roll shafts
       and tighten the turnbuckle to push the roll shafts away from the centerline of pass, removing the
       clearance between the roll shaft and Clevite bore and the eccentric outside diameter and the front
       plate bore. Make the following dimensional checks with the spreader bar assembled as described
       above, but when it is necessary to adjust the position of the bronze nuts at the eccentrics or to turn
       the adjusting screw, remove the spreader bar. Refer to figure 25.
              o   For dimension "A", use a planer gage with a range of at least 225 mm or use a
                  175/225 mm inside micrometer.

              o   For dimension "B", use a 300/350 mm outside micrometer for the 230 mm housing.

              o   Measure dimension "A". Subtract dimension "A" from dimension "C" which is stamped on
                  Reference "X". Multiply the result by 2. Adjust dimension "B" to this value.

       NOTE: The dimension stamped on reference "X" is the exact measurement for that surface to the
       centerline of the housing bores.

                  calculated in step 3. Pass line setting is now complete.

The lift test is an important overall inspection of the film bearing clearances and should be made for each
rebuilt housing. Results should be recorded for future comparison when in the mill lift tests are
conducted as part of your preventive maintenance program

inspection sheet) should be set at the top of the shaft and should be perpendicular to the shaft surface. The total lift,
bearing clearance plus eccentric clearance, should also be measured and recorded.

7.0    Drive Housing
On the 230 reducing mill the drive housing is the link in the drive train between motor and rolls. The
drive housing contains two horizontal parallel non-integral bevel gear shafts, two bevel gear shafts at 45° to
the horizontal and 90° to each other, and two idler pinion shafts.
The two drive shafts mesh with the two bevel gear shafts at 45°. The shafts are supported by a single row
roller bearings on one end and angular contact single ball bearings on the other end. The gears and bearings
are pressure lubricated from the reducing/sizing mill lube oil system.
The two input shafts are coupled to a floating shaft via a rigid-flexible coupling. The opposite end of the
floating shaft couples to a clutchable drive box via a similar coupling. The input is transmitted by a non
integral gear.
The two bevel gear shafts provide a continuation of the drive train from the bevel drive shafts to the rolls.
Each bevel gear shaft is supported by rolling element bearings and each one is situated at 45° to the horizontal
and 90° to each other. Each bevel gear shaft is driven by the drive shaft through a pair of precision spiral
bevel gears. The ratio of the spiral bevels are designed to give the correct speed relationship between stands
based on the rolling schedule.
In addition to the drive bevel gear, the drive shaft also carries a helical gear that meshes with a similar pinion
carried on the idler shaft. These two helical gears form the drive for the roll shafts.
On the 150 sizing mill a major component of a roll unit is the combination drive. This drive also is the
link in the drive train between motor and rolls. The drive housing contains three horizontal parallel non
integral helical gear shafts (2 input shafts and 1 intermediate drive shaft), two bevel gear shafts at 45° to the
horizontal position and 90° to each other, and two idler pinion shafts enclosed in a pinion housing.
Each input shaft is coupled to one end of a floating shaft via a flexible-rigid coupling. The opposite end of
the floating shaft couples to a clutchable drive box via a similar coupling. The first input is transmitted by a
line shaft to a pair of non-integral helical gears coupled directly to a bevel output shaft. The second input
shaft is also a bevel output. All shafts are supported by a single row roller bearings on one end and a pair of
duplex ball bearings on the other end. The gears and bearings are pressure lubricated from the sizing mill
lube oil system.
The two bevel gear shafts mounted at 45° provide a continuation of the drive train from the bevel output
shafts to the rolls. Each bevel gear shaft is supported by roller and duplex ball bearings and is mounted at
45° to the horizontal and 90° to each other. The horizontal bevel shaft drives each bevel gear shaft
through a set of precision spiral bevel gears. The ratio of the spiral bevels is designed to give the correct
speed relationship between stands based on the rolling schedule.
In addition to the driven bevel, the driven shaft also carries a helical gear which meshes with a similar
pinion carried on the idler shaft. These two helical gears form the drive for the roll shafts.

      A.    DRIVE HOUSING SAFETY PROCEDURES

WARNING: BEFORE ATTEMPTING ANY MAINTENANCE TASK ON THE REDUCING/SIZING
MILL (RSM) COMPONENTS, CLOSE THE SNAP SHEAR IMMEDIATELY BEFORE THE RSM TO
PREVENT ACCIDENTAL ENTRY OF ROD INTO THE REDUCING/SIZING MILL. DE-ENERGIZE
ALL DRIVE MOTORS AND COMPLY WITH ALL COMPANY PROCEDURES RELATING TO
SAFETY.

WARNING: THIS EQUIPMENT IS CAPABLE OF INFLICTING SEVERE AND FATAL
INJURIES. ELECTRICAL VOLTAGES IN BOTH THE POWER AND THE CONTROL
CIRCUITS ARE CAPABLE OF RENDERING FATAL SHOCKS. OBSERVE ALL SAFETY
PRECAUTIONS.
       NOTE: Consider disassembly/reassembly of this equipment potentially hazardous at all times.
       NOTE: The disassembly/reassembly procedures following are for the complete removal and
       Disassembly of the drive housing. In actual service, and as time dictates, remove and disassemble
       parts only to the extent necessary to service individual parts.
       NOTE: The bevel gear shafts with idler shafts and the two parallel bevel gear shafts, may be
       Assembled and disassembled as separate units. In the following procedures, the bevel gear drive
       shaft with idler shaft assemblies will be referred to as the "upper housing" and the two parallel bevel
       gear shaft assemblies will be referred to as the "lower housing." Also, note that the (2) horizontal
       bevel gear shafts cannot be removed from the drive housing without first disassembling a portion of
       the upper housing.
       B.      REMOVING THE ROLL UNIT FROM THE MILL
               1.  Open the cobble guard cover to its fully open position.
               2.     Traverse the roll unit from the on line position to the off-line position.
                      This motion automatically disconnects the drive couplings from the drive unit. Drive
                      couplings are fixed to the main drive and will be supported in a cradle on the fixed
                      bed below the driveside platform. Service couplings automatically disconnect all
                      fluid and electrical services.

               3.     Inspect the main drive couplings. These couplings are pressure lubricated from the
                      main drive and roll unit lube systems. The couplings are enclosed within fabricated
                      metal housings which support the couplings when the roll units are disengaged and
                      also contain and drain the lube oil. Periodically, remove the enclosure top section and
                      inspect the lip type seal, oil spray tubes and coupling gear teeth. Inspect the oil seal
                      and sealing surface on the roll unit for damage. Replace the seal if necessary. Confirm
                      that the oil spray tubes are firmly in position and are pointed at the approximate
                      center of the gear teeth.

               4.     Located on each output shaft on the main drive is a liquid spring, O-ring, and
                      bushing. Inspect these items for damage or wear whenever drive couplings are
                      disassembled. See manufacturer’s literature for operating instructions and
                      maintenance procedure.

7.2    CLEANING, INSPECTION AND REFURBISHMENT
Using a suitable solvent, thoroughly wash then air dry all parts. Remove all pipe plugs from the lube oil
passages in the drive housing. Pressure flush the passages, then blow them out with compressed air. Inspect
the passages and remove all traces of scale, dirt or any other restrictive material or contamination. If pressure
flushing alone cannot remove the scale accumulation, use a drill, reamer or other suitable device to break it
loose. Blow the passage out again with compressed air. When the lube oil passages are clear, reinstall the
pipe plugs. Block all entry ports to guard against contamination until reassembly.

       WARNING:        BLOWING OUT THE LUBE OIL PASSAGES WITH COMPRESSED AIR CAN BE

       Remove all spray nozzles from their associated tubing and clean. Remove, inspect and clean the spray nozzle
       filters. If necessary, install new filters and nozzles. Inspect all old gaskets for damage or for having acquired a
       set whose condition would prevent effective sealing and compromise the oil tight integrity of the housing.
       Replace with new gaskets. Discard all O-rings and seals removed during disassembly and replace with spares
       at reassembly.
       Inspect gear teeth for wear or damage. If gears were nicked or burred during disassembly, remove by
       Light grinding or hand stoning. Do not remove material from tooth flanks that would change the shape
       of the tooth.
       The best maintenance practice is to replace any bearing that has been removed with a new one. If
       availability of spares makes this impractical, thoroughly clean and inspect bearings. If there are no
       visible signs of damage or excessive wear, it may be possible to reuse the bearing, at least temporarily.
       Inspect the mounting surfaces for the input shaft seals. These seals are labyrinth type made in two pieces.
       One half mounts to the bearing retainer and the other rides on the shaft spacer. Make sure the mounting
       surfaces are free of damage and wear. Repair or replace if necessary. After completely disassembling
       the drive housing, thoroughly clean the inside of the drive box and protect until time to reassemble.
       Cover all subassemblies with plastic or other grease resistant material while awaiting reassembly.
             A.     BEARING JOURNALS ON SHAFTS
             In the event of a bearing failure, it is possible for the inner race to be pulled around the shaft if the
             bearing seized, causing considerable wear on the bearing surface of the shaft. Replacement of the shaft
             is recommended. Consult Morgan for assistance.
             B.       DRIVE HOUSING (MACHINING)
             The drive housing, the front bearing mounting plates, the driven bevel shaft lower bearing mounting
             plates and driveside end plates are machined as an assembly. These parts are not interchangeable with
             similar parts in the other drive housings. If parts are damaged and require repair, consult Morgan for
             assistance.
             C.        GEARS
             Hand stone any minor damage to gear teeth, such as burr or bruise, carefully removing just enough
             material to correct the damage without reducing the contact area of the tooth.

D.         SETUP AND CHECKS OF SPIRAL BEVEL GEARS
           1.    Check the gear tooth backlash of the bevel gears:
CAUTION: THE PROCEDURES OUTLINED IN THE FOLLOWING STEPS ARE OF CRITICAL
IMPORTANCE. POOR GEAR CONTACTS DUE TO IMPROPERLY POSITIONED BEVEL GEARS
CAN RESULT IN BROKEN TEETH. CONTACTS THAT ARE HARD ON THE ENDS OF THE
TEETH CREATE HIGH STRESSES THAT CAUSE FATIGUE CRACKS.

                     a.      Lock the selected driven bevel gear shaft in the lower housing to prevent any rotation.
                     b.      Position the dial indicator on the heel end of the bevel gear tooth with the plunger
                             normal to the convex side of the gear tooth.
                     c.      Rock the driven bevel gear shaft gently thru the available clearance. Note the reading
                             on the dial indicator and compare it to the value etched on the face of the horizontal
                             bevel gear. Move either the horizontal bevel gear or the 45° bevel gear by adjusting
                             the shim pack thickness until backlash values agree.
                     d.      Determine the required shim change to correct the backlash. On the horizontal shafts,
                             remove the bolts holding the outboard bearing cartridge in place. Change the shims to
                             the new thickness and refasten the cartridge. On the 45° driven bevel shaft, remove the
                             outboard bearing retainer and split bearing cartridge. Adjust the shim thickness as
                             required. Reassemble and check the backlash again.

      NOTE: It may be necessary to move one or both of the bevel gear shafts to obtain the correct backlash.

          2.    Check the tooth contact pattern when backlash has been correctly set:

                 a.        Apply a thin film of red lead or brown gear compound to the load carrying faces of all
                           teeth on the smaller of the two bevel gears.

                 b.        Apply a thin film of Prussian blue to the load carrying faces of all teeth on the larger
                           bevel gear.

      NOTE: Color films must be thin to accurately reflect small errors in contact.

                 c.        Apply a braking load to the driven bevel shaft and turn the driving shaft through five
                           revolutions in the direction of rotation.

                 d.        Examine the patterns on the loaded side of the pinion teeth and compare them with those
                           appearing on the contact record card. Note: Each bevel set has its own record, so be
                           certain to match gear set numbers.

6.    CLEANING, INSPECTION, AND REFURBISHMENT

       Using a suitable solvent, thoroughly wash then air dry all parts. Remove all pipe plugs from the lube
       oil passages in the housing, pressure flush the passages, then blow them out with compressed air.
       Inspect the passages and remove all traces of scale, dirt or any other restrictive material or
       contaminant. If pressure flushing alone cannot remove the scale accumulation, use a drill, reamer or
       other suitable device to break it loose. Blow it out again with compressed air. When the lube oil
       passages are clear, reinstall the pipe plugs. Block all entry ports to guard against contamination until
       reinstallation.

WARNING:       PETROLEUM BASED SOLVENTS ARE FLAMMABLE AND THEIR VAPORS ARE
               HARMFUL.

WARNING:       BLOWING OUT THE LUBE OIL PASSAGES WITH COMPRESSED AIR CAN BE
               DANGEROUS. USE CAUTION WHEN USING COMPRESSED AIR.

       Remove all spray nozzles from their associated tubing and clean.

       Discard all O-rings and seals removed during disassembly and replace with new spares at reassembly.

       Inspect teeth of gears and pinions for excessive wear or damage. Remove slight scratches or burrs by
       grinding lightly.

       The best factory practice is to replace any bearing removed from its shaft with a new one from spares.
       If there are no visual signs of damage or excessive wear, it may be possible to reuse the bearing, at
       least temporarily.

       Inspect the sealing and bearing surfaces of the line shaft for signs of nicks, scratches, or any other
       defect that could impair the serviceability of these areas. Polish grind slight scratches to provide a
       suitable surface. Replace or repair shafts that have deep scratches or nicks.

       Cover all subassemblies with plastic or other grease resistant material while waiting to reassemble.

              DRIVE HOUSING (MACHINING)
             Each drive housing is machined as an assembly with both end plates bolted and doweled in
             place. End plates from other drive housings are not interchangeable. If any of these parts are
             damaged and require repair, consult Morgan for assistance.

        Accelerometers and cables for vibration sensing are all mounted internally in both the 230 Reducing

        drive housings, remove sensors and store them safely to prevent damage. Also, protect the internal
        cables and connectors from damage while disassembling and reassembling the roll units.

        sensor from its mounting surface. Almost all of the sensors can be accessed through removable
        inspection covers or upon removal of the roll housings.

8.0    Mill Drives

The mill drive is the main drive train between the motor and mill rolls. The drive box is made up of
four sections of fabricated steel construction bolted together. The lower section, the sub base plate,
is bolted directly to the foundation and grout embedded. The Drive input and the output is through
spline bore flexible couplings.

Each shaft assembly in the drive is supported on cylindrical roller bearings with the axial thrust controlled
by a deep groove ball bearing and THRUST ISOLATOR washers. Gear ratio changes are obtained
through clutches which either engage or disengage selected clutch gears. Servo motors operate the
clutches. The clutch gears are supported on tapered roller bearings with the correct end play obtained with
an adjustable locknut. The remainder of the gears are pressed and keyed on to the shafts.

Lubrication is supplied to each drive from the mill lubrication system which feeds to an internal piping
arrangement to pressure feed bearings, gear meshes and the driving half of the disengaging couplings. The
tapered roller bearings, however, which support the idler gears are pressure fed from the mill lubrication
system through a system of axial and radial holes in their respective shafts.

External Gear Drive Arrangement See E.C.S. 695-W for additional Main Drive Control information
The Reducing/Sizing Mill (RSM) stands are mechanically tied through an external gear drive arrangement and
driven by a single motor. The external gear drive consists of one gearbox with four (4) stages of gearing. The
stages are denoted as “A” (clutches 1 through 3), “B” (clutches 4 and 5), “C” (clutches 6 and 7) and “D”
(clutches 8 and 9).

The clutch positions are obtained by servo motors and are indicated by resolvers. By changing the clutch
configurations of each stage in the external gear drive the total reduction within the Reducing / Sizing Mill
(RSM) can be varied allowing multiple finished products to be rolled. Refer to ECS 695-W as a guide

Clutch Arrangement

All clutches (1 through 9) are 3-position, operated by servo motors. The clutch positions are: “A” (Clutch
fork location is towards RSM Housing), “B” (Clutch fork location is away from RSM Housing) and “N”
(Clutch fork is in neutral position) See Table 2 gear selection and corresponding clutch fork and servo motor
positions. When shifting, first bring the clutch to the neutral position and then move to the selected gear.
Important: Energize the two solenoid valves sequentially, not at the same time.

             1.    Make sure RSM drive is at complete stop and prevented from running.
             2.    Shift clutches to desired gear ratio in sequence. Note: If any clutch fails to engage, return it to
                   neutral position and proceed to the next clutch to be shifted.
             3.    At end of sequence, verify All Clutches are in desired operating positions. Note: Once clutch is
                   engaged it is assumed to be in position. Verify only at the end of the sequence.
             4.    If clutch is not in desired position, Jog motor at slow speed (5 r/min or less) for
                   approximately 0.5 seconds and repeat shifting procedure.

       8.1     DISASSEMBLY PROCEDURES
       The main drive box consist of similar components - fabricated housings, shaft assemblies
       (including gears) and clutch arrangements. The disassembly, reassembly and maintenance of these
       components are common and addressed in this section. For the following procedures it is assumed
       that all of the bearings, seals and gaskets are being replaced (mandatory replacement). Refer to
       Figure 38 for housing shaft assembly designation and location arrangement.
       CAUTION: The housing sections are enormously heavy. Use extreme care when rigging and
       lifting housing assemblies. The Upper and Intermediate housing sections may be removed
       together as one unit if adequate lifting cranes are used. DO NOT attempt to remove more than
       one housing, if load capacity of crane is exceeded.
       CAUTION: In order to remove shaft and gear assemblies from the mill drive, the housing
       sections must be removed. Disconnect all bearing retainers, piping, wiring and external
       components as needed to remove the applicable housing sections.
              A..        REMOVING SHAFT ASSEMBIES FROM DRIVE BOX
              CAUTION: Shaft assemblies are exceedingly heavy. Use extreme care when rigging and
              lifting shaft assembly from drive housing.
                         1.       With the drive box isolated from all services (hydraulic, air and electric) and the
                                  clutch in the neutral position - remove the bolts from the bearing cartridges.
                         2.       To remove the drive box housings - remove the bolts from the bearing
                                  caps/retainers and the bolts where the housings splits.
                         3.       Remove the coupling bolts and split the coupling.
                         4.       Disconnect the external feed pipe from the oil nozzle.
                         5.       Remove the shaft assembly from the drive box and move it to a clean area
                                  (service area) for disassembly and reassembly.
              B.         DISASSEMBLY OF SHAFT COMPONENTS Refer to Figures 43 through 48 for
                         specific shaft assemblies.
              The shaft assembly must be in a horizontal position to begin disassembly and carefully
              blocked to prevent movement or damage to components. To replace all bearings on this
              shaft it is necessary to remove the gears, bearing block, bearing cartridges, sleeves and
              coupling. To accomplish this certain procedures should be followed:
                     •        Ensure that the shaft assembly is in a clean area before beginning to disassemble.
                     •        Wear gloves when handling parts such as gears and bearing cartridges etc.
                     •        Wire shims together with the part with which they were removed.
                     •        Wherever possible, use a puller on the inner race when removing bearings from shafts.
                     •        Use a hydraulic puller to remove bearings.
                     •        Do not attempt to loosen the adjustable locknuts, holding the clutchable gears
                              before the clamp screws have been slackened off.

       8.2     CLEANING AND INSPECTION

       Using a suitable solvent, thoroughly wash then air dry all parts. Remove all set screws (orifices)
       from the lube oil passages in the shaft, pressure flush the passages, then blow them out with
       compressed air. Inspect the passages and remove all traces of scale, dirt or any other restrictive
       material or contaminant. When the lube oil passages are clear, reinstall the set screws, with LOCTITE.
       Block the entry port on the end of the shaft to guard against contamination until reinstallation.

       WARNING: PETROLEUM BASED SOLVENTS ARE FLAMMABLE AND THEIR VAPORS
       ARE HARMFUL.

       WARNING: BLOWING OUT THE LUBE OIL PASSAGES WITH COMPRESSED AIR CAN
       BE DANGEROUS. USE CAUTION WHEN USING COMPRESSED AIR.

       Discard all gaskets, THRUST ISOLATOR washers or seals removed during disassembly and replace with
       new spares at reassembly. Inspect teeth of gears and pinions for excessive wear or damage.

       The best factory practice is to replace any bearing removed from its shaft with a new
       one from spares. If availability of spares makes this impractical, thoroughly clean and
       inspect the bearings. If there are no visual signs of damage or excessive wear, it may be
       possible to reuse the bearing, at least temporarily.

       Inspect the sealing and bearing surfaces of the line shaft and sleeves for signs of nicks,
       scratches, or any other defect that could impair the serviceability of these areas. Polish
       grind slight scratches to provide a suitable surface. Replace or repair shafts that have
       deep scratches or nicks in these areas.

       Cover all sub-assemblies with plastic or other grease resistant material while waiting to
       reassemble.

               A. BEARING JOURNALS ON SHAFTS

               In the event of a bearing failure, it is possible for the inner race to be pulled
               around the shaft if the bearing seized, causing considerable wear on the bearing
               surface of the shaft.

               B. GEARS

               Hand stone any minor damage to gear teeth, such as a burr or bruise, carefully
               removing just enough metal to correct the damage without reducing the contact
               area of the tooth.

               C. CLUTCH PLUNGER

               Only if the plunger is to be replaced should it be removed and the threads in the hub cleaned.

             A. TORQUE REQUIREMENTS
             Components of each shaft assembly need to be reassembled and tightened to specific torque

             B. SHAFT ASSEMBLY
             Before starting the shaft assembly:
                  •   Verify all measurements of shaft and housings for proper design/rebuild specifications.
                  •   Clean ALL mating surfaces, shaft seats and bearing & gear bores with mineral spirit cleaner.
                      Apply a very thin coat of light machine oil (ISO VG 32) with a clean lint free cloth to the shaft
                      seats and bearing bores.
                  •   Make sure all preservative has been cleaned off the entire bearing using a petroleum based
                      solvent.
                  1. Installation and Adjustment for clutchable helical gears.

                  Start with the shaft in a supported vertical position, to allow access to the bearing journal
                  nearest to the clutch splines.

                    a. Install with installation tools, the bearing cups and outer races into the bores of the
                        clutchable gears. The outer races are a transitional fit in the bores and it may be

NOTE:    The tapered roller bearings are under a statically loaded condition when transmitting torque
         and are unloaded when there is any differential speed between the gear and the shaft. The

               b. Once the outer races are installed, apply a thin film of ISO VG 100 lubricating oil to
                  each outer raceway.

               c. The bearing inner races (cones) are an interference fit on the shaft so it will be
                  necessary to heat them (230° F to 250° F) using a bearing heater or oven. The shaft
                  and the bearing bore are to be free of any grease or oil. After heating, assemble the
                  inner race on the shaft being sure that it is properly seated against the shaft

               d. Next assemble the gear complete with both bearing outer races (cups) onto the shaft
                  so the gear rests on the bearing race previously installed against the shoulder.
               e. The heated second bearing inner race can now be installed using shim stock (about 0. 1 mm
                  thick) between the rollers and the outer race in the gear to prevent the bearing from
                  completely seating. Note: If allowed to seat tightly against the outer race in the gear, all the
                  bearing end play would be removed and correct seating of the bearing would be very
                  difficult to achieve.
                  f. Allow the assembly to cool to room temperature (24 hours) before proceeding with the
                     final bearing setting.
                     When the assembly has cooled, remove the shim stock from between the rollers
                     and the outer race and install the adjustable locknut until it contacts the bearing.
                     Note: The threads both on the shaft and in the locknut are to be free from oil and
                     grease).

                  g. Using a dial indicator with it's stylus contacting the top face of the gear to measure
                      the relative movement (run out) between the gear and the shaft, check the bearing end
                     play by pulling up on the gear while rotating it to make sure the rollers are correctly

        THAT THE SHAFT IS ADEQUATELY SUPPORTED AND RESTRAINED AGAINST
        ROTATION. IT WILL BE HELPFUL TO USE A SUITABLE SPANNER WRENCH TO
        TIGHTEN THE LOCKNUT.

   WARNING: THE POWER SUPPLY TO THE STEPPER MOTORS MUST BE SHUT OFF

             The clutch arrangement (gear ratio change arrangement) works through the engagement of
             internal splines in the splined coupling with the external splines on the shaft and the external

             on the drive box, is activated. Perform any maintenance on the clutch with the spherical rod

                      The splines (internal and external) should be given the same consideration as

                      contact area of the spline faces and to assure no interference between mating
                      parts during gear changes.

                     Maximum. Insert the shaft into fork until shaft flange seats on bore shoulder.

       WARNING: Do not exceed equipment ratings. Never attempt to press on or lift a load weighing
       more than the capacity of the cylinder. Overloading causes equipment failure
       and possible personal injury.

       Never set the relief valve to a higher pressure than the maximum rated pressure of the pump.
       Higher settings may result in equipment damage and/or personal injury.

       WARNING: The system operating pressure must not exceed the pressure rating of the lowest
       rated component in the system. CHECK pressure gauges in the system to monitor operating
       pressure.
       CAUTION: Avoid damaging connected hoses. Avoid sharp bends and kinks when routing
       hoses. Using a bent or kinked hose will cause severe back-pressure. Sharp bends and kinks will
       internally damage the hose leading to premature hose failure.

       Do not drop heavy objects on hose. A sharp impact may cause internal damage to hose wire
       strands. Applying pressure to a damaged hose may cause it to rupture. DO NOT lift or pull
       equipment by hoses or couplers. Rig and secure equipment for safe transport.

       CAUTION: Keep hydraulic equipment away from flames and heat. Excessive heat will soften
       packing and seals, resulting in fluid leaks. Heat also weakens hose materials and packings. For
       optimum performance do not expose equipment to temperatures of 65°C [150°F] or higher.
       Protect all hoses and cylinders from weld spatter and extreme heat.

       DANGER: Do not handle pressurized hoses. Escaping oil under pressure can penetrate the
       skin, causing serious injury. If oil is injected under the skin, see a doctor immediately.

       WARNING: Only use hydraulic cylinders in a coupled system. Never use a cylinder with
       unconnected couplers. If the cylinder becomes extremely overloaded, components can fail
       catastrophically causing severe personal injury. Never bleed system to exposed atmosphere.

       WARNING: Immediately replace worn or damaged parts. Never Bypass safety devices!
       IMPORTANT: Qualified trained technicians must only service Mill equipment.

       WARNING: Do not use electrical equipment in an explosive atmosphere. Adhere to all local
       and national electrical codes. Keep hands clear of moving parts and pressurized hoses.

1.0     Safety Procedures

                    IMPORTANT: All Safety Devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to assure
                    the safety of the operators. Stay clear of machinery when in operation.
                    WARNING: CONSIDER ALL EQUIPMENT AS POTENTIALLY HAZARDOUS
                    AT ALL TIMES.
Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices make the
elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the process and/or
product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be constrained to follow a
prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble. Cobbles occur at random times
and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently
caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment, and
stock temperature are also causes of cobbling anywhere along the length of a bar in process in the rolling
train. The following recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe manner.
        1.1     Visibility and Communications
                Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration.
                Locations of pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of
                equipment controlled from that point.
                A. Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight.
                B. Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper
                   lighting can be used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or cloud
                   the reflective surface and that the mirror location does not make it liable to breakage.
        1.2     Audible Communications
                Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as
                substitutes only when visual contact is not possible.
        1.3     Safety Stops
                Guide adjustments may be made only when the Mill Line is shut down. Mechanical or
                electrically operated stops must be used to block any stock from inadvertently entering
                into the mill.
                Make sure mill is shut down and material can not run through the stand. Make sure that
                stops remain in place as long as personnel making adjustments are in the hazard area. For
                example, the snap shear will be closed ahead of the NTM.
        1.4     Alarms
                The alarms as described in the control specifications will have a warning system to alert
                the operators of new oncoming front ends.
                A prominently located light board should be used with the warning system to indicate the
                strand in use and the progress of the stock in the mill.

Intelligent Pinch Roll                                                                                         Operation and
At Laying Head                                                                                        Maintenance Instructions

Note: For efficient operation of the pinch roll, operators are required to constantly monitor all
components. Listed below are operation descriptions of the Pinch Roll and preventive steps and
procedures to help ensure optimal operation.

SYSTEMS AND COMPONENTS Refer to Figures 1 through 8 as a reference.
1.0     Pinch Roll Cover Assembly
A protective hood covers the pinch rolls during operation. The cover is opened and closed manually. The
Cover Closed proximity switch indicates the closed position. Note: The cover must be closed to run the
pinch roll.

In order for the pinch rolls to operate, certain interlocking conditions must take place. In addition, other
interlocking steps and procedures are required from the Laying Head. Refer to other interlocking steps and
procedures for existing systems and components that may effect the operation of the entire mill. The
following interlocks steps and procedures are required in both manual and automatic mode for operation of
the Pinch Rolls. INTERLOCK NOTE: The pinch roll drive is allowed to operate only when the cover is
fully closed, as indicated by the proximity switch.
2.0     Pinch Rolls
The pinch roll consists of an upper and lower roll which are driven through an internal speed increaser by a
speed regulated motor. Rolls are closed by servo motor with force controlled by a torque regulator. When
closed, rolls grip the product and permit the motor to exert a pull on the product or control speed of rod
during tailout.

The regulator set points, high and low, are adjusted from the pulpit. Adjustment of the "PINCH" force
prevents marking the rod by the rolls, but maintains sufficient force so that the roll can establish required rod
tension or speed without slipping.

Rolls are opened by servo motor with speed regulator. Linkage within the pinch roll unit causes each roll to
move by equal amounts, but in opposite directions.

3.0     Pinch Roll Open and Close
There are three automatic operating modes for the pinch roll unit selectable by operator. Operating logic for
the three modes is as follows:
 Mode                      Action                                          Comments
                                                    Commonly used in mills where it is not necessary to
  Tail     CLOSE - tail end at CD/HMD1              use the pinch rolls to maintain tension in the water
  Only     OPEN - tail end at pinch rolls           boxes. The pinch roll is only required to obtain good
                                                    tail end control.
           CLOSE - front end at pinch rolls         Commonly used when rolling ribbed rod products.
  Head     OPEN - 5 seconds after closing           The pinch rolls are used to prevent a cobble when the
 & Tail CLOSE - tail end at CD/HMD1                 water is switched on and to obtain good tail end
           OPEN - tail end at pinch rolls           control.
                                                    It is used to ensure that a small amount of tension is
 Entire CLOSE - front end at pinch rolls            maintained through the water boxes and in order to
  Bar      OPEN - tail end at pinch rolls           maintain good tail end control. A stable, well-tuned
                                                    control system is required.

By Morgan Construction Co.                                                                                     Page 8
15 Belmont Street, Worcester, MA 01605                                                                          Rev A
www.morganco.com
                                      Copyright © Morgan Construction Company   All Rights Reserved

Intelligent Pinch Roll                                                                                         Operation and
At Laying Head                                                                                        Maintenance Instructions
In addition to the normal closing signals above, rolls are signaled to close whenever scrap cutting is
initiated when rod is present at the NTM Exit HMD, RSM entry HMD1. This is because the new tail end
generated by the scrap cutting action does not pass in front of CD/HMD1 and it is desirable to close the
rolls to control the tail rings.

4.0     Pinch Roll Tension Regulator
Tension is automatically applied to the rod when the pinch roll closes onto the rod with the tail end still in
the delivery stand of the RSM. The amount of torque applied is operator adjustable using the "TORQUE
LIMIT" control, and is used to directly control the rod tension. Tension feedback is actual motor torque
minus no-load torque required to overcome friction and windage.

Normally pinch roll motor is running with max current limit allowed to accelerate or to decelerate the pinch
roll. Lowering current limit is required when the pinch roll is closed, and product is still in the mill delivery
stand. Pinch roll current limit can be set at a lower level before rolls close on product.

Speed “HOLD” on tail ends freezes speed correction to the pinch roll to obtain tension. "HOLD" prevents
rolls from accelerating to lead speed when tail end clears the finishing stand yet maintains tension until tail
end exits finishing stand. “HOLD” is turned on before tail end is leaving No-Twist® Mill. Speed hold
mode is turned off after pinch rolls are told to open. Speed correction of tension regulator to be displayed
in pulpit.

Positive indication of slip; an alarm is activated if the rolls slip on the rod which is detected by the speed
feedback without dropping at current limit setting.

Incorrect settings for tension control are evidenced as follows:

        Too Low:
        The motor cannot maintain tension between the pinch rolls and the last rolling stand. The rod will
        be fluttering in the water boxes and recovery zones. The motor amps are very low. The pinch rolls
        cannot control the tail ends effectively.

        Too High:
        The pinch rolls are always trying to maintain the preset lead speed setting. When the pinch rolls are
        closed the “pinch rolls slipping” alarm is displayed. When rolling small products the laying head
        ring pattern changes as the pinch rolls are closed. Tail ends tend to be uncontrolled.

Note: It is also important to understand that it will be necessary to make small adjustments to the
original data settings in order to obtain the best operating conditions. The final settings will ultimately
depend on operating speed of the mill, material grade and temperature of the material at the laying head.

5.0     Tail End Speed Step Down

The tail end speed step down function is used to slow down smaller, high speed products to maintain or
reduce the ring diameter as the product tails out of the laying head. This is required to minimize the
tendency for the tail end to exit the laying head in an uncontrolled manner.

Initially set for 1% speed slowdown, the speed is operator adjustable.

At Laying Head                                                                                         Maintenance Instructions
Stepdown of speed occurs when tail end clears the RSM delivery stand as indicated by a tracking system
and stepdown reference is greater than zero percent.

A step speed change is applied to the pinch roll drive only. The Laying Head is not required to slowdown at
this moment. There is no speed match issue for tail end slowdown between pinch roll and laying head.

The pinch rolls are to decelerate until the tail end clears the pinch roll.

Pinch torque switches from LOW to HIGH before the rod leaves the NTM® unless stepdown is set at zero
percent. An adjustable ramp is required when transitioning between high and low speed, this should not be a
step function.

6.0     Tail End Speed Up

The Tail End Speed Up function speeds up larger, slower speed products to provide sufficient energy for rod
tail end to clear the laying head.

The Reducing/sizing mill (RSM), pinch roll and laying head accelerate at the same rate, up to max. 30 m/sec.
This reduces the possibility of ring size deviation on the tail end of a bar. Acceleration rate is calculated so
delivery speed is reached just as tail end arrives at pinch roll. Pinch rolls can accelerate up to maximum of
rated motor torque.

For speed synchronization among the RSM, pinch roll and laying head, the pinch roll control will calculate
the ratio of pinch roll speed correction (actual speed : hold speed) before tail out of NTM in real time. This
ratio is used for the RSM and laying head to correct speed in real time.

One analogue input is required in the RSM and Laying Head speed control. This can be set to 10 volt = 50%
speed correction. This analog input is set to zero volts while the laying head is not required to speedup. So the
RSM and laying head is applied the normal speed reference without any speed correction to laying head drive
while it is not in speedup mode.

The speed-up delivery speeds are adjustable in the logic to suit the rolling speed. This is not an operator-
adjustable parameter but shall be easily modified by turn supervisor.

Typical values are:               < 16 mm -               not used
                                  16 mm -                 16 m/sec
                                  18 mm -                 22 m/sec
                                  20 mm -                 24 m/sec

Acceleration starts when tail end clears the mill delivery stand of NTM. This is determined by tracking tail
end through the NTM®. Pinch pressure switches from LOW to HIGH just as acceleration begins. This
function can be switched ON if rolling speed is less than the speed-up preset and the Speed-Up selection
switch is ON.

Tail end at pinch roll turns off tail end speedup function.
