       1.2    Monitoring
       The Laying Head Area is designed for manual and automatic operation. Operating stations help test,
       monitor and adjust conditions that may occur through the automated system.
       Note: For efficient operation of the Laying Head, operators are required to constantly monitor
       all components and control systems

       A.     Monitor Main Control Pulpit. Refer to the following switches and indicators for proper
              operation.

              1. Laying Head speed reference selection, NORMAL – TEST: When the NORMAL
                 position is selected, the laying head speed follows the rod speed with an adjustable
                 plus/minus trim. In the TEST position, the laying head speed follows a preset
                 reference.

              2. Laying Head Speed Adjustment: The Laying Head speed adjustment ranges from a Plus
                 10% to a Minus 5%. Speed adjustment rate precision of 0.1% increments is required.
                 Speed adjustments are to be made with either a joystick or separate, discrete RAISE and
                 LOWER pushbuttons. These are NOT to be “soft” devices shown on an MMI screen and
                 accessed via a mouse or keyboard. The operator must have real-time precise adjustment
                 control as the ring pattern is observed via the television camera.

              3. Laying Head Speed Indicator: Indicates the speed in m/sec.

              4. Laying Head RUN/STOP with indicator: Indicates the operating mode.

              5. Wobble selection TEST – OFF – AUTO: In TEST mode position, the wobble is turned
                 on without the rod traveling through the mill. In OFF position, there is no wobble
                 operation. In AUTO position, the wobble turns on and off by rod front end and tail end
                 signal detection.

              6. Wobble Amplitude Adjustment: The amplitude adjustment ranges from 0% to 10%
                 with a minus value limit of 5%.

              7. Wobble Rate Adjustment: The rate adjustment ranges from 0% to 100% (maximum
                 accelerate/decelerate).

              8. Laying head ampere load indication, positive and negative.

              9. HMD (Hot Metal Detector) indicator and TEST:

                  NTM Entry HMD indicates rod entering NTM.
                  NTM Exit HMD indicates rod exiting NTM.
                  The Laying Head HMD indicates rod traveling through the laying head.

              10. Unbalance detector monitor with ALARM and SHUTDOWN settings. The ALARM
                  mode is set at 7 mm/sec peak velocity and SHUTDOWN mode is set at 10 mm/sec
                  peak velocity which initiates an automatic shutdown (signal must be active for 5
                  seconds).

                  gaps are greater than 5 seconds, the purge will purge an empty pipe until the new front
                  end arrives. In any case, the purge should be on before the new front end arrives and
                  remain on for 15 seconds.

PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS
Preventative maintenance is routine maintenance that, if performed as scheduled, helps to keep the laying head
assembly in good operating condition. Its primary purpose is to reduce the incidence of operating failures,
which require costly downtime for repairs. The recommended routine maintenance schedule below represents
the anticipated minimum requirements for maintaining the laying head. Table 2 is provided as a quick
reference guide for frequent periodic maintenance requirements for the laying head assembly.

Special Attention should be given to the deflector plates and pipe support when inspecting for
cracks and abnormalities. Use the Laying Head Addendum as a guide for inspection criteria and
repair procedures for the deflector plates and pipe support.
Important Note: Due to the high temperature condition that the laying head is exposed to, additional
“RAPID” cooling through an external water supply (i.e. manually hosing down of deflector plates
and pipe support assembly) is NOT recommended. Deterioration, cracking and weakness of
components will occur, affecting the normal life expectancy of the laying head.


IMPORTANT

Always isolate shutoff and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic and electrical power supply sources
before performing any repairs or maintenance. Read safety instructions and warnings for each system
and component prior to working on machinery.

Make sure the mill process stations in front of laying head assembly have been shut down.

WARNING:         Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or disconnect all
power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any stored energy from components.
Restrain and secure any part or system that could cause injury.

WARNING: The laying head assembly is potentially dangerous and capable of inflicting severe
bodily injuries and fatal electric shock. Before starting any maintenance task, comply with all
company policies relating to safety. Also, be thoroughly familiar with the general safety
requirements.

CORRECTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS
DEFINITION

Corrective maintenance encompasses those repair procedures required to return the laying head assembly to
satisfactory operating condition. Such repairs do not necessarily return the equipment to like-new
condition. Rather, the objective is to make it operational again as soon as possible. It is recommended to
replace faulty parts/components and sub-assemblies with new or previously refurbished spare

1.0     General Maintenance Criteria

The following is a list of maintenance actions to perform whenever dismantling equipment for repairs.

        1.1     Electric controls and power cables -- Before disconnecting any wiring that does not have
                plug-in connectors, make sure that color coding is clearly identifiable or tag each wire
                carefully for reference at re-assembly.

        1.2     Rigging parts for removal/replacement -- Many parts that make up this equipment are much
                too heavy to be handled by one person. Provide adequate rigging for lifting and supporting
                heavy parts before attempting to dismantle any equipment. Refer to Morgan rigging and
                lifting procedures and Figure 9 for the deflector plate and pipe support assembly removal
                and installation.

        1.3     Cleaning -- Clean all parts with a suitable solvent (mineral spirits, SAVASOL no.5, or
                equivalent) to remove all scale, grease, grime, or dirt. Use a clean wiper; do not use cotton
                waste. Air dry after cleaning.

        1.4     Bearings and Sealing Surfaces -- Closely inspect bearings and sealing surfaces for signs of
                wear, nicks, scratches, gouges, or build-up of scale or other foreign substances. Replace
                bearings that show any signs of deterioration.

                To clean roller bearings, soak in clean solvent long enough to loosen any sludge, then gently
                slosh each bearing around near the top of the container to dislodge all pockets of grease.
                Scrub away stubborn accumulations with a small brush that has bristles that do not break off.
                Do not spin dirty bearings, but rotate races slowly while washing and scrubbing.

                Rinse the bearings in clean solvent and air dry. Hold both races when blowing with clean,
                dry compressed air. Do not allow the air jet to spin the bearing; rather, turn each race by
                hand to expose all surfaces to the drying air. If the bearing is to be stored for later reuse,
                lubricate and wrap it in wax paper or other grease-proof wrapping.

                CAUTION: A bearing may be defective without the defect being visually evident: replace
                any bearing removed during any maintenance task with new bearing at re-assembly.

                New bearings are packed with a rust-preventative grease (or other protective coating) and
                wrapped in grease-resistant paper before they are shipped. Do not unwrap the bearing until
                time for installation. Unwrap and thoroughly wash the new bearing and air dry. Pre-
                lubricate immediately with Mobil 525 (or equivalent).

                NOTE: For ease of installation of bearings, heat the bearings at a maximum temperature
                of 121°C (250°F) in oil for one hour minimum, or in an electric furnace for 1-1/2 hours
                minimum, or by bearing induction heater for 15 minutes minimum.

        1.5     Oil Seals – Replace (Mandatory Replacement) all seals, O-rings and gaskets that are
                removed or disturbed during disassembly procedure. Make sure seals and O-rings seat
                properly upon re-assembly.

VISUAL INSPECTION (VT)
Visual inspection is often the most cost-effective method, but it must be conducted throughout the entire
welding process from start to finish helping ensure proper weldment. Additionally, visual inspection is also
required when conducting Magnetic Particle (MT) testing and Liquid Particle (PT) inspections. Visual
inspection requires little equipment. Equipment for VT includes a flashlight, pocket rule, a weld size gauge,
a magnifying glass (magnifier), and either a straight edge or square for checking straightness and alignment.
Prior to welding, materials should be examined to see if they meet specifications for quality, type, size,
cleanliness and freedom from defects. Grease, paint, oil, oxide film or heavy scale is not acceptable and
should be removed. Joining pieces should be checked for alignment, joint fit-up straightness and
dimensional accuracy. Process and procedure requirements should be verified, including electrode size and
type, equipment settings and provisions for preheat or post heat/stress relief.

The root pass of a multipass weld is the most critical to weld soundness. It is especially susceptible to
cracking, and because it solidifies quickly, it may trap gas and slag. On subsequent passes, conditions caused
by the shape of the weld bead or changes in the joint configuration can cause further cracking, as well as
undercut and slag trapping. Repair costs can be minimized if visual inspection detects these flaws before
welding progresses. Inspection of each layer before depositing another layer should be the accepted practice.

Visual inspection at an early stage of production can also prevent under-welding and over-welding conditions.
Welds that are smaller than called for in the specifications cannot be tolerated. Beads that are too large can
cause distortion through added shrinkage stress. Detection of surface flaws, including cracks, porosity and
unfilled craters, dimensional variances, warpage and appearance flaws, as well as weld size characteristics,
can be evaluated.

Before checking for surface flaws, welds must be cleaned of slag. Shot blasting should not be done before
examination, due to the peening action possibly sealing in fine cracks and making them invisible.

Note: AWS D1.1 Structural Welding Code does not allow peening on the root or surface layer of the weld or
the base metal at the edges of the weld.

Inspection Requirements

        1. Visual inspection shall be performed prior to other required nondestructive tests, except as noted
           in paragraph 5 below, in an adequately lighted area and, unless otherwise specified, under no
           magnification. When a borescope or magnifier is necessary to conduct the inspection, evaluation
           shall be based upon comparison with a workmanship sample viewed under the same conditions.

        2. Visual inspection may be accomplished with the aid of a variety of mechanical instruments and
           optical comparators. Weld and fillet gauges, calipers, scales and other special devices may be
           used when necessary to completely examine the weld.

        3. Personnel performing visual inspections of welds shall be thoroughly familiar with required
           procedures, techniques and use of equipment, and shall be certified in accordance with Level II
           (Inspector) or Level III (Examiner) status.

        4. Weld surfaces to be inspected and at least one (1) inch of the adjacent base material shall be in
           the unpainted condition and free of weld spatter, scale, rust, slag, and any other foreign material
           that may interfere with evaluation of the weld.

        5. Final Weld examination shall be visually examined in the final surface and final heat treated
           condition. When surface blending or contouring is required for other non-destructive tests, then
           visual inspection shall be performed after conditioning. For welds that are to be subsequently
           machined, the weld size is to be verified prior to machining and the machined surface shall be
           inspected for all other attributes contained herein. Welds may be inspected in the as-welded
           condition. Weld contour and size attributes may be verified prior to stress relief treatments, but
           all other attributes must be verified after completion of stress relief.

        6. Completed weld surfaces shall be visually inspected for the entire length of the weld noting any
           defect attributes.

LIQUID PENETRANT INSPECTION (PT)
Liquid penetrant inspection is often referred to as an extension of the visual inspection method. Surface cracks
and pinholes that are not visible to the naked eye can be located by liquid penetrant inspection. It is widely
used to locate leaks in welds and can be applied with austenitic steels and nonferrous materials where
magnetic particle inspection would be useless.
Two types of penetrating liquids can be used, fluorescent or visible dye. With fluorescent penetrant
inspection, a highly fluorescent liquid with good penetrating qualities is applied to the surface of the part to be
examined. Capillary action draws the liquid into the surface openings, and the excess is then removed. A
"developer" is used to draw the penetrant to the surface, and the resulting indication is viewed by ultraviolet
(black) light. The high contrast between the fluorescent material and the object makes it possible to detect
minute traces of penetrant that indicate surface defects.
Dye penetrant inspection works in a similar manner, except that vividly colored dyes visible under ordinary
light are used. Normally, a white developer is used with the dye penetrant that creates a sharply contrasting
background to the vivid dye color. This method allows greater portability by eliminating the need for
ultraviolet light. Note: The part to be inspected must be clean and dry, because any foreign matter could close
the cracks or pinholes and exclude the penetrant. Penetrants can be applied by dipping, spraying or brushing,
but sufficient dwell time must be allowed for the liquid to be fully absorbed into the discontinuities.
Inspection Requirements
        1        Liquid penetrant inspection shall be performed using a solvent-removable visible dye, with
                 associated relevant indication defined as an indication caused by an unnatural break in part
                 geometry, such as cracks, penetrant remover and a wet non-aqueous developer. The liquid
                 penetrant process is intended to detect only discontinuities that are open to the surface.

        2        Equipment used to process parts per this procedure will include a light source to adequately
                 illuminate the part surface for evaluation of indications, a timer with both audio and visible
                 alarm, and a means of ventilation to remove excess particulate when spraying parts with
                 penetrant or developer. A fan may also be used to circulate shop air in the drying cycle. Parts
                 may be processed in the open shop or in dedicated areas, so long as all applicable safety
                 regulations are observed. Personnel should not breathe solvent fumes, which may be toxic.
                 They should wear gloves and suitable clothing during testing to keep cleaner and penetrant
                 off the skin.

MAGNETIC PARTICLE TESTING (MT)
Magnetic particle inspection is a method of locating and defining discontinuities in magnetic materials. This
method is excellent for detecting surface defects in welds, including discontinuities that are too small to be
seen with the naked eye and those that are slightly below the surface.

This method may be used to inspect plate edges prior to welding, in process inspection of each weld pass or
layer, post weld evaluation and to inspect repairs. It is a good method for detecting surface cracks of all sizes in
both the weld and adjacent base metal, subsurface cracks, incomplete fusion, undercut and inadequate
penetration in the weld, as well as defects on the repaired edges of the base metal. Note: Magnetic particle
testing should not be a substitute for radiography or ultrasonic for subsurface evaluations.

The Magnetic Particle process entails placing probes on each side of the area to be inspected, as a high
amperage is passed through the workplace between them. A magnetic flux is produced at right angles to the
flow of current. When these lines of force encounter a discontinuity, such as a longitudinal crack, they are
diverted and leak through the surface, creating magnetic poles or points of attraction. A magnetic powder
dusted onto the surface will cling to the leakage area more tenaciously than elsewhere, forming an indication
of the discontinuity.
Note: For this indication to develop, the discontinuity must be angled against the magnetic lines of force.
Thus, when current is passed longitudinally through a work piece, only longitudinal flaws will show. Putting
the work piece inside a solenoid coil will create longitudinal lines of force that cause transverse and angular
cracks to become visible when the magnetic powder is applied.

A joint between a base metal and a weld metal of different magnetic characteristics will create magnetic
discontinuities that may be falsely interpreted as unsound (false indication). On the other hand the powder
clinging over the harmless magnetic discontinuity can obscure a true defect. Sensitivity decreases with the
size of the defect and is also less with round forms such as gas pockets. It is best with elongated forms, such
as cracks, and is limited to surface flaws and some subsurface flaws, mostly on thinner materials.
Because the field must be distorted sufficiently to create the external leakage required to identify flaws, fine-
elongated discontinuities, such as hairline cracks, seams or inclusions that are parallel to the magnetic field,
will not show up. Note: Changing the direction of the field can develop them, and it is advisable to apply the
field from two directions, preferably at right angles to each other.
Magnetic powders may be applied dry or wet. The dry powder method is used for inspecting heavy weldment,
while the wet method is often used in inspecting precision, high stressed components (i.e. aircraft
components). Dry powder is dusted uniformly over the work with a spray gun, dusting bag or atomizer. The
finely divided magnetic particles are coated to increase their mobility and are available in gray, black and red
colors to improve visibility.
In the wet method, very fine red or black particles are suspended in water or light petroleum distillate. This
can be flowed or sprayed on, or the part may be dipped into the liquid. The wet method is more sensitive than
the dry method, because it allows the use of finer particles that can detect exceedingly fine defects.
Fluorescent powders may also be used for further sensitivity and are especially useful for locating
discontinuities in corners, keyways, splines and deep holes.
Inspection Requirements

        1       Personnel performing MT shall be qualified and thoroughly familiar with the procedure,
                methods, techniques and equipment, and shall be certified to Level I (Operator) minimum.
                Personnel interpreting and reporting results shall be certified to Level II (Inspector) or Level
                III (Examiner).

        2       The magnetic particle inspection system shall have the proven ability to detect a 1/16" long
                by 0.006” wide by 0.02” deep notch (max. dimensions) machined into a 3/8" thick low alloy
                steel plate. The plate shall be oriented in the vertical position and the magnetic flux shall be
                90 degrees to the notch.

        3       MT shall be performed using either the dry continuous or wet continuous method of
                magnetization with contact prods and color contrasting dry powder, or contact clamps with
                oil-based magnetic particle bath. For longitudinal MT of cylindrical parts such as shafts and
                circumferential welds such as for pipe, coils and/or cable wrapping is permitted. In all cases,
                MT shall be performed in two essentially perpendicular directions.

WELDING INSPECTION
DEFINITIONS
The following definitions along with Table 1 are provided as a guide to help assist in the inspection of
weldment, surface cracking, fusion deficiencies and imperfections.
        Arc Strike: Any localized heat affected zone caused by an electrical arc when passing current
        through the work piece, generally recognizable by evidence of melting of the material surface at
        the location of the arc strike, causing a scar like marking.
        Capillary Action: (PT) Pertaining to Liquid Penetration Inspection, it is the tendency of certain
        liquids to travel or climb into surface openings.
        Circular Magnetization: Magnetization of a piece of ferromagnetic material in such a way that
        the magnetic flux path is completely contained within the article. Usually produced by passing
        an electric current directly through the piece. Running a central conductor through a hollow
        piece may also produce a circular field. Magnetic flux density is strongest close to the surface
        on the test piece that is in contact with the central conductor.
        Concavity: A depression or hollow in the surface of the weld metal whereby the weld is not
        flush with a plane connecting the toes of the weld.
        Continuous Method: (MT) Application of ferromagnetic particles to the test surface while the
        magnetizing current is being applied.
        Convexity: Reinforcement of a weld extending beyond a plane connecting the toes of the weld.
        Crater Pit: A rounded depression in the stop of the weld bead.
        Developer: (PT) A white powder material similar to talc that blots up any residual dyed
        penetrant and provides a contrasting background. Spots of red in the white background are
        called “indications”.
        Discontinuity: (MT) Any interruption in the magnetic lines of force in the part being tested
        which causes a break in the magnetic line force and results in a magnetic particle indication.
        Discontinuity: (PT) An interruption in the normal physical structure or configuration of a part
        which may or may not affect its usefulness.
        Dwell Time: (PT) This is the time allowed for capillary action to occur after applying the
        penetrant to the test piece and before the visual inspection process starts. Generally 10 to 15
        minutes is the minimum allowable dwell time. While more sensitive applications will require an
        extended dwell time.

        False indication: (MT) An ambiguous or misleading indication caused by surface
        contamination or surface irregularities that are not attributed to the test procedure.

       Field Strength Indicator: (MT) A device used to indicate and /or measure the strength
       and direction of a magnetic field. Gauss meters are normally used to measure residual

       Indication: (MT) Any magnetic particle pattern on the surface of a part being tested.

       Indication: (PT) The trace of the Penetrant on a part indicating a discontinuity. An indication
       may be larger than the imperfection that caused it; however, the size of the indication is the
       basis of acceptance evaluation.
       Inspection Area: The weld and the accessible adjacent base material for a distance of ½ inch
       from the toes of the weld.
       Joint Offset: The amount of misalignment in groove welds between the base materials that are

       Linear Indication: An indication with a length greater than three (3) times its width and greater
       than 0.06 inches in length.

       Longitudinal Magnetization: (MT) Magnetization of a material in such a way that the
       magnetic lines of force run substantially parallel to the long axis of the part, completing the path
       through air outside of the material. Usually produced by a coil of current carrying nonmagnetic
       insulated conductor wrapped around the test piece. The magnetic field is strongest close to the
       inside surfaces of the coil.
       Magnetic Particle Test Bar: (MT) A bar of low carbon steel, which has holes drilled in the
       edge at varying distances from the top surface of the bar, and a machined and epoxy-filled
       groove in the top face. The test bar enables one to evaluate the capability of the magnetic field
       to detect discontinuities.
       Magnetic Writing: A loose fuzzy indication, caused by distortion of the magnetic field through
       contact of the test part with another magnetized metallic surface or by proximity of the
       conductor cables to the test piece. This may be corrected by separating the articles, moving the
       cables, and by demagnetizing the test part.

All welding processes inherently have conditional welding parameters that result in possible weld
discontinuities and imperfections. Imperfections may not render a part as unsuitable for its intended
application; however it does affect the expected life span of the component. Refer to applicable
standards for acceptance levels of discontinuity.
Imperfections and discontinuity and its causes can be classified into two general categories. Those
produced during fabrication and those formed as a result of adverse conditions during service. Types of
imperfections/discontinuities that can occur include: Inclusions, porosity, undercutting, incomplete
fusion (root and penetration), and cracking.
Poor welding techniques and improper choice of welding parameters are major causes of weld
discontinuities, but they can also be caused by the use of improper base metal, filler metal, or shielding
gas. The base metal and filler metal should also be cleaned to avoid creation of a discontinuity. The
causes of common discontinuities that can occur with gas metal arc welding (GMAW), Gas Tungsten
arc welding (GTAW) and shielded metal arc welding (SMAW) are provided below.
        Inclusions
        Inclusions cause a weakening of the weld and often serve as the initiation and starting point of
        cracks. The basic types of inclusions that occur in arc welding are slag, oxide and tungsten
        inclusions.
                Slag Inclusions: Slag inclusions occur when slag particles created from the shielding
                flux on the electrode become trapped inside the weld. This can occur by welding over
                the slag particles during a multiple pass weld. The best prevention to this problem is to
                thoroughly clean the weld bead using a slag pick, wire brush and cone shaped grinding
                bit. Special attention should be given to the toes of the weld where slag can easily be
                trapped.
                Other contributing causes of slag inclusions include:                                Slag Inclusion

                •        Erratic travel speed to the electrode.

                •        Too low amperage setting.

                •        Too large a size of electrode.

                •        Weaving motion of electrode is too wide.

                •        Electrode angle that allows slag to travel ahead of the arc.

                Oxide Inclusions: Oxide inclusions occur when oxide particles from the surface of the
                base metal are mixed into the molten weld pool. Certain surface oxides have very high
                melting temperatures (magnesium and aluminum oxides). The best method in
                preventing oxide inclusions is to thoroughly clean the joint area before welding
                (grinding, wire brushing and chemical cleaning as applicable). Reducing the welding
                speed and increasing the voltage may also help with preventing oxide inclusions.

                Tungsten Inclusions: Tungsten inclusions occur when small pieces of the tungsten tip
                break off and enter the pool weld. The following conditions contribute to tungsten
                inclusion and should be avoided and eliminated from the welding process.
                •        The tip of the tungsten electrode makes contact with the molten metal pool.

                •        Use of improper shielding gas type. Only inert gases should be used and lines
                         purged.

                •        The maximum electrical current for a given electrode size has been exceeded.

Porosity
Porosity is a discontinuity caused by gas pockets in the weld metal that may be scattered in small
clusters or along the entire length of the weld. These gas pockets leave a void in the weld that can cause
it to be weakened. Porosity may be inside the weld and/or on the surface of the weld bead.
Discontinuity is caused by one or more of the following:
         •       Inadequate shielding gas flow rate.

        •       Wind drafts that deflect the shielding gas coverage.

        •       Blockage of the shielding gas flow when spatter
                builds up on the nozzle (GMAW).

        •       Contaminated or wet shielding gas.

        •       Excessive welding current.

        •       Excessive welding voltage.

        •       Excessive electrode extension.

        •       An excessive travel speed that causes freezing of the weld pool before gases can escape.

        •       Rust, grease, oil, moisture or dirt on the surface of the base metal, welding wire or filler
                metal rod.

        •       Impurities in the base metal, such as sulfur and phosphorous.

        •       Excessive moisture in the electrode coating. Note: SMAW flux covered electrodes
                should be kept in a heated holding oven to prevent moisture content and to help
                eliminate hydrogen cracking.

        •       Too short an arc length with covered electrodes except when using low hydrogen or
                stainless steel electrodes.

       Undercut

       Undercutting occurs when an unfilled groove melts into the base metal next to the toe or root of
       a weld. This is a predominantly a problem with fillet welds. Undercutting can weaken the joint
       at the toe of the weld and is usually an initiation point for a crack. The primary causes of
       undercut include:

       •       Excessive welding current.

       •       Arc voltage too high.

       •       Excessive travel speed that does not
               allow enough filler metal to be added.

       •       Erratic feeding of the welding wire.

       •       Excessive weaving speed.

       •       Incorrect electrode angles, especially on vertical and horizontal positions.

       Incomplete Weld Fusion
       Incomplete fusion occurs when the weld metal is not completely fused to the base metal or
       adjoining weld beads. This can happen between the weld metal and the base metal or between
       passes in multiple pass welding. Incomplete fusion between the weld metal and the base metal
       usually results from inadequate joint penetration. Although it can occur with all welding
       processes, it is often a major problem with the GMAW process “Short-Arc” mode of metal
       transfer.
       When short-Arc welding is done, wider root openings are often used to allow better penetration,
       and more care should also be taken when using a weaving technique. Welding over a previous
       weld bead that has excessive convexity often causes incomplete fusion between passes in a
       multiple pass weld. If an excessively convex weld bead is created, the surface should be ground
       off enough so that complete fusion can be made with the next pass.

       Major causes of incomplete fusion include:
       •       Excessive travel speed, which causes an
               excessively convex weld bead and does
               not allow adequate joint penetration.


       •       Letting the weld metal get ahead of the arc or letting the                                     Incomplete
               weld layer get too thick, which keeps the arc away from                                          Fusion
               the base metal.

       •       Too small a bevel angle.

       •       Failure to remove sufficient metal when back grinding and gouging a double sided weld.

       Cracks
       Weldment cracking can be caused by improper welding procedures, welding techniques and
       materials preparation. Cracks are either transverse or longitudinal to the weld. Transverse cracks
       are perpendicular to the axis of the weld and can result from longitudinal shrinkage strains
       acting on excessively hard and brittle weld metal. Longitudinal cracks are often caused by high
       joint restraint and high cooling rates. Preheating will often help to reduce these problems.
       Cracking can be classified as either hot or cold cracking.
       Hot cracking occurs at elevated temperatures and generally happens just after the weld metal
       starts to solidify. This type of cracking can be caused by excessive element (sulfur,
       phosphorous, and lead) composition in a steel base metal. In nonferrous metals, it can be caused
       by sulfur or zinc. Hot cracking can also be caused by an improper method of breaking the arc or
       in a root pass when the cross-sectional area of the weld bead is small compared to the mass of
       the base metal.
       Hot cracking often occurs in deep penetrating welds, and it can continue through successive
       layers if it is not repaired. Hot cracking can be prevented or at least minimized by performing
       the following tasks.
           •    Preheating to reduce shrinkage stresses in the weld.
           •    Using clean or uncontaminated shielding gas.
           •    Increasing the cross-sectional area of the bead.
           •    Changing the contour of the weld bead.
           •    Using base metal with very low contents of those elements that tend to cause hot
                cracking.
           •    With steel, using filler metals that are high in manganese.

       Cold cracking occurs after the weld metal solidification is complete. Cold cracking may occur
       several days after welding and is generally caused by hydrogen embrittlement and moisture
       containment, excessive joint restraint, and rapid cooling.
           •    Thorough cleaning of the joint area of moisture, oils and solvents, preheating, the use of
                lowhydrogen electrodes and dry high purity shielding gas help reduce this problem.

          Crater Cracks                                                                             Crater Cracks

          Crater cracks are shallow hot cracks
          that are commonly caused by improperly
          breaking the arc. The initiation of the crack
          starts at the crater pit indention and travels in a
          spider web formation or along the center line of
          the weld. Crater cracks can be prevented, by
          reversing the travel of the electrode back into
          the weld bead a little way, gradually reducing
          the welding current at the end of the weld, or by
          stopping the travel before breaking the arc.

       Centerline Cracks
       Centerline cracks are cold cracks that often occur in single pass concave fillet welds. A
       centerline crack is a longitudinal crack that runs down the center of the weld. This problem may
       be caused by:
                                                                                            Centerline Cracks
       •       A weld bead that is too small for the thickness
               of the base metal.
       •       Poor fit up and preparation.
       •       High joint restraint.
       •       An extension of a crater crack.

       Under Bead Cracks
       Under Bead Cracks and base metal cracks are cold
       cracks that form in the heat affected zone of the base metal. These types of cracking are caused
       by excessive joint restraint, entrapped hydrogen, or a brittle microstructure. Rapid cooling can
       cause a brittle microstructure or excessive heat input.    Under Bead Cracks


       Under Bead and base metal cracking can be reduced or
       eliminated by using preheat and taking precautions
       against introducing hydrogen into the weld. The
       hydrogen bonds with oxygen to form moisture (H20) in
       the base metal and consequently induces cracking under the weld bead.

INTRODUCTION Refer to Figures 1 and 2 for pipe bending fixture general layout.

The Pipe Bending Fixture is used to bend heated pipes to a shape that will be used as a guide pipe in the
laying head assembly. To rotate the fixture at the appropriate speed, the pipe bending assembly consists
of a 1 HP motor with a 1247 to 1 ratio motor reducer and is controlled at the electrical assembly and
control pendant. Twenty clamps on the fixture assembly are used to hold the bent pipe in position
while the pipe cools. A hold down roller restrains the pipe from rotating and allows the operator to
guide the pipe into position onto each toggle clamp mechanism and saddle.

Each revolution (360°) of the pipe bending fixture takes approximately 42 seconds. The fixture rotates
approximately 480° to complete the pipe bend in less than a minute (55 seconds). Controls for the pipe
bending fixture includes a forward and reverse feature on the control pendant to aid in the removal of
the pipe.

Note: For efficient operation of the Pipe Bending Fixture, operators are required to constantly
monitor all components.

inspections, however, do not reduce the lubrication frequency.

  1.0     Safety Procedures

                      IMPORTANT: All Safety Devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to

                      HAZARDOUS AT ALL TIMES.
  Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices make the
  elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the process and/or
  product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be constrained to follow a
  prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble. Cobbles occur at random times
  and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently
  caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment, and
  stock temperature are also causes of cobbling anywhere along the length of a bar in process in the rolling
  train. The following recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe manner.
          1.1     Visibility and Communications
          Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations of pulpits
          and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment controlled from that point.
                   A. Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight.
                  B. Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper lighting
                     can be used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or cloud the
                     reflective surface and that the mirror location does not make it liable to breakage.
          1.2     Audible Communications
                  Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as
                  substitutes only when visual contact is not possible.
          1.3     Safety Stops
                  Guide adjustments may be made only when the Mill Line is shut down. Mechanical or
                  electrically operated stops must be used to block any stock from inadvertently entering

  IMPORTANT: Always read Safety Instructions and Warnings for each system and component

  INTRODUCTION

  See the applicable ECS for more information.

  Morgan’s Horizontal Compactor provides the ability to automatically compress and bind coils for further
  transport to shipping and loading area. A Hook Carrier system transports the coils to and from the
  compactor. Coils are placed in position for tying through the hook carrier system and by the platens (pressure
  plates PP1 & PP2) of the compactor. A compactor table lifts the coil (with hook in place), the press plates
  compress the coil and the feed and strapping unit feeds the strap around the coil and joins it. Once
  compressed and bound, the coil is lowered back onto the hook and transported to its final destination.

  The main components of the Compactor Unit include:

          •   A lifting table that elevates the coil off of the Coil-hook during the compacting cycle.
    Note: The Coil Hook stays in position while coil is compressed.
          •   Two press plates, moveable on wheels, actuated by hydraulic cylinders.
          •   Mounted on Press Plate #1 are four (4) strapping units. The strapping units have arrangements
              for feeding, stretching, crimping, notching and cutting strapping material.
          •   Four (4) strapping dispensers, each comprising of a strap Reel and magazine assembly and
              strapping accumulator, are located adjacent to Press Plate #1 end of compactor.
          •   Hydraulic Power Unit (HPU) System consisting of a power unit with four feed pumps, one
              circulating pump, operating tank and accumulator.

1.0     Lift Table

  The compactor has a mechanism to lift a coil from the hook prior to compacting and then to lower the coil
  back onto the hook once compacting and tying is completed. Lifting action is produced by a hydraulic
  cylinder that is controlled by Table Lift solenoid valve (3 position).

  The table positions are indicated by the Table Down Position proximity switch, Table Maximum Up
  Position proximity switch and the Table Mid Position proximity switch.

  The Table Mid Position proximity switch stops lifting action of the table anytime it is reached with the
  PP Coil Detector photoelectric sensors not detecting the edges of coil being compacted.

  The Table Maximum Up proximity switch stops lifting action of table anytime it is reached.

  Interlocking required: The table cannot be raised unless external signal to Hook Carrier system is set to
  prevent movement of a hook in or out of compactor.

Press Plates

Press plates are hydraulically actuated to compact the coil to a preset (by operator) force. Each press plate is
controlled by a PP Traverse electro hydraulic proportional direction valve. The valve acts as both a
directional control valve and a proportional flow control valve and is supplied complete with the electronics
mounted on the valve.

          A +20mA speed and direction signal is used to control acceleration/deceleration, speed and
          direction of the Press plates.

                  A positive value extends the cylinder.
                  A negative value retracts the cylinder.

          References to valves are always ramped.
                 Acceleration rate is 8% per 0.05 seconds
                 Deceleration rate is 8% per 0.05 seconds

          Retract speed is limited to 30% whenever PP is within 200 mm of park position.
          Extend speed is limited to 30% whenever PP is within 200 mm of being fully extended.

  For maximum speed extending press plates to coil, the PP Traverse Regen 2-position, single solenoid
  valves are energized. This connects rod end of cylinders to their cap ends.

          The PP Traverse Regen solenoid valves are also kept energized during press for compacting
          forces less than 20 ton.

          For press forces 20 tons or greater, the PP Traverse Regen solenoid valves are de-energized
          during the final compression cycle, commonly referred to as Direct mode.

                  Note: This valve must be de-energized anytime its PP Traverse valve is requesting an
                        "out" (retract) motion.

  The PP Traverse Position transducers are mounted internally in the press plate cylinders.

          Calibrate transducers to produce a 4-20mA (0-2525 mm) position feedback signal for the PLC to
          allow synchronization and positioning of the Press plates during the compacting cycle. The
          cylinder travel is mechanically limited to 2425 mm.

          Transducers are also used to calculate size of coil.

  The PP1 Cap End Pressure transducer monitors the full bore side (cap end) of the #1 Press Plate traverse
  cylinder.

          This transducer produces a 4-20mA (0-207 bar) pressure feedback signal for the PLC to ensure
          that the correct compacting force is achieved when compacting.

  The PP1 Rod End Pressure transducer monitors the rod end of the #1 Press Plate traverse cylinder.

          This transducer produces a 4-20mA (0-207 bar) pressure feedback signal for the PLC to ensure
          that the correct compacting force is achieved when compacting.

  The force exerted by the Press Plates during the final compacting cycle is determined by setting of the PP1
  Pressure Limit proportional relief valve which limits hydraulic pressure in cap end of cylinder for PP1.

          A 0-20ma (0-100%) signal from the PLC is used to set the relief pressure where 14.3 ma will limit
          pressure to 125 bar or 1800 psi which will limit force exerted to 40 metric ton in direct mode (PP
          Traverse Regen valve de-energized) and 20 metric ton when in regen mode.

  The characteristic of the relief valve is non-linear. Use the following equations for other forces:

       Force < 20 tons and > 8 tons (Regen Mode)
        Valve setting (%) = (4.344 x Force) - 18.2 IF Force < 15.7, ELSE = (5.026 x Force) -28.95 .

       Force > 20 tons and < 40 tons (Direct Mode)
        Valve setting (%) = (2.172 x Force) - 18.2 IF Force < 31.4, ELSE = (2.513 x Force) -28.95 .

  The PP1 Pressure Limit Enable single solenoid valves are energized to connect PP1 Pressure Limit
  valve to cap end of cylinder for PP1. This allows PP1 Pressure Limit valve to be easily disabled during
  high speed closing of press plates.

  When the PP Unlock single solenoid valve is de-energized, flow of oil out of piston end of traverse
  cylinder is prevented. This solenoid must be energized whenever it is desired to retract its associated press
  plate.

  The Press plate fully retracted (rear position) is indicated by the PP Retracted proximity switch.

  The PP Coil Detector photoelectric sensors mounted on PP1 & PP2 detect edge of coil being compacted.

  The Press plates are synchronized electronically and move together to ensure that the coil is compacted
  evenly and centered on hook after compacting is done.

  Interlocking required:

          Plates cannot move in towards coil unless external signal to Hook Carrier system is set to prevent
          movement of a hook in or out of compactor.

          Plates cannot move in towards coil unless all tying heads are fully retracted as indicated by the
          Tying Head Retract prox switches.

2.0     PP1 Strapping Heads (4)

  Press plate #1 has four (4) strapping heads each mounted on its own traversing frame. The strapping head
  is a manufactured assembly that consists of a feed roll, tension roll, sealing jaw, strap shear, a strap guide
  as well as the controlling solenoid valves, proximity switches and encoder.

  The Strapping Head is traversed to and from the coil by a hydraulic cylinder.

          Traverse is controlled by its Strap Head Traverse 3-position, double solenoid valve.

          The Strap Head Retract proximity switch detects that the strapping unit carriage is fully retracted
          which is the strap feeding position.

          The Strap Head Extend pressure switch detects that the strapping unit carriage is up against the
          coil that is the crimping position.

          Important Note: The pressure switch monitors the pressure in the rod end of cylinder that goes to
          zero when head is stopped by coil. Since pressure in rod end is also zero when head is first
          extended towards coil, it is necessary for the Retract proximity switch to inhibit detection of
          pressure loss until cylinder moves off proximity switch. Detection logic should be extend solenoid
          energized a minimum of 0.5 seconds, retract proximity switch false and pressure switch false (zero
          pressure).

  Each Strapping Head has a Feed Roll used to feed the strapping through the head and guides thus feeding
  the strapping around the coil. Once the strapping is around the coil and clamped in the jaw, the feed roll is
  reversed to tighten the strapping around the coil (“stretching “the strapping back).

          The feed roll is rotated by a pneumatic motor that is controlled by its Feed Forward single
          solenoid valves (A & B) and its Feed Reverse single solenoid valves (A & B).

  Each Strapping Head also has a Tension Roll used to fully tighten the strapping around the coil. This roll
  can only be run in reverse direction.

          The tension roll is rotated by a pneumatic motor that is controlled by its Strap Tensioning single
          solenoid valves (A & B).

  The Feed Roll and Tension Roll are closed on the strap using the same mechanical mechanism. When
  Feed Roll is closed, the Tension Roll is opened and visa versa.

          The Feed Roll is opened/closed (tension roll closed/opened) by a pneumatic cylinder that is
          controlled by its Feed/Tension Select 2-position, double solenoid valve.

          The Feed Roll is detected being closed by its Feed Roll Closed proximity switch.

          The Feed Roll is detected being open by its Feed Roll Open proximity switch.

  The Holding Jaw is a pneumatic powered mechanism that operates in three positions, Full Open, Half
  Close (pinch position) and Full Close (seal & cut).

          Full Open position is obtained by energizing the Jaw Open solenoid coil with Jaw Half Close &
          Jaw Seal/Cut solenoid coils de-energized.

          Half Close position is obtained by energizing the Jaw Half Close solenoid coil with Jaw Open &

  The Head Guide Flap is a pneumatic powered mechanism that supports the front end of the strapping
  through Strapping Head. It is then opened prior to tightening strap around coil.

          The Guide is controlled by the Guide Flap 2-position, double solenoid valve.

          The Guide is detected being closed by its Guide Flap Closed proximity switch.

          The Guide is detected being opened by its Guide Flap Open proximity switch.

  Each Strapping Head has a curved guide on PP1 that steers strapping returning from PP2 around end of
  coil and back into the head.

  The guide doors are maintained closed by springs. The doors are pulled open by the strapping when it is
  being stretched around the coil.

3.0     PP2 Strapping Guides

  Press plate #2 has four (4) strapping guides that are mounted on one (1) moveable carriage. The guides are
  used to feed (thread) the strapping around the coil and back to the strapping heads on press plate #1.

  The guide carriage is controlled by a PP2 Guide Traverse electrohydraulic proportional direction valve.
  The valve acts as both a directional control valve and a proportional flow control valve and is supplied
  complete with the electronics mounted on the valve.

              4.0     Strap Payoff Dispenser and Accumulators

                The banding strap used by the compactor comes in reels (one for each strap head). The Dispenser
                Unwinder rotates the reels to payoff the strapping to its accumulator. The Feed Roll on the Strap Head
                then pulls strapping from the accumulator as required.

                The Dispenser Unwinder is powered by a 0.55 kW, AC electric motor, and is controlled by its Inverter
                located in the Drive Cabinet that is located in the Electric Room. The amount of strap remaining on the
                unwinder is monitored by its Strap Detector photo sensor.

                The Dispenser Accumulator consists of top and bottom sheaves where the bottom ones are free to raise
                and lower with the strapping. The weight of the bottom sheave assembly provides tension in strapping and
                energy source to lower sheaves to bottom when not being supported by strap.

                The position of the bottom sheaves is monitored by two limit switches. The Accumulator Full indicates
                accumulator is full of strap (sheaves at bottom). The Accumulator Empty indicates the accumulator is
                empty (sheaves at top).

  Hyd Feed Pump Suction Valves

  Valves are located at inlet of each feed pump. These are manual valves. Each valve has a Pump Suction
  Valve limit switch to indicate when the valve is open. The switch is closed with valve in fully open
  position. A pump cannot run unless its suction valve is open.

  Hyd Feed Pump Loading Valves

  Each pump has a Pump Loading single solenoid valve. When the solenoid is energized, associated pump
  can develop full pressure. The solenoid is de-energized by PLC when pump is stopped or starting and
  whenever Compactor is E-Stopped. Power is also removed from these valves during a Compactor E-
  Stop by contactors. The solenoid is energized by PLC 5 seconds after pump has started or 5 seconds after
  Compactor E-Stop is reset with pump running.

  Hydraulic Accumulator

  There is a pressure accumulator for the hydraulic system output header. Whenever the system is not in use,
  the accumulator pressure must be discharged for safety. The accumulator pressure is relieved by
  Accumulator Blowdown single solenoid valve. When the solenoid is de-energized, the accumulator will
  discharge to tank.

          The solenoid is automatically energized whenever one of the pump motor starters is energized.
          Power is removed from this valve during a Compactor E-Stop by contactors in OS6.

  Pump Header Blowdown & Accumulator Isolation Valves
  The Pump Header Blowdown valve connects the pump feed header to tank return line when its solenoid
  is de-energized. The Accumulator Isolation valve blocks the accumulator from the pump feed header
  when its solenoid is de-energized. Both solenoids are de-energized by PLC whenever Compactor is E-
  Stopped. Power is also removed from these valves during a Compactor E-Stop by contactors.

  The Header Blowdown solenoid is energized by PLC when Compactor E-Stop is reset. The
  Accumulator Isolation solenoid is energized by PLC 1 second after Header Blowdown solenoid has
  been energized.
  Hyd Feed Pump Filters
  Each feed pump has a simplex filter located downstream of its discharge. Each filter has a Filter Dirty
  pressure switch which will indicate when the filter is dirty and requires maintenance. Alarm is generated
  whenever normally closed pressure switch opens on high pressure. Pump is shut down if alarm persists
  for 1 hour.

  Hydraulic Tank Level Switch

  There is a Tank Level float switch. Provides alarm for LOW and LOW-LOW level. Feed pumps and
  circulating pump cannot run under LOW-LOW level condition. Also, the heaters are de-energized.

  Hydraulic Circulating Pump

  A circulating pump is used to circulate oil through the heat exchanger for cooling and through duplex
  filters for cleaning. The pump is driven by squirrel cage induction motor with FVNR control. The
  hydraulic feed pumps cannot be started if circulating pump is not running.

  Hydraulic Duplex Oil Filter

  The circulating pump has a duplex filter located downstream of its discharge. Each filter has a Filter
  Dirty pressure switch which will indicate when the filter is dirty and requires maintenance. Alarm is
  generated whenever normally closed pressure switch opens on high pressure. Pump is shut down if alarm
  persists for 1 hour.

  Hydraulic Fluid Temperature Control

  Tank Temp thermostats TT1 & TT2 are used to control heating and cooling of oil.

          TT2 contact is closed below 30oC and open above 33oC.
          TT3 contact is closed below 42oC and open above 45oC.
          TT1 contact is closed below 60oC and open above.

  Electric heaters are used for heating hydraulic fluid.

          The heaters are energized when the temperature is below 30oC and are de-energize when the
          temperature is above 33oC.

          A temperature above 60oC is to signal a HIGH TEMPERATURE alarm and is to de-energize the
          heater circuit. All of the hydraulic pumps are also shutdown after current compacting cycle
          completes or after 2 minutes (whichever occurs first).

          A temperature below 30oC is to signal a LOW TEMPERATURE alarm.

          A temperature below 30oC is to prevent starting the pump motors but will not shut pump down.

  A water heat exchanger system is used to cool the tank hydraulic fluid.

  The Cooling Water single solenoid valve is energized to supply water to heat exchanger.

          Solenoid is energized whenever temperature is above 45oC and circulating pump is running.

  AUTO Operation

     Auto 0    In AUTO mode awaiting hook with coil.
               1. Go to Step 1 when Initial Conditions to Start are "true", Compactor Done is "false"
                   AND one of following is true:
                   a) Operator presses START COMPACTOR pushbutton.
                   b) Compact Permissive is "true" and AUTO INITIATE is selected ON.

     Auto 1    Compact coil & setup guides
               1. Initiate following sequences simultaneously
                  Compress coil (Seq 0, then Seq 3)
                  Table up (Seq 1)
                  Guide setup sequence (Seq 2)
               2. Once force reached with guides in position, go to Auto 2 for each strapping unit

     Note: Each strapping unit has its own Auto 2-5 that run independently.

     Auto 2    Feed (thread) strap through strapping head and guides.
               1. Initiate Seq X1 for each strapping unit.
               2. Go to Auto 3 for strapping head when its Seq X1 finishes.

     Auto 3    Position strapping head
               1. Initiate strapping head to coil (Seq X2) for strapping unit
               2. Go to Auto 4 for strapping head when its Seq X2 finishes.
               3. After 2.5 sec initiate PP2 guide carriage to retract position (Seq 7)

     Auto 4    Tighten (stretch) strap around coil.
               1. Initiate strap stretching to coil (Seq X3) for strapping unit
               2. Go to Auto 5 for strapping head when its Seq X3 finishes.

     Auto 5    Seal strap
               1. Initiate seal sequence (Seq X4) for strapping unit
               2. Once Seq X4 for strapping head is completed, set seal complete flag to allow Auto 6

     Auto 6    Clear Auto Compact cycle
               1. Latch Compactor Done logical to allow Hook Carrier system to remove/deliver coil.
               2. Initiate dispensers to payoff strapping (accumulator sheaves to down position).
               3. Go to Auto 0

  PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS

  DEFINITION: Preventive maintenance is routine maintenance that if performed as scheduled helps to keep
  the Horizontal Compactor Binding Unit in good operating condition. Its primary purpose is to reduce the
  incidence of operating failures, which require costly downtime for repairs. The recommended routine
  maintenance schedule below represents the anticipated minimum requirements for maintaining the Compactor
  Assembly.

  IMPORTANT: Always isolate, shutoff and/or disconnect Water, Air, Hydraulic and Electrical power
  supply sources before performing any repairs or maintenance. Read Safety Instructions and Warnings
  for each system and component prior to working on machinery. Always Refer to Safety section. Make
  sure the Mill process stations and pass line have been shut down. All Surrounding Equipment should
  be locked-out /tagged-out and secured.

  WARNING: CONSIDER ALL MILL EQUIPMENT AS POTENTIALLY HAZARDOUS AT ALL TIMES.
  IT IS CAPABLE OF CRUSHING ANY BODY PART CAUGHT IN IT.

  WARNING: ELECTRICAL VOLTAGES IN BOTH POWER AND CONTROL CIRCUITS ARE CAPABLE
  OF RENDERING SEVERE AND FATAL SHOCKS.

  WARNING: HOT PRODUCT TRAVELLING THROUGHOUT THE MILL CAN MAKE ALL
  EQUPIMENT SURFACES A HIGH TEMPERATURE CONDITION. CONSIDER ALL SURFACES
  THROUGHOUT THE MILL AS HOT!!

  WARNING: BEWARE OF PINCH POINTS. BLOCK AND RESTRAIN ROTATING AND MOVING
  PARTS BEFORE REMOVING AND PERFORMING ANY MAINTENANCE OF EQUIPMENT.
  CAUTION: EQUIPMENT THROUGHOUT THE MILL PRODUCES EXCESSIVE NOISE.
   ALWAYS WEAR HEARING PROTECTION.
  Important:     Make sure Main Hydraulic Power unit is shut off and locked out. Make sure there is no
  hydraulic pressure in the entire compactor assembly. Make sure the Compactor hydraulic accumulator
  Pressure (“p”) line has zero pressure = (0 Bar)

  INTRODUCTION
  Routine and Preventive Maintenance of the Horizontal Compactor Binding Unit assembly is required to ensure
  extended and proper operation. Table 3 is provided as a quick reference guide for frequent periodic
  maintenance requirements for the Horizontal Compactor Binding Unit assemblies. Refer to the Safety section
  and to the applicable manufacturers’ technical manual for maintenance requirements and procedures of
  specific components of the horizontal Compactor Binding Units. Refer to Morgan assembly drawings as a
  guide.

  WARNING: Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or disconnect all power
  supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any stored energy from components. Restrain and
  secure any moving parts of a component or system that could cause injury.

  WARNING: The Horizontal Compactor Binding Unit Assembly is potentially dangerous and capable
  of inflicting severe bodily injuries and fatal electric shock. Before starting any maintenance task,
  comply with all company policies relating to safety. Also, be thoroughly familiar with all SAFETY
  REQUIREMENTS.

  CORRECTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS
  DEFINITION
  Corrective maintenance encompasses those repair procedures required to return the Horizontal Compactor
  Binding Unit assembly to satisfactory operating condition. Such repairs do not necessarily return the
  equipment to like-new condition. Rather, the objective is to make it operational again as soon as possible.
  It is recommended to replace faulty parts/components and sub-assemblies with new or previously
  refurbished spare parts/components and sub-assemblies. Those parts removed may then be refurbished or
  reconditioned after the main equipment has been returned to service.
  IMPORTANT
  Always isolate, shutoff and/or disconnect Water, Air, Hydraulic and Electrical power supply sources
  before performing any repairs or maintenance. Read Safety Instructions and Warnings for each system
  and component prior to working on machinery. Refer to Safety section.

  INTRODUCTION
  Corrective Maintenance of the Horizontal Compactor Binding Unit Assembly as defined above is intended to
  keep down time at a minimum by replacing components and then dismantling and overhauling the removed
  component in a service area away from the mill. Once refurbished, the component becomes a spare shelf part,
  ready to be utilized as a replacement when needed.
  No disassembly procedures are given herein of components being replaced. Components that require
  overhaul/refurbishment should be maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Refer to
  the manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance and torque requirements and procedures of specific
  components of the Horizontal Compactor Binding Unit Assembly
  General guidelines and maintenance criteria are provided below when corrective maintenance of a component or
  sub-assembly is required. These are minimum guidelines and should be used in conjunction with the specific
  maintenance requirements from the component manufacturer.

  Upon re-assembly, tighten all bolts, screws, nuts and fasteners in accordance with Morgan reference drawings
  torque requirements. Torque specific components in accordance with the manufacturer’s requirements.
          WARNING: Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or disconnect
          all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any stored energy from
          components. Restrain and secure any moving parts of a component or system that could
          cause injury.
          WARNING: The Horizontal Compactor Binding Unit Assembly is potentially dangerous
          and capable of inflicting severe bodily injuries and fatal electric shock. Before starting any
          maintenance task, comply with all company policies relating to safety. Also, be thoroughly
          familiar with all safety requirements

  The following is a list of maintenance actions to perform whenever dismantling equipment for repairs. In
  addition, some general maintenance practices for the horizontal Compactor Binding Unit are provided.

          1.1     Electric controls and power cables -- Before disconnecting any wiring that does not have

          1.2     Rigging parts for removal/replacement -- Many parts that make up this equipment are

                  supporting heavy parts before attempting to dismantle any equipment.
          1.3     Cleaning – When disassembling components, clean all parts with a suitable solvent
                  (mineral spirits, SAVASOL no.5, or equivalent) to remove all scale, grease, grime, or dirt.
                  Use a lint free clean wiper; do not use cotton rags. Air dry after cleaning.
          1.4     Bearings and Sealing Surfaces -- Closely inspect bearings and sealing surfaces for signs
                  of wear, nicks, scratches, gouges, or build-up of scale or other foreign substances.
                  Replace bearings that show any signs of deterioration.

  CAUTION: A bearing may be defective without the defect being visually evident. Replace any bearing
  removed during any maintenance task with new or cleaned bearing at re-assembly.

  New bearings are packed with rust-preventative grease (or other protective coating) and wrapped in
  grease-resistant paper before they are shipped. Do not unwrap the bearing until time for installation.
  Unwrap and thoroughly wash the new bearing and air dry.
  NOTE: For ease of installation of bearings, heat the bearings at a maximum temperature of 121°C
  (250°F) in oil for one hour minimum, or in an electric furnace for 1-1/2 hours minimum, or by bearing
  induction heater for 15 minutes minimum.
          1.5      Oil Seals – Replace (Mandatory Replacement) all seals, o-rings and gaskets that are
                   removed or disturbed during disassembly procedure. Make sure seals and o-rings seat
                   properly upon re-assembly.
          1.6     Oil Passages -- Pressure flush oil passages and blow dry with compressed air.
          1.7     Pre-lubrication Prior to Re-assembly -- Lightly lubricate all seals, bearings, bushings, and
                  gears with oil before installation
          1.8     Aligning Parts during Re-assembly -- Because of the weight of large parts, use guide studs
                  during re-assembly to ensure proper pilot hole and dowel pin alignment.
          1.9     Clean all parts and inspect for scratches, cracks, burrs, flaking, pitting, scaling or
                  discoloration of mating or load-bearing surfaces.

         2.1     Strapping Head Unit Removal and Installation (Quick Change).
                 Removal Procedure

                 A. Disconnect all electric connections and hydraulic hoses from the unit. Make sure to
                    plug all hydraulic pipes to prevent dirt and dust from entering the hydraulic system.
                 B. Install eye bolts and jam nuts to binding unit for unit removal. Rig and Secure
                     Binding Unit for lifting. Provide some tension on the slings for balancing the unit
                     prior to removal.
                 C. Loosen the bolts connecting the strapping head unit to the carriage. Then put additional
                     lifting tension on the slings.
                 D. Remove the bolts completely and remove binding unit to service area for
                     reconditioning.

                 Installation Procedure
                 E. Reverse steps and procedures from above. Use the steps below as a guide.

                              pin. Thread and install the first bolt to ensure a proper alignment and seating of
                              the locator pin. Install remaining bolts and tighten binding unit to carriage
                              assembly. Torque bolts in sequence to 200 Nm.

INTRODUCTION

In Steel Rolling Mills there are many lubrication systems. In general, the function of each system is to provide
a reliable source of oil (the load-carrying element) for the bearings and gears at a specified quantity,
temperature, and cleanliness. Lubrication systems in steel mills can be classified in several different ways:

    The first classification is based on the lubricant and the operation of the system.
    1. Oil lubrication systems.
    2. Air/Oil lubrication systems.
    3. Grease lubrication systems.
    4. Oil mist systems (not recommended for industrial applications).

    This chapter focuses primarily on oil lubrication systems. These systems are classified based on the type
    of supply to the mechanical equipment:
    1. Splash lubrication in enclosed gearboxes.
    2. Self-contained lubrication for gearboxes.
    3. Centralized lubrication systems.

    However, the most important classification is based on the interaction with the mechanical equipment and
    other fluids, in particular water. With this in mind there are two different types of systems:
    1. Dry systems.
    2. Wet systems.

    Lubrication systems can also be classified by the system operating pressure:
    1. Low pressure systems
    2. High pressure (hydrostatic) systems

    Additionally, the lubrication systems can be classified based on the oil viscosity that is also associated to
    the equipment speed, the type of oil and other operating conditions such as temperature and flow. Each
    different system type has different design, operating and maintenance conditions and requirements.

    The emphasis in this chapter is on centralized lubrication systems as they are the most important system
    type used in the industry.

    In the Attachment, generalized fluid recommendations are presented for Morgan Construction Company
    equipment.

Centralized Lubrication Systems:

One or several gearboxes can be supplied from a centralized lubrication system. A main tank or tanks are
used to store the oil and pumps are used to send the required flows to the mechanical equipment, passing also
through filters and heat exchangers. Depending on the application, some additional equipment can be also
included such as oil accumulators, return filters, off-line cleaning and heating systems, etc. This is the most

Dry and Wet System Considerations
Dry Lubrication Systems: These are systems not subject to water ingress and/or large water contamination.
      Typical systems are for enclosed gearboxes; also gearboxes with splash lubrication and self-contained
      lubrication systems normally fall within this classification.

        Gearboxes located away from the sources of water in the rolling process are typically considered dry
        systems. All the gearboxes that drive the breakdown mill, roughing and intermediate mill stands are
        connected to dry lubrication systems. Typically these are known as the low speed equipment.
        Although there is a potential for water ingress throughout the seals or pipes in the lubrication
        system’s heat exchangers, statistically this is a very rare event and the system can be considered to
        have a low probability of water ingress.

        Humidity present in the ambient air can contaminate the lubrication systems. Water condensation
        from the environment can occur due to temperature changes and/or high relative humidity in the air.
        Knowing the ambient parameters from site helps design the system with the appropriate devices to
        control condensation.

        The design of this type of systems is typically simpler than wet systems, the system itself is cheaper
        and the maintenance requirements are small.

        Some facts concerning dry systems:
        • Different oil chemistries can be used in dry systems that can provide better protection to bearings
           and gears.
        • Oils typically do not need special demulsibility characteristics.
        • Oil contamination comes mostly from the mechanical equipment.
        • Oils may require special additives to reduce foaming and/or may require not having some other
           additives that may increase the air entrainment in the oil.
        • Lower oil degradation and additive loss.
        • Reduced chances of corrosion and associated bearing failures.

Wet Lubrication Systems: These are systems subject to water ingress and water and humidity
     contamination. Typical systems are for high-speed rod mills including Pre-Finishing Mills, No-Twist®
     Mills, Reducing/Sizing mills, Mini-Finishing mills and Mini-blocks and for low-speed/high-load
     Morgoil® chock bearing lubrication systems.

       It is important to note that the main source of water ingress in rolling mill equipment is the roll cooling
        used on the mill stands for low and high speed equipment.

      The design of these types of systems could be very complicated depending upon, among many other
       factors:
      •         Water quality.
      •         Water ingress rates.
      •         Oil chemistry required.
      •         Operating temperatures.
      •         Oil limit temperatures.

      Wet lubrication systems normally require larger tanks (settling times must be based on the final oil
      viscosity and oil type), water removal units and analysis of the water effect on the overall operation of
      the equipment to define filter types, heat exchangers and auxiliary equipment.

      Morgan has performed several studies to determine the most efficient water removal techniques and
      recommends the use of the Morgan Vacuum Dehydrators in this type of lubrication system.

      Due to the additional requirements, the wet lubrication systems are typically more complicated, require
       larger space, are more expensive and the maintenance is more severe.

      Some facts concerning wet systems:
      •       Special oil chemistries must be used in wet systems that can provide good water separation
               and at the same time good protection to bearings and gears.
      •       Oils may require special additives to reduce foaming and/or may require not having some
               other additives that may increase the air entrainment in the oil.
      •       In most cases the oil contamination comes from the water.
      •       Higher probabilities of oil degradation and additive loss.
      •       Increased chances of corrosion and associated bearing failures.

      The maximum water content tolerated in the oil is based on the operating speeds and loads of the
       bearings lubricated by the system. The higher the speeds the lower the water content allowed.

      Morgan typically uses Clevite® bearings on the high-speed equipment that have low tolerance to water
      contamination due to the small tolerances and high precision required for high-speed operation. The
      maximum water content allowed is 0.2% (2 000 ppm).

      Morgoil® bearings have a higher tolerance to water in the oil and allow the operation of lubricants
      highly contaminated with water. The maximum water content permissible is 2% (20 000 ppm).

      Roller bearings have very low tolerance to water. The lubrication system must be kept very clean and
       with very low water content. Typically the maximum water content allowed is also 0.2% (2 000
       ppm).
