Lubrication System Pressure Classifications

As stated above, there are two classes of hydraulic systems based on pressure:

       Low Pressure Lubrication Systems: These are systems that operate at a maximum pressure of 10 bar
       (150 PSI) at the pump. These systems are used for lubrication and heat removal purposes only.

       High Pressure Lubrication Systems: These are systems that operate at pressures above 10 bar (150
       PSI) at the pump; typically in the range of 200 to 300 bar (3000 to 4500 PSI). These systems are used
       for Morgoil® hydrostatic applications. They consist of two different supply lines; one of which
       function is to provide lubrication and heat removal, and the other to enhanced the load carrying
       capacity of the fluid.

OILS FOR ROLLING MILLS

Rolling Mills require highly refined mineral oils. Although there are a few applications using synthetic oils,
the main stream of lubricants is still based on mineral oils.

Generalized specifications for the different oils used in Morgan equipment are listed in Attachment 1.

Oil chemical specifications for Rolling Mill lubrication systems are:
1. NTM® oil for high-speed equipment.
2. Gear oil with EP additives for low-speed equipment enclosed gearboxes and Reducing/Sizing Mill
    gearbox(es).
3. Morgoil® oils. Classified in Standard and Super-Demulsibility oils.

Different viscosities of the specified oils are used in different parts of the mill. The viscosity is selected based
on the equipment speed and loads.

The ISO classification of oils is normally used to identify the different oil viscosities. They are typically in
the ranges of ISO VG-100 to ISO VG-680 for oil lubrication systems and ISO VG-46 to ISO VG-320 for
air/oil systems; however some special oils may not fully agree with this classification.

One of the main parameters for oil selection is the oil chemistry that must be fully compatible with all the
parts of the mechanical equipment, especially materials and seals and also provide specific operating
properties to the oil during the lubrication process.

TYPICAL OPERATING PARAMETERS OF OIL LUBRICATION SYSTEMS

In a lubrication system, the most important operating parameters are:
    1. Pressure
         • Supply pressure at the pumps: typically 6 to 10 bar
         • Supply pressure at the equipment: typically 1.5 to 3 bar

        Note: Refer to Morgan circuit drawings for specific values and settings.

    2. Temperature
       • Tank storage temperature: typically 49°C
       • At the pump outlet: Typically 50°C
       • At the heat exchanger outlet: typically 40°C (*)
       • At the equipment: typically 40°C (*)
       (*) Temperature may vary depending on the oil used and equipment operating and design parameters.
       For high-speed mill stands: 38°C

        Note: Refer to Morgan circuit drawings for specific values and settings.

    3. Flow
       • Vary depending on the bearing size, speed and loads.

        Note: Refer to Morgan circuit drawings for specific values and settings.

    4. Water content.
       • At the tank: maximum allowable 2% (20,000 ppm), however quantities can be much higher
       • At the equipment:
         - 2% (20,000 ppm) maximum for Morgoil® bearings.
         - 0.2 % (2,000 ppm) maximum for Clevite® bearings
         - 0.2 % (2,000 ppm) maximum for roller bearings

    5. Air content
       • At the tank: maximum allowable 1%, however quantities can be much higher
       • At the equipment: 0.5% maximum

    6. Viscosity
       • Viscosity is directly proportional to the oil temperature and the oil Viscosity Index; therefore the
           temperature control is very important in lubrication systems. The Morgan maximum allowance
           in viscosity variance is 8% for every ISO grade.

    7. Oil cleanliness
       • Measured based on ISO cleanliness levels. Continuous oil cleanliness monitoring is always
           recommended to evaluate the filter’s efficiency, protect the mechanical equipment and avoid
           premature failures of the mechanical and lubrication system equipment.

LUBRICATION SYSTEM MAIN FILTER(S)
Morgan recommends that lubricating oil sent to the mill equipment should be passed through a set of duplex
filters that will filter the fluid to a level that meets the Morgan equipment requirements.
The oil cleanliness requirements depend on the equipment speeds and loads. Normally the higher the speed
the higher the cleanliness requirement; however the actual oil cleanliness level will also depend on the
condition of the equipment, the type, quality and quantity of contaminants and most importantly of the filter
beta number and filter efficiency.

The multi-pass test ISO 16889 measures the filter performance in a wide particle-size range. This gives a
series of Beta ratios for the filter as opposed to a percentage efficiency. The filter beta number specifies the
efficiency of a filter element based on the absolute size of the particles tested and the amounts of
contaminants upstream and downstream of the filter. The higher the beta number for an absolute particle size
the higher the filter efficiency and therefore the better the filter performance and cleaner the oil.

        Beta x micron =Number of particles upstream (x micron and larger)
                       Number of particles downstream (x micron and larger)

Where x is the determining size of particle for the Beta ratio. The following Figure illustrates the Morgan
filter-element efficiencies.




For many years cleanable filter elements were used in lubrication systems, unfortunately the beta ratios and
efficiencies of these are extremely low. The latest technology uses synthetic fiber disposable filter elements
that can provide up to six months of continuous operation with the same efficiency and only increases in
pressure drop. Maximum allowable pressure drop is typically set at 1.5 bar through the filter housing.
The new filtration technology allows the operation of a high-speed lubrication system with one main
duplex filter of Beta12(c) >1000, which provides better filtration than a typical 10 micron filter
(Beta10(c) = 200)


MORGAN FILTER RECOMMENDATIONS

Based on ISO 4406-1999, The following filtration levels are required for Morgan mill equipment:
        Low speed: Beta22(c) >= 1000
        High speed: Beta12(c) >= 1000

        Note that high speed equipment includes: PFM, NTM, RSM, PR, LH

Past practice at most mills was to compare the results of lab analysis against a set of "Mobil Modified NAS

Water Removal with Vacuum Dehydrator

In lubrication systems with possible water ingress, Morgan recommends the Morgan Vacuum Dehydrator be
used to remove the water from the oil. The vacuum dehydrator is deemed to be a better way to remove water
than a centrifuge. The dehydrator is normally sized to remove water in 12 hours of continuous operation.

Vaccum dehydrators remove water by lowering the boiling point of the water at pressures lower than the
atmospheric pressure. It is very important that the vacuum dehydrator provide a controlled heating of the oil
and that the oil is returned at almost the same temperature as it is extracted from the tank.

Morgan’s special design Vacuum Dehydrator includes a low power density heating system in two steps that
provides a controlled heating process and also returns the oil to the tank at a temperature similar to the oil
inlet temperature. The advantages of this design is that it does not interfiere with the main lubrication system
temperature control and does not have direct contact with electric heaters.

The unit also comes with a Beta12(c) or Beta22(c) main filter that after the heating process can be used as an of-
line filtration system.

For low viscosity oils (up to 150 cSt) the unit uses coalescer filters to enhance the water removal rate of free
water present in the oil.

The unit uses special disperser filters in the vacuum chamber that increase the oil surface exposed to vacuum
in order to thin out the oil and promote higher water removal. The unit controls the water removal with a
variable frequency driven pump controlled by level which at the same time controls the foam level.

LUBRICATION SYSTEM INSPECTION PROGRAM

IMPORTANT: The following information should be used as a guide for implementing an inspection
program for each lubrication system. It is important that recording separate inspection data and information
for each lube system and mill area be thorough and complete. Each area of the mill has its own unique
system and the inspection program should be tailored to the specifications of that system.
Because of the high speed, close tolerance bearings and precision gearing employed throughout the
mill, it is essential that a simple, yet effective maintenance program be established to assure that the
lubricating system, as well as the lubricating oil, be kept in prime condition. Therefore, this section
of the manual covers general recommendations as well as typical forms that can be utilized for setting
up mill inspection and maintenance programs.
Since it is literally impossible to build a mill and lubricating system that will remain 100% free of
contamination, it is important to first recognize the various possible sources of contamination and
then the ways in which steps can be taken to fight this contamination.
Some of the sources of contamination include:
    •   Ingress of roll pass water through the roll neck seals of the mill housings.
    •   Ingress of water and rust through condensation on the underside of the top of the receiving tank.
    •   Scale from the rod carried in with the roll pass water.

    •   Pipe scale from inside of gravity drain piping.
    •   Airborne iron oxides entering through the breathers on the mill housings and receiving tanks.

    •   Chemical composition of the roll pass water, such as PH, chlorides, detergents, etc., and particle
        contamination from suspended solids.
    •   Poor housekeeping practices during filter cleaning, tank inspection, addition of make-up oil,
        rebuilding of mill housings, etc.

REFERENCES
Generally, mill installations vary as to the number of strands, mill stands per strand, mill speeds, etc.; likewise,
there are similar variations in the associated lubricating systems such as tank size, pump capacity, type and size,
as well as the quantity and location of filters, etc. It must be recognized that this write-up does not apply
to any one specific lubricating system but is generally applicable to all systems.
It is suggested that these procedures be edited by the user to make them applicable to the specific mill
installation and lubricating system at hand. At the same time, actual plant practices could be added under
various items as felt necessary, the result of which, would then be a practical maintenance procedure
handbook for the given installation.

For engineering details applying specifically to the lubricating system for this mill installation, refer to the
Morgan Construction Company Lubrication circuit drawing for the oil specifications.

The oil is filtered at the main duplex filter station in the oil cellar. The elements used in the filters are
disposable for 12 micron (High speed equipment) and 22 micron (Low speed equipment). Pressure
differential gages and switches on the duplex filter assembly indicate, by means of the pressure drop
across the bank, the relative conditions of cleanliness of the filter elements. In addition, a pressure
transmitter at the supply header to the equipment sounds an alarm when the pressure to the equipment
falls to an unsafe level.

Note: Refer to Morgan circuit drawings for specific values and settings.

TYPICAL INSPECTION CHARTS

The forms at the end of this manual are presented as typical of the type that can be prepared for a
maintenance inspection program. Through the use of such forms, it will be possible to maintain a log
or history of both the lubricating system and the lubricating oil. Such a log will be a valuable tool in
preventing problems from getting out of hand and which, if not corrected, could shut down the mill.
When preparing the actual forms to be used for this inspection program, obviously they will have to
be altered from that shown in order to include the actual components contained in the lubricating
system at hand. At the same time, it may be desirable to change the format to be more compatible
with plant forms currently in use.
Also, as experience is gained in the operation of the mill and lubricating system, it may be found
advantageous to alter the various forms to add any items or change the frequency of inspection to
better suit the actual operating conditions encountered.
TYPICAL INSPECTION CHARTS FOR LUBRICATING SYSTEMS
CHECK LIST FOR MAINTENANCE

A Check List Chart should be made available for maintenance and operation personnel that list the
major components of the system with recommendations of what to check for and the frequency at
which it should be checked.
It is suggested that similar full size charts be made from these pages by the user and hung on the wall
in the oil cellar convenient for ready reference by maintenance.
DAILY INSPECTION REPORT
The report form shown on pages 40, 42 and 43 are an example of the type of information that should
be recorded on a daily basis. The Superintendent of Maintenance is to establish the frequency at
which this report is to be made; i.e., at the start or end of each shift or on a daily basis.
Upon completion of this inspection report, it must be checked against the previous report and any
changes noted are to be reported in writing to the Superintendent of Maintenance or his appointed
representative. The Daily Inspection Reports are to be properly filed for easy reference.

INSPECTION OF DRIP LEG SIGHT GLASSES
The main purpose of this chart is to make sure that the sight glass in the drain line from each of the applicable
mill housings is inspected at least once during each shift. Whether or not the chart is filled in on a shift or
daily basis is purely a matter of preference. It is felt that close surveillance of the sight glasses is the best
insurance in detecting the major source of ingress of water into the system. Presence of water in one of the
sight glasses is generally a sign that something is amiss with the roll neck seals on that stand or that there is
misalignment of the roll pass water spray nozzles. When free water is detected in a sight glass, this fact
should be reported to the mill maintenance personnel so they can check this stand further. It may also be
noted that the color of the oil in the sight glass may change from the clear amber tone of the original oil. This
may be an indication of a minor leak or a form of aeration, etc., which bears closer watching to determine the
need for further action. Should water be detected in a sight glass, it is suggested that a quick check be made
for the presence of water in the receiving tank by cracking slightly the opening drain cocks at the bottom of
the tank in operation.

A more accurate method to determine the conditions of the roll housing seals is to do the following during the
normal maintenance shut-down:
   • Shut down the equipment and then the roll cooling.
   • Shut down the lubrication system.
   • Take oil samples from the drip-legs and observe the color and condition of the oil in the drip legs.
   • Drain the drip legs completely.
   • Start-up the roll cooling and leave it running for approximately 30 to 60 minutes and inspect the drip
       legs during this time.
   • If water starts filling up the drip legs it is an indication of seal problems in the particular stand where
       water is found.
   • Replace the seals in the failed stand(s) as necessary.
MONTHLY INSPECTION REPORT
It is suggested that at monthly intervals a check to the condition of components which change at a
relatively slow rate be made. It will also serve an important maintenance function by providing data on
such things as total operating hours, quantity of make-up oil added, number of filter changes, repairs made,
etc. As with all other charts, this one should be compared against the previous month's chart and
abnormalities reported to the Superintendent of Maintenance.
VISUAL INSPECTION PROGRAM
In order to assure that the lubricating oil is being maintained in good condition and to prevent minor
adverse conditions from compounding into major problems, it is recommended that a simple monthly
visual inspection program be established. Such a program will provide the maintenance personnel
first hand knowledge relative to the general condition of the oil in the system at all times. Without
such a program, total dependence is placed upon a laboratory for analysis of samples which is a costly
and, more important, a time consuming process.
The center of this visual inspection program is the combination light box/storage rack. The purpose
of this rack is to provide a specific place to store samples while at the same time providing the means
to visually examine an individual sample as well as compare that sample against previous samples.

Naturally, many liberties can be taken in making a storage rack. However, it is important that it is
well illuminated in order to "see through" the samples of oil. One word of caution - do not store oil
samples where they may be exposed to direct sunlight since ultraviolet rays can have an effect on the
color of the oil.
The standard infant nursing bottles are an example of the type of bottle that can be used for sample
bottles since they are readily available, inexpensive, * sterile, graduated and capped. Naturally,
any other type container having these features could be used.
The primary step in initiation of this program is to obtain a master sample against which all
successive samples are to be compared. It is recommended that this sample be obtained at the time
new oil is delivered from the refinery for installation in the system.
In the supply pipe header for the equipment and on the back of the No-Twist mill and RSM is located
a sample cock and test ports which are to be used when drawing oil samples for inspection. The
sample cock should be cleaned with a filtered solvent, using lint free wipers, such as Kim wipes,
before drawing a sample. Naturally, the lubricating system must be operating and then a gallon or
two of oil flushed from the sample cock before the actual sample bottle is filled. A sample thus
obtained is representative of the oil being delivered to the equipment. Such a sample should be drawn
at predetermined monthly intervals and the sample bottle placed in the rack for comparison against
the previous and master samples.
NOTE: The sample bottles must be kept in their plastic wrapped protective bag until needed.
Used bottles must be cleaned and sterilized prior to use.

Note: The following points are to be checked during visual inspection of the sample:
Color
Water, dirt, air, etc., are all factors that may have an effect on the color of the oil. Entrained water
will settle out on the bottom of the bottle quite readily. However, if an emulsion is in the process of
being formed, this will impart a hazy appearance to the oil starting with a very light haze going all the
way to a cream colored milky appearance. Entrained air will have a tendency to impart a hazy
appearance but can be distinguished from water by closer inspection. Although heavier or larger
particles of contamination will settle out on the bottom of the bottle, it is possible for lighter particles
to remain in suspension.
Water and/or Emulsion
Within an hour of drawing a sample, most of the water, if present, will collect on the bottom of the
bottle and is easily distinguished from the oil. The maximum allowable water content and/or
emulsion in the sample is 0.2% (2000ppm) which can be read directly from the scale on the bottle.
Should this amount of water be present, then steps must be taken immediately to:
    •   Assure the Vacuum Dehydrator (preferred) or centrifuge is in operation.
    •   Inspect the sight glasses in the drain lines at the back of the mill to see if any stand is admitting water.
    •   Check the bottom of the tank for accumulation of water.

Odor
By merely sniffing the sample bottle for a rotten egg smell one can readily determine that the oil has been
overheated. Associated with the detection of this odor is a distinct change in color to a dark brown and is a
signal that another sample should be taken and sent to the laboratory for further tests.
Contamination
It is possible to detect 40 micron particles of dirt with the naked eye and, therefore, the bottom of the bottle
should be examined closely. If specks are noticed on the bottom, the previous months' samples should be
examined to compare whether or not there appears to be a noticeable increase in quantity. A collection of a
few dots of pepper across the bottom should not be cause for alarm but, of course, if the entire bottom is
covered, then an immediate check should be made on all filter elements in the lubricating system. Also,
another sample should be drawn and sent to the laboratory for further analysis and identification of the nature
of the contamination.
The photograph of oil sample vials (Page 19) has been prepared by Mobil to serve as a guide or comparison
against samples taken for the Visual Inspection Program. Reading the photograph from left to right (samples
1 through 4) we have:
Sample #1
New NTM® oil (Mobil Vacuoline 525 oil typical). The master, or standard, sample in the storage rack
should compare favorably with this picture since it is a sample of new oil as delivered to the mill.
Sample #2
This vial contains NTM® oil (Mobil Vacuoline 525 oil typical) taken from the sample cock after having been in
circulation approximately six months. The oil shows a slight haze and the color is somewhat darker than the
master sample. Should a sample drawn have a much darker color than this, then the supplier of the oil should be
contacted to discuss further testing to determine the identification and source of contamination. Also, as
previously discussed, the bottom of the bottle should be examined closely for the degree of "pepper" spread
across the bottom which is our indication of particle contamination. 5% water was purposely added to this
sample and then agitated. The clear separation of water developed within an hour as shown at the bottom of the
vial. Should any free water be observed the steps described in the Water and/or Emulsion section must be taken.
Sample #3
This is also used NTM® oil (Mobil Vacuoline 525 oil typical) with water dispersed throughout thus creating the
cloudy appearance. Should the drawn sample appear close to this example then the system must be watched
closely since the condition could get worse rather quickly. The tank in service should be switched over to
stand-by, the vacuum dehydrator (preferred) run or centrifuged and then allowed to rest. In the meantime, all
sight glasses in the drain line at the applicable mill station should be inspected for water ingress as well as all
other possible sources of water contamination.
Sample #4
This again, is used NTM® oil (Mobil Vacuoline 525 oil typical) oil which is partly emulsified with water.
The bottom cream colored layer represents a heavy emulsion and must be treated with an emulsion breaker
before continued service. Should a sample be drawn that compares to this, then immediately the tank in
service should be switched to stand-by and the oil supplier notified of the condition at hand.

TYPE OF LUBRICATING OIL
IMPORTANT: Extreme caution must be exercised to assure that NO OTHER OIL THAN THE
TYPE SPECIFIED FOR THE SPECIFIC LUBRIACTION SYSTEM of the applicable mill area
be used. This is particularly true when make-up oil is to be added to the system. Check that the
proper oil is ordered and check again upon delivery before adding to the system. Extra caution must
be employed when make-up oil is added via barrels to make certain that no "foreign" barrels, such as
hydraulic fluid, gear oil, kerosene, etc., get mixed in by mistake. To the casual observer it may
appear that the mixing of one barrel of "foreign" oil into a 38,000 liter (10,000 gallon) system would
have little effect. However, to the contrary, the resulting chemical reaction could contaminate the
entire tank and quickly place the entire mill area in jeopardy.
To assist in understanding the complexity of the oil used for lubrication to specific mill areas, the
following is intended to express in layman's terms how an oil can be designed or "built" for a specific
purpose and explains why an "ordinary oil" cannot be used.

Skipping over the details of processing crude oil into refined oil, it is sufficient to state that the oil for
each mill area is made from a "Base Stock". Since not all base stocks are alike, it is necessary to limit
the type used and, therefore, the statement from the specifications..."The oil must be formulated from
high quality, solvent refined paraffinic straight mineral base stocks...".
Thus starting with a good base stock oil it is then possible by means of additives to literally design,
build or develop an oil that will provide the physical qualities necessary to properly lubricate the
different pieces of equipment throughout the mill.
Note: Refer to Morgan circuit diagrams for specific details and specifications about the oil required.
Example: Although not for use in rod mills, a somewhat similar example of oil "built" to suit a
specific application is that of the common "Multi-Viscosity" motor oil. Years ago, motor oils
contained few, if any, additives. With the advent of high horsepower automobile engines, the oils no
longer were able to provide the protection required of these new engines and thus the oil industry
"built" or developed a new series of oils to suit this need. Starting with a base stock, an additive was
introduced to provide multi-viscosity; an additive for protection against wear; one for anti-rust and
so on, until an oil able to provide excellent protection against many conditions was produced.
In like manner, but entirely different than motor oils, the NoTwist Vee and RSM mill oil has been
developed specifically to meet the operating conditions of these high speed mills. Briefly, some of the
built-in features provided by the additives used in this oil include:
Protection Against Water
This feature is required in order for the oil to quickly shed water that may ingress into the system by
way of the roll neck seals. By having this ability to shed water quickly and also providing a large
reservoir in which this can take place, it is then possible to drain off the accumulation of water from
the bottom of the reservoir.

Protection Against Rust

An inhibitor is provided to protect against the formation of rust which could be caused by the
presence of both water and also condensation within the NoTwist Vee mill housings, receiving tanks,
gravity drain piping, etc.

Wear and Load Protection
These types of additives, in somewhat general terms, can be considered as additional insurance. They
are present and to a certain degree help with the general workload of lubricating the gearing and
bearings. However, in times of emergency, such as encountering an overload on the mill, they come
into play by providing extra muscle or film strength during the emergency.
Breakdown Protection

This type of additive is intended to provide a measure of protection against oxidation of the oil when
exposed to high temperatures.
For certain applications some other built-in features must be provided in the oil:
    • Air entrainment resistance (de-aeration).
    • Foaming resistance.
    • Extreme pressure (EP) additives (EP oil not to be used with high speed equipment such as
        NTM®, PFM, RSM, PR, LH).
LUBRICATING OIL VISUAL INSPECTION PROGRAM
IMPORTANT: The following information should be used as a guide for implementing an
inspection program for each lubrication system. It is important that recording separate inspection
data and information for each lube system and mill area be thorough and complete. Each area of
the mill has its own unique system and the inspection program should be tailored to the
specifications of that system.
In our continuing search for new ways and/or methods to maintain the oil in the cleanest condition
possible, these pages are issued to describe two additional procedures that we feel valuable toward
maintaining clean oil.
Procedure I - Daily Visual Inspection Program
Perhaps the single, most serious problem faced in mills is the sudden ingress of water into the
lubricating system. This is why, as noted on the check list, the need to open the drain cocks on the
bottom of the reservoirs daily to drain off any collection of water.

This new procedure does not change or alter any previous instructions; it merely is an attempt to
stress the value of inspecting the oil on a shift or daily basis. Some mills in operation have
experienced cases where the lubricating system practically runs by itself for long periods of time and,
other than the routine cleaning of filters, maintenance practices begin to relax somewhat. Then there
is a sudden change; i.e., during a roll change or some other unrelated condition, there will be a sudden
ingress of water into the system that is not detected as quickly as it normally should. For

example; the oil level in the tank has been allowed to fall below normal and the high/ low level switch
improperly adjusted to suit this condition and therefore the ingress of water is much greater than
normally permitted. Likewise, the inspector failed to open the cock on the bottom of the tank

daily as suggested and as a result, the increased volume in the tank escaped detection. From this
point on, the progression of events can occur quite rapidly. Due to the relaxed attitude of inspection
and since the oil level is low and the amount of water accumulated on the bottom of the tank has
increased considerably, the nozzle on the end of the floating suction is at a level which can pick up
free water along with the oil. Thus water and oil enters the suction side of the pump whereupon it
becomes thoroughly mixed going through the gears in the pump. Likewise this solution is carried on
to the mill where again it is mixed by going through the gear meshes in the mill. Perhaps this is a
rather graphically excessive description of the process but nevertheless illustrates how quickly a
seemingly perfect tank of oil can be transformed into a creamy tight emulsion. Therefore, for
Procedure I we are recommending that, in addition to opening the drain cocks at the bottom of the
tanks daily that a baby bottle of oil also be inspected at least once a day and preferably once a shift.

The preferable place to draw a sample of oil is, of course, at the petcock or test ports on the headers to
the equipment, as applicable. A sample drawn here will actually show the oil being delivered to the
mill. It will be quite obvious to anyone inspecting samples whether or not there has been a radical
change in appearance of the oil between the morning and evening samples. Should any change in
appearance be noted, action can be taken at once to determine what may be causing this rapid change
and correct the problem long before it gets out of hand. We cannot overstress the importance of
frequent periodic inspection as an aid in keeping the oil in good condition.

Procedure II - Contamination Levels
It has been our experience over the years in dealing with various bearing problems encountered in the
No-Twist Mill and Reducing-Sizing Mill area that those mills maintaining the cleanest lubricating
systems have, by a wide margin, very few problems as compared to the extremely high incidence of
problems experienced by mills whose lubricating systems are known to be contaminated.

Procedure II consists of two parts, namely: Part 1 - How to process a No-Twist Vee Mill /RSM oil
sample and Part 2 - How to classify the results .

Since our expertise is with the mill equipment we will only touch on the highlights of Procedure II
and recommend that the mill oil supply representative or other knowledgable persons specializing in
the subject be contacted by the Mill Maintenance Department to explain the details of testing the oil
and subsequent classification of same.

Procedure II - Part 1 - The Processing of a Sample:

Mill Maintenance personnel, working in conjunction with the oil supply representative or other
“expert” determine a schedule for regular sampling, and method for reporting results and maintaining
records of sample results.
Once having processed an oil sample the next step is to classify the results which is Part 2 of this procedure.

Procedure II - Part 2 Classification of Results:

The results of the sample processed in Part 1 then needs to be analyzed to determine the level of
cleanliness/contamination. As stated earlier, past practice was to compare the results against a set of
"Mobil Modified NAS 1638" reference photographs. (Using the National Aerospace Standard
1638, Mobil had developed a series of photographs of the various levels of contamination 1 thru 12 ).
The current Morgan recommendation is that samples be taken and analyzed in accordance with the
relevant ISO 4406-1999 (and related procedures). The results should be compiled and tracked over
time to allow a fuller picture of the lubrication system performance.

LABORATORY SAMPLING

For several years now major oil suppliers and others have been working with mills in setting up
regular programs for monitoring lubricating systems oils. Such a regular program is recommended by
Morgan. The basis of these programs is to establish a schedule for taking and processing samples of
mill oil, analyze them and report back what specific action, if any, is required by the mill, all within a
short period of time. The recommendations take into account the results from past samples on the
system(s) oil so that a history is established for each system.

As stated, it is recommended that the Superintendent of Maintenance make arrangements with the
mills oil supply representative or other to establish such a program. The representative will assign a
number or some identifier to each tank requesting this service which then establishes a history file for
this mill. Frequency of sending samples for analysis should not exceed the following schedule:
        •   Sample every 500 hours for the first 2000 hours
        •   Sample every 1000 hours for the next 2000 hours
        •   Sample every 2000 hours thereafter
The oil samples as received at the laboratory are identified by the identifying code number and
processed. The results of the tests should be reported on a standard form and, for example, should
this particular oil sample be the 3rd 500 hour sample, then the standard form would also show the
results of the first two samples. Thus the report received back at the mill would show the results of
the three samples tested to date. This is a most important feature of this procedure, for it permits the
mill personnel to see whether or not there has been any change in the results of any one test over a
period of time, as well as the rate at which the change has occurred.
Provided this or similar program is used diligently and maintenance practices kept alert we believe
this approach to be a decided improvement over the old method of testing and reporting on oil
samples.

MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS
IMPORTANT
Always isolate, shutoff and/or disconnect Water, Air, Hydraulic and Electrical power supply sources before
performing any repairs or maintenance. Read Safety Instructions and Warnings for each system and
component prior to working on machinery. Refer to Safety section in this manual.
INTRODUCTION
Routine and Preventive Maintenance of the Fluid Systems is required to ensure extended and proper operation.
Table 6 is provided as a quick reference guide for frequent periodic maintenance requirements for the cooling and
lubrication systems. Trouble Shooting information is also provided for each system in Tables 1 through 5.
General maintenance instructions are also provided as a guide for components of the lube tank system. Refer to
the manufacturers technical manual for maintenance requirements and procedures of specific components of the
fluid system. Refer to the General Maintenance section as a guide for corrective maintenance.
        Warning: Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or
        disconnect all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any stored
        energy from components. Restrain and secure any moving parts of a component or
        system that could cause injury.
1.0     Hydraulic Systems
        Daily
        1.1        Check reservoir fluid level and fill as necessary. Monitor temperature of tank.
        1.2        Inspect for leaks and loose connections. Tighten or replace as necessary.
        Weekly
        1.3        Check for pressure drop across filters. Change filters if drop range is 10-15 psi.
        1.4        Inspect heat exchanger for leaks and corrosion.
        Monthly
        1.5        Clean and inspect air breathers. Replace as necessary. Keep equipment free and clean from dirt.
        1.6        Inspect and tighten any loose solenoids.
        3 Months
        1.7        Inspect pipe supports, piping lengths and bolts and fittings. Tighten or replace as required.
        1.8        Test and check operation of relief valves, pressure switches and level gages. Check accumulator
                   pre-charge.
        1.9        Clean and inspect heat exchanger. Replace anodes as required.
        6 Months
        1.10       Check pumps and motors for excess noise and vibration.

CORRECTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS
DEFINITION

Corrective maintenance encompasses those repair procedures required to return the applicable fluid system to
satisfactory operating condition. Such repairs do not necessarily return the equipment to like-new condition.
Rather, the objective is to make it operational again as soon as possible. It is recommended to replace faulty
parts/components and sub-assemblies with new or previously refurbished spare parts/components and sub-
assemblies. Those parts removed may then be refurbished or reconditioned after the main equipment has
been returned to service.

IMPORTANT

Always isolate, shutoff and/or disconnect Water, Air, Hydraulic and Electrical power supply sources before
performing any repairs or maintenance. Read Safety Instructions and Warnings for each system and
component prior to working on machinery.

INTRODUCTION

Corrective Maintenance of the Fluids Systems as defined above, is intended to keep down time at a
minimum by replacing components and then dismantling and overhauling the removed component in a
service area away from the mill. Once refurbished, the component becomes a spare shelf part, ready to be
utilized as a replacement when needed.

No disassembly procedures are given herein of components being replaced. Components that require
overhaul/refurbishment should be maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Refer to
the manufacturers technical manual for maintenance and torque requirements and procedures of specific pre-
manufactured components for the applicable fluid system.

General guidelines and maintenance criteria are provided below when corrective maintenance of a
component or sub-assembly is required. These are minimum guidelines and should be used in conjunction
to the specific maintenance requirements from the component manufacturer.

Upon re-assembly, tighten all bolts, screws, nuts and fasteners in accordance with Morgan reference
drawings torque requirements. Torque specific components in accordance with the manufacturer’s
requirements.

        WARNING: Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or
        disconnect all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any stored
        energy from components. Restrain and secure any moving parts of a component or
        system that could cause injury. Make sure covers are secure with locking pin and all
        interlocks are in place before performing any maintenance.
        WARNING: The lube and hydraulic systems are potentially dangerous and capable of
        inflicting severe bodily injuries. Before starting any maintenance task, comply with all
        company policies relating to safety. Also, be thoroughly familiar with the general requirements.

1.0     General Maintenance Criteria
The following is a list of maintenance actions to perform whenever dismantling equipment for repairs.
        1.1     Electric controls and power cables -- Before disconnecting any wiring that does
                not have plug-in connectors, make sure that color coding is clearly identifiable or tag each
                wire carefully for reference at re-assembly.
        1.2     Rigging parts for removal/replacement -- Many parts that make up this equipment are much
                too heavy to be handled by one man. Provide adequate rigging for lifting and supporting
                heavy parts before attempting to dismantle any equipment.
        1.3     Cleaning -- Clean all parts with a suitable solvent (mineral spirits, SAVASOL no.5, or
                equivalent) to remove all scale, grease, grime, or dirt. Use a clean wiper; do not use cotton
                waste. Air dry after cleaning.
        1.4     Bearings and Sealing Surfaces -- Closely inspect bearings and sealing surfaces for signs of
                wear, nicks, scratches, gouges, or build-up of scale or other foreign substances. Replace
                bearings that show any signs of deterioration.
                To clean roller bearings, soak in clean solvent long enough to loosen any sludge,
                then gently slosh each bearing around near the top of the container to dislodge
                all pockets of grease. Scrub away stubborn accumulations with a small brush
                that has bristles that do not break off. Do not spin dirty bearings, but rotate races
                slowly while washing and scrubbing.
                Rinse the bearings in clean solvent and air dry. Hold both races when blowing with clean,
                dry compressed air. Do not allow the air jet to spin the bearing; rather, turn each race by
                hand to expose all surfaces to the drying air. If the bearing is to be stored for later reuse,
                wrap it in wax paper or other grease-proof wrapping.
                CAUTION: A bearing may be defective without the defect being visually evident: replace
                any bearing removed during any maintenance task with new or cleaned bearing at re-
                assembly.

                New bearings are packed with rust-preventative grease (or other protective coating) and
                wrapped in grease-resistant paper before they are shipped. Do not unwrap the bearing until
                time for installation. Unwrap and thoroughly wash the new bearing and air dry. Pre-
                lubricate immediately with Mobil Vacuoline 525 (or equivalent).

        NOTE: For ease of installation of bearings, heat the bearings at a maximum temperature of 121°C
        (250°F) in oil for one hour minimum, or in an electric furnace for 1-1/2 hours minimum, or by
        bearing induction heater for 15 minutes minimum.

        1.5     Oil Seals -- Replace all seals and gaskets that are removed or disturbed during disassembly
                procedure. Make sure seals seat properly upon re-assembly.

        1.6      Oil Passages -- Pressure flush oil passages and blow dry with compressed air. Make sure
                 passages are clear of debris or blockage.

        1.7      Pre-lubrication Prior to Re-assembly -- Lightly lubricate all seals, bearings, bushings, and
                 gears with oil before installation
        1.8      Aligning Parts During Re-assembly -- Because of the weight of large parts, use guide studs
                 during re-assembly to ensure proper bolt hole and /or dowel pin alignment.
        1.9      Clean all parts and inspect for scratches, cracks, burrs, flaking, pitting, scaling or discoloration
                 of mating or load-bearing surfaces.
        1.10     Hand scrape any bushing that have not become out-or-round to remove burrs, small scratches or
                 accumulated foreign substances. Replace any bushing showing gross deformation or cracking.
        1.11     Check shafts and pivot pins for straightness with v-blocks and dial indicator. It is possible to
                 straighten bent shafts in a hydraulic press, but if spares are available, it is much better to
                 replace the parts. Never straighten bent castings; replace them. Weld cracked steel castings
                 only if no spares are available, but replace them whenever possible.
        1.12     If roller surfaces become badly worn, rough, pitted, scaled or blistered, dress them on a lathe
                 or grind them clean as long as the design tolerances are maintained. Otherwise, replace the parts.

MAINTENANCE OF LUBRICATING SYSTEM COMPONENTS
Receiving Tanks
In addition to serving as a storage tank for the oil, the receiving tank also provides a place for
contamination to settle out. One of the features of the oil used in the lubricating system is its ability
to shed water. Therefore, since the receiving tank is the ideal place to permit this to take place, it has
purposely been sized to provide a minimum of 21 minutes "rest" time for the oil (high speed
equipment) and 10 to 13 minutes “rest” time for low speed equipment. Also, the bottom of the tank is
sloped from back to front so that as the water drops out of the oil it will collect along the front side of
the tank where it may readily be drained off by means of the cocks or drain valves provided. On a
daily basis, it is important that these valves be used to drain off any accumulation of water. If this is
not done, the increase in volume of water allowed to accumulate can quickly lead to further problems.
One of the problems that can be encountered is that of emulsification, the blending or mixing of oil
and water. Should the water content of the oil be allowed to build up, then the process of
emulsification can be started by the mixing action of the rotors in the system pumps, by the gears and
pinions and also the rolling element bearings within the mechanical equipment, as applicable.

Once an emulsion has started to form, it will "tighten" quite rapidly if not checked and can reach a
point where the lubrication of the applicable mill area will be endangered. Should such a situation
develop, the first step to be taken is to start the vacuum dehydration system.

In the case of an existing stand-by tank** then also switch over from the "service" tank to the

**Note: The Morgan standard is the use of one tank and a Morgan Vacuum Dehydrator. Other
systems exist which use two tanks and a Vacuum Dehydrator, or two tanks and a centrifuge.

Cooling and Lubrication                                                                                Maintenance Instructions
"standby" tank in order to prevent further emulsification of the oil in the service tank. In so doing,
leave the return line drain valves open on the first tank for a few minutes while the system pump
draws from the second tank in order to allow most of the emulsified oil still in circulation in the
system to drain into the first tank. Then switch the drain valves to drain into the second tank thus
returning the system to normal operation.

If not already in operation, the next step is to place the vacuum dehydrator (preferred) or centrifuge in
operation on the emulsified tank of oil and then have a call placed to the oil supplier to inform him of
the condition at hand and request his assistance to apply corrective measures. Because special
treatment is required in order to break an emulsion and such treatment, if not properly exercised, can
have the adverse effect on the additives of the oil, the treatment should only be made by the supplier
of the oil. After contacting the oil supplier, it is important that the applicable mill area/system be
inspected to determine the source of ingress of water into the lubricating system. Also, in the case of
a two tank system, the tank just switched over to service should be closely watched for the ingress of
water and, of course, promptly drained if present. In addition, the vacuum dehydrator (preferred) or
centrifuge should be switched for operation on this tank.
Another form of contamination that will collect on the bottom of the tank is dirt or sludge. This
sludge is a composite of many varieties of materials such as pipe scale, foreign matter carried in with
the water, air born dirt, etc. A simple tool should be made, similar to the common garden hoe, for
checking the accumulation of sludge on the bottom of the tank. Once a month, by standing on top of
the tank, the hoe can be lowered thru the hatch and gently dragged across the bottom in order to
collect a sample of any sludge that may be present. Once proof has been established that sludge is
indeed accumulating, past records should be checked to establish how many months have elapsed to
this point. From this data, a date should be established for the draining, cleaning and inspection of
the tank interior. Regardless of whether or not sludge is present, it is suggested that the tanks be
drained, cleaned and inspected on a yearly basis.

Whenever it is necessary to open the hatch covers for any reason, it is essential to clean the cover itself,
and the area around it to prevent dirt from falling into the tank. The covers should remain open only as
long as is absolutely necessary, and be closed carefully, so as not to damage the sealing material.
Examination of the tank interior coating is also advisable on a monthly basis. The inside top of the
tank is highly susceptible to condensation and rusting, and therefore, should be inspected frequently.
Severe rusting problems, where "stalactites" of rust form, should be corrected as soon as possible
since if allowed to progress, only further increases the problem of contamination of oil in the
receiving tank.
While checking the tank interior coating, it is a good practice to take a look at the floating suction if
applicable (Wet systems use a floating suction while dry systems do not) just to make sure that it can
swing free and is in fact floating at the proper level. It is possible that the float could have become
jammed for some unknown reason, or even sunk, which, of course, could be the source of some other
unexplained problem.

Cooling and Lubrication                                                                                Maintenance Instructions
For systems utilizing two tanks it is recommended that the tanks be alternated weekly between service
and stand-by. One of the purposes in alternating tanks is to give the oil a rest period to permit
entrained water, air and contaminants to settle out. It is recommended that as soon as the "service"
tank is switched to stand-by that its contents be immediately processed through the vacuum
dehydrator (preferred) or centrifuge.

This procedure assures that most of the entrained contamination is removed instead of being allowed
to accumulate on the bottom of the receiving tank. It also assures that a relatively clean tank of oil is
available in the event of a problem arising with the tank in service. Since the vacuum dehydrator is
equipped with a preheater, it is not necessary to change the setting of the electric heater or steam
temperature regulator to raise the bulk temperature of the oil above the normal operating temperature.
After cleaning and allowing the tank to rest the remainder of the week, the drain cocks on the bottom
of the tank should be opened daily to drain off any further accumulation of free water.

Contrary to general assumptions, new oil as received in drums, or in bulk, from the oil supplier is not
necessarily "clean". Therefore, when adding oil to the system, make sure that it is filtered. If not
already so equipped, it is recommended that the fill connection on each receiving tank be fitted with a
22 micron absolute filter for low speed equipment systems, or 12 micron disposable element type
filter for high speed equipment systems. If oil is to be added by means of a transfer pump, then it is
important that a pump be provided for this specific purpose only. A transfer pump and hoses
"borrowed" from elsewhere in the mill must not be permitted due to the danger from contamination
with hydraulic oil, solvents, or whatever fluid the pump may have previously been used for.
Receiving Tank - High and Low Level Switch Assembly with Visual Indication

An oil level alarm is provided to give warning of either rising or falling oil level. A rising level in the
reservoir is an indication that water is entering the system, usually by way of a damaged roll neck
seal. Note: Falling oil level points to an oil leak in the system.
The setting of the strikers which contact the switch should be checked each day, and reset when
necessary to bring it as close as possible to the switch. This will insure the sounding of the level
alarm with a minimum oil loss or water ingress. As an example, in a 10,000 gallon (37,850 liters)
tank there are approximately 150 gallons (567.8 liters) per inch (25.4 mm) of depth, an arbitrary
setting of several inches above or below the switch will allow too much oil loss or water ingress
before the alarm sounds.
As noted, the strikers are to be adjusted daily to set as close as practical to the arm of the level switch.
About the only other maintenance required is to check that the alarm system indicating "high or low
level" is in proper working order. This can automatically be done whenever the system is shut down
since the rise in oil level should activate the alarm.
Receiving Tank - Liquid Level Gage
The main purpose of the liquid level gage on the front of the tank is to provide a visual check on the
operating oil level in the tank. By means of the scale calibrated in gallons, it can readily be
determined how much oil is needed to bring the operating level up to normal.

The liquid level gage is not to be used as an indicator to show the condition of the oil within the tank.
This is because of the configuration, location and minute quantity of oil in the glass in relation to the
entire volume of the tanks that it is impossible for this gage to show a true representative sample.
It is cautioned that the operating oil level must not be allowed to fall below more than 10% to 15% of
the total volume. This is because the rest or settling time of the oil will be greatly reduced which in
turn could promote further problems if the system were operated with less oil in the tank than this
minimum level.

For example, with a given size 10,000 gallon (37800 liter) tank, there are approximately 150 gallons
per 1" (25.4 mm) of depth. With a full tank of oil there should be about 6 inches of air space between
the oil level and the top of the tank. Then, with the system in operation, assume 450 gallons (1703
liters) of oil in the piping and No-Twist mill housings, etc., which would drop the oil level 3 inches
(76.2 mm). Thus, the normal "Operating Level would be 9 inches (228.6 mm) down from the top of
the tank.

A 15% oil loss, or 1500 gallons (5677.5 liters) would cause the level to drop an additional 10 inches
(254 mm) for a total of 19 inches (482.6 mm) down from the top of the tank. This 19 inches (482.6
mm) would be the minimum allowable oil level for this particular example. It is suggested that a
sticker, or nameplate, be placed alongside the level gage at this point stating to the effect "Minimum
oil level. Do not allow level to drop below this mark".

Naturally, these figures will vary in accordance with the actual tank dimensions and are given as a
guide in determining the allowable minimum oil level. As the level in the tank recedes toward the
minimum level, procedures should be automatically initiated for the addition of make-up oil to the
system.

Receiving Tank - Air Breather

The filter element of the air breather should be inspected on a monthly basis and cleaned as required.

Receiving Tank - Fan
The fan must be operated continuously to promote air flow over the oil level and remove humidity
from the tank.

Receiving Tank -Thermometer

Although this thermometer does provide an indication of the average oil temperature in the tank, it is
not to be used in determining the setting of the temperature regulating control.

Caution:       The temperature of the oil in the tank must never be raised above 150°F (66°C) nor be
               held at such an elevated temperature for more than 8 hours.

Receiving Tank - Temperature Transmitter

The temperature transmitter will send a 4-20 ma signal to the PLC to maintain the tank temperature
stable and switch on and off the different heater banks.

Receiving Tank - Heating Coils
At such time as the tank is drained for cleaning, the coils should be thoroughly inspected for leaks or
any other type of damage.
Receiving Tank - Return Line Filters
Some systems are equipped with return filters that are sometimes directly mounted on the receiving
tank. In that case the drain line filters mounted on the top of the tank at the return end are equipped
with an easily removable bolted cover. The units should be alternated periodically and inspected for
contamination. It is recommended that spare clean elements be available so that as an element
becomes dirty, it is only necessary to remove same and replace it immediately with a clean spare
element. Then the dirty element can be cleaned at a more convenient time. It is suggested that the
elements be checked weekly until such time as it can be established that less frequent cleaning
intervals are required. Cleaning procedures for these elements are described in Systems Filters
section of this manual.
Receiving Tank - Temperature Regulating Control
In order for the cooler, to operate properly, it is necessary that the proper temperature be maintained
in the receiving tank in service. The required tank temperature is that which will deliver oil at the
inlet connection of the cooler at the design temperature. Assuming the design inlet temperature to be
120°F (49°C), then the tank temperature control valve must be adjusted so as to provide this
temperature of oil going into the cooler. The pump discharge header thermometer, and the cooler
inlet thermometer, are used to determine the set point of the temperature regulating valve.

The tank heating system must remain on at all times even though the mill may shut down nights,
week-ends, etc. This is necessary in order to maintain the receiving tanks at operating temperature
ready for mill start-up. When shutting down the lubricating system for an extended period, the
supply line drain-down valve is to be opened to allow the oil in the supply line to the mill to drain
back to the receiving tank.

Note: In cold climates, it may be found advantageous to keep the lubrication system in operation
when the mill is shut down. This is especially true if the mill building is cold which in turn allows the
mass of steel in the mechanical equipment in the mill to become cold. Such things as raising the
setting of the temperature regulating valve, by-passing the cooler, etc., will allow the circulation of
warm oil through the housings to off-set somewhat the chilling effect of cold weather and thus
attempting to keep the mill ready for start-up.
Caution:       Do not raise the temperature of the oil in the tank above the design inlet temperature of
               the cooler. If, for any reason, such as aid in the removal of entrained air and/or water,
               it is desired to raise the temperature of the oil IN THE IDLE TANK to 150°F (66°C),
               then at such times the tanks must not be left unattended.
Service and Standby Pumps

It is recommended that the service and standby pumps be alternated weekly so as to equalize their
time in service. Refer to the pump manufacturer's instructions for maintenance requirements.

The pump relief valves should be checked occasionally to assure their settings have not been
disturbed and they are not leaking.

System Filters

A procedure for inspection and cleaning of filter elements should be developed prior to the start-up of
the lubricating system so that there will be no confusion or mill delays by waiting for a filter change.
In reality, there is no excuse for the alarm system to signal a dirty filter since good housekeeping
practices should dictate that an element be changed before the point at which the alarm will sound.
For example: assume the pressure of the No-Twist mill housings to be 40 PSI (2.81 Kg/sq. cm) with a
clean element and the low pressure alarm is set for 30 PSI (2.11 Kg/sq. cm). Maintenance practices
should know from daily inspections that the pressure is slowly falling at the No-Twist mill and when
the pressure has reached 33 PSI (2.32 Kg/sq. cm) a new element should be installed instead of waiting
until the alarm goes off at 22 PSI (1.55 Kg/sq. cm) and then change the filter.

Note: Refer to Morgan circuit diagrams for settings and specifications for each system.
Although Morgan Construction Company uses disposable synthetic filter elements for maximum
protection of mill bearings and ease of filter change, there may be mills still using cleanable strainers.
For these mills Morgan recommends the filters be upgraded to comply with the latest standards.
Morgan does not guarantee mechanical equipment not complying with the latest filtration and
cleanliness levels specified by Morgan.

The following Service Instructions are applicable to the Morgan Construction Co. Duplex Filter Assembly for
replacement of disposable filter elements. (Refer to figure below).

        1. Check arrow location on transfer valve for on-line filter housing.
                 (Arrow points to in service filter housing)
        2. Open commuter valve.
        3. Open bleed valve of stand by filter vessel.
        4. Close bleed valve upon appearance of fluid.
        5. Turn transfer valve handle in the direction of the stand by filter assembly.
        6. Close commuter valve.
        7. Open drain plug of the to be service filter vessel.
        8. Open bleed valve of the to be serviced filter vessel.
        9. Loosen and swing bolts away from top plate.
        10. Lift and swing cover back.
        11. Remove old elements from housing by pulling up on the handle provided on the filter element
                 and replace with a new set.
        12. Check cover o-ring and replace, if necessary.
        13. Re-install drain plug.
        14. Swing cover plate back in place and secure with swing bolts. Torque to 90 ft-lbs.
        15. Open commuter valve.
        16. Close bleed valve upon appearance of fluid.

      The following procedure is suggested for Return Line Filters.

      The basic procedure at filter changing time should be: remove the dirty element and replace it immediately
      with a clean element. Do not attempt to remove a dirty element, take it away to clean and then put it back.
      By following the recommended procedure, several dirty elements can be cleaned at the convenience of the
      operator and a much more thorough job of cleaning can be accomplished.
      On the subject of cleaning of stainless steel wire cloth filter elements it is unfortunate that concise instructions
      are difficult to establish. However, perhaps one negative statement can be made which is: Filter elements
      cannot be thoroughly cleaned by swishing them around in a bucket of solvent for half a minute!

      Many methods have been developed over the years by various plants for the cleaning of elements. The
      following are some of the ways by which effective methods can be developed. One method is to first
      immerse a dirty element in a bucket of hot soapy water consisting of a solution of household detergent and
      ammonia. This will wash off the heavy concentration of oil that in turn increases the lift of the subsequent
      cleaning solvent wash.

The cleaning of elements in solvent can be accomplished in many ways. Circulation of solvent through the
element and time seem to be the important considerations. One method is to use a chamber in which the
element can be submerged in cleaning solvent. The chamber is fitted with an air header that causes agitation
of the solvent about the element. Another somewhat similar method is to use a chamber to contain the element
and employ a pump to positively circulate solvent thru the element. The advantage of such method is that
elements can be left unattended while cleaning for many hours.
Perhaps the ultimate in cleaning methods today is that of ultrasonic. Best results using this method are
achieved by first washing the element in the detergent solution to remove heavy deposits. A second
cleaning via the circulating solvent method may also be advisable to improve the efficiency of the final
ultrasonic cleaning.

Whichever method is selected, it must be performed in a clean area, preferably a clean room, set aside for
this purpose.
A simple, yet effective way to assure they are thoroughly clean is to visually inspect them. This can be done
by means of using a 100 watt, or larger, bare light bulb suspended from the ceiling to a convenient eye-level
height.

The element to be inspected is held at eye-level and slowly rotated with the light bulb suspended inside the
element. Any contamination can readily be seen as dark areas or gray patches on the element in which case,
the element should be re-cleaned.

While inspecting the element for dark areas of contamination, it should also be carefully inspected for bright
spots which would indicate physical damage to the wire cloth. These bright spots of light would be an
indication of holes or punctures, tears, etc., in the mesh proper. In addition, the ends of the filter element
must be inspected thoroughly to assure the wire cloth is properly seated in the end caps. Any element
showing signs of physical damage must not be returned to service but instead, should be sent to the
manufacturer for re-conditioning.
Clean elements must be placed in heavy polyethylene bags, sealed and stored in a locker or other dust tight
enclosure to protect them until ready for use.

Accumulator

State and local codes for unfired pressure vessels should be checked for any required periodic inspections of
this tank and entered on the master check list as a reminder.

It is suggested that at six month intervals, a pressure test be made to assure that no leaks have developed
in the air piping from the tank to the control panel. Shut off the oil supply valve to the tank and open the
air supply valve to charge the tank to 8.5 bar (123 PSI). Check pressure after 1 hour and readjust to 8.5
bar. Note the time, and four hours later check the pressure again. The pressure should not have dropped
 more than 0.2 bar (3 PSI) during this time. If it has, then check all pipe joints, valve stem packing, sight
glass joints, etc., with a soap solution to find the source of the air leak.

At least once a month the drain cock in the oil supply line to the tank should be cracked to check for the
presence of water that should be allowed to drain off if present. In the event there ever is a serious problem

 with the oil that should require draining from the main receiving tank, then the pressure tank and supply
piping should also be drained.

Pressure Control Valve

Little should be required in the way of maintenance on this valve other than perhaps a yearly inspection of
the condition of the diaphragm and valve stem packing.

Pressure Intensifier
Some systems are equipped with an air pressure intensifier that will increase the instrument air pressure
supplied to the accumulator in order to maintain a constant level of oil

Heat Exchanger

Proper lubrication of the gears and bearings of the mechanical equipment dictates that the temperature of
the oil at the mill must not vary more than +/- 1°C (1.8°F) above or below 38°C (100°F) at the inlet
connection to the mills. To this end, the heat exchanger temperature controller and the water control valve
combine to form a team to maintain this required oil temperature. Since this is a separate control system
within the lubricating system it is important to understand its operation. Basically, a sensing bulb,
connected to a temperature transmitter, in the discharge oil line from the cooler tells the PLC the
temperature of the oil being delivered from the heat exchanger to the mill. The PLC will make a calculation
between the desired oil temperature at the heat exchanger outlet and the actual temperature measured by the
temperature transmitter and reposition the valve opening to allow more or less water into the heat
exchanger. The calculation is repeated until the difference in temperature is no more than +/- 0.5°C or +/-
1.0° C depending on the application. All systems have a second temperature transmitter located within the
interconnecting piping that will create an offset to the desired temperature in order to compensate for
temperature losses through the piping.

If the oil is too hot, for example, the controller tells the water valve to open a little more to allow more
water to flow through the heat exchanger. A greater water flow rate through the heat exchanger will chill
the oil and this decrease in temperature is detected by the sensing bulb and sent back to the controller to
complete the cycle. This is a constantly varying process and is influenced by variables on the inlet side of
the heat exchanger, such as water temperature and pressure, and oil temperature and flow rate.
It is important that the water supply to the heat exchanger be clean and free from pressure fluctuations.
Sediment in the water can settle out in the tubes of the heat exchanger. To provide a means of checking
water flow, a sight flow indicator is provided in the discharge water line from the heat exchanger, a pressure
reducing valve, and if necessary, a filter, is to be provided in the water supply line to be set at a pressure
which will remain steady irrespective of fluctuations that may occur upstream in the main supply line. The
water supply should be inspected monthly to assure everything is in proper working order.

Note: Refer to water quality specifications on pages 11 and 12.

Responsibility for operation of the temperature controller and the daily changing of the chart usually
falls under the "Instrument Department". Since the flow modulating valve is pneumatically operated,
it is important that the air filter to the controller be inspected weekly and cleaned as required. Also,

 it is suggested that the air control piping between the controller and the water control valve be
checked at six month intervals to assure no leaks have developed.

Vacuum Dehydrator (preferred) or Centrifuge

For new systems utilizing one oil tank and a Morgan Vacuum Dehydrator, the Dehydrator must be
operated as soon as there is any signs of water ingress into the oil and should be operated for at least
12 hours every 2 days, or as required.

For other systems the standard operating practice for a two tank lubricating system dictates that one
tank be in service for a period of a week after which the alternate tank be placed in service for a week.
As soon as the first tank is changed over to a stand-by, the oil in the stand-by tank should
immediately be processed through the dehydrator or centrifuge. This will "clean up" the oil having
been in service for a week and assure its readiness for operation in the event of trouble on the service
tank. In addition, using the vacuum dehydrator or centrifuge will aid materially in lessening the
degree or rate of build-up of contamination both in the oil and on the bottom of the tank.

For a two tank system only, after the stand-by tank has been processed, the dehydrator (preferred) or
centrifuge can be switched over to the service tank and allowed to run continuously.

The vacuum dehydrator or centrifuge is a valuable tool that should be employed to the fullest extent
for the removal of contamination. Its proper use in preventing the build-up of contamination will in
turn repay dividends in the area of maintenance, for example, by increasing the time between filter
changes.

Under certain conditions, it may be found that continuous use of the vacuum dehydrator or centrifuge
results in elevating the oil temperature in the tank. This is caused by the fact that the centrifuge
discharges heated oil. Should this condition promote a problem with over-temperature, then reducing
the heat supply to the centrifuge heater or the addition of a small oil cooler on the discharge side of
the centrifuge, should provide better control.

Pressure Gauges, Thermometers and Pressure Switches

All instruments should be removed, inspected for wear, and calibrated on a yearly basis.
Replacements should be made as required.

Alarm System

The importance of the alarm system is obvious. All components should be checked periodically for
proper working conditions. Each time the lubricating system is started or stopped, an observer at the
various signal panels can check for burned out bulbs or nonfunctioning components, and report such
conditions to the department responsible for their replacement or repair.

Dump Pump

In large systems, a dump pump is used to drain the oil from the filter housings and accumulator (if
installed). The system has its own control system and it is used only for maintenance purposes.

3.0    SAFETY

       Important:     Always read the safety instructions and warnings for each system and
                      component prior to operating and maintaining this machinery. Follow all
                      safety precautions to avoid personal injury or property damage during
                      system operation. Refer to this section and the Safety Sections of each
                      component manual for general safety steps and procedures. Read all
                      instructions, warnings, and cautions carefully.

       Important:     Only trained personnel should operate and maintain mill equipment and
                      tools including rigging and lifting procedures. Do not work on equipment
                      on which you have not been trained!

       Important:     All safety devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to assure
                      the safety of the operators.

       Important:     Always wear personal protection equipment. Always wear proper safety
                      gear when in the mill. Minimum Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
                      should include safety hat, boots and gloves as well as eye and ear protection.
                      Wear proper protective gear when operating and maintaining mill
                      equipment.

       Caution:       Equipment throughout the mill produces excessive noise. Always wear
                      hearing protection.

       Warning:       Consider all equipment as potentially hazardous at all times. It is capable of
                      crushing any body part caught in it.

       Caution:       Working with high pressure components (i.e. hoses and cylinders) may be
                      dangerous if equipment is misused. Never use faulty equipment.

       Danger:        Electrical voltages in both power and control circuits are capable of
                      rendering severe and fatal shocks.

       Warning:       Hot product traveling throughout the mill can raise the temperature of all
                      equipment surfaces. Consider all surfaces throughout the mill to be hot!

       Warning:       Beware of pinch points. Block and restrain rotating parts before removal
                      and mounting equipment.

       Warning:       Do not exceed equipment ratings. Never attempt to press on or lift a load
                      weighing more than the capacity of the cylinder. Overloading causes
                      equipment failure and possible personal injury.

       Caution:       Working with high pressure may be dangerous if equipment is misused.
                      Never set the relief valve to a higher pressure than the maximum rated

       Warning:       The system operating pressure must not exceed the pressure rating of the
                      lowest rated component in the system. Check pressure gauges in the system
                      to monitor operating pressure.

       Caution:       Avoid damaging connected hoses. Avoid sharp bends and kinks when
                      routing hoses. Using a bent or kinked hose will cause severe back-pressure.
                      Sharp bends and kinks will internally damage the hose leading to premature
                      hose failure.

                      Do not drop heavy objects on hoses. A sharp impact may cause internal
                      damage to hose wire strands. Applying pressure to a damaged hose may
                      cause it to rupture. DO NOT lift or pull equipment by hoses or couplers.
                      Rig and secure equipment for safe transport.

       Caution:       Keep hydraulic equipment away from flames and heat. Excessive heat will
                      soften packing and seals, resulting in fluid leaks. Heat also weakens hose
                      materials and packing. For optimum performance do not expose equipment
                      to temperatures of 65°C [150°F] or higher. Protect all hoses and cylinders
                      from weld spatter and extreme heat.

       Danger:        Do not handle pressurized hoses. Escaping oil under pressure can penetrate
                      the skin, causing serious injury. If oil is injected under the skin, see a doctor
                      immediately.

       Warning:       Only use hydraulic cylinders in a coupled system. Never use a cylinder with
                      unconnected couplers. If the cylinder becomes extremely overloaded,
                      components can fail catastrophically causing severe personal injury. Never
                      bleed system to exposed atmosphere.

       Warning:       Immediately replace worn, or damaged parts.

       Important:     Only qualified and trained technicians are allowed to service mill
                      equipment.

       Warning:       Do not use electric pumps in an explosive atmosphere. Adhere to all local
                      and national electrical codes. Start the pump with the valve in the neutral
                      position to prevent accidental cylinder operation. Keep hands clear of
                      moving parts and pressurized hoses.

       Caution:       To prevent damage to electric motors, check specifications. Use of incorrect
