Operation and
No-Housing Stands                                                           Maintenance Instructions


       3.1     Safety Procedures

       Important:      All safety devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to assure
                       the safety of the operators.

       Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices
       make the elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the
       process and/or product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be
       constrained to follow a prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble.
       Cobbles occur at random times and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is
       unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed
       path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment, and stock temperature are also causes of
       cobbling anywhere along the length of a bar in process in the rolling train. The following
       recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe manner.

       3.2     Visibility and Communications

       Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations of
       pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment controlled from
       that point.

       Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight confirmation.

       Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper lighting can be
       used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or cloud the reflective surface and
       that the mirror location does not make it liable to breakage.

       3.3     Audible Communications

       Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as substitutes only
       when visual contact is not possible.

       3.4     Safety Stops

       Guide adjustments may be made only when the Mill Line is shut down. Mechanical or
       electrically operated stops must be used to block any stock from inadvertently entering into the
       mill.

       Ensure mill is shut down and material can not run through the stand. Ensure that stops remain in
       place as long as personnel making adjustments are in the hazard area.

       3.5     Alarms

       The alarms as described in the control specifications will have a warning system to alert the
       operators of new oncoming front ends.

       A prominently located light board should be used with the warning system to indicate the strand
       in use and the progress of the stock in the mill.

       3.6     Restart of Mill

       When a service operation is completed, the Mill must be restarted in the following sequence:

       1. All mechanical stops will be moved.
       2. All Guards will be in place.
       3. All personnel will clear the hazardous area.
       4. Permissive switches will be placed in “ALLOW RESTART” position and all interlocks
          engaged.
       5. Operators at control stations will be notified that the Mill Line may be restarted.

       Operators must not restart the mill until they are completely satisfied that restarting will not
       present hazards to personnel. An audible signal will be given by the operator to indicate that
       restart is imminent.

       3.7     Safety Shutoff and Lockout/Tag out

       Important:       Operators must be familiar with all Main Pulpit (Mill Desk) and Local
                        Control Station switches, indicators and controls. Operators must also
                        know where all power supply shutoff and isolation locations are in the
                        water, air, hydraulic, lubrication and electrical systems.

       Important:       Always isolate, shutoff, and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic and electrical
                        power supply sources before performing any repairs, maintenance or roll
                        and guide changes. Read all safety instructions and warnings for each
                        system and component prior to working on machinery. Read and refer to
                        Safety section of this manual before performing any maintenance or repairs.

                        Lockout and tag out isolation valves located in the supply lines before
                        performing maintenance, or repairs. Lockout and Tag out control switches at the
                        Local Control Station and Main Pulpit.

       Important:       Ensure the mill process stations and pass line have been completely shut
                        down and interlocks are working properly. All safety devices must be
                        properly maintained and never bypassed to assure the safety of the
                        operators. ALWAYS verify zero energy state before working on equipment.

       3.12    Hydraulics

       Interlocking with Hydraulic Power Unit: Control circuits for operating hydraulically powered
       equipment is effective only when one of the associated hydraulic pumps is running. This
       safeguard is designed to prevent unexpected movement of hydraulic cylinders or motors merely
       by starting a hydraulic pump.

       Hydraulic System: To isolate the Hydraulic System, shutoff valves located at the HPU and at the
       corresponding component manifold block must be manually turned off. The hydraulic system
       can now be Locked Out and Tagged Out. Refer steps and procedures below as a guide. Lockout
       and Tagout the valves while performing any type of maintenance or repair. ALWAYS - Verify
       Zero Energy State before working on equipment.

       De-energize hydraulics before services equipment. Use reference drawings as a guide for
       component fluid piping systems, manifold blocks and valve locations.

       Warning:        Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or
                       disconnect all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any
                       stored energy from components. Restrain and secure any moving parts of a
                       component or system that could cause injury. Always verify zero energy
                       state before working on equipment. Follow steps and procedures below.

       1. Ensure the mill has stopped. Ensure no product is on line before shutting down.

       2. Shut off and isolate supply lines at power unit. The power unit should be turned off.

       3. Connect pressure gauges in each supply and return line of component to be worked on. Test
          gauge ports are in each manifold block of for both cylinders.

       Note:           There are other test (gauge) ports for the supply and drain lines throughout
                       the system. Another pressure gauge should be connected as applicable to
                       related component. The pressure in this gauge should be zero.

       4. The corresponding component solenoid valve when in the center position should allow fluid
          to drain, however for safety, the solenoid valve should be energized and moved to using
          solenoid A to allow full drainage of the component piping end. Pressure in the gauge
          connected to this line (ports A) should be lowered to zero.

       5. The solenoid valve then should be moved using solenoid B to drain the other direction of the
          component piping. Pressure should be check until it gets down to zero.

       6. For safety verification, repeat step 5 and confirm and verify pressure to be zero.

       Important:      Never bleed or vent hydraulics to the atmosphere.

4.0    OPERATION

       Important:      Always read all safety instructions and warnings for each system and
                       component prior to operating and working on machinery. Refer to Safety
                       Section for general safety steps and procedures.

       4.1     Introduction

       There are a total of 16 No-Housing Stands. Stands 1V-6H comprise the roughing mill. Stands 7H
       – 16H comprise the intermediate mill. “V” indicates vertical. “H” indicates horizontal. There
       are three different roll housing sizes (NH30, NH23, and NH19) with three different maximum roll
       diameters will be used for the mill train to accommodate the required billet size.

       Each stand assembly contains the following assemblies: Drive Assembly (including main drive
       motor, gearbox, and spindles), Spindle Carrier, Roll Container, and the Transfer Car. The roll
       container is removed and replaced as a unit, allowing minimum downtime between product
       rolling. Each stand includes hydraulically powered device to clamp, traverse, align, and position
       the stand. All hydraulic functions will be under manual control via a local floor station. Solenoid
       valves are rated to be continuously energized. Hydraulic power for Stands 1V-6H is provided by
       Hydraulic System A-A-1. Hydraulic power for Stands 7H – 16H is provided by Hydraulic System
       A-A-2.

       4.2     Components

               4.2.1   No-Housing Stand Assembly Roll Unit

       Note:           For efficient operation of mill stand, operators are required to constantly
                       monitor all components. Listed below are operation descriptions and
                       preventive steps/procedures to help ensure optimal operation.

               The No-Housing Stand Assembly as stated above contains a self-contained removable
               stand. Each No-Housing stand consists of sub-assemblies that include; upper and lower
               chock assemblies, a parting mechanism assembly, screw post assemblies and a container
               assembly. Parting adjustment of the rolls is symmetrically adjustable along the pass
               centerline. The upper roll is axially adjustable by a worm screw mechanism. Roll
               parting is not possible while product is in the mill.

              4.2.2    Upper Chock Assembly

              Main components of the upper chock assembly include a mill roll, the work side and
              drive side chocks with bearings and seals, and the axial adjustment mechanism (worm
              gear). The function is to hold the upper roll against the forces of rolling. All bearings and
              seals are air/oil lubricated. All seals wear on replaceable rings and retainers.

              Axial adjustment of the upper roll is by a manually adjusted worm gear mechanism
              located on the work side chock. It is used to align grooves of the upper roll to the
              grooves on the fixed lower roll. Upper chock assemblies are mounted onto the screw
              posts along with the lower chock assemblies. Before being placed back onto the mill, all
              No-housing sub-assemblies should be completely assembled in a remote maintenance
              location.

              Figure 5 – Typical Upper Chock Assembly




              4.2.3   Lower Chock Assembly

              Main components of the lower chock assembly include a mill roll and work side and
              drive side chocks with bearings and seals. There is no axial adjustment mechanism as the
              roll is fixed in position by a thrust bearing in the work side chock. All other features are
              similar to the upper chock assembly. See illustration (below) for guidance.

               4.2.4   Roll Parting Mechanism Assembly

               The parting mechanism assembly consists of two (2) gear boxes connected by a quick-
               connect coupling between the input worm shafts (see Figure 7 below). These units
               mount on top of the screw posts with a reducer to provide control of the symmetric roll
               parting.

               The No-housing stands’ roll parting is adjustable through the operation of a hydraulic
               motor that couples onto the drive side unit or by manual input to the worm shaft on the
               work side unit which activates two sets of interconnected screw jacks. This motor is
               controlled by the Screwdown double solenoid valve. Change in parting is indicated by a
               dial indicator which is mounted on top of the screw posts. High speed screw down
               adjustment can be accomplished by simultaneously energizing the Screwdown Speed
               Fast single solenoid valve while the Screwdown solenoid valve is activated in either
               direction.

               Roll leveling (i.e. adjusting the work side and drive side screw posts independently to
               have parallel rolls) is accomplished by disconnecting the coupling on the worm shaft
               extensions. Then the two gearboxes may be operated separately moving either end of the
               roll as required.

       Note:           The roll parting mechanism is not designed to operate while rolling is in
                       progress. The Screw down pushbuttons on the operator stations should be
                       active only at times when rod is not in the mill.

              4.2.5   Screw Post Assemblies

              The screw post assemblies connect the upper and lower chock assemblies, provide
              mounting for the parting mechanism assembly (screw post shaft ends) and includes the
              foot/bushing for mounting to the container assembly and is also used to secure the chock
              supports when using the roll change unit. Main components of the screw post assemblies
              include the screw post nuts, pre-load nuts, foot/bushing, and mounting lugs.

              Each screw post has right and left hand threads, which allow for the symmetrical roll
              parting. All four rods turn in unison by the parting mechanism assembly. Once the
              screw post assemblies are mounted in the chocks, and the parting mechanism is attached,
              there is no required disassembly for roll changes.

              Roll parting cannot be adjusted while rolling. Hydraulic motor is connected to a 4.08:1
              gear ratio. When the output shaft is rotating 1 turn it will close the roll gap with 0.26 mm.
              Roll gap will close 0.26/4.08= 0.0637 mm per hydraulic motor turn (30 pulses).

              4.2.8    Spindle Carrier

              The spindle carrier assembly is located near the coupling between the roll container and
              the spindles. It supports the outer ends of the spindles when the roll container is
              removed. Spindle carrier can slide along a machined way. The spindle carrier is moved
              by the pass alignment hydraulic Cylinder. Movement of spindle carrier is used to both
              align the roll groove and to push the stand’s roll container to the off-line position where it
              can be removed. The spindle carrier employs a locking pin that engages the roll
              container. When the locking pin is engaged the container moves together with the
              spindle carrier. When the locking pin is disengaged the spindle carrier can be moved
              independent of the roll container. See illustration (below) for details.

              4.2.9   Container Locking Pins

              The container locking pins connect and disconnect the spindle carrier and the roll
              container. When the locking pins are engaged the container moves together with the
              spindle carrier. When the locking pins are disengaged the spindle carrier can be moved
              independent of the roll container.

              The locking pins are engaged and disengaged from the spindle carrier by hydraulic
              cylinder controlled by Container Locking Pin double solenoid valve. The locking pins
              are detected as engaged by Feed Side Engaged and Exit Side Engaged proximity
              switches. The locking pins are disengaged when the container is to be removed for roll
              change.

              Vertical Stands only:

              The locking pins cannot be disengaged unless the transfer car is in the on-line position
              under the roll container as sensed by the Transfer Car In proximity switch. The locking
              pins cannot be disengaged unless the spindle carrier is fully extended, i.e. the roll
              container is on the transfer car at mill floor level, as sensed by the Pass Align Extended
              proximity switch.

              4.2.10 Spindle Spotting

              The Spindle Spotting Position proximity switch detects when the spindle is in correct
              alignment for stand engagement. Refer to Main Drive Control Specification for details
              concerning spindle spotting.

              4.2.11 Stand Pass Alignment

              The pass alignment Cylinder moves the spindle carrier, which in turn moves the container
              with the roll package, providing that the container-locking pin is engaged. Each
              hydraulic Cylinder’s direction is controlled by a Pass Alignment double solenoid valve.

              High speed pass alignment can be accomplished by simultaneously energizing the Pass
              Alignment Fast single solenoid valve while the Pass Alignment solenoid valve is
              energized in either direction. The Spindle Carrier Retracted (or Pass Align
              Retracted) proximity switch detects when the spindle carrier is in its fully retracted
              position, i.e. in its maximum drive side position.

              Vertical Stands Only:

              To prevent interference the spindle carrier must be in its fully retracted position before
              the roll container is traversed in or out. Note that when the transfer car is off-line, the
              spindle carrier can be extended further for correct pass alignment. The Spindle Carrier
              Extended (or Pass Align Extended) proximity switch must be active, i.e. roll container
              on transfer car at mill floor level, before the container coupling pin can be disengaged.
              See illustration (below) for details.

               4.2.12 Pass Alignment Cylinders

               When the container locking pins are engaged, the pass alignment cylinder moves the spindle
               carrier, which in turn moves the container assembly with the No-housing roll assembly. A
               double solenoid valve controls each hydraulic cylinder’s direction.

               A High-speed pass alignment can be accomplished by simultaneously energizing the Pass
               Alignment Fast Speed single solenoid valve and the Pass Alignment solenoid valve in either
               direction.

               NOTE: The control should allow the spindle carrier to be retracted when the clamps are
               clamped and the container locking pins are retracted. The Stand Clamps will hold the stand in
               place while separating the spindle carrier from the Stand. This sequence is required to remove
               the spindle carrier from the stand. See Stand Removal procedure.

               Note: For Vertical Stands, the spindle carrier must be in its fully retracted position before the
               roll container is traversed in or out with the Transfer Car to prevent interference. The control
               system should provide Jog pushbuttons located on the Remote Pendant to allow for local pass
               alignment adjustments

               4.2.13 Transfer Car Assembly Stand Traverse (Vertical Stands Only)

               The transfer car assembly is located below the roll container assembly. When the roll
               container and No-housing assemblies are disconnected form the spindle carrier assembly,
               the transfer car must be in place to receive them. Once the Container and No-housing
               assemblies are loaded onto the transfer car, the car traverses to the off-line location where
               an overhead crane can remove the stand for maintenance or roll changes.

               A traverse hydraulic cylinder pulls and pushes the transfer car between the on-line and
               off-line positions. The traverse cylinder is controlled by the Traverse double solenoid
               hydraulic valve. High-speed traverse can be accomplished by simultaneously energizing
               the High Speed single solenoid valve and the Traverse solenoid valve. Note: The
               Traverse valve can be activated in either direction.

               The Transfer Car in Position proximity switch detects the transfer car in the in-line
               position. The proximity switch is used for the interlocking system and for stand change
               functions.

               To prevent drift, the PLC (logic control) shall maintain directional output to Traverse
               solenoid valve once car reaches the extreme travel proximity switch for that direction
               until opposite direction command is given. Transfer Car Fast solenoid valve will also
               be disabled at this time.

       4.3     Mill Drive Assemblies

       Horizontal stands are driven by a combination parallel shaft reducer and pinion stand with
       horizontal output shafts. Vertical stands are each driven by a combination right angled bevel gear
       reducer and pinion stand with input shaft horizontal and dual output shafts vertical downward.
       Pinion shafts are straight and include a single key to accommodate bolted connection hub for
       universal type spindle. Pinions and gear shafts are supported by rolling element bearings.

       4.4     Interlocking

       The following interlocks steps and procedures are required in both manual and automatic
       operation. Refer to other operation sections of all mill equipment for additional interlocking steps
       and procedures of specific components.

       In order for the mill stands to start and operate, certain interlocking conditions must take place.
       In addition, other interlocking steps and procedures are required for stand changes and installation
       as well as existing equipment interlocks. Refer to other interlocking steps and procedures for
       Stand Change (See Stand Change section of manual) as well as for existing systems and
       components that may effect the operation of the mill stands. The following interlocks steps and
       procedures are required in both manual and automatic mode for start-up and operation of the mill
       stands. Important: Operators should be familiar and experienced with all interlocking
       systems.

               4.4.1    Stand Start-up and Operation Interlocks.

                       A. The spindle carrier assembly must be fully retracted to allow Vertical

                       B. The spindle carrier must be fully extended with cylinder pressurized before

                      proximity switch before the spindle carrier assembly can be extended. For
                      Vertical Stands, the transfer car must be fully in-line or off-line.

6.0    PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS

       6.1    Definition

       Preventive maintenance is routine maintenance that if performed as scheduled helps to keep the
       No-Housing Stand Assemblies in good operating condition. Its primary purpose is to reduce the
       incidence of operating failures, which require costly downtime for repairs. The recommended
       routine maintenance schedule below represents the anticipated minimum requirements for
       maintaining the No-Housing Stands. As you accumulate operating experience, it may be feasible
       to reduce the frequency of checks and inspections, however, do not reduce the lubrication
       frequency.

       Important:     Always isolate, shutoff, and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic, and
                      electrical power supply sources before performing any repairs or
                      maintenance. Read safety instructions and warnings for each system and
                      component prior to working on machinery. Refer to the Safety sections in
                      the beginning of your mill’s manual as well as in this manual chapter.

       6.2    Introduction

       Routine and Preventive Maintenance of the No-Housing Stand Assemblies is required to ensure
       extended and proper operation.
             3
       Table is provided as a reference guide for frequent periodic maintenance requirements for the
       No-Housing Stand Assemblies. Refer to the General Maintenance section and applicable
       manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance requirements and procedures for specific
       components. Refer to Morgan assembly drawings as a guide for additional information.

       Warning:       Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or
                      disconnect all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any
                      stored energy from components. Restrain and secure any moving parts of a
                      component or system that could cause injury.

       Warning:       Exposed moving parts can cause severe injury. LOCK OUT and TAG OUT
                      POWER before removing guards or performing maintenance. NEVER
                      remove a guard, shield cover or other protective devices while the
                      equipment is running!

       Warning:       This equipment is potentially dangerous and capable of inflicting severe
                      bodily injuries. Before starting any maintenance task, comply with all
                      company policies relating to safety. Also, be thoroughly familiar with the
                      general safety requirements.

       Warning:       Always stop machinery before entering or adjusting the equipment. Know
                      where all e-stop buttons are located before operating or performing
                      maintenance on this equipment.

       6.3     General Maintenance Schedule

               6.3.1    Lubrication

       Note:            It is of critical importance that the location of all grease fittings are known
                        and addressed with each lubrication cycle. Refer to Morgan Reference
                        drawings for the locations of grease fittings.

       Important:       A Maintenance program must be implemented for tracking of all bearing
                        lubrication. A general deterioration of in service grease results in build up
                        of lubricant residue and consequent destruction of bearings. Apply fresh
                        grease to bearings on a regular basis and record date of lubrication to
                        establish regular lube routine.

               Daily
               • Inspect the re-circulating lube oil system for correct pressure and fluid level. Change
                  filters and breather as required.

               Weekly or Each Roll Change
               • Lubricate coupling box assemblies. See Morgan reference drawings for location of
                 grease fittings.

               Monthly or Each Roll Change

       Note:            The following lubrication steps should be performed at the interval that is
                        most frequent. Always apply grease to subassemblies before reinstalling
                        onto stand.

               •    Lubricate foot/bushing on screw post assemblies. See Morgan reference drawings
                    for grease fitting locations
               •    Lubricate Locking Pin assemblies.
               •    Lubricate Spindle Carrier assemblies. See Morgan reference drawings for grease
                    fitting locations.

                    A. Lubricate Connector Rod Pivot Pin
                    B. Lubricate Liners
                    C. Lubricate Guide Rail

               •    Lubricate Container assemblies. See Morgan reference drawings for grease fitting
                    locations.
               •    Lubricate Parting Mechanism assembly. See Morgan reference drawings for grease
                    fitting locations.
               •    Inspect Lube air/oil block assemblies on no housing for debris or blockage. Make
                    sure there is no blockage of internal lubrication holes.
               •    Lubricate cylinder pivot areas of transfer car (vertical stands) base/bed assemblies
                    (all stands) and connector lever arm (convertible stands).

7.0    CORRECTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS

       7.1     Definition

       Corrective maintenance encompasses those repair procedures required to return the No-Housing
       Stand assemblies to satisfactory operating condition. Such repairs do not necessarily return the
       equipment to like-new condition. Rather, the objective is to make it operational again as soon as
       possible. It is recommended to replace faulty parts/components and sub-assemblies with new or
       previously refurbished spare parts/components and sub-assemblies. Those parts removed may
       then be refurbished or reconditioned after the main equipment has been returned to service.

       Important:      Always isolate, shutoff, and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic, and
                       electrical power supply sources before performing any repairs or
                       maintenance. Read safety instructions and warnings for each system and
                       component prior to working on machinery. Refer to Safety Section in this
                       manual chapter.

       7.2     Introduction

       Corrective Maintenance of the No-Housing Stand assemblies as defined above is intended to keep
       down time at a minimum by replacing components and then dismantling and overhauling the
       removed component in a service area away from the mill. Once refurbished, the component
       becomes a spare shelf part, ready to be utilized as a replacement when needed.

       No disassembly procedures are given herein of components being replaced. Components that
       require overhaul/refurbishment should be maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s

       7.3       General Maintenance Criteria

       The following is a list of maintenance actions to perform whenever dismantling equipment for
       repairs:

       1. Electric controls and power cables: Before disconnecting any wiring that does not have plug-
          in connectors, make sure that color coding is clearly identifiable or tag each wire carefully for
          reference at re-assembly.

       2. Rigging parts for removal/replacement: Many parts that make up this equipment are too
          heavy to be handled by one person. Provide adequate rigging for lifting and supporting
          heavy parts before attempting to dismantle any equipment.

       3. Cleaning: Clean all parts with a suitable solvent (mineral spirits, SAVASOL no.5, or
          equivalent) to remove all scale, grease, grime, or dirt. Use a clean wiper; do not use cotton
          waste. Air dry after cleaning.

       4. Bearings and Sealing Surfaces: Closely inspect bearings and sealing surfaces for signs of
          wear, nicks, scratches, gouges, or build-up of scale or other foreign substances. Replace
          bearings that show any signs of deterioration.

             To clean roller bearings, soak in clean solvent long enough to loosen any sludge, and then
             gently move each bearing around near the top of the container to dislodge all pockets of
             grease. Scrub away stubborn accumulations with a small brush that has bristles that do not
             break off. Do not spin dirty bearings, instead rotate the races slowly while washing and
             scrubbing.

             Rinse the bearings in clean solvent and air dry. Hold both races when blowing with clean,
             dry compressed air. Do not allow the air jet to spin the bearing; rather, turn each race by
             hand to expose all surfaces to the drying air. If the bearing is to be stored for later reuse,
             wrap it in wax paper or other greaseproof wrapping.

       Caution:          A bearing may be defective without the defect being visually evident.
                         Replace any bearing removed during any maintenance task with new or
                         cleaned bearing at re-assembly.

             New bearings are packed with rust-preventative grease (or other protective coating) and
             wrapped in grease-resistant paper before they are shipped. Do not unwrap the bearing until
             time for installation. Unwrap and thoroughly wash the new bearing and air dry. Pre-lubricate
             immediately with Mobil 500 series oil (or equivalent).

       Note:             For ease of installation of bearings, heat the bearings at a maximum
                         temperature of 121°C (250°F) in oil for one hour minimum, or in an electric
                         furnace for 1-1/2 hours minimum, or by bearing induction heater for 15
                         minutes minimum.

              7.4.2   Stand Change Procedure (Vertical Stands)

              The following steps describe a stand change operation. Note that this is not an
              automatic operation. The operators must take responsibility to ensure that
              procedures are performed in a manner which cannot cause personal injury or
              equipment damage. Particular care must be exercised when removing and
              replacing the roll container using the overhead crane.

              1. Clear mill, stop drive.
              2. Local floor station selector switch to STAND CHANGE position.
              3. Ensure that transfer car is in position under roll container.
                  Open stand clamps.
              4. Extend pass alignment cylinder to lower spindle carrier and roll container to
                  transfer car at mill floor level.
              5. Disengage container locking pin.
              6. Retract pass alignment cylinder to raise spindle carrier to full up driveside
                  position. This provides clearance to prevent damage to spindle carrier as roll
                  container is traversed on transfer car.
              7. Traverse transfer car to off-line position.
              8. Remove roll container from transfer car with overhead crane.
              9. Replace roll container on transfer car with overhead crane.
              10. Traverse transfer car to on-line position.
              11. Extend pass alignment cylinder to lower spindle carrier to coupling position.
              12. Engage container locking pin.
              13. Retract pass alignment cylinder to raise spindle carrier and roll container to
                  desired working position.
              14. Close stand clamps.
              15. Adjust screwdown.
              16. Local floor station selector switch to ROLLING position.

              7.4.3   Stand Change Procedure (Horizontal Stands)

              Stand Change Procedure:

              The following steps describe a stand change operation. Note that this is not an
              automatic operation. The operators must take responsibility to ensure that
              procedures are performed in a manner which cannot cause personal injury or
              equipment damage. Particular care must be exercised when removing and
              replacing the roll container using the overhead crane.

              REMOVAL:
              1. Move screwdown to correct opening for new roll package.
              2. Refer to guide setup operational notes on the applicable Morgan drawing.
              3. Guide clear.
              4. Unclamp.
              5. Traverse CONTAINER to max workside position.
              6. Clamp.
              7. Disengage locking pin.
              8. Retract SPINDLE CARRIER to max driveside position.
              9. INSERT STAND REMOVAL RIG.
              10. Remove STAND with crane.

              INSTALLATION:
              1. Insert new roll package.
              2. ADJUST SPINDLE CARRIER CENTERS (MANUALLY) TO MATCH

              4. Engage locking pin.
              5. Unclamp.
              6. Traverse to correct pass position.
              7. Move guide close to roll (not full stroke).
              8. Jog traverse to align with guide gauge.
              9. Clamp.
              10. Fully extend guide.
              11. Manually insert static guide (see operational notes on the applicable Morgan

       7.5     Roll Change Instructions

       Note:           Due to the complexities involved with changing No-Housing Stand rolls,
                       Section 7.5 is formatted slightly different than a typical Morgan O & M
                       manual section. In effort to make the following procedures alphanumeric
                       number is continuous throughout the entire section (i.e. 7.5.3 has procedure
                       with the letter “A.” In section 7.5.4 the first procedure starts with the letter
                       “B.” Normally when a subsection starts alphanumeric numbers restart.
                       Alphanumeric numbering correlates with Figures 16 through 18 (below).
                       This method is used to correlate procedures in this section across multiple
                       Figures.

       The roll change assemblies are located in the roll housing maintenance shop and are used to
       remove used rolls from roll housing and replace them with a new pair of rolls.

       The change unit is foundation mounted and operated by two hydraulic cylinders for in and out
       positioning. Two (2) traversable (work side and drive side) chock support carriages are used for
       chock removal and replacement. A roll support assembly is used to move used and new rolls into
       position.

               7.5.1   Roll Change Overview

               •   The No-housing stand is removed for the mill stand and moved off line.
               •   If a Vertical stand is being changed, the No-housing unit is rotated to the Horizontal
                   Position at the Downender Assembly.
               •   No-housing unit is moved to the Maintenance Roll Shop.
               •   No-housing unit is separated from the container assembly, cleaned and inspected.
               •   No-housing unit moved and placed on roll change assembly.
               •   Chock Assemblies are now separated from the rolls.
               •   The used rolls are removed from the roll change unit.
               •   New rolls are set-up and moved to roll change unit.
               •   Work side and drive side chocks (both upper & lower) are traversed onto the new
                   rolls.
               •   The new roll package in removed from roll change unit and placed back on container
                   assembly.
               •   No-housing unit is rotated to vertical position at down ender station, if applicable.
               •   The new no-housing is then returned and installed in the mill stand on-line.

       7.8     Reassembly

       Always follow reference drawings for alignment, torque requirements, and clearance information.
       Follow manufacturer’s maintenance instructions for reassembly of vendor components. Use
       inspection charts as a guide for cleaning and inspection prior to reassembly.

               7.8.1   Reconditioning Components in Service Area

               For best results provide an area where components can be disassembled, cleaned,
               inspected and reassembled in a clean environment. Follow General Maintenance criteria
               as described in Section 7.3. The shop should have the capability of handling all
               components and parts that require periodic inspection and rebuild as well as emergency
               repair. Ideally the following equipment should be installed in the shop:

               A disassembly bench or steel saw horses that are capable of holding the weight of the
               equipment. Wooden blocks with at least 400 mm clearance to allow for access of parts
               located on underside of component. In this position all components all parts will be
               readily accessible for removal.

               A cleaning tank of sufficient size for cleaning parts, as well as an air hose for drying parts
               after cleaning the parts. From the cleaning bath, the parts would be passed to the
               component assembly bench for subassembly of bearings, shafts, etc. Final assembly
               would be made on an assembly table separate form the other maintenance table

               Crane, lifting equipment and wooden pallets for transporting components back to the
               Mill. All necessary tools and power supply for tools to disassemble clean and inspect
               components.

       7.9     Cleaning and Inspection

       Clean and inspect all parts. Replace parts as necessary. Reverse steps and procedures outlined in
       component removal section. See Notes below.

       Using a suitable solvent, thoroughly wash then air dry all parts. Remove all pipe plugs from the
       lube oil passages in the drive housing. Pressure flush the passages, and then blow them out with
       compressed air. Inspect the passages and remove all traces of scale, dirt or any other restrictive
       material or contamination.

       If pressure flushing alone cannot remove the scale accumulation, use a wire brush or other
       suitable device to break it loose. Blow the passage out again with compressed air. When the lube
       oil/grease passages are clear, reinstall the pipe plugs. Block all entry ports to guard against
       contamination until reassembly.

1.0     Safety Procedures

                    IMPORTANT: All Safety Devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to
                    assure the safety of the operators. Stay clear of machinery when in operation.

                    WARNING: CONSIDER ALL EQUIPMENT AS POTENTIALLY
                    HAZARDOUS AT ALL TIMES.
Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices make the
elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the process and/or
product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be constrained to follow a
prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble. Cobbles occur at random times
and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently
caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment,
and stock temperature are also causes of cobbling anywhere along the length of a bar in process in the
rolling train. The following recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe
manner.
        1.1     Visibility and Communications
        Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations of
        pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment controlled from that
        point.
                 A. Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight.
                B. Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper lighting
                   can be used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or cloud the
                   reflective surface and that the mirror location does not make it liable to breakage.
        1.2     Audible Communications
                Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as
                substitutes only when visual contact is not possible.
        1.3     Safety Stops
                Guide adjustments may be made only when the Mill Line is shut down. Mechanical or
                electrically operated stops must be used to block any stock from inadvertently entered
                into the mill
                Ensure mill is shut down and material can not run through the stand Ensure that stops remain
                in place as long as personnel making adjustments are in the hazard area.
        1.4     Alarms
                The alarms as described in the control specifications will have a warning system to alert the
                operators of new oncoming front ends.
                A prominently located light board should be used with the warning system to indicate the
                strand in use and the progress of the stock in the mill.

   No-housing Roll Change Removal and Installation
   In order to change rolls, the No-housing sub-assemblies (chock insert package) must be removed from the
   container assembly and transferred to the roll change unit. The following steps and procedures are
   provided as a guide for roll removal and installation on the no-housing assembly.
   IMPORTANT: Always read Safety Instructions and Warnings for each system and component prior to
   operating and working on machinery. Refer to Safety Section for general safety steps and procedures.

           Roll Change Overview:
               A. The No-Housing stand is removed from the mill stand and moved off line.
               B. No-Housing unit is moved to the Maintenance Roll Shop.
               C. No-Housing unit is separated from the container assembly, cleaned and inspected.
               D. No-Housing unit is moved and placed on roll change assembly.

   PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS
   DEFINITION

   Preventive maintenance is routine maintenance that if performed as scheduled helps to keep the
   Stand assemblies in good operating condition. Its primary purpose is to reduce the incidence of
   operating failures, which require costly downtime for repairs. The recommended routine maintenance
   schedule below represents the anticipated minimum requirements for maintaining the no housing
   assembly. As you accumulate operating experience, it may be feasible to reduce the frequency of
   checks and inspections, however, do not reduce the lubrication frequency.

   IMPORTANT

                 Always isolate, shutoff and/or disconnect Water, Air, Hydraulic and Electrical power
                 supply sources before performing any repairs or maintenance. Read All Safety
                 Instructions and Warnings for each system and component prior to working on
                 machinery. Refer to Safety section. Make sure the Mill process stations and pass
                 line has been shut down.

   INTRODUCTION

   operation. Table 1 is provided as a quick reference guide for frequent periodic maintenance
   requirements for the Stand assemblies. Refer to the Safety and General Maintenance section and to the
   applicable manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance requirements and procedures of specific
   components. Refer to Morgan assembly drawings as a guide and for additional information.

   CORRECTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS
   DEFINITION
   Corrective maintenance encompasses those repair procedures required to return the Roll Change Unit
   assembly to satisfactory operating condition. Such repairs do not necessarily return the equipment to
   like-new condition. Rather, the objective is to make it operational again as soon as possible. It is
   recommended to replace faulty parts/components and sub-assemblies with new or previously
   refurbished spare parts/components and sub-assemblies. Those parts removed may then be
   refurbished or reconditioned after the main equipment has been returned to service.

   IMPORTANT
               Always isolate, shutoff, and/or disconnect Water, Air, Hydraulic, and Electrical power
               supply sources before performing any repairs or maintenance. Read Safety Instructions
               and Warnings for each system and component prior to working on machinery. Refer to
               Safety section.

   INTRODUCTION
   Corrective Maintenance of the No-housing Stand Assembly as defined above, is intended to keep down time
   at a minimum by replacing components and then dismantling and overhauling the removed component in a
   service area away from the mill. Once refurbished, the component becomes a spare shelf part, ready to be
   utilized as a replacement when needed.

   No disassembly procedures are given herein of components being replaced. Components that require
   overhaul/refurbishment should be maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Refer to the
   manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance and torque requirements and procedures of specific

            1.1     Electric controls and power cables -- Before disconnecting any wiring that does not

           1.2     Rigging parts for removal/replacement -- Many parts that make up this equipment are
                   much too heavy to be handled by one person. Provide adequate rigging for lifting and
                   supporting heavy parts before attempting to dismantle any equipment.
           1.3     Cleaning -- Clean all parts with a suitable solvent (mineral spirits, SAVASOL no.5,
                   or equivalent) to remove all scale, grease, grime, or dirt. Use a clean wiper; do not
                   use cotton waste. Air dry after cleaning.
           1.4     Bearings and Sealing Surfaces -- Closely inspect bearings and sealing surfaces for
                   signs of wear, nicks, scratches, gouges, or build-up of scale or other foreign
                   substances. Replace bearings that show any signs of deterioration. Scrape bushings
                   slightly, being careful not to exceed the tolerance limits.
           To clean roller bearings, soak in clean solvent long enough to loosen any sludge, then gently
           wash each bearing around near the top of the container to dislodge all pockets of grease.
           Scrub away stubborn accumulations with a small brush that has bristles that do not break
           off. Do not spin dirty bearings, but rotate races slowly while washing and scrubbing.
           Rinse the bearings in clean solvent and air dry. Hold both races when blowing with clean,
           dry compressed air. Do not allow the air jet to spin the bearing; rather, turn each race by
           hand to expose all surfaces to the drying air. If the bearing is to be stored for later reuse,
           wrap it in wax paper or other greaseproof wrapping.
           CAUTION: A bearing may be defective without the defect being visually evident. Replace
           any bearing removed during any maintenance task with new or cleaned bearing at re-
           assembly.
           New bearings are packed with rust-preventative grease (or other protective coating) and
           wrapped in grease-resistant paper before they are shipped. Do not unwrap the bearing until
           time for installation. Unwrap and thoroughly wash the new bearing and air dry. Pre-
           lubricate immediately with Mobil 500 series oil (or equivalent).
           NOTE: For ease of installation of bearings, heat the bearings at a maximum temperature of
           121°C (250°F) in oil for one hour minimum, or in an electric furnace for 1-1/2 hours
           minimum, or by bearing induction heater for 15 minutes minimum.
           1.5     Oil Seals – Replace (Mandatory Replacement) all seals, o-rings and gaskets that are
                   removed or disturbed during disassembly procedure. Make sure seals and o-rings
                   seat properly upon re-assembly.

           1.6     Oil Passages -- Pressure flush oil passages and blow dry with compressed air.
           1.7     Pre-lubrication Prior to Re-assembly -- Lightly lubricate all seals, bearings, bushings,
                   and gears with oil before installation

       3.1          Safety Procedures

       Important:                All Safety Devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to
                                 assure the safety of the operators.

       Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices
       making the elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the
       process and/or product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be
       constrained to follow a prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble.
       Cobbles occur at random times and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is
       unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed
       path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment, and stock can also cause cobbling anywhere
       along the length of a bar in process in the rolling train. The following recommended guidelines
       will help to produce a quality product in a safe manner.

       3.2          Visibility and Communications

       Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations of
       pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment controlled from
       that point.

       Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight. Where line-of-sight
       visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper lighting can be used provided that the
       immediate environment will not dirty or cloud the reflective surface and that the mirror location
       does not make it liable to breakage.

       3.3          Audible Communications

       Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as substitutes only
       when visual contact is not possible.

       3.4          Safety Stops

       Guide adjustments may be made only when the mill line is shut down. Mechanical or electrically
       operated stops must be used to block any stock from inadvertently entering into the mill.

       Ensure mill is shut down and material can not run through the stand. Ensure that stops remain in
       place as long as personnel making adjustments are in the hazard area.

       3.5          Alarms

       The alarms as described in the control specifications will have a warning system to alert the
       operators of new oncoming front ends.

       A prominently located light board should be used with the warning system to indicate the stand in
       use and the progress of the stock in the mill.

       4.1          Introduction

       The Downender is comprised of a main stationary frame grouted in place to the mill floor and a
       rotating frame barrel for supporting the no-housing stand units. An electric motor powers a gear
       drive reducer that rotates the frame barrel through a chain and sprocket drive shaft arrangement.

       The function is to down end (rotate to horizontal position) the vertical no-housing stands after
       removal from the mill in preparation for roll changing. Upon re-installing back onto the vertical
       stand, the stands are upended (rotate) from the horizontal orientation back to the vertical
       orientation position. Operation is by manual control through a hand held control pendant.

       Note:                     For efficient operation of the Downender assembly, operators are required
                                 to constantly monitor all components. Listed below are operation
                                 descriptions of the Downender assembly and preventive steps/procedures to
                                 help ensure optimal operation.

Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices make
the elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the process and/or
product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be constrained to follow a
prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble. Cobbles occur at random times
and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently
caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment,
and stock temperature are also causes of cobbling anywhere along the length of a bar in process in the
rolling train. The following recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe
manner.
        1.1     Visibility and Communications
        Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations of
        pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment controlled from that
        point.
                 A. Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight.
                B. Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper lighting
                   can be used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or cloud the
                   reflective surface and that the mirror location does not make it liable to breakage.
        1.2     Audible Communications
                Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as
                substitutes only when visual contact is not possible.
        1.3     Safety Stops
                Guide adjustments may be made only when the Mill Line is shut down. Mechanical or
                electrically operated stops must be used to block any stock from inadvertently entered
                into the mill.
                Make sure mill is shut down and material can not run through the stand. Make sure that
                stops remain in place as long as personnel making adjustments are in the hazard area.
        1.4     Alarms
                The alarms as described in the control specifications will have a warning system to alert
                the operators of new oncoming front ends.
                A prominently located light board should be used with the warning system to indicate the
                strand in use and the progress of the stock in the mill.

INTRODUCTION Refer to Figures 1 and 2 as a guide.
The main purpose of the Cropping and Cobble (C & C) Shear, located after stand 6H is to crop front and
tail ends of processed sections during delivery through the mill. The shear may also be used for
continuous cobble cutting. The short crop and cobble lengths drop into a scrap chute.
The C & C Shear consists of two knives mounted on two parallel overhung crankshafts. Tail rods
extending from the knife holders are guided by follower link arms to keep the knives parallel to each
other and perpendicular to the stock during cutting. The crankshafts are geared together and driven by a
pinion gear. The ratio between the pinion gear and the crankshaft gear is 1:1.
During crop cutting, the shear starts from the rest position, and then accelerates to the preset cutting speed.
The rotating knife blades then engage the stock at the bite angle and continue the cut. When a cut stroke is
completed, the shear stops and the blades are automatically moved to the rest or parked position by the
position regulator. The position regulator will hold the shear in the rest or parked position between cut
cycles.

For cobble cutting, the shear knives are started and accelerated from their parked position and are rotated
continually. When cobble cutting is signaled to stop, the shear completes one more cut, decelerates and
stops. The blades are again automatically moved to their rest position.
The C & C Shear is designed for manual and automatic operation, operating stations (Main Pulpit and
Local) help test, monitor and adjust conditions that may occur through the automated system. Refer to
Table 1 for description of electrical devices used in the C & C Shear Assembly.

       1.1       Shear Speed and Control Refer to applicable Morgan ECS for more detailed
                 information.

       Shear speed is regulated to follow the speed of the previous stand. Speed regulation will be
       accomplished by variable voltage, variable frequency (VVVF) operation.

       Control is through a fully regenerative, reversing, Thyristor power converter with overcurrent,
       undervoltage, and field loss protection. Following each cut, the shear will stop by regenerative
       braking.

       The drive stops the shear between 90° and 270° position, and the position regulator operates the
       drive in reverse or forward direction to position the shear to the 90° parked position.

       The shear should return to the parked position as quickly as possible to be ready for a cobble
       function in the event of a front-end cobble in the mill. Absolute accuracy of parked position is
       not necessary for cobble cut initiation.

       The following control strategy is used to minimize the slowing of the shear during the cut:

             1. Use ramp reference to control acceleration of shear from park position to bite angle.
             2. Ramp time is always minimum possible so shear just reaches cut speed when blades
                reach bite angle. ramp_time(seconds) = [degrees_motor_travel] / [3 x motor_rpm].
             3. Continue ramping speed reference at same rate until 5% over reference is obtained or
                blades pass cut complete position (0 degrees).
             4. Utilize inertia compensation (direct input to current controller) during accel/decel.

       The following additional impact correction circuit may be required to reduce the slowing of the
       shear during the cut.
           1. Current reference is increased in anticipation of the shear load as the knives enter the cut
               zone.
           2. Exact location within the shear cycle and amount of increase is determined by the
               section area and speed of the shear.

       1.2       Crop Cut Length and Accuracy

       Crop cut length is adjustable within the range of 75 mm to 450 mm. The required
       accuracy is +50 mm for front and tail ends for 95% of cuts.

       1.6     Detector for Crop Cut Signal

       The Crop HMD1 (Hot Metal Detector 1) is located after delivery guide of stand 6H. Crop
       HMD2 initiates a counter and upon completion of a preset count, causes the shear to
       automatically make a front or tail crop. Product speed calculation using motor RPM, stand gear
       ratio and effective roll diameter is used to track the front and tail ends from Crop HMD1.
       Also a speed trap between HMD 1 and 2 will be used to confirm/ adjust the calculated speed.

       1.7     Automatic Head Cut Counter Control

       A preset counter system is used to provide consistent length of front end crop cuts. The counter
       counts pulses supplied from the pulse generator or an internal clock. Operator adjustment of the
       head crop length is provided. Note: This adjustment must have minimum and maximum
       allowable settings outside which the operator may not adjust. This is to prevent premature cuts
       and crop lengths too long for scrap handling.

       When the front end of a rod is detected at the Crop HMD1, the system starts updating the preset
       value for the CUT counter using calibrated speed of Intermediate Mill 6H delivery stand.

       In order to compensate for variations in the shear reaction time, it is necessary to subtract the
       number of counts representing the shear reaction or delay time from the calculated transport time
       delay.

       A shear REACTION time counter accumulates elapsed pulses from cut-initiate signal to knife
       overlap (as indicated by the shear position encoder 0° position). This count is updated every
       time the shear makes a cut. Any difference from the calculated reaction time and the measured
       REACTION time is used to calculated preset for CUT counter.

       accelerated by 50 % to propel the bar.

2.0     Sequence of Cutting Operation

The following is a description of the intended sequence of operation. Data is calculated based on 873
rpm (max) of the motor, 106.4 rpm (max) of the shear knife shaft. Refer to Figure 1 as a guide.
Important: Always operate all mill equipment with Safety Guards closed.

        2.1 The position where the knives overlap and are fully engaged is the 0° position.

        2.2 Between cuts, the shear is held at the parked position which is 90°.

        2.3 When the shear is signaled to cut, it accelerates to 873 rpm in 228°, .71 second, at 1.8 per
            unit average torque.

        2.4 At 318.6°, the approximate bite angle, the knives contact the stock and commence the cut.

        2.5 At 0° the encoder signals that the cut is complete.

        2.6 At 42°, the encoder signals that the knives are clear and signals the drive to stop by
            regenerative braking.

        2.7 The shear decelerates to a stop in 229°, .71 second at 1.8 per unit average torque.

        2.8 The shear comes to a stop at the 270° position.

        2.9 The shear will then reverse direction and travel from the 270° position to the 90° parked
            position.

        2.10 When the shear has position regulated to a stop at the 90° position the position regulator
             will continue to hold the shear in position between cut cycles.

PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS
DEFINITION

Preventative maintenance is routine maintenance that, if performed as scheduled, helps to keep the Crop
& Cobble (C&C) shear assembly in good operating condition. Its primary purpose is to reduce the
incidence of operating failures, which require costly downtime for repairs. The recommended routine
maintenance schedule below represents the anticipated minimum requirements for maintaining the C &
C Shear.

IMPORTANT
Always isolate shutoff and/or disconnect Water, Air, Hydraulic and Electrical power supply sources before
performing any repairs or maintenance. Read Safety Instructions and Warnings for each system and
component prior to working on machinery. Refer to Safety section.
INTRODUCTION
Routine and Preventive Maintenance of the C & C Shear assembly is required to ensure extended and
proper operation. Table 2 is provided as a quick reference guide for frequent periodic maintenance
requirements for the C & C Shear assembly. Refer to the General Maintenance section and to the
applicable manufacturers technical manual for maintenance requirements and procedures of specific
components. Refer to Morgan assembly drawings as a guide and for additional information.
        WARNING: Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or disconnect all
        power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any stored energy from components.
        Restrain and secure any moving parts of a component or system that could cause injury. Never open
        inspection doors on the shear housing while the shear is operating.

        WARNING: The C & C Shear Assembly is potentially dangerous and capable of inflicting severe
        bodily injuries. Before starting any maintenance task, comply with all company policies relating
        to safety. Also, be thoroughly familiar with the general safety requirements.

        Refer to Gear Reducer manufacturer’s recommendations for lubrication.
        Daily

                  area. Replace seals as necessary.

        1.5       Lubricate main drive coupling in accordance with manufacturer’s requirements.

CORRECTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS
DEFINITION
Corrective maintenance encompasses those repair procedures required to return the C & C shear
assembly to satisfactory operating condition. Such repairs do not necessarily return the equipment to
like-new condition. Rather, the objective is to make it operational again as soon as possible. It is
recommended to replace faulty parts/components and sub-assemblies with new or previously refurbished
spare parts/components and sub-assemblies. Those parts removed may then be refurbished or
reconditioned after the main equipment has been returned to service.
IMPORTANT

Always isolate shutoff and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic and electrical power supply sources before
performing any repairs or maintenance. Read Safety Instructions and Warnings for each system and
component prior to working on machinery. Refer to Safety section.

INTRODUCTION
Corrective Maintenance of the C & C Shear Assembly as defined above is intended to keep down time
at a minimum by replacing components and then dismantling and overhauling the removed component
in a service area away from the mill. Once refurbished, the component becomes a spare shelf part, ready
to be utilized as a replacement when needed.

No disassembly procedures are given herein of components being replaced. Components that require
overhaul/refurbishment should be maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Refer
to the manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance and torque requirements and procedures of
specific components of the C & C Shear Assembly.

General guidelines and maintenance criteria are provided below when corrective maintenance of a
component or sub-assembly is required. These are minimum guidelines and should be used in
conjunction with the specific maintenance requirements from the component manufacturer.

Upon re-assembly, tighten all bolts, screws, nuts and fasteners in accordance with Morgan reference
drawings torque requirements. Torque specific components in accordance with the manufacturer’s
requirements.

Removal procedures are also provided for components and sub-assemblies that may require corrective
maintenance. Refer to the General Safety and Maintenance section and applicable Morgan reference
drawings as a guide.

        WARNING: Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or
        disconnect all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any stored
        energy from components. Restrain and secure any moving parts of a component or
        system that could cause injury.

        WARNING: The C & C Shear Assembly is potentially dangerous and capable of inflicting
        severe bodily injuries. Before starting any maintenance task, comply with all company
        policies relating to safety. Also, be thoroughly familiar with the general requirements.

1.0     General Maintenance Criteria

The following is a list of maintenance actions to perform whenever dismantling equipment for repairs.

        1.1     Electric controls and power cables -- Before disconnecting any wiring that does not have
                plug-in connectors, make sure that color coding is clearly identifiable or tag each wire
                carefully for reference at re-assembly.

        1.2     Rigging parts for removal/replacement -- Many parts that make up this equipment are
                much too heavy to be handled by one person. Provide adequate rigging for lifting and
                supporting heavy parts before attempting to dismantle any equipment.

        1.3     Cleaning -- Clean all parts with a suitable solvent (mineral spirits, SAVASOL no.5, or
                equivalent) to remove all scale, grease, grime, or dirt. Use a clean wiper; do not use
                cotton waste. Air dry after cleaning.

        1.4     Bearings and Sealing Surfaces -- Closely inspect bearings and sealing surfaces for signs
                of wear, nicks, scratches, gouges, or build-up of scale or other foreign substances.
                Replace bearings that show any signs of deterioration.

              To clean roller bearings, soak in clean solvent long enough to loosen any sludge, then
              gently slosh each bearing around near the top of the container to dislodge all pockets of
              grease. Scrub away stubborn accumulations with a small brush that has bristles that do
              not break off. Do not spin dirty bearings, but rotate races slowly while washing and
              scrubbing.

              Rinse the bearings in clean solvent and air dry. Hold both races when blowing with
              clean, dry compressed air. Do not allow the air jet to spin the bearing; rather, turn each
              race by hand to expose all surfaces to the drying air. If the bearing is to be stored for
              later reuse, wrap it in wax paper or other grease-proof wrapping.

              CAUTION: A bearing may be defective without the defect being visually evident:
              replace any bearing removed during any maintenance task with new or cleaned bearing
              at re-assembly.

              New bearings are packed with a rust-preventative grease (or other protective coating)
              and wrapped in grease-resistant paper before they are shipped. Do not unwrap the
              bearing until time for installation. Unwrap and thoroughly wash the new bearing and air
              dry. Pre-lubricate immediately with compatible system lubricant.

              NOTE: For ease of installation of bearings, heat the bearings at a maximum
              temperature of 121°C (250°F) in oil for one hour minimum, or in an electric furnace for
              1-1/2 hours minimum, or by bearing induction heater for 15 minutes minimum.

       1.5    Oil Seals -- Replace all seals and gaskets that are removed or disturbed during
              disassembly procedure. Make sure seals seat properly upon re-assembly.

       1.6    Oil Passages -- Pressure flush oil passages and blow dry with compressed air. Make
              sure passages are clear of debris or blockage.

       1.7    Pre-lubrication prior to re-assembly -- Lightly lubricate all seals, bearings, bushings, and
              gears with oil before installation.

       1.8    Aligning parts during re-assembly -- Because of the weight of large parts, use guide
              studs during re-assembly to ensure proper bolt hole and /or dowel pin alignment.

       1.9    Clean all parts and inspect for scratches, cracks, burrs, flaking, pitting, scaling or
              discoloration of mating or load-bearing surfaces.

       1.10   Hand scrape any bushing that have not become out-or-round to remove burrs, small
              scratches or accumulated foreign substances. Replace any bushing showing gross
              deformation or cracking.

       1.11   Check shafts and pivot pins for straightness with v-blocks and dial indicator. It is
              possible to straighten bent shafts in a hydraulic press, but if spares are available, it is
              much better to replace the parts. Never straighten bent castings; replace them. Weld
              cracked steel castings only if no spares are available, but replace them whenever
              possible.

       1.12   If roller surfaces become badly worn, rough, pitted, scaled or blistered, dress
              them on a lathe or grind them clean as long as the design tolerances are maintained.
              Otherwise, replace the parts.

3.0    Component Removal

The procedures below are for removing components and sub-assemblies that may require overhaul or
refurbishment from the C & C Shear Assembly. This work should be done only by qualified personnel
who have been trained on the equipment involved. The steps describe the work in general, and are not
intended to be a comprehensive guide. Refer to the General Safety, Lockout/Tagout, and Maintenance
section and applicable Morgan reference drawings as a guide.

       3.1     Shear Housing disassembly and Shaft Removal
               A. Visually check to see that the shear drive is stopped.
               B. Isolate, shutoff and/or disconnect all applicable water, air, lubrication, hydraulic,
                    and electrical power supply sources and control wiring.
               C. Ensure that all the systems in item “B” have been properly locked out and tagged.
               D. Disconnect all power lines from the shear drive.
               E. Disconnect electrical leads to the encoder.
               F. Remove the shear trough(s) if necessary to gain sufficient access to move shear
                    housings.
               G. Disconnect and bleed lube piping to the shear.
               H. Drain the lubricant from the Shear housing. Disconnect drain piping.
               I.   Clean the exterior of Shear housing and components.
               J.   Disconnect and disassemble the drive coupling between the drive and the Shear. The
                    coupling half on the Shear input shaft may be left in place.

Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices make the

quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be constrained to follow a prescribed path. Any

1.0     Toggle Shear Assembly

A two-strand toggle shear is mounted at the entry to stand 7. The toggle shear is an emergency-dividing shear
consisting of a pair of knives and is used primarily to cut a bar in the event of a cobble in the mill, thus limiting
the amount of material fed into the cobble.

The two pairs of knife blades each close by means of a separate air cylinder. The knives, in closing, contact the
moving bar. The bar then pulls the knives to complete the cut. The Toggle Shear dividing action is obtained by
bringing the knives into contact with the moving bar. The knives are arranged so that continued forward
movement of the bar causes them to fully engage to sever the bar.

Each pair of knives are closed and opened by the action of a double-acting air cylinder. Each double-acting air
cylinder is controlled by a double solenoid air valve. Energizing one solenoid causes the shear knives to close,
while energizing the other solenoid causes the shear knives to open. Note: With the air cylinder retracted, the
knives are open and bar may pass between them, and into the mill stand.

Extending the cylinder, the knives move forward, contact and sever the bar and then come together blocking the
passage of the remaining length of bar. Reverse action of the cylinder causes the knives to disengage and return
to the fully-opened position.

The toggle shear assembly is designed for manual and automatic operation. Operating stations (pulpit and local
stations) help test, monitor and adjust conditions that may occur through the automated system. Refer to Table 1
for a description of the electrical equipment used in the toggle shear assembly.
