                show any signs of deterioration.
                To clean roller bearings, soak in clean solvent long enough to loosen any sludge, and then gently
                slosh each bearing around near the top of the container to dislodge all pockets of grease. Scrub
                away stubborn accumulations with a small brush that has bristles that do not break off. Do not
                spin dirty bearings, but rotate races slowly while washing and scrubbing.
                Rinse the bearings in clean solvent and air dry. Hold both races when blowing with clean, dry
                compressed air. Do not allow the air jet to spin the bearing; rather, turn each race by hand to
                expose all surfaces to the drying air. If the bearing is to be stored for later reuse, wrap it in wax
                paper or other grease-proof wrapping.
                CAUTION: A bearing may be defective without the defect being visually evident: replace any
                bearing removed during any maintenance task with new or cleaned bearing at re-assembly.

                New bearings are packed with rust-preventative grease (or other protective coating) and wrapped
                in grease-resistant paper before they are shipped. Do not unwrap the bearing until time for
                installation. Unwrap and thoroughly wash the new bearing and air dry. Pre-lubricate
                immediately with same oil in lube system (or equivalent).
        NOTE: For ease of installation of bearings, heat the bearings at a maximum temperature of 121°C
        (250°F) in oil for one hour minimum, or in an electric furnace for 1-1/2 hours minimum, or by bearing
        induction heater for 15 minutes minimum.
        1.5     Oil Seals -- Replace all seals and gaskets that are removed or disturbed during disassembly
                procedure. Make sure seals seat properly upon re-assembly.

        1.6     Oil Passages -- Pressure flush oil passages and blow dry with compressed air. Make sure
                passages are clear of debris or blockage.

        1.7     Pre-lubrication Prior to Re-assembly -- Lightly lubricate all seals, bearings, bushings, and gears
                with oil before installation

        1.8     Aligning Parts during Re-assembly -- Because of the weight of large parts, use guide studs
                during re-assembly to ensure proper bolt hole and /or dowel pin alignment.

       WARNING: Do not exceed equipment ratings. Never attempt to press on or lift a load

       Never set the relief valve to a higher pressure than the maximum rated pressure of the pump.
       Higher settings may result in equipment damage and/or personal injury.

       WARNING: The system operating pressure must not exceed the pressure rating of the lowest
       rated component in the system. CHECK pressure gauges in the system to monitor operating
       pressure.

       CAUTION: Avoid damaging connected hoses. Avoid sharp bends and kinks when routing
       hoses. Using a bent or kinked hose will cause severe back-pressure. Sharp bends and kinks
       will internally damage the hose leading to premature hose failure.


       Do not drop heavy objects on hose. A sharp impact may cause internal damage to hose wire
       strands. Applying pressure to a damaged hose may cause it to rupture. DO NOT lift or pull
       equipment by hoses or couplers. Rig and secure equipment for safe transport.

       CAUTION: Keep hydraulic equipment away from flames and heat. Excessive heat will soften
       packing and seals, resulting in fluid leaks. Heat also weakens hose materials and packings.
       For optimum performance do not expose equipment to temperatures of 65°C [150°F] or
       higher. Protect all hoses and cylinders from weld spatter and extreme heat.


       DANGER: Do not handle pressurized hoses. Escaping oil under pressure can penetrate the
       skin, causing serious injury. If oil is injected under the skin, see a doctor immediately.

       WARNING: Only use hydraulic cylinders in a coupled system. Never use a cylinder with
       unconnected couplers. If the cylinder becomes extremely overloaded, components can fail
       catastrophically causing severe personal injury. Never bleed system to exposed atmosphere.

       WARNING: Immediately replace worn or damaged parts.
       IMPORTANT: Qualified trained technicians must only service Mill equipment.


       WARNING: Do not use electric pumps in an explosive atmosphere. Adhere to all local and
       national electrical codes. Start the pump with the valve in the neutral position to prevent
       accidental cylinder operation. Keep hands clear of moving parts and pressurized hoses.


       CAUTION: To prevent damage to electric motors, check specifications. Use of incorrect

1.0     Safety Procedures

WARNING: CONSIDER ALL EQUIPMENT AS POTENTIALLY HAZARDOUS AT ALL TIMES.
Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices make the
elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the process and/or
product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be constrained to follow a
prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble. Cobbles occur at random times
and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently
caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment, and
stock temperature are also causes of cobbling anywhere along the length of a bar in process in the rolling
train. The following recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe manner.
        1.1     Visibility and Communications
        Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations of
        pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment controlled from that
        point.

                A. Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight.

                B. Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper
                   lighting can be used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or cloud
                   the reflective surface and that the mirror location does not make it liable to breakage.

        1.2     Audible Communications

                Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as
                substitutes only when visual contact is not possible.

        1.2     Safety Stops

                Guide adjustments may be made only when the Mill Line is shut down. Mechanical or
                electrically operated stops must be used to block any stock from inadvertently entering into
                the mill.

                Make sure mill is shut down and material can not run through the stand. Make sure that
                stops remain in place as long as personnel making adjustments are in the hazard area.

        1.3     Alarms

                The alarms as described in the control specifications will have a warning system to alert
                the operators of new oncoming front ends.

                A prominently located light board should be used with the warning system to indicate the
                strand in use and the progress of the stock in the mill.

OPERATION

IMPORTANT: Always read safety instructions and warnings for each system and component prior
to operating and working on machinery. Refer to Safety Section for general safety steps and
procedures.

INTRODUCTION Refer to Figures 1 through 8 as a guide.

There are two Crop and Cobble (C&C) shears after stand 12H, one shear for each of the mill strands. The
main purpose of the C & C Shears is to crop front and tail ends of processed sections during delivery
through the mill. The shear may also be used for continuous cobble cutting. The short crop and cobble
lengths drop into a scrap chute to a scrap bucket.

The shears have a traverse function to allow each shear to be traversed by hydraulic cylinder out of the mill
line for maintenance.

The C & C Shear consists of two knives mounted on two parallel shafts on 700 mm centers that are geared
together (1:1 ratio). The direct drive pinion gear is powered by an electric motor.

Each knife shaft has 3 blades located 120 degrees apart from each other. One blade is the full width of the
knife holder while the other 2 blades are narrower.

There are 2 paths through the shear as determined by a switching trough ahead of the shear. In one path,
only the wide blades cut the stock. This is the normal crop cut operation. The other path is used for cobble
cutting where all 3 blades make a cut thus producing 3 cuts per shear revolution.

For each crop cut, the shear will accelerate from rest through approximately 250 degrees to the wide blade
cut position. When a crop cut stroke is completed, the shear stops and the wide blades are automatically
moved to the parked position by a position regulator. The position regulator will hold the shear in the
parked position between cut cycles when rolling billets.

For cobble cutting, the shear runs continually until stopped by the operator. Note: When cobble cutting is
signaled to stop, the shear completes one more cut, decelerates and stops. The blades are again
automatically moved to their rest position.

The C & C Shear is designed for manual and automatic operation, operating stations (Main Pulpit and
Local) help test, monitor and adjust conditions that may occur through the automated system. Refer to
Table 1 for a description of the electrical devices used in the C & C Shear Assembly.

FUNCTION, OPERATION, AND CONTROL DESCRIPTION Refer to Figures 1 through 8.
Note: For efficient operation of the C & C Shear, operators are required to constantly monitor all
components. Listed below are operation descriptions of the C & C Shear Assembly.

  1. C & C Shear Assembly, Entry Switch, and Exit Deflector

       1.1     Shear Control

       The Shear motor is to be fully regenerative, reversing, VVVF inverter with overcurrent,
       undervoltage, and field loss protection. VVVF type speed regulator is required maintaining
       cutting speed within plus or minus 1% of the selected speed.

       Following each cut, the shear will stop by regenerative braking. The drive stops the shear
       between 40° and 270° position, and position regulator operates the drive in reverse or forward
       direction to position shear to the 90° parked position.

       The shear should return to the parked position as quickly as possible to be ready for a cobble
       function in the event of front-end cobble in the mill. Absolute accuracy of parked position is not
       necessary for cobble cut initiation.

       Shear speed is regulated to follow product speed reference of the previous stand. SHEAR
       SPEED adjustment permits adjustment and presetting of the ratio between the shear speed and the
       speed of the stock.

       The following control strategy is used to minimize the slowing of the shear during the cut:
       • Use ramp reference to control acceleration of shear from park position to bite angle.
       • Ramp time is always minimum possible so shear just reaches cut speed when blades reach
          bite angle. ramp_time(seconds) = [degrees_motor_travel] / [3 x motor_rpm]
       • Continue ramping speed reference at same rate until 5% over reference is obtained or blades
          pass cut complete position (0 degrees).
       • Utilize inertia compensation (direct input to current controller) during accel/decel.

       The following additional impact correction circuit may be required to reduce the slowing of the
       shear during the cut:
           • Current reference is increased in anticipation of the shear load as the knives enter cut
               zone.
           • Exact location within the shear cycle and amount of increase is determined by the section
               area and speed of the shear.

       1.2     Crop Cut Length and Accuracy

       Crop cut length: Head - adjustable 100 mm to 300 mm
                                Tail - adjustable 100 mm to 500 mm

       Required accuracy +40 mm front and tail ends for 95% of cuts.

       1.3     Holding Brake

       A spring set, electrically released Holding Brake is installed onto the motor. The brake is used for
       holding only, including holding the knife assembly when changing knife blades. It is not used for
       stopping.

       When there is no stock detected between the furnace and the shear, the brake will de-energize and
       set after a time delay. Time delay is set initially for 15 seconds. The brake is released whenever
       stock is detected between the furnace and the shear.

       1.4     Shear Lubrication

       Shear is lubricated from the mill lube system. A Shear Lube Pressure switch at the shear signals
       when lube pressure is correct. An annunciated alarm will signal when lube pressure is not correct.

       1.5     Detector for Crop Cut Signal

       The Crop HMD (Hot Metal Detector) is used to initiate automatic crop cuts. A hot metal detector is
       located after stands 12. The detector initiates a counter and upon completion of a preset count, causes
       the shear to automatically make a front crop.

       Detection of a tail end initiates a tail crop if selected.

Shear Assembly                                                                        Maintenance Instructions

       1.7     Manual Positioning of Shear

       For maintenance purposes such as blade changing or adjusting, all power must be disconnected
       from the shear drive before attempting to move the shear by hand. A Jog function is included to
       enable the operator to position the shear.

       1.8     Automatic Head Cut Counter Control

       A preset counter system is used to provide consistent length of front-end crop cuts. The counter
       counts pulses supplied from the pulse generator or an internal clock.

       Operator adjustment of the crop length is provided. Note: This adjustment must have a minimum
       and maximum allowable settings outside which the operator may not adjust. This is to prevent
       premature cuts and crop lengths too long for scrap handling.

       In order to compensate for variations in the shear reaction time, it is necessary to subtract the number
       of counts representing the shear reaction or delay time from the calculated transport time delay.

       A shear REACTION time counter accumulates elapsed pulses from cut-initiate signal to knife overlap
       (as indicated by the shear position encoder 0° position). This count is updated every time the shear
       makes a cut. Any difference from the calculated reaction time and the measured REACTION time is
       used to calculated preset for CUT counter.

       Initially, or after a mill delay, or after a change in product size which calls for a different shear speed,
       the shear must be dry-run through one or two cycles by operator in order to establish the correct shear
       delay count.

       When the front end of a rod is detected at the Crop HMD before shear, the CUT counter starts
       counting. Upon reaching the preset count, the counter system produces a cut initiate signal.

       The CUT counter re-establishes the preset count each time the shear is put through a cut cycle,
       whether automatically or by hand.

       1.9     Automatic Tail Cut Counter Control

       The same counting system is used to initiate a tail cut. Operator adjustment of the tail crop
       length is provided. This adjustment must also have a minimum and maximum allowable setting
       outside which the operator may not adjust. This is to prevent premature cuts and crop lengths too
       long for scrap handling.

       Since the calculation of product speed using motor RPM, stand gear ratio and effective roll diameter
       represents exit speed, reduction of material in entry stand of stand 12 must be used as well to
       calculate material speed.

       When the tail end of a rod is detected at the Crop HMD before shear, the CUT counter starts
       counting. Upon reaching the preset count, the counter system produces a cut initiate signal.

       The CUT counter re-establishes the preset count each time the shear is put through a cut cycle,
       whether automatically or by hand.

       1.10     Cobble Cutting

       When cobble cutting at slow product speeds, the end of the bar sometimes can stall in the delivery
       troughs to the shear once the product has tailed out of the upstream stand. Accelerating the shear
       once the product tails out of the upstream stand provides additional inertia to the remaining piece
       of bar so that it does not stall.

       Acceleration begins as the product tails out of stand 12. The shear accelerates to maximum shear
       operating speed. Acceleration rate is controlled by torque limit of the drive. Shear runs
       continuously until stopped by the operator.

       1.11     Entry Traversing Switch Trough

       There are two paths through the shear. The entry switch trough directs the bar into the selected
       path. One path is the CROP CUT path at the driveside. In this position, only the shear wide
       blade cuts the rod. The switch is normally in this position and moves only for cobble cutting.

       The other path is the COBBLE CUT path at the workside. In this position, all 3 blades cut the
       rod.

       The entry switch proximity switches indicate the 2 positions. Close coordination and fast action
       is required between the shear and switch when cobble cutting is to start. The entry switch trough
       motion is produced by an air cylinder which is controlled by a double solenoid valve.

       When cobble cutting is to start, the shear must accelerate up to speed for the first cut to be made
       by the wide blades. After the first cut, the rod must be in the narrow blade path so the narrow
       blade following the wide blade makes the second cut.

       When the narrow blade ahead of the wide blade is about 20 degrees past the zero position, the
       switch is signaled to move to the narrow, 3 blade position. At max shear speed, it must complete
       the move in 0.08 seconds. There is a shock absorber at the end of the cylinder stroke.

       It may be necessary to signal the switch to move early to compensate for reaction time. The
       reaction time compensation can be achieved automatically by logging the following signals:

           1.    Solenoid energized
           2.    CROP position proximity switch signal lost
           3.    COBBLE position proximity switch signal made

       The switch returns to CROP position when cobble cutting stops.

           1.12    Shear Traverse Refer to figures 2 and 3.

           A sliding base assembly under each shear and shear motor allow the shear and motor assembly to
           be traversed from the on-line operating position to an off-line position for maintenance. A
           hydraulic cylinder is utilized to provide the motion. Sliding base clamp bolts must be loosened
           prior to traversing. Refer to applicable Morgan reference drawing for procedure.

           Two solenoid valves control the traverse motion. Solenoid ‘a’ is energized to move the shear
           online and solenoid ‘b’ is energized to move the shear offline.

           Proximity switches indicate the position of each shear.

           1.13    Scrap Chute Operation Refer to figures 1 through 3.

           Two scrap buckets are located at the lower level beneath the shear. Cut pieces are directed into one
           bucket or the other by the scrap chute deflector. The chute deflector is operated by an air cylinder
           which is controlled by manual valve.

           The bucket is removed by a fork truck and replaced with an empty box when the box is full.

2.     Sequence of Shear Cutting Operation Refer to Figure 4 as a guide.

The following is a description of the intended sequence of operation. Data is calculated based on 527.2 rpm
(max) of the motor, 97.2 rpm (max) of the shear knife shaft.

     2.1       The position where the knives overlap and are fully engaged is the 0° position.

     2.2       Between cuts, the shear is held at the parked position which is 90°.

     2.3       When the shear is signaled to cut, it accelerates to 97.2 rpm in 250.172°, 0.8579 seconds, at 1.80
               per unit average torque.

     2.4       At 340.172°, the approximate bite angle, the knives contact the stock and commence the cut.

     2.5       At 0° the encoder signals that the cut is complete.

     2.6       At 19.828°, the encoder signals that the knives are clear and signals the drive to stop by
               regenerative braking.

     2.7       The shear decelerates to a stop in 250.172°, 0.8579 seconds at 1.80 per unit average torque.

     2.8       The shear comes to a stop at the 270° position.

     2.9       The shear will then reverse direction and travel from the 270° position to the 90° parked position.

     2.10      When the shear has position regulated to a stop at the 90 degree position the position regulator
               will continue to hold the shear in position between cut cycles.

3.0     Monitoring Refer to applicable ECS for additional descriptions.

The C & C Shear is designed for manual and automatic operation, operating stations (Main Pulpit and Local)
help test, monitor and adjust conditions that may occur through the automated system.

Note: For efficient operation of the C & C Shear, operators are required to constantly monitor all
components and control systems. Make sure all safety guards are closed and interlocks are working
properly.

The operator's control devices for the crop and cobble shear are to be located in the Main Mill Pulpit and on
the Mill Floor Station for the Shear.

Some of the devices are noted for mounting on a set-up panel. The remaining are to be desk mounted. This
list is intended to describe the functions required.

Note: The term "discrete" signifies a device that is immediately available such as a panel mounted
pushbutton, as opposed to a "soft" device requiring screen menu paging.

A duplicate set of controls for the following devices is required for each 700mm C&C shear.

        3.1     Monitor Main Control Pulpit. Refer to the following switches and indicators. Refer to
                section 3.3 below for a description of the function of these devices.

          a. 1 - PRODUCT SPEED digital readout type indicator, calibrated in M/sec.

          b. 1 - SHEAR SPEED REFERENCE, digital readout indicator, calibrated in M/sec.

          c. 1 - SHEAR SPEED FEEDBACK, digital readout indicator, calibrated in M/sec.
                  horizontal speed of shear at 20° bite angle.

          d. 1 - STAND ROLL DIAMETER compensation. (Same as used for Main Drive)

          e. 1 - SHEAR SPEED REFERENCE selection. (Set-up Panel)
                  2-position, maintaining contact, marked NORMAL - TEST

          f. 1 - SHEAR MODE selection. (Set-up Panel)
                  4-position, maintaining contact, marked JOG - OFF - HAND - AUTO

          g. 1 - HEAD CROP LENGTH adjustment. (Set-up Panel)

          h. 1 - HEAD CROP LEAD SPEED adjustment. (Set-up Panel)

          i. 1 - TAIL CROP selection. (Set-up Panel)
                  2-position, maintaining contact, marked OFF – ON.

          j. 1 - TAIL CROP LENGTH adjustment. (Set-up Panel)

          k. 1 - TAIL CROP LEAD SPEED adjustment. (Set-up Panel)

       3.3     Operator’s Control Devices – Functions.

       The following describes the function of devices listed in section 3.1 and 3.2 above:

       a.,b.,c. The PRODUCT SPEED indicator, as well as the SHEAR SPEED REFERENCE and
                FEEDBACK indicators, are used for setting the shear speed. By observing these displays and
                by means of the Shear LEAD SPEED adjustments (devices "h" and "k", the operator may
                arrive at a setting for the shear speed suited for the speed of the product.

               For the head crop, the shear lead speed should be set about 12% higher than the mill stand
               speed due to also to the speed drop which occurs during the shearing operation. The
               correction for the 15° bite angle is done automatically by the control system.

               Shear speed set higher than necessary does not directly result in cobbles; however, shear
               speed set too low could cause a cobble. To arrive at the proper shear speed setting for cutting

              a particular section, the shear speed should be set conservatively high and the cutting action
              observed. If the shear speed is higher than necessary, the crop length would be thrown
              forward; if the shear speed is set too low, the front end of the remaining length of product
              after the cut would have a tendency to buckle.

       d.     The ROLL DIAMETER compensation is preset by the operator to affect proper Stand motor
              RPM and calibration of the SHEAR PRODUCT SPEED indicator by compensating for
              various roll diameters. This also modifies the shear speed reference signal to provide a signal
              directly proportional to the speed of product going through shear.

       e.     The SPEED REFERENCE selection switch permits selection of either stand product speed or
              a test reference for speed regulation and cut length counting equipment.

              In the NORMAL condition, the relative speed of the shear is regulated to follow the delivery
              speed of the stock from Intermediate Mill #2 for a head cut and Bar Finishing Mill take in
              speed for a tail cut. A change in the stock speed provides an equal percentage adjustment in
              the speed reference for the shear.

              In the TEST condition, an independent speed reference is provided for the shear to permit
              operation of the shear for test and maintenance purposes when the mill is not running stock.
              Test reference should be adjustable through full range of shear (5-100%). The HEAD CROP
              LEAD SPEED adjustment, device "h", may be used to adjust test reference if desired.

       f.     The SHEAR MODE selection permits selection of either remote jog, hand, or automatic
              operation of the shear.

              Selection of OFF prevents operation of the shear.

              It is necessary to return the select OFF to reset the circuit before the shear may be operated
              after a control power outage.

              The shear position regulator must not move the knives to the parked position, when the power
              is switched on, until the mode selection is cycled through OFF.

              Selection of AUTO provides for automatic head crop operation of the shear from the crop
              length counter equipment. The crop cut length is set with the HEAD CROP LENGTH
              adjustment (device "g"). Selection of AUTO also permits auto cobble cutting.

              Manual initiation of a cut cycle may be made by means of the SINGLE CUT or COBBLE
              CUT pushbuttons (devices “n”, “o” and “s”) while the SHEAR MODE is in either AUTO or
              HAND.

              Selection of HAND prevents automatic operation of the shear from the crop cut length
              counter or the auto cobble cut circuits.

              In the JOG condition, the SHEAR JOG switch (device "v") is operative for jogging the shear
              either forward or reverse at reduced speed (10%). Jogging is independent of the shear
              stopping sequence.

               To initiate another cut cycle the above pushbutton must be released and again depressed.

       p.      The SHEAR READY indicating light, when illuminated, indicates that the shear drive power

               ready for operation and in its parked position. This light flashes when the CROP AND

       h.,k.   The HEAD CROP & TAIL CROP LEAD SPEED adjustments provide the means for
               adjusting the shear speed. With the SPEED REFERENCE selection in TEST the HEAD
               CROP LEAD SPEED adjustment can set the motor speed between 10% and 100%.

               With the SPEED REFERENCE selection in NORMAL the HEAD CROP LEAD SPEED (0
               to 15%) and the TAIL CROP LEAD SPEED (0 to -15%) adjustments set the relationship of
               the shear speed to the PRODUCT SPEED.
               Either the HEAD CROP LEAD SPEED or the TAIL CROP LEAD SPEED adjustment will
               be effective depending on the type of cut being made.

               For head crop cuts and cobble cuts, the shear peripheral speed should be set about 12%
               higher than the rod speed to offset the speed drop which occurs during the shearing operation.
               Compensation for the bite angle of about 15° is done by the control system. The knives start
               to bite into the stock about 15° before the knives reach the 0 degree position. To arrive at the
               proper speed setting for a particular product, the shear HEAD CROP LEAD SPEED should
               be set at 10% and the cutting action observed.

               For tail cuts, the shear speed reference is set to a lower lead speed in order that the rotating
               shear knives do not overtake and deform the severed end of the bar proceeding to next stand.
               Initially set the TAIL CROP LEAD SPEED to -10%.

       g.,j.   The CROP LENGTH ADJUSTMENTS are used to increase or decrease the respective crop
               cut length when the SHEAR MODE selection is in the AUTO position.

               detector is functioning. The illuminated portion associated with the pushbutton glows while
               the sensor detects stock.

               automatic control equipment for the shear.

               Depressing the CROP HMD TEST pushbutton has the same effect on the control circuits as
               when the sensor detects the arrival of stock head end. Releasing the pushbutton simulates the
               arrival of a stock tail end.

PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS
DEFINITION

Preventative maintenance is routine maintenance that, if performed as scheduled helps to keep the C & C
shear assembly in good operating condition. Its primary purpose is to reduce the incidence of operating
failures, which require costly downtime for repairs. The recommended routine maintenance schedule
below represents the anticipated minimum requirements for maintaining the C & C Shear. As you
accumulate operating experience, it may be feasible to reduce the frequency of checks and inspections,
however, do not reduce the lubrication frequency.
IMPORTANT
Always isolate shutoff and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic and electrical power supply sources
before performing any repairs or maintenance. Read all safety instructions and warnings for each
system and component prior to working on machinery. Refer to Safety section.
INTRODUCTION
Routine and preventive maintenance of the C & C Shear assembly is required to ensure extended and
proper operation. Table 2 is provided as a quick reference guide for frequent periodic maintenance
requirements for the C & C Shear assembly. Refer to the General Maintenance section and to the
applicable manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance requirements and procedures of specific
components. Refer to Morgan assembly drawings as a guide and for additional information.
       WARNING: Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or
       disconnect all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any stored energy
       from components. Restrain and secure any moving parts of a component or system that
       could cause injury. Never open inspection doors on the shear housing while the shear is
       operating.
       WARNING: The C & C Shear Assembly is potentially dangerous and capable of inflicting
       severe bodily injuries. Before starting any maintenance task, comply with all company
       policies relating to safety. Also, be thoroughly familiar with the general safety
       requirements.
1.0    Lubrication
       Daily
       1.1       Inspect lubrication system and piping for leaks. Refer to fluids maintenance instructions.
       Weekly
       1.2       Lubricate air cylinder pivot pin to switch trough assembly with Mobile AW-10 or
                 equivalent. Lubricate manual grease points on sliding base.
       Monthly
       1.3       Inspect all seals for leaks. Note: Some minor leaking is acceptable. Wipe and monitor
                 leakage area. Replace seals as necessary.
       4 Months
       1.4       Inspect internal gearing and bearings for proper lubrication.
       6 Months
       1.5       Lubricate drive couplings in accordance with manufacturer’s requirements.

DEFINITION
Corrective maintenance encompasses those repair procedures required to return the C & C shear assembly
to satisfactory operating condition. Such repairs do not necessarily return the equipment to like-new
condition. Rather, the objective is to make it operational again as soon as possible. It is recommended to
replace faulty parts/components and sub-assemblies with new or previously refurbished spare
parts/components and sub-assemblies. Those parts removed may then be refurbished or reconditioned after
the main equipment has been returned to service.
IMPORTANT

Always isolate shutoff and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic and electrical power supply sources before
performing any repairs or maintenance. Read all safety instructions and warnings for each system and
component prior to working on machinery. Refer to Safety section.

INTRODUCTION

Corrective Maintenance of the C & C Shear Assembly as defined above, is intended to keep down time at
a minimum by replacing components and then dismantling and overhauling the removed component in a
service area away from the mill. Once refurbished, the component becomes a spare shelf part, ready to be
utilized as a replacement when needed.

No disassembly procedures are given herein of components being replaced. Components that require
overhaul/refurbishment should be maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Refer to
the manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance and torque requirements and procedures of specific
components of the C & C Shear Assembly.

General guidelines and maintenance criteria are provided below when corrective maintenance of a
component or sub-assembly is required. These are minimum guidelines and should be used in
conjunction with the specific maintenance requirements from the component manufacturer.

Upon re-assembly, tighten all bolts, screws, nuts and fasteners in accordance with Morgan reference
drawings torque requirements. Torque specific components in accordance with the manufacturer’s
requirements.

Removal procedures are also provided for components and sub-assemblies that may require corrective
maintenance. Refer to the General Safety and Maintenance section, and applicable Morgan reference
drawings as a guide.

        WARNING: Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or
        disconnect all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any stored energy
        from components. Restrain and secure any moving parts of a component or system that
        could cause injury.

        WARNING: The C & C Shear Assembly is potentially dangerous and capable of inflicting
        severe bodily injuries. Before starting any maintenance task, comply with all company
        policies relating to safety. Also, be thoroughly familiar with the general maintenance
        requirements.

1.0     General Maintenance Criteria

The following is a list of maintenance actions to perform whenever dismantling equipment for repairs.

        1.1     Electric controls and power cables -- Before disconnecting any wiring that does not have
                plug-in connectors, make sure that color coding is clearly identifiable or tag each wire
                carefully for reference at re-assembly.

        1.2     Rigging parts for removal/replacement -- Many parts that make up this equipment are
                much too heavy to be handled by one person. Provide adequate rigging for lifting and
                supporting heavy parts before attempting to dismantle any equipment.

        1.3     Cleaning -- Clean all parts with a suitable solvent (mineral spirits, SAVASOL no.5, or
                equivalent) to remove all scale, grease, grime, or dirt. Use a clean wiper; do not use
                cotton waste. Air dry after cleaning.

       1.4    Bearings and Sealing Surfaces -- Closely inspect bearings and sealing surfaces for signs of
              wear, nicks, scratches, gouges, or build-up of scale or other foreign substances. Replace
              bearings that show any signs of deterioration.

              To clean roller bearings, soak in clean solvent long enough to loosen any sludge, and then
              gently slosh each bearing around near the top of the container to dislodge all pockets of
              grease. Scrub away stubborn accumulations with a small brush that has bristles that do not
              break off. Do not spin dirty bearings, but rotate races slowly while washing and scrubbing.

              Rinse the bearings in clean solvent and air dry. Hold both races when blowing with clean,
              dry compressed air. Do not allow the air jet to spin the bearing; rather, turn each race by
              hand to expose all surfaces to the drying air. If the bearing is to be stored for later reuse,
              wrap it in wax paper or other grease-proof wrapping.

              CAUTION: A bearing may be defective without the defect being visually evident: replace
              any bearing removed during any maintenance task with new or cleaned bearing at re-
              assembly.
              New bearings are packed with rust-preventative grease (or other protective coating) and
              wrapped in grease-resistant paper before they are shipped. Do not unwrap the bearing until
              time for installation. Unwrap and thoroughly wash the new bearing and air dry. Pre-
              lubricate immediately with Mobil 525 (or equivalent).

              NOTE: For ease of installation of bearings, heat the bearings at a maximum temperature of
              121°C (250°F) in oil for one-hour minimum, or in an electric furnace for 1-1/2 hours
              minimum, or by bearing induction heater for 15 minutes minimum.
       1.5    Oil Seals -- Replace all seals and gaskets that are removed or disturbed during disassembly
              procedure. Make sure seals seat properly upon re-assembly.
       1.6    Oil Passages -- Pressure flush oil passages and blow dry with compressed air. Make sure
              passages are clear of debris or blockage.
       1.7    Pre-lubrication prior to re-assembly -- Lightly lubricate all seals, bearings, bushings, and
              gears with oil before installation.
       1.8    Aligning parts during re-assembly -- Because of the weight of large parts, use guide studs
              during re-assembly to ensure proper bolt hole and /or dowel pin alignment.
       1.9    Clean all parts and inspect for scratches, cracks, burrs, flaking, pitting, scaling or
              discoloration of mating or load-bearing surfaces.
       1.10   Hand scrape any bushing that have not become out-or-round to remove burrs, small
              scratches or accumulated foreign substances. Replace any bushing showing gross
              deformation or cracking.

       1.11   Check shafts and pivot pins for straightness with v-blocks and dial indicator. It is possible
              to straighten bent shafts in a hydraulic press, but if spares are available, it is much better to
              replace the parts. Never straighten bent castings; replace them. Weld cracked steel castings
              only if no spares are available, but replace them whenever possible.

3.0     Component Removal
The procedures below are for removing components and sub-assemblies that may require overhaul or
refurbishment from the C & C Shear Assembly. This work should be done only by qualified personnel
who have been trained on the equipment involved. The steps describe the work in general, and are not
intended to be a comprehensive guide. Refer to the General Safety, Lockout/Tagout, and Maintenance
section and applicable Morgan reference drawings as a guide.
       3.1     Shear Housing Removal from Mill
               A. Visually check to see that the shear drive is stopped.
               B. Disconnect all power from the shear drive.
               C. Disconnect electrical leads to the encoder.
               D. Remove the shear troughs if necessary to gain sufficient access to remove the shear
                  housings.
               E. Shut off the lube oil supply to shear. Disconnect and bleed lube piping to the shear.
               F. Separate the drive and shear coupling halves.
               G. Remove all hardware securing the housing.

               H. Disconnect lube piping from between the intermediate housing sections.
               I.   Rig the entire shear assembly for lifting and remove to service area.

       3.2     Housing Disassembly (Disassembly is similar for each housing section)
               A. Remove the drive shaft seal retainer hardware from the drive side of the shear. Hang the
                  retainer on the pinion shaft.
               B. Remove the drive shaft seal.

               C. Remove the drive shaft bearing retainer hardware from the drive side of the shear. Pull
                  the bearing retainer and shim pack off the housing a hang them on the pinion shaft. Tie
                  the shims together as an aid for re-use at re-assembly.

               D. Remove the bearing cartridges, retainers and applicable shims from each shaft assembly.

               E. Remove all hardware connecting each housing section to be removed.

               F. Rig the housing section for lifting. Carefully hoist the housing off the other housing
                  section using care not to damage gear teeth or internal lube piping.

               G. Rig the shaft assembly for lifting and remove from the shear. Use caution when
                  disengaging the gear teeth and in moving the assembly to prevent damage to the
                  assembly.
               H. Rig the drive shaft assembly for lifting and remove from the shear. Use caution in
                  moving the assembly to prevent damage to the assembly.

4.0     Component Installation
        4.1     Reverse steps and procedures outlined in Section 3.0. Follow the additional steps and
                procedures listed below.
                A. Select proper shim sizes. Shims are tied together as an aid for re-assembly.
                B. Use new seals, gaskets, o- rings, and bearings. Pre-lubricated seals and bearings prior to
                   re-assembly. Make sure o-ring seals are seated properly.
                C. Use Sealtite or equivalent on all housing joint/seams.
                D. Check shafts free rotation. Make sure shafts and gears have clear oil lines.
                E. Check to see that gears and pinions mesh properly.

                F. Torque all fasteners in accordance with Morgan reference drawing requirements.

                G. Restore lubrication piping. Make sure internal lubrication is properly aligned with gearing
                   and bearings.
                H. Restore all power supplies to the shear. Refer to Section 5.0.

                I.   Run the shear through several cut cycles to test the operation.

       3.1     Safety Procedures

       Important:      All safety devices must be properly maintained and never bypassed to assure
                       the safety of the operators.

       Stock presents serious hazards and the nature of the hazards and rolling mill operating practices
       make the elimination or control of these hazards extremely difficult. For operator control of the
       process and/or product quality, the stock must be generally visible and accessible, yet be
       constrained to follow a prescribed path. Any deviation from the path is referred to as a cobble.
       Cobbles occur at random times and places and the direction taken by the cobbled stock is
       unpredictable. Cobbles are most frequently caused by front ends failing to follow a prescribed
       path. Improper speed regulation, guide adjustment, and stock temperature are also causes of
       cobbling anywhere along the length of a bar in process in the rolling train. The following
       recommended guidelines will help to produce a quality product in a safe manner.

       3.2     Visibility and Communications

       Visibility from a control point to machinery is an important safety consideration. Locations of
       pulpits and other control points should provide an optimum view of equipment controlled from
       that point.

       Where possible and practical, visibility should be realized by line-of-sight confirmation.

       Where line-of-sight visibility is impossible or impractical, a mirror with proper lighting can be
       used provided that the immediate environment will not dirty or cloud the reflective surface and
       that the mirror location does not make it liable to breakage.

       3.3     Audible Communications

       Intercoms, telephone, and radio communications can be used to supplement or as substitutes only
       when visual contact is not possible.

       3.4     Safety Stops

       Guide adjustments may be made only when the Mill Line is shut down. Mechanical or
       electrically operated stops must be used to block any stock from inadvertently entering into the
       mill.

4.0    OPERATION

       Important:      Always read all safety instructions and warnings for each system and
                       component prior to operating and working on machinery. Refer to Safety
                       Section for general safety steps and procedures.

       4.1     Introduction

       The purpose of the Snap Shears, located at the entry to Pre-finishing Mill (PFM) stands 17 and 18
       are to close the rod travel path and sever the rod. The Snap Shears are used as safety devices to
       prevent stock from entering the PFM when interlock safety systems are activated (i.e. Safety
       Guards Open). They also protect the downstream mechanical mill equipment in the event of low
       lubrication, cooling water malfunction, and electrical power loss. The Snap Shears must also be
       closed when performing any maintenance on the downstream mill machinery.

       The Snap Shears are also used as an emergency cutting shear when a cobble occurs in the PFM or
       beyond. This prevents excess material from entering the PFM when rod travel has slowed down
       or stopped downstream. The Snap Shears are designed for manual and automatic operation,
       operating stations (Main Pulpit and Local) help test, monitor and adjust conditions that may occur
       through the automated system. Refer to Table 1for a description of electrical equipment used in
       the Snap Shear Assemblies.

             Table 1 – Description of Electrical Equipment
         DESCRIPTION                                                          DESIGNATOR

         Cut Solenoid Valve                                                   -        1SS/EV1
         Shear Opened Proximity Switch                                        -        1SS/PLS1
         Shear Closed Proximity Switch                                        -        1SS/PLS2
         Shear Open Signal Lantern                                            -        1SS/VIS2
         Shear Closed Signal Lantern                                          -        1SS/VIS1
         PFM Low-Low Lube Oil Pressure Switch                                 -        PFM/PS3.1, 3.2

         Local Floor Station near Snap Shear                                  -        OS14

       The Snap Shear can accommodate various feed size diameter stock. Knife deflectors, guide
       inserts and guide shoes are interchangeable for the applicable rod size. See Morgan reference
       drawings for appropriate guide information.

       4.2     Components

               4.2.1. Snap Shear Assembly Operation

               The Snap Shear single solenoid valve controls the Snap Shear. The Shear Opened and
               Shear Closed proximity switches indicate the open and closed positions. The valve is
               energized to open the knives (air actuating cylinder) from the rod travel path and de-
               energized to close and cut the rod (spring loaded return in the cylinder). The air cylinder
               rotates the knives into the vertical position with sufficient force to bite into the traveling
               rod. The rod then pulls the knives to the final closed position, against the stops, and the
               knife blades severs the rod.

               •     The following conditions cause an immediate closing of the snap shear:

                     1. Operation of a SNAP SHEAR CLOSE button.

                     2. Indication that the Pre Finishing mill stand drive motor has stopped or is to be
                        stopped by a loss of power or fault condition as described in the Main Drive
                        control specification.

                     3. Indication of Low-Low Lube oil pressure in either one of the lubrication
                        system header for the Pre finishing mill.

                     4. Low Mill Cooling Water pressure in Pre Finishing mill.

                     5. Auto Cobble Detection proximity switch in the PFM.

               •     Conversely, once the snap shear is closed, the following conditions will prevent the
                     opening of the snap shear :

                     1. Loss of power on the Pre Finishing mill drive.

                     2. Fault in the PFM lubrication system.

                     3. Fault in the roller entry guide lube system of the PFM.

                     4. Pre Finishing mill cobble guard door not closed.

                     5. Low pressure in the Pre Finishing mill roll cooling water.

       Note:                    See Section 4.4.2 for interlocking.

              4.2.2. Interlocking

              The following interlocks steps and procedures are required in both manual and automatic
              operation. Refer to other operation sections of all mill equipment for additional
              interlocking steps and procedures of specific components.

              •   The mill door cannot open unless the snap shear is closed. Also, the snap shear
                  cannot open unless the door is closed.

              •   The Sidelooper persuader roll and lifting guide remains in its existing position when
                  the snap shear is signaled to close.

              •   Upstream crop and cobble shear automatically starts cobble cutting when snap shear
                  closes and hot metal is detected at loop scanner or HMD before this shear.

              •   Permit the manual stopping of the crop and cobble shears when desired.

5.0    MONITORING

       5.1     Monitoring

       The Snap Shear is designed for manual and automatic operation, operating stations (Main Pulpit
       and Local) help test, monitor and adjust conditions that may occur through the automated system.

       Note:           For efficient operation of the Snap Shear, operators are required to
                       constantly monitor all components and control systems.

               A.      Ensure the following elevated warning devices are working properly:

                       •   Shear Open Signal and Shear Closed Signal lantern type lamps:

                           Red = closed.
                           Green = open.

               B.      Monitor Main Control Pulpit. Refer to the following switch and indicators for
                       proper operation:

                       •   Snap shear CUT initiation and indication.

                       •   Snap shear OPEN indication.

               C.      Monitor Local Station. Refer to the following switch and indicators for proper
                       operation of Snap Shear:

                       •   CUT illuminated button.

                       •   OPEN illuminated button.

                           OPEN can be initiated only at this location.

               D.      Ensure water is flowing through spray tube and cooling knife assembly.

               E.      Make sure cylinder is actuating properly. Test without stock for complete knife
                       travel/rotation. Adjust flow control valves if necessary, so that knife assembly
                       opens and closes quickly and completely against stops.

               F.      Check that knives close together with a maximum gap of 0.5 mm. Adjust and
                       shim if necessary.

6.0    PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS

       6.1     Definition

       Preventive maintenance is routine maintenance that if performed as scheduled helps to keep the
       Snap Shear assembly in good operating condition. Its primary purpose is to reduce the incidence
       of operating failures, which require costly downtime for repairs. The recommended routine
       maintenance schedule below represents the anticipated minimum requirements for maintaining
       the Snap Shear. As you accumulate operating experience, it may be feasible to reduce the
       frequency of checks and inspections, however, do not reduce the lubrication frequency.

       Important:      Always isolate, shutoff, and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic, and
                       electrical power supply sources before performing any repairs or
                       maintenance. Read safety instructions and warnings for each system and
                       component prior to working on machinery. Refer to the Safety sections in
                       the beginning of your mill’s manual as well as in this manual chapter.

       6.2     Introduction

       Routine and Preventive Maintenance of the Snap Shear assembly is required to ensure extended
       and proper operation. Table 2 is provided as a reference guide for frequent periodic maintenance
       requirements for the Snap Shear assembly. Refer to the General Maintenance section and
       applicable manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance requirements and procedures for
       specific components. Refer to Morgan assembly drawings as a guide for additional information.

       Warning:        Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or
                       disconnect all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any
                       stored energy from components. Restrain and secure any moving parts of a
                       component or system that could cause injury.

       Warning:        Exposed moving parts can cause severe injury. LOCK OUT and TAG OUT
                       POWER before removing guards or performing maintenance. NEVER
                       remove a guard, shield cover or other protective devices while the
                       equipment is running!

       Warning:        This equipment is potentially dangerous and capable of inflicting severe
                       bodily injuries. Before starting any maintenance task, comply with all
                       company policies relating to safety. Also, be thoroughly familiar with the
                       general safety requirements.

       Warning:        Always stop machinery before entering or adjusting the equipment. Know
                       where all e-stop buttons are located before operating or performing
                       maintenance on this equipment.

       6.3       Lubrication

       Per Shift

       1. Inspect air regulator/lubricator/filter system for correct pressure and fluid level. Adjust

       Weekly

       Daily

       2. Inspect all air connections and hoses for leaks, cuts, abrasions and excess wear. Tighten
          connections and replace hoses as required.

7.0    CORRECTIVE MAINTENANCE INSTRUCTIONS

       7.1     Definition

       Corrective maintenance encompasses those repair procedures required to return the Snap Shear
       assembly to satisfactory operating condition. Such repairs do not necessarily return the
       equipment to like-new condition. Rather, the objective is to make it operational again as soon as
       possible. It is recommended to replace faulty parts/components and sub-assemblies with new or
       previously refurbished spare parts/components and sub-assemblies. Those parts removed may
       then be refurbished or reconditioned after the main equipment has been returned to service.

       Important:      Always isolate, shutoff, and/or disconnect water, air, hydraulic, and
                       electrical power supply sources before performing any repairs or
                       maintenance. Read safety instructions and warnings for each system and
                       component prior to working on machinery. Refer to Safety Section in this
                       manual chapter.

       7.2     Introduction

       Corrective Maintenance of the Snap Shear assembly as defined above is intended to keep down
       time at a minimum by replacing components and then dismantling and overhauling the removed
       component in a service area away from the mill. Once refurbished, the component becomes a
       spare shelf part, ready to be utilized as a replacement when needed.

       No disassembly procedures are given herein of components being replaced. Components that
       require overhaul/refurbishment should be maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s
       instructions. Refer to the manufacturer’s technical manual for maintenance and torque
       requirements and procedures of specific components of the Snap Shear Assembly.

       General guidelines and maintenance criteria are provided below when corrective maintenance of
       a component or sub-assembly is required. These are minimum guidelines and should be used in
       conjunction with the specific maintenance requirements from the component manufacturer.

       Upon re-assembly, tighten all bolts, screws, nuts and fasteners in accordance with Morgan
       reference drawings torque requirements. Torque specific components in accordance with the
       manufacturer’s requirements.

       Warning:        Before performing any maintenance on mill equipment, shutoff or
                       disconnect all power supply sources. De-energize, dissipate and exhaust any
                       stored energy from components. Restrain and secure any moving parts of a
                       component or system that could cause injury. Make sure covers are secure
                       with locking pin before performing any maintenance.

       Warning:        The Snap Shear assembly is potentially dangerous and capable of inflicting
                       severe bodily injuries. Before starting any maintenance task, comply with

       7.3     General Maintenance Criteria

       The following is a list of maintenance actions to perform whenever dismantling equipment for
       repairs.

       1. Electric controls and power cables: Before disconnecting any wiring that does not have plug-
          in connectors, make sure that color coding is clearly identifiable or tag each wire carefully for
          reference at re-assembly.

       2. Rigging parts for removal/replacement: Many parts that make up this equipment are much
          too heavy to be handled by one man. Provide adequate rigging for lifting and supporting
          heavy parts before attempting to dismantle any equipment.

       3. Cleaning: Clean all parts with a suitable solvent (mineral spirits, SAVASOL no.5, or
          equivalent) to remove all scale, grease, grime, or dirt. Use a clean wiper; do not use cotton
          waste. Air dry after cleaning.

       4. Bearings and Sealing Surfaces: Closely inspect bearings and sealing surfaces for signs of
          wear, nicks, scratches, gouges, or build-up of scale or other foreign substances. Replace
          bearings that show any signs of deterioration.

       5. Air Cylinder Seals: Replace (Mandatory Replacement) all seals, o-rings and gaskets that are
          removed or disturbed during disassembly procedure. Make sure seals and o-rings seat
          properly upon re-assembly.

       6. Pre-lubrication Prior to Re-assembly: Lightly lubricate all seals, bearings, bushings, and
          gears with oil before installation

       7. Aligning Parts During Re-assembly: Because of the weight of large parts, use guide studs
          during re-assembly to ensure proper bolt hole and /or dowel pin alignment as necessary.

       8. Clean all parts and inspect for scratches, cracks, burrs, flaking, pitting, scaling or
          discoloration of mating or load-bearing surfaces.

       9. Hand scrape any bushing that have not become out-or-round to remove burrs, small scratches
          or accumulated foreign substances. Replace any bushing showing gross deformation or
          cracking.

       10. Check shafts and pivot pins for straightness with v-blocks and dial indicator. It is possible to
           straighten bent shafts in a hydraulic press, but if spares are available, it is much better to
           replace the parts. Never straighten bent castings; replace them. Weld cracked steel castings
           only if no spares are available, but replace them whenever possible.

       7.4    Air Cylinder Assembly

              7.4.1. Air Cylinder Removal

              Refer to Figure 3 (below) for guidance.

              1. De-energize the cylinder control valve solenoid circuit. Isolate and disconnect the air
                 supply. Release air pressure using the pressure relief on directional control valve.
                 Bleed both ends (flow control) of the cylinder. Disconnect the hoses at the cylinder.
                 Dissipate any stored energy left in the air cylinder.

              2. Disconnect the rod end clevis from the pivot link arm assembly.

              3. Remove cap screws, lock washers and locking bar plate from linking arm.

              4. Remove pin from clevis. Use a pin driver if necessary.

              5. Remove trunnion block and shims holding cylinder to housing. Carefully remove the
                 hydraulic cylinder to a service area for refurbishment.

              7.4.2. Air Cylinder Refurbishment

              1. Dismantle and repair cylinder in accordance with manufacturer’s maintenance
                 instructions.

       Caution:       Stay clear of end caps of air cylinder when dismantling.

              2. A compression spring inside the cylinder could cause serious injury. Place cylinder
                 in a vice and restrain caps. Remove caps with extreme care.

              7.4.3. Air Cylinder Reinstallation

              Refer to Figure 3 (below) for guidance.

       Important:     The special heavy duty designed air cylinder must be replaced with exact the same
                      model. Any substitute model air cylinder may cause damage to the snap shear and
                      other mill equipment.
              1. Rotate knife assembly to closed position (vertical) and knife holders register against
                 stops.

              2. Thread clevis all the way onto cylinder rod until thread bottoms out on shoulder of
                 cylinder rod. Align holes and insert parallel pin into clevis and cylinder rod.

       7.6    Knife Refurbishment

              See Figure 6 for proper knife blade angle.

               A.     Inspect knife blades for excess wear or damage. Grind or machine damaged area
                      to a smooth surface. Surface finish of blade should be 6.3√ at a 25° angle on both
                      sides.

             Figure 6 – Knife Blade Dressing Illustration




       7.7    Returning the Equipment to Service

       Important:     If a hydraulic/air cylinder or hydraulic motor has been removed and
                      replaced, cycle the cylinder/motor several times with its bleed valves open to
                      remove entrapped air before attempting any operation of the equipment.

       Warning:       Before starting any of the equipment, make sure all personnel are at their
                      work areas or in the areas that have been designated as safe when the
                      equipment is in operation. This is the responsibility of the mill owner and
                      his authorized supervisor of operating personnel.

       Warning:       Before returning the power systems to service, ensure that all personnel are
                      clear of the equipment being returned to service. Controls may have been
                      repositioned while the maintenance was being performed causing
                      unexpected movements of equipment.

       After complying with the above WARNINGS, return all power systems to service and
       remove all tags from controls.
